title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
text:
The data


Code
# a chart of Our World in Data as a table: one row for each country or region and each year
owid <- function(chart) {
  read.csv(paste0(
    "https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/",
    chart,
    ".csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true"
  ))
}
continents <- owid("continents-according-to-our-world-in-data")
population <- owid("population")
land <- owid("land-area-km")

# the DFO Global Flood Records, version 0.9.0 (CC0): one row for each large flood
dfo_url <- "https://zenodo.org/records/19288171/files/Global_Flood_Records.csv"
dfo_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
download.file(dfo_url, dfo_file, quiet = TRUE)
dfo <- read.csv(dfo_file, encoding = "UTF-8", check.names = FALSE)
# the column names, in the order of the file
names(dfo) <- c("id", "glide", "start", "end", "country", "area", "source", "cause", "dead", "displaced", "severity", "magnitude")

# the EM-DAT country profiles: the yearly figures of each country, from the page of the dataset on the
# Humanitarian Data Exchange, which gives the address of the latest file
hdx <- fromJSON("https://data.humdata.org/api/3/action/package_show?id=emdat-country-profiles")$result
emdat_url <- hdx$resources$url[grepl("xlsx$", hdx$resources$url)][1]
emdat_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(emdat_url, emdat_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
# the second row of the sheet holds codes, not data
emdat <- read_xlsx(emdat_file, col_types = "text")[-1, ]
names(emdat) <- c("year", "country", "iso", "group", "subgroup", "type", "subtype", "events", "affected", "dead", "damage", "damage_adjusted", "cpi")




Code
# the countries: rows with a country code that Our World in Data puts on a continent (its regions
# have no code or one that starts with OWID_, except Kosovo's)
continents <- continents[nzchar(continents$code) & (!grepl("^OWID_", continents$code) | continents$code == "OWID_KOS"), ]
country_codes <- continents$code
# the continents of Our World in Data count all of Russia in Europe: Russia is on its own here
group_of <- function(code) {
  continent <- continents$owid_region[match(code, continents$code)]
  ifelse(code == "RUS", "Russia", ifelse(continent == "Europe", "Europe without Russia", continent))
}
# the name of a country in a sentence (with the same names as Our World in Data)
name_of <- function(code) continents$entity[match(code, continents$code)]
with_the <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    x %in% c("Central African Republic", "Democratic Republic of Congo", "United States", "United Kingdom", "Gambia", "Netherlands", "Philippines", "Dominican Republic"),
    paste("the", x),
    x
  )
}
# the land area of each country (the latest year that the World Bank has) and its population
land_now <- land[land$code %in% country_codes & !is.na(land$ag_lnd_totl_k2), ] |>
  group_by(code) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()
land_of <- function(code) land_now$ag_lnd_totl_k2[match(code, land_now$code)]
pop_key <- setNames(population$population_historical, paste(population$code, population$year))
pop_of <- function(code, year) unname(pop_key[paste(code, year)])




Code
# the dates: month, day and year of two digits ("1/6/24")
dfo$start_date <- as.Date(dfo$start, "%m/%d/%y")
dfo$year <- as.integer(format(dfo$start_date, "%Y"))
dfo$month <- as.integer(format(dfo$start_date, "%m"))
dfo$area <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", dfo$area))
dfo$row <- seq_len(nrow(dfo))
n_records <- nrow(dfo)
last_dfo_year <- 2023 # the last year that the archive covers
n_after <- sum(dfo$year > last_dfo_year)

# a flood can hit more than one country: the countries are written in one cell, separated by commas
# and with names of the United Nations; they are given the names of Our World in Data here
renamed <- c(
  "Azores Islands" = "Portugal",
  "Bolivia (Plurinational State of)" = "Bolivia",
  "Canary Islands" = "Spain",
  "Côte d’Ivoire" = "Cote d'Ivoire",
  "Réunion" = "Reunion",
  "Democratic Republic of the Congo" = "Democratic Republic of Congo",
  "Democratic People's Republic of Korea" = "North Korea",
  "Germany Federal Republic" = "Germany",
  "Hong Kong Special Administrative Region" = "Hong Kong",
  "Iran (Islamic Republic of)" = "Iran",
  "Lao People's Democratic Republic" = "Laos",
  "Micronesia (Federated States of)" = "Micronesia (country)",
  "Netherlands (Kingdom of the)" = "Netherlands",
  "Republic of Korea" = "South Korea",
  "Republic of Moldova" = "Moldova",
  "Russian Federation" = "Russia",
  "State of Palestine" = "Palestine",
  "Syrian Arab Republic" = "Syria",
  "Taiwan (Province of China)" = "Taiwan",
  "Timor-Leste" = "East Timor",
  "Türkiye" = "Turkey",
  "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland" = "United Kingdom",
  "United Republic of Tanzania" = "Tanzania",
  "United States of America" = "United States",
  "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)" = "Venezuela",
  "Viet Nam" = "Vietnam"
)
parts <- strsplit(gsub("\\s+", " ", gsub("'", "'", dfo$country)), ",\\s*")
places <- data.frame(row = rep(dfo$row, lengths(parts)), name = trimws(unlist(parts)))
places$name <- ifelse(places$name %in% names(renamed), renamed[places$name], places$name)
places$code <- continents$code[match(places$name, continents$entity)]
places$group <- group_of(places$code)
gone <- sort(unique(places$name[is.na(places$code)]))
n_gone <- length(unique(places$row[is.na(places$code)]))
n_multi <- sum(lengths(parts) > 1)

# the cause: written freely in the file (with typing mistakes and names of storms), sorted here
cause_of <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  case_when(
    grepl("monso|monoo", x) ~ "Monsoon rain",
    grepl("cyclone|tropical|typhoon|hurricane", x) ~ "Cyclone",
    grepl("dam|levy|levee", x) ~ "Dam or levee failure",
    grepl("snow|\\bice\\b|avalan", x) ~ "Snowmelt or ice",
    grepl("rain|torrential", x) ~ "Heavy rain",
    TRUE ~ "Other or not given"
  )
}
dfo$cause_group <- cause_of(dfo$cause)

# tsunamis are not floods (EM-DAT sorts them with the earthquakes): DFO has four records with the cause
# "tsunami", and one more that it calls a tidal surge, of 26 December 2004 in Thailand, the day of the
# tsunami of the Indian Ocean
dfo$tsunami <- grepl("tsunami", tolower(dfo$cause)) | (dfo$start_date == as.Date("2004-12-26") & dfo$country == "Thailand")
n_tsunami <- sum(dfo$tsunami)
thai <- dfo[dfo$tsunami & dfo$country == "Thailand", ]

# the floods used on this page: not tsunamis, and in the years that the archive covers
floods <- dfo[!dfo$tsunami & dfo$year <= last_dfo_year, ]
places <- places[places$row %in% floods$row, ]
places_ok <- places[!is.na(places$code), ]
first_dfo_year <- min(floods$year)
n_floods <- nrow(floods)




Code
for (v in c("year", "events", "affected", "dead")) emdat[[v]] <- as.numeric(emdat[[v]])
# the Canary Islands have a code of their own in EM-DAT
emdat$iso[emdat$iso == "SPI"] <- "ESP"
emdat_date <- as.Date(sub(".*_(\\d{4}_\\d{2}_\\d{2})\\.xlsx$", "\\1", emdat_url), "%Y_%m_%d")
# the floods, with the glacial lake outburst floods that EM-DAT lists apart
em_flood <- emdat[emdat$type %in% c("Flood", "Glacial lake outburst flood"), ]
n_glof <- sum(em_flood$type == "Glacial lake outburst flood")
first_em_year <- min(emdat$year)
partial_year <- max(emdat$year) # the year that is not over
n_partial <- sum(em_flood$events[em_flood$year == partial_year])
em_flood <- em_flood[em_flood$year < partial_year, ]
last_em_year <- max(em_flood$year)
# the rows whose country Our World in Data does not have (the former Serbia and Montenegro)
em_lost <- em_flood[!em_flood$iso %in% country_codes, ]
em_flood <- em_flood[em_flood$iso %in% country_codes, ]
# a missing figure of deaths (or of people affected) is a figure that nobody reported, not a zero
share_no_dead <- 100 * mean(is.na(em_flood$dead))
share_no_affected <- 100 * mean(is.na(em_flood$affected))
n_years_em <- last_em_year - first_em_year + 1




Code
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the map and the calendar (water: blue)
blues <- c("#eff3ff", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c", "#08306b")

# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}

# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
# millions of people: whole numbers from 10 million, one decimal below
million <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) >= 1e7, number(x / 1e6), one(x / 1e6))
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}


The archive and the countries. The DFO archive has 5,503 records; 2 of them start in January 2024, after the end of the years it covers, and are left out. 424 records name more than one country, and a flood counts once for each country it hit. 18 records name only Czechoslovakia, Serbia Montenegro, Soviet Union and Yugoslavia, which no longer exist as countries, and are left out of the figures by country.
Tsunamis are not floods. DFO’s records have 5 tsunamis: 4 with the cause “tsunami”, and the record of 26 December 2004 in Thailand, which DFO calls a “tidal surge” and gives 160,000 dead: the date of the earthquake and tsunami in the Indian Ocean, which left 227,898 people dead or missing in all the countries on its shores (NOAA). EM-DAT counts the Thai tsunami with the earthquakes, with 8,345 dead and missing. These 5 are left out, which leaves 5,496 floods from 1985 to 2023.
EM-DAT: the years, and the empty cells. The yearly figures of EM-DAT that this page uses start in 2000, and they are those of the version of 25 November 2026. 2026 is not over, and its 61 floods so far are left out: the figures run from 2000 to 2025. In 24% of the rows of floods (a country, a year and a kind of flood) no number of dead is given, and in 6% no number of people affected. EM-DAT cannot tell an unreported number from none (EM-DAT FAQ), so a total here is a minimum, and the rows without a figure are counted as zero. A flood that hit several countries is a record in each. 5 rows for former countries are left out. EM-DAT includes 7 country-years of glacial lake outburst floods, which are kept.

title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
section: 1. Where in the world do the large floods happen?
text:
1. Where in the world do the large floods happen?


Code
# the groups: the continents, with Russia on its own
groups_all <- c("Africa", "Asia", "Europe without Russia", "North America", "Oceania", "South America", "Russia")
# the floods of each group: a flood that hit two groups counts in both
by_group <- places_ok |>
  distinct(row, group) |>
  count(group, name = "n_floods")
group_land <- tibble(code = country_codes, km2 = land_of(country_codes), group = group_of(country_codes)) |>
  filter(!is.na(km2)) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(km2 = sum(km2))
by_group$km2 <- group_land$km2[match(by_group$group, group_land$group)]
by_group$per_area <- by_group$n_floods / by_group$km2 * 1e6
by_group <- by_group[order(-by_group$n_floods), ]
of_group <- function(g, column) by_group[[column]][by_group$group == g]
n_distinct_floods <- n_distinct(places_ok$row)

# the countries
by_country <- places_ok |>
  count(code, name = "n_floods") |>
  mutate(name = name_of(code), km2 = land_of(code), per_area = n_floods / km2 * 1e6) |>
  arrange(desc(n_floods))
top_count <- head(by_country, 5)
# per square kilometre, the countries of more than 10,000 square kilometres (the smallest ones
# would lead with a handful of floods)
min_km2 <- 25000
n_small <- sum(by_country$km2 < min_km2, na.rm = TRUE)
top_area <- by_country |>
  filter(km2 >= min_km2) |>
  arrange(desc(per_area)) |>
  head(5)
in_country <- function(name, column) by_country[[column]][by_country$name == name]
# the share of the floods of each part of the world in the first three groups
share_asia <- 100 * of_group("Asia", "n_floods") / n_distinct_floods

# a second record: the events that EM-DAT counts in each country from 2000 to the last year that
# both records have
both_from <- 2000
both_to <- min(last_dfo_year, last_em_year)
em_count <- em_flood |>
  filter(year >= both_from, year <= both_to) |>
  group_by(code = iso) |>
  summarise(n_em = sum(events))
dfo_count <- places_ok |>
  filter(row %in% floods$row[floods$year >= both_from]) |>
  count(code, name = "n_dfo")
top_em <- head(em_count$code[order(-em_count$n_em)], 10)
top_dfo <- head(dfo_count$code[order(-dfo_count$n_dfo)], 10)
shared_top <- intersect(top_em, top_dfo)
only_em <- setdiff(top_em, top_dfo)
only_dfo <- setdiff(top_dfo, top_em)
europe <- places_ok[places_ok$group %in% c("Europe without Russia"), ]
n_europe <- n_distinct(europe$row)
greece_n <- sum(places_ok$code == "GRC")
greece_years <- em_flood[em_flood$iso == "GRC", ] |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE))
greece_worst <- greece_years[which.max(greece_years$dead), ]


Asia: more than two in five of the large floods. DFO’s 5,496 large floods from 1985 to 2023 include 5,479 in at least one country that has a continent (a flood that crosses a border counts in each continent it touches). 43% of these floods were in Asia: 2,361 floods, one for every 13,160 square kilometres of land. In South America there were 501, in North America 886, in Africa 913, in Europe without Russia 481, in Oceania 249 and in Russia 115. Per square kilometre, Europe without Russia has 2.7 times as many large floods as Africa does, which may say as much about how much news reaches DFO as about floods: its notes say that news from poorer countries tends to arrive later and in less detail (DFO notes on the archive).


Code
bars <- by_group[order(by_group$n_floods), ] # the largest at the top
bars$group <- factor(bars$group, levels = bars$group)
bar_colors <- ifelse(bars$group == "Asia", red, gray)
left <- plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~n_floods,
  y = ~group,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = bar_colors),
  text = ~ number(n_floods),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} large floods<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
)
right <- plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~per_area,
  y = ~group,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = bar_colors),
  text = ~ one(per_area),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} large floods per million km²<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
)
hidden_axis <- list(title = "", showticklabels = FALSE, showgrid = FALSE, zeroline = FALSE)
panel_title <- function(text, axis) {
  list(
    text = text,
    xref = paste(axis, "domain"),
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = 1,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "bottom",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 13)
  )
}
subplot(left, right, shareY = TRUE, margin = 0.04, widths = c(0.55, 0.45)) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Large floods, ", first_dfo_year, "–", last_dfo_year),
    "DFO Global Flood Records v0.9.0; land areas: World Bank (FAO), via Our World in Data.",
    x_axis = c(hidden_axis, list(range = c(0, 1.25 * max(bars$n_floods)))),
    xaxis2 = c(hidden_axis, list(range = c(0, 1.3 * max(bars$per_area)))),
    annotations = list(
      panel_title("Floods", "x"),
      panel_title("Floods per million km² of land", "x2")
    ),
    margin = list(l = 150, t = 90, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.06
  )






The most large floods are in a few large countries. The most large floods were in the United States (509), China (380), India (316), Indonesia (247) and the Philippines (215): large countries, with a lot of land for a flood to hit. Per square kilometre of land, the list changes. Of the countries of more than 25,000 square kilometres, Haiti, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, the Dominican Republic and Burundi come first, with 1,488, 1,115, 885, 788 and 740 large floods per million km²; the United States has 56. The 38 countries of less than 25,000 square kilometres are not ranked, because a handful of floods would put them first.


Code
on_map <- by_country[!is.na(by_country$n_floods), ]
classes <- c(0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, Inf)
class_names <- c("Under 10", "10–24", "25–49", "50–99", "100–199", "200 or more")
on_map$class <- as.integer(cut(on_map$n_floods, classes, right = FALSE))
# a colour scale of six steps, one colour for each class
shades <- blues[2:7]
steps <- do.call(c, lapply(seq_along(shades), function(i) {
  list(list((i - 1) / 6, shades[i]), list(i / 6, shades[i]))
}))
plot_ly(
  on_map,
  type = "choropleth",
  locations = ~code,
  z = ~class,
  zmin = 0.5,
  zmax = 6.5,
  colorscale = steps,
  marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.3)),
  text = ~ paste0(
    name,
    ": ",
    number(n_floods),
    " large floods<br>",
    ifelse(is.na(per_area), "", paste0(number(per_area), " per million km²"))
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text",
  colorbar = list(
    title = list(text = "Large<br>floods"),
    tickvals = 1:6,
    ticktext = class_names,
    len = 0.8,
    thickness = 14
  )
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Large floods in each country, ", first_dfo_year, "–", last_dfo_year),
    "DFO Global Flood Records v0.9.0. Grey: no large flood in the record.",
    geo = list(
      showframe = FALSE,
      showcoastlines = FALSE,
      showland = TRUE,
      landcolor = "#e8e8e8",
      projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
      lataxis = list(range = c(-57, 85))
    ),
    margin = list(t = 50, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )






EM-DAT, a different record, finds much the same countries. Counting the floods that EM-DAT records in each country from 2000 to 2023, and the large floods of DFO in the same years, 8 of the 10 countries with the most floods are the same in both records. Pakistan and Colombia come in the top 10 of EM-DAT only, Australia and Russia in the top 10 of DFO only.
Europe. 481 large floods hit Europe without Russia, 33 of them Greece, which also has 22 floods in EM-DAT from 2000 to 2025. 2017 is the year with the most dead and missing in the floods of Greece in EM-DAT (23).

title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
section: 2. Where do floods kill the most people?
text:
2. Where do floods kill the most people?


Code
# EM-DAT, the years from first_em_year to last_em_year: the floods of each country, their dead and the
# people affected, and the average population of the country in those years
em_country <- em_flood |>
  group_by(code = iso) |>
  summarise(n_em = sum(events), dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE), affected = sum(affected, na.rm = TRUE))
average_pop <- population[population$code %in% country_codes & population$year %in% first_em_year:min(last_em_year, max(population$year)), ] |>
  group_by(code) |>
  summarise(pop = mean(population_historical))
em_country$pop <- average_pop$pop[match(em_country$code, average_pop$code)]
em_country$name <- name_of(em_country$code)
# deaths a year for each million people, and the share of the people affected each year
em_country$per_million <- em_country$dead / em_country$pop * 1e6 / n_years_em
em_country$affected_share <- 100 * em_country$affected / em_country$pop / n_years_em
total_dead <- sum(em_country$dead)
top_dead <- em_country |>
  arrange(desc(dead)) |>
  head(10)
# per million people: the countries of more than one million people
min_pop <- 1e6
top_rate <- em_country |>
  filter(pop >= min_pop) |>
  arrange(desc(per_million)) |>
  head(10)
top_affected <- em_country |>
  filter(pop >= min_pop) |>
  arrange(desc(affected_share)) |>
  head(5)
of_dead <- function(name, column) em_country[[column]][em_country$name == name]
world_dead_rate <- total_dead / sum(em_country$pop) * 1e6 / n_years_em


Most of the dead are in a few large countries. From 2000 to 2025, EM-DAT counts 142,432 dead and missing in floods. India (36,103), China (13,447) and Pakistan (11,356) come first, and the ten countries with the most dead have 63% of all of them: India alone has 25%. But a large country has a lot of people to lose. Per million people, a different list leads: Haiti (12.6 a year), Afghanistan (5.3 a year) and Nepal (5.1 a year), against 0.8 a year for all the countries together.


Code
left_panel <- top_dead |>
  transmute(panel = "Dead and missing, total", name, value = dead, label = number(dead))
right_panel <- top_rate |>
  transmute(panel = "A year for each million people", name, value = per_million, label = one(per_million))
dots <- rbind(left_panel, right_panel)
dots$panel <- factor(dots$panel, levels = c("Dead and missing, total", "A year for each million people"))
dots$name <- sub("Democratic Republic of Congo", "DR Congo", dots$name)
dots$key <- paste(dots$panel, dots$name, sep = "___")
dots$key <- factor(dots$key, levels = rev(dots$key))
dots$highlight <- dots$name %in% c(top_dead$name[1], top_rate$name[1])
ggplot(dots, aes(x = value, y = key, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.6, colour = "grey20") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub(".*___", "", x)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = red, "FALSE" = gray), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Where floods killed most, ", first_em_year, "–", last_em_year),
    subtitle = "EM-DAT: dead and missing in floods",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = paste0("Data: EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via the Humanitarian Data Exchange; population: Our World in Data.\nRight: countries of over ", number(min_pop / 1e6), " million people")
  ) +
  theme_page(12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
  )









The people affected: a different list again. Deaths are one measure; EM-DAT also counts the people affected (injured, affected or homeless, counted again each time they are hit). In an average year of 2000–2025, the countries of over 1 million people with the largest share of their people affected are South Sudan (3.0%), Cambodia (2.9%), Slovenia (2.9%), Bangladesh (2.8%) and Thailand (2.8%). Read these with care: how many people are “affected” depends on who counts, and EM-DAT takes the number that its source gives (EM-DAT).

title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
section: 3. When does each part of the world flood?
text:
3. When does each part of the world flood?


Code
# the share of the floods of each group that start in each month (a flood that crosses two groups
# counts in both)
season <- places_ok |>
  distinct(row, group) |>
  mutate(month = floods$month[match(row, floods$row)]) |>
  count(group, month, name = "n") |>
  group_by(group) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
season <- merge(expand.grid(group = groups_all, month = 1:12), season, all.x = TRUE)
season$share[is.na(season$share)] <- 0
# the three months in a row in which each group floods the most (December to February included)
three <- function(shares) sapply(1:12, function(m) sum(shares[(m - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1]))
best <- season |>
  arrange(group, month) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(start = which.max(three(share)), share = max(three(share)))
season_months <- function(g) {
  s <- best$start[best$group == g]
  (s - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1
}
season_text <- function(g) {
  m <- season_months(g)
  paste(month.name[m[1]], "to", month.name[m[3]])
}
season_share <- function(g) percent(best$share[best$group == g])
# the causes: the share of the floods of a group that DFO puts down to each
cause_share <- function(g, cause, from = 1:12) {
  rows <- places_ok$row[places_ok$group == g]
  rows <- unique(rows)
  fl <- floods[floods$row %in% rows & floods$month %in% from, ]
  100 * mean(fl$cause_group == cause)
}
asia_months <- floods[floods$row %in% unique(places_ok$row[places_ok$group == "Asia"]), ]
asia_jjas <- 100 * mean(asia_months$month %in% 6:9)
asia_jul <- 100 * mean(asia_months$month == 7)
monsoon_share <- 100 * mean(asia_months$cause_group == "Monsoon rain")
monsoon_in_jjas <- 100 * mean(asia_months$cause_group[asia_months$month %in% 6:9] == "Monsoon rain")
heavy_in_jjas <- 100 * mean(asia_months$cause_group[asia_months$month %in% 6:9] == "Heavy rain")
all_causes <- floods |>
  count(cause_group) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
of_cause <- function(x) all_causes$share[all_causes$cause_group == x]


Each part of the world floods in its own wet season. The calendar shows, for each group, the share of its large floods that start in each month, from 1985 to 2023. If floods came evenly through the year, each month would have 8% to 9%.


Code
season$class <- cut(
  season$share,
  c(-Inf, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15, Inf),
  labels = c("Under 5%", "5–7.5%", "7.5–10%", "10–12.5%", "12.5–15%", "15% or more"),
  right = FALSE
)
ggplot(season, aes(x = month, y = factor(group, levels = rev(groups_all)), fill = class)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = blues[2:7], drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "When each continent floods",
    subtitle = paste0("Share of its large floods that start in each month, ", first_dfo_year, "–", last_dfo_year),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Data: DFO Global Flood Records v0.9.0"
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8)))









Asia floods in the summer of the north. 53% of the large floods of Asia start from June to September, 18% in July alone. DFO puts 19% of them down to monsoon rain. Of the floods that start from June to September, 29% are put down to monsoon rain and 56% to heavy rain, so DFO’s word for the cause is not a count of monsoon floods. In South America and Oceania the floods come in the other half of the year: South America floods most from January to March (41% of its floods), Oceania from January to March (53%). Africa’s season is August to October (33%), North America’s August to October (34%) and Europe’s, without Russia, September to November (32%); Russia’s floods come in May to July (49%).
What causes them, in DFO’s words. DFO writes down one main cause for each flood. For all the floods of the record, 77% are down to heavy or torrential rain, 9% to a cyclone (including a tropical storm), 8% to monsoon rain, 3% to snowmelt or ice, and 1% to the failure of a dam or levee. The rest is another cause, or none is given. The names are written freely in the file, with typing mistakes and storm names, and are sorted here by the words they contain.

title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
text:
4. Which were the worst floods?


Code
# EM-DAT's dead for the floods and the storms (the group that holds tropical cyclones, which DFO
# counts as floods) of each country and year
em_deadly <- emdat[emdat$type %in% c("Flood", "Glacial lake outburst flood", "Storm"), ] |>
  group_by(iso, year) |>
  summarise(dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
em_dead_of <- function(codes, y) {
  sum(em_deadly$dead[em_deadly$iso %in% codes & em_deadly$year %in% c(y, y + 1)])
}
# the floods with the most dead in DFO, and the dead that EM-DAT has for the same countries in the
# year of the flood and the year after (EM-DAT starts in 2000)
worst <- floods |>
  arrange(desc(dead)) |>
  head(25)
worst$codes <- lapply(worst$row, function(r) places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r])
worst$em_dead <- ifelse(
  worst$year >= first_em_year,
  mapply(function(codes, y) em_dead_of(codes, y), worst$codes, worst$year),
  NA
)
worst$where <- sapply(worst$codes, function(codes) and_list(with_the(name_of(codes))))
worst$where_plain <- sapply(worst$codes, function(codes) and_list(name_of(codes)))
# a record whose dead are more than ten times those of EM-DAT for the same countries and years
worst$doubtful <- !is.na(worst$em_dead) & worst$dead > 10 * worst$em_dead
doubtful <- worst[worst$doubtful, ]
worst_ok <- worst[!worst$doubtful, ]
top_worst <- head(worst_ok, 10)
all_dead <- sum(floods$dead[!floods$row %in% doubtful$row])
top_share <- 100 * sum(top_worst$dead) / all_dead
# the people displaced: a number larger than the population of the countries of the flood is wrong
floods$pop_of_places <- sapply(floods$row, function(r) {
  codes <- places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r]
  if (length(codes) == 0 || floods$year[floods$row == r] > max(population$year)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  sum(pop_of(codes, floods$year[floods$row == r]), na.rm = TRUE)
})
too_many <- floods[!is.na(floods$pop_of_places) & floods$displaced > floods$pop_of_places, ]
too_many_text <- paste0(
  sapply(too_many$row, function(r) and_list(with_the(name_of(places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r])))),
  " ",
  too_many$year,
  ": ",
  million(too_many$displaced),
  " million displaced, ",
  million(too_many$pop_of_places),
  " million people"
)
displaced_ok <- floods[!floods$row %in% too_many$row, ]
top_displaced <- displaced_ok |>
  arrange(desc(displaced)) |>
  head(8)
top_displaced$codes <- lapply(top_displaced$row, function(r) places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r])
top_displaced$where_plain <- sapply(top_displaced$codes, function(codes) and_list(name_of(codes)))
top_displaced$share <- 100 * top_displaced$displaced / sapply(seq_len(nrow(top_displaced)), function(i) {
  sum(pop_of(top_displaced$codes[[i]], top_displaced$year[i]), na.rm = TRUE)
})
# the flood of Storm Daniel in Greece, in DFO and EM-DAT
daniel <- floods[floods$start_date == as.Date("2023-09-05") & grepl("Greece", floods$country), ]
daniel_em <- emdat[emdat$iso == "GRC" & emdat$year == 2023 & emdat$type == "Flood", ]
libya <- floods[floods$year == 2023 & floods$country == "Libya", ]
libya_em <- emdat[emdat$iso == "LBY" & emdat$year == 2023 & emdat$type == "Storm", ]


A handful of floods kill most of the people. Leaving out the 4 doubtful records named below, DFO’s floods have 507,360 dead. The 10 floods in the table, 0.2% of all the floods, have 60% of them. The table is the floods with the most dead in DFO’s record, after two checks: the tsunami is out (see the data), and so are the records that give more than ten times the dead that EM-DAT has, for the same countries in the year of the flood and the year after, in floods and storms together: Uganda, September 2020 (12,000 dead in DFO, 40 in EM-DAT), Costa Rica and Nicaragua, November 2016 (4,000 dead in DFO, 44 in EM-DAT), Tanzania, December 2000 (3,600 dead in DFO, 41 in EM-DAT) and Nicaragua and Honduras, October 2005 (2,000 dead in DFO, 73 in EM-DAT). EM-DAT starts in 2000, so the floods before it cannot be checked this way.

    start = format(top_worst$start_date, "%d %b %Y"),

    em_dead = ifelse(is.na(top_worst$em_dead), "–", number(top_worst$em_dead)),
    displaced = number(top_worst$displaced)
  ),

The storm brought record rain to Greece on 5 and 6 September, with a reported 750 mm in 24 hours at a station in Zagora, and heavy floods in Libya a few days later, where two old dams burst above the city of Derna (WMO). title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
section: 5. Are floods more frequent or deadlier than they were?
text:
5. Are floods more frequent or deadlier than they were?


Code
# DFO: the large floods that start in each year
dfo_year <- floods |>
  count(year, name = "n")
# EM-DAT: the floods, the dead and the people affected each year
em_year <- em_flood |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(n = sum(events), dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE), affected = sum(affected, na.rm = TRUE))
world_pop <- population[population$entity == "World", ]
# the population of the world is known up to the last year of Our World in Data's file
em_year$per_million_world <- em_year$dead / world_pop$population_historical[match(em_year$year, world_pop$year)] * 1e6
rate_years <- em_year[!is.na(em_year$per_million_world), ]
last_pop_year <- max(rate_years$year)
dfo_early <- dfo_year[dfo_year$year < 2000, ]
dfo_late <- dfo_year[dfo_year$year >= 2000, ]
peak <- dfo_year[which.max(dfo_year$n), ]
after_peak <- dfo_year[dfo_year$year > peak$year, ]
low_after <- min(after_peak$n)
low_after_years <- after_peak$year[after_peak$n == low_after]
low_first <- dfo_year[which.min(dfo_year$n), ]
em_peak <- em_year[which.max(em_year$n), ]
# what a rank test says of a trend: "no clear trend" unless the chance of the pattern without a trend is
# under 5 in 100
trend_text <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p >= 0.05) "no clear trend" else if (cor(x, years, method = "kendall") > 0) "a rise" else "a fall"
}
em_dead_peak <- em_year[which.max(em_year$dead), ]


There is no clear trend in the floods since 2000, and the older years do not compare. The count of large floods in DFO’s record went from 45 in 1987 to 297 in 2003, and down to 102 in 2013, 2014 and 2015: swings of that size over a few years say more about how floods were found and written down than about floods (from 2000 to 2023 a rank test finds no trend in this count: by chance, 12 in 100). DFO warns that the quality and the quantity of the information about a flood is “not always in proportion to its actual magnitude”, and that news from some countries arrives later and with less detail (DFO notes on the archive). EM-DAT warns of the same, the more so for the years before 2000: the rise in the number of disasters recorded from the 1960s on “largely reflects improvements in reporting, communication technology, and the growth of the database itself”, and it advises leaving the years before 2000 out of any study of trends (EM-DAT FAQ). So the figures for EM-DAT keep to 2000 onwards.
From 2000 to 2025, EM-DAT records 124 to 224 floods a year, with 224 in 2006 and 2021, and a rank test finds no clear trend: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 93. For the dead it finds no clear trend (by chance, 91 in 100); the dead range from 2,875 to 9,820 a year, most in 2013. For the dead of floods per million people in the world, from 2000 to 2023, the last year of the population data, it finds no clear trend (1.0 in 2000, 0.9 in 2023; by chance, 20 in 100). For the people affected it finds a fall (by chance, 1 in 100), but a few years dominate the total, such as 2010, with 189 million.


Code
panels <- c(
  paste0("Large floods a year (DFO, from ", first_dfo_year, ")"),
  paste0("Floods a year (EM-DAT, from ", first_em_year, ")"),
  paste0("Dead and missing a year (EM-DAT, from ", first_em_year, ")")
)
series <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = panels[1], year = dfo_year$year, value = dfo_year$n),
  data.frame(panel = panels[2], year = em_year$year, value = em_year$n),
  data.frame(panel = panels[3], year = em_year$year, value = em_year$dead)
)
series$panel <- factor(series$panel, levels = panels)
peaks <- series |>
  group_by(panel) |>
  slice_max(value, n = 1)
ggplot(series, aes(x = year, y = value)) +
  geom_line(colour = dark_gray, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = dark_gray, size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = peaks, colour = red, size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = peaks, aes(label = paste(year, "·", number(value))), colour = "grey20", hjust = -0.15, vjust = 0.5, size = 3.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1990, 2020, 10), limits = c(first_dfo_year - 1, last_dfo_year + 8)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) number(x), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15)), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "More floods, or more reporting?",
    subtitle = "Red: the year with the most",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: DFO Global Flood Records v0.9.0; EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via the Humanitarian Data Exchange"
  ) +
  theme_page(12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))

title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
text:
So, what does it mean?

Asia has the most large floods. 43% of the large floods of the record, and the countries with the most are the United States, China and India. Per square kilometre, Haiti and Sri Lanka lead.
A few large countries have most of the dead, and other countries have the most for each person. The ten countries with the most dead have 63% of the deaths in EM-DAT since 2000; per million people, Haiti leads, with 12.6 a year.
Every part of the world has its wet season. Asia floods in June to September, South America and Oceania in the first months of the year.
A few floods kill most of the people. The 10 deadliest floods have 60% of the dead of DFO’s floods, and 5 of them came with a cyclone.
The records do not show a clear rise in floods or in flood deaths since 2000. Older counts rise and fall with the way floods were recorded.

What this does not show. Neither record is a count of all floods: DFO records the large floods that the news and government reports tell of, and EM-DAT those that meet its entry criteria, so a country with little news coverage or few reports may have more floods than it shows. A flood that kills nobody, in a country that does not ask for help, may appear in neither. The counts are of floods, not of how long they lasted or how much land they covered, and the estimates of the dead, the missing and the displaced differ between sources. Nothing here says what causes floods, or whether climate change is changing them: for that, a record must be built to measure it. And the table of the worst floods leaves out the records that did not agree with the other source, which may include a true record that EM-DAT lists differently.
For the overview of all the hazards, see Natural Disasters; for another hazard of the weather, Tornadoes; for the fire that follows the dry season, Where the World Burns.

title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World

DFO, Global Archive of Large Flood Events – Notes (archived copy of the notes on the columns of the archive, from the Internet Archive).
EM-DAT, the International Disaster Database, CRED / UCLouvain, Brussels, Belgium (emdat.be): Frequently asked questions, Data accessibility, Human impact variables; the yearly totals for each country are the EM-DAT country profiles of the Humanitarian Data Exchange. EM-DAT is free for non-commercial use under its Database License Agreement and is not open data; the country profiles are published under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and this page shows totals and counts worked out from them, not the data.

title: Climate Data Visualisation in R
text:
1. Arctic Sea Ice Animated GIF

The data
The NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0 provides monthly sea ice extent as shapefiles — one zip per month per year. The September minimum is the most-cited indicator of Arctic sea ice loss.
URL pattern:
https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/north/monthly/shapefiles/shp_extent/09_Sep/
  extent_N_YYYYMM_polygon_v4.0.zip


Download helper


Code
sf::sf_use_s2(TRUE)   # spherical geometry needed for polar projections

month_dirs <- c("01_Jan","02_Feb","03_Mar","04_Apr","05_May","06_Jun",
                "07_Jul","08_Aug","09_Sep","10_Oct","11_Nov","12_Dec")

fetch_ice_extent <- function(year, month = "09", pole = "N",
                             tmpdir = file.path(tempdir(), "nsidc_ice")) {
  dir.create(tmpdir, showWarnings = FALSE)
  mm       <- sprintf("%02d", as.integer(month))
  yymm     <- paste0(year, mm)
  pole_dir <- ifelse(pole == "N", "north", "south")
  mon_dir  <- month_dirs[as.integer(mm)]

  url <- paste0(
    "https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/",
    pole_dir, "/monthly/shapefiles/shp_extent/", mon_dir, "/",
    "extent_", pole, "_", yymm, "_polygon_v4.0.zip"
  )

  zip_path <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm, ".zip"))
  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000)
    tryCatch(download.file(url, zip_path, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb"),
             error = function(e) NULL)

  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000) return(NULL)

  exdir <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm))
  suppressWarnings(unzip(zip_path, exdir = exdir, overwrite = FALSE))
  shp <- list.files(exdir, "\\.shp$", full.names = TRUE)[1]
  if (is.na(shp)) return(NULL)

  tryCatch(sf::st_read(shp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
}




Base layers
These objects are computed once and reused for every frame. The world basemap and the circular clip boundary never change between years — only the ice extent polygon does.


Code
crs_polar <- "+proj=stere +lat_0=90 +lat_ts=70 +lon_0=0 +datum=WGS84 +units=m"

world_proj <- sf::st_transform(
  ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf"), crs_polar
)

# circular clip: 5.5 million metres from the pole (~55°N+)
clip_circle <- sf::st_buffer(
  sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point(c(0, 90)), crs = 4326) |> sf::st_transform(crs_polar),
  dist = 5.5e6
)

world_clip <- sf::st_intersection(sf::st_make_valid(world_proj), clip_circle)

clip_year <- function(shp) {
  proj <- sf::st_transform(shp, crs_polar) |> sf::st_make_valid()
  tryCatch(sf::st_intersection(proj, clip_circle), error = function(e) NULL)
}



Why st_make_valid()? NSIDC shapefiles occasionally contain self-intersecting rings — a geometry error that causes st_intersection() to throw a TopologyException and abort. st_make_valid() repairs the polygon before clipping, at a negligible performance cost.


Why North Pole stereographic? A standard lat/lon projection distorts the Arctic — Greenland appears enormous and the pole is a line, not a point. The stereographic projection (+proj=stere +lat_0=90) places the pole at the centre and gives a circular, undistorted view of the region.



1979 reference outline
The 1979 September extent — the earliest year in the NSIDC record — is drawn as a red outline on every frame. It acts as a fixed reference so viewers can immediately see the cumulative loss without needing to compare frames mentally.


Code
raw_1979 <- fetch_ice_extent(1979)
ice_1979 <- if (!is.null(raw_1979)) clip_year(raw_1979) else NULL




Extent values from NSIDC CSV
The shapefile does not contain the area value as a label-ready number. NSIDC publishes a companion CSV with the monthly extent in million km².


Code
areas_csv <- read.csv(
  "https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/north/monthly/data/N_09_extent_v4.0.csv",
  strip.white = TRUE
)
head(areas_csv)


  year mo source_dataset region extent area
1 1979  9     NSIDC-0051      N   7.05 4.58
2 1980  9     NSIDC-0051      N   7.67 4.87
3 1981  9     NSIDC-0051      N   7.14 4.44
4 1982  9     NSIDC-0051      N   7.30 4.43
5 1983  9     NSIDC-0051      N   7.39 4.70
6 1984  9     NSIDC-0051      N   6.81 4.11




Frame loop
Each year is rendered as an independent ggplot and saved to PNG. gifski then stitches all PNGs into a single GIF.
Processing years independently — rather than binding all shapefiles into one sf object — avoids CRS incompatibility errors. NSIDC shapefiles from different years may carry slightly different WKT representations of the same projection, which causes rbind to fail. The per-year approach sidesteps the issue entirely.


Code
years_all  <- 1979:2026
frames_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "arctic_frames")
dir.create(frames_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

plots <- list()

for (yr in years_all) {
  raw <- fetch_ice_extent(yr)
  if (is.null(raw)) { message("skip ", yr); next }

  ice_yr <- clip_year(raw)
  if (is.null(ice_yr) || nrow(ice_yr) == 0) { message("skip ", yr); next }

  area     <- areas_csv$extent[trimws(as.character(areas_csv$year)) == as.character(yr)]
  area_lbl <- if (length(area) && !is.na(area[1])) sprintf("%.2f M km²", area[1]) else ""

  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = clip_circle, fill = "#1a3a5c", color = NA) +
    { if (!is.null(ice_1979))
        geom_sf(data = ice_1979, fill = NA, color = "#FF5252",
                linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.75) } +
    geom_sf(data = ice_yr,     fill = "#E3F4FF", color = "#90CAF9", linewidth = 0.1) +
    geom_sf(data = world_clip, fill = "#5D4037", color = "#3E2723", linewidth = 0.2) +
    labs(title    = paste("Arctic Sea Ice — September", yr),
         subtitle = paste0(area_lbl, "   |   red outline = 1979 extent"),
         caption  = "Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0") +
    theme_void(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#0D1B2A", color = NA),
      plot.title    = element_text(color = "white",  face = "bold", size = 18,
                                   hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(14, 0, 4, 0)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#90CAF9", size = 10,
                                   hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(0, 0, 8, 0)),
      plot.caption  = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 7.5,
                                   hjust = 1,  margin = margin(6, 10, 8, 0)),
      plot.margin   = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )

  plots[[as.character(yr)]] <- p
  message("frame ", yr, " ready")
}




Stitch into GIF


Code
dir.create(frames_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
frame_paths <- character(length(plots))
for (i in seq_along(plots)) {
  path <- file.path(frames_dir, sprintf("frame_%04d.png", i))
  ggsave(path, plots[[i]], width = 10, height = 10, dpi = 600, bg = "#0D1B2A")
  frame_paths[i] <- path
}

gifski::gifski(frame_paths,
               gif_file = "arctic_ice_animated.gif",
               width = 800, height = 800, delay = 1)


[1] "C:\\Users\\dzach\\Documents\\GitHub\\vignettes\\quarto\\illustration\\arctic_ice_animated.gif"












Rendering time: Expect 1–2 hours for all 47 frames at dpi=600. Set dpi=150 for a quick preview — the GIF file size drops from ~200 MB to ~10 MB and rendering takes a few minutes.

title: Climate Data Visualisation in R
text:
2. ggplot2 Climate Spiral GIF
A frame-by-frame recreation of the Ed Hawkins climate spiral — the animated polar chart that went viral in 2016 and was shown at the opening ceremony of the Rio Olympics.
Each frame is a ggplot saved to PNG; gifski stitches the PNGs into a GIF. This avoids gganimate entirely, which means full control over every frame and no compatibility issues between gganimate and sf geometries.
Data: NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 — monthly global surface temperature anomalies (deviation from the 1951–1980 baseline), freely available as a CSV.

Prepare data
The CSV has one row per year and one column per month. pivot_longer reshapes it to long format (one row per year-month), and match(month, month.abb) converts the month abbreviation to a number 1–12. January is then repeated as month 13 to close the spiral loop — without this, the path from December back to January leaves a visible gap.


Code
df_nasa_raw<-read.csv("https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv", header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = "***", skip = 1)
df_long <- df_nasa_raw[, c("Year", month.abb)] |>
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(month.abb), names_to = "month", values_to = "temp") |>
  mutate(
    temp      = as.numeric(temp),
    month_num = match(month, month.abb)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(temp), Year >= 1880)

years   <- sort(unique(df_long$Year))
n_years <- length(years)

# repeat January as month 13 to close the loop
closed <- df_long |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  arrange(month_num) |>
  group_modify(~ bind_rows(.x, filter(.x, month_num == 1) |>
                                  mutate(month_num = 13))) |>
  ungroup()




Reference geometry
Three static elements appear on every frame and never change:

Dashed circles at 0°C, 1.5°C, and 2.0°C — the Paris Agreement warming targets
Radial spokes — one per month, running from the centre to just inside the label ring
Month labels — positioned at label_r = 1.85, just outside the outermost circle



Code
# Paris Agreement target circles
circle_df <- expand.grid(
  month_num = seq(1, 13, length.out = 200),
  r         = c(0, 1.5, 2.0)
)

# month label positions
month_labels <- data.frame(month_num = 1:12, label = month.abb)

temp_lim <- c(-1.0, 1.6)
label_r  <- 1.85

# radial spokes
spokes_df <- data.frame(
  month_num = rep(1:12, each = 2),
  temp      = rep(c(temp_lim[1], label_r - 0.05), 12),
  grp       = rep(1:12, each = 2)
)




Frame loop
For each year, two data subsets are drawn:

past — all years up to (but not including) the current year, coloured with the viridis “inferno” palette scaled from earliest (dark) to most recent (bright)
curr — the current year only, drawn in white at double thickness so it stands out

The yr_idx column (year index / total years) maps each past year to a position in the 0–1 colour range, ensuring consistent colouring across all frames.


Code
frames_dir  <- file.path(tempdir(), "spiral_frames")
dir.create(frames_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
frame_paths <- c()

for (i in seq_along(years)) {
  yr           <- years[i]
  years_so_far <- years[seq_len(i)]

  past <- closed |>
    filter(Year %in% years_so_far, Year != yr) |>
    mutate(yr_idx = match(Year, years) / n_years)

  curr <- closed |> filter(Year == yr)

  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_path(data = spokes_df,
              aes(x = month_num, y = temp, group = grp),
              color = "gray25", linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_path(data = circle_df,
              aes(x = month_num, y = r, group = r),
              color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.35, linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = c(0, 1.5, 2.0) + 0.04,
             label = c("0°C", "1.5°C", "2°C"),
             color = "gray50", size = 2.8, hjust = 1) +
    geom_path(data = past,
              aes(x = month_num, y = temp, group = Year, color = yr_idx),
              linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_color_viridis_c(option = "B", limits = c(0, 1), guide = "none") +
    geom_path(data = curr,
              aes(x = month_num, y = temp),
              color = "white", linewidth = 1.6, alpha = 0.95) +
    geom_text(data = month_labels,
              aes(x = month_num, y = label_r, label = label),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "gray70", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
    coord_polar(theta = "x", start = -pi / 6, clip = "off") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 13), breaks = 1:12, labels = NULL) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(temp_lim[1], label_r + 0.1)) +
    labs(title   = as.character(yr),
         caption = "NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis v4  |  Anomaly vs 1951-1980 baseline") +
    theme_void(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#050510", color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#050510", color = NA),
      plot.title   = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 38,
                                  hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(16, 0, 0, 0)),
      plot.caption = element_text(color = "gray40", size = 7.5, hjust = 0.5,
                                  margin = margin(0, 0, 12, 0)),
      plot.margin  = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )

  path <- file.path(frames_dir, sprintf("frame_%04d.png", i))
  ggsave(path, p, width = 1800/150, height = 1900/150, dpi = 150, bg = "#050510")
  frame_paths <- c(frame_paths, path)
  message("frame ", i, "/", n_years, "  (", yr, ")")
}

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
text:
Floods, storms, earthquakes, heatwaves and droughts: somewhere in the world, a disaster caused by nature is recorded about once a day, and a few of them kill tens of thousands of people. This page is the overview of a series on natural disasters, and asks five questions:

Which disasters happen most often?
Which kill the most, and has that changed?
Which affect the most people?
Where do disasters kill the most?
Where is the Earth itself restless?

Each kind has a page of its own: earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, floods, tornadoes, and wildfires, in the world and in Greece.
The data are downloaded when the page is rendered:

EM-DAT, the International Disaster Database of the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED) at UCLouvain, as published by Our World in Data (Natural disasters): the disasters recorded in the world each year, by kind, and the people killed and affected in each country each year since 1900. EM-DAT records only disasters that meet its entry criteria, and defines a disaster as “a situation or event which overwhelms local capacity, necessitating a request to the national or international level for external assistance” (EM-DAT, definitions).
The population of each country, for deaths per person (Our World in Data).
Earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more since 1900, from the catalogue of the US Geological Survey (USGS); volcanoes, from the Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program (Volcanoes of the World); and the boundaries of the Earth’s tectonic plates (Bird 2003).

The kinds of disaster are those of EM-DAT. A storm includes tropical cyclones (hurricanes and typhoons) and tornadoes; an earthquake includes its aftershocks and the tsunamis it causes; extreme temperature means heatwaves, cold waves and severe winters (EM-DAT classification). Deaths are the confirmed dead and the missing.

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "sf"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(sf)

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
text:
The data


Code
# a chart of Our World in Data as a table: one row for each country or region and each year
owid <- function(chart) {
  read.csv(paste0(
    "https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/",
    chart,
    ".csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true"
  ))
}
# EM-DAT: the people killed and affected in each country each year, by kind of disaster, and the
# disasters recorded in the world each year, by kind
deaths <- owid("natural-disasters-deaths")
affected <- owid("natural-disasters-people-affected")
events <- owid("number-of-natural-disaster-events")
population <- owid("population")
continents <- owid("continents-according-to-our-world-in-data")

# the earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more since 1900 (USGS)
quakes <- read.csv(paste0(
  "https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=csv",
  "&starttime=1900-01-01&minmagnitude=7&orderby=time-asc"
))
# the volcanoes that have erupted in the last 12,000 years (Smithsonian); the geological summary of
# each volcano has line breaks inside its quotes, which read.csv reads correctly
volcanoes <- read.csv(paste0(
  "https://webservices.volcano.si.edu/geoserver/GVP-VOTW/ows?service=WFS&version=2.0.0",
  "&request=GetFeature&typeName=GVP-VOTW:Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Volcanoes&outputFormat=csv"
))
# the boundaries of the tectonic plates (Bird 2003, as GeoJSON)
plates <- st_read(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json",
  quiet = TRUE
)




Code
# the kinds of disaster: the columns of EM-DAT's tables, their names in its table of events, and
# their names on this page
kinds <- data.frame(
  key = c(
    "flood",
    "extreme_temperature",
    "extreme_weather",
    "drought",
    "earthquake",
    "volcanic_activity",
    "landslide",
    "wildfire"
  ),
  event_name = c(
    "Flood",
    "Extreme temperature",
    "Extreme weather",
    "Drought",
    "Earthquake",
    "Volcanic activity",
    "Landslide",
    "Wildfire"
  ),
  label = c(
    "Flood",
    "Extreme temperature",
    "Storm",
    "Drought",
    "Earthquake",
    "Volcano",
    "Landslide",
    "Wildfire"
  )
)
# the charts with colours show the five deadliest kinds and put the other three together
kinds$group <- ifelse(kinds$key %in% c("volcanic_activity", "landslide", "wildfire"), "Other", kinds$label)
group_levels <- c("Flood", "Extreme temperature", "Storm", "Drought", "Earthquake", "Other")
label_of <- setNames(kinds$label, kinds$key)
group_of <- setNames(kinds$group, kinds$key)

# a table of EM-DAT with one row for each place, year and kind; a year without a recorded disaster of
# a kind has no value there, which means that none was recorded: zero
to_long <- function(x, prefix) {
  y <- do.call(rbind, lapply(kinds$key, function(k) {
    data.frame(entity = x$entity, code = x$code, year = x$year, kind = k, value = x[[paste0(prefix, k, "_yearly")]])
  }))
  y$value[is.na(y$value)] <- 0
  y
}
dead <- to_long(deaths, "total_dead_")
hit <- to_long(affected, "total_affected_")
first_year <- min(dead$year)
last_year <- max(dead$year)
recent <- 2000:last_year

# the countries: rows with a code that Our World in Data puts on a continent (its regions have no
# code, or one that starts with OWID_)
country_codes <- continents$code[nzchar(continents$code)]
continent_of <- setNames(continents$owid_region, continents$code)

# the population of each place and year; the data end in 2023, and the years after it take the
# population of 2023
names(population)[names(population) == "population_historical"] <- "people"
last_population <- max(population$year)
carried <- do.call(rbind, lapply((last_population + 1):last_year, function(y) {
  transform(population[population$year == last_population, ], year = y)
}))
population <- rbind(population[population$year >= first_year, ], carried)




Code
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# the kinds of disaster, in the order of the stacked bars: the first five colours of a palette whose
# neighbours were checked for colour blindness, and grey for the rest
group_colors <- c(
  Flood = "#2a78d6",
  "Extreme temperature" = "#eb6834",
  Storm = "#1baf7a",
  Drought = "#eda100",
  Earthquake = "#e87ba4",
  Other = "#bdbdbd"
)
# one hue, from light to dark, for the deaths per person on the map
reds <- c("#fee5d9", "#fcbba1", "#fc9272", "#fb6a4a", "#ef3b2c", "#cb181d", "#99000d")

# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom", traceorder = "normal")

# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
thousand <- function(x) number(x / 1000)
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# country names that take "the" in a sentence
with_the <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    x %in% c("Democratic Republic of Congo", "Central African Republic", "United States", "Philippines"),
    paste("the", x),
    x
  )
}


More disasters are recorded than before, which is not the same as more happening. EM-DAT recorded 6 disasters in 1900, 84 in 1970 and 405 in 2000, and since 2000 between 325 and 451 a year. Our World in Data warns that “the historical increase largely reflects improvements in data reporting” (Our World in Data), so this page counts disasters only from 2000. Deaths are another matter: the great disasters of the past were recorded too, and the page follows deaths since 1900.
The population of each country comes up to 2023; for 2024–2025 the page uses that of 2023.

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
text:
1. Which disasters happen most often?


Code
per_year <- sapply(kinds$event_name, function(k) {
  sum(events$n_events[events$entity == k & events$year %in% recent]) / length(recent)
})
often <- data.frame(label = kinds$label, per_year = per_year)
often <- often[order(-often$per_year), ]
all_per_year <- mean(events$n_events[events$entity == "All disasters" & events$year %in% recent])
of_often <- function(label) often$per_year[often$label == label]


Floods, then storms. Since 2000, EM-DAT has recorded 393 disasters a year: 167 floods and 110 storms, 71% of them. Earthquakes, droughts and extreme temperatures come next, 27, 26 and 25 a year, then landslides (20), wildfires (13) and volcanic eruptions (5).


Code
often$label <- factor(often$label, levels = rev(often$label))
plot_ly(
  often,
  x = ~per_year,
  y = ~label,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(often$label %in% c("Flood", "Storm"), red, gray)),
  text = ~ round(per_year),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.0f} a year<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Disasters recorded a year, 2000–", last_year),
    "EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via Our World in Data.",
    x_axis = list(showticklabels = FALSE, showgrid = FALSE, zeroline = FALSE, range = c(0, 1.15 * max(often$per_year))),
    margin = list(l = 140, t = 60, b = 50, r = 20),
    note_y = -0.08
  )

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
section: 2. Which kill the most, and has that changed?
text:
2. Which kill the most, and has that changed?


Code
world_dead <- dead[dead$entity == "World", ]
since_2000 <- world_dead[world_dead$year %in% recent, ] |>
  group_by(kind) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
of_since <- function(k) since_2000$deaths[since_2000$kind == k]
all_since <- sum(since_2000$deaths)

# deaths a year per 100,000 people in the world, by decade and kind
world_people <- population[population$entity == "World", c("year", "people")]
decades <- world_dead |>
  inner_join(world_people, by = "year") |>
  mutate(decade = 10 * (year %/% 10), group = group_of[kind]) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  mutate(person_years = sum(people[kind == kinds$key[1]])) |>
  group_by(decade, group) |>
  summarise(rate = 1e5 * sum(value) / first(person_years), .groups = "drop")
decade_total <- decades |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(rate = sum(rate))
worst_decade <- decade_total$decade[which.max(decade_total$rate)]
rate_of <- function(d) decade_total$rate[decade_total$decade == d]
last_decade <- max(decade_total$decade)

# the deadliest years of single countries: since 1900 and since 2000
country_dead <- dead[dead$code %in% country_codes, ]
worst_ever <- country_dead |>
  group_by(entity, year) |>
  slice_max(value, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(desc(value))
worst_recent <- worst_ever[worst_ever$year %in% recent, ]


Since 2000, earthquakes. Disasters killed 1,595 thousand people from 2000 to 2025: 796 thousand in earthquakes and the tsunamis they caused, 377 thousand in heatwaves and cold, 228 thousand in storms and 142 thousand in floods. A few events make most of these numbers. The deadliest years of single countries since 2000:

    country = worst_recent$entity[1:10],
    year = worst_recent$year[1:10],
    kind = label_of[worst_recent$kind[1:10]],
    deaths = number(worst_recent$value[1:10])

Over the century, far fewer. In the 1920s, disasters killed 26.6 people a year for every 100,000 people in the world; in the 2020s so far, 0.75. The deadliest years ever recorded in one country were China in 1931 (flood, 3,700,000 dead), China in 1928 (drought, 3,000,000) and Bangladesh in 1943 (drought, 1,900,000). The last year in which disasters killed a million people or more in a single country was 1943.


Code
decades$group <- factor(decades$group, levels = group_levels)
decades$label <- paste0(decades$decade, "s")
p <- plot_ly()
for (g in group_levels) {
  x <- decades[decades$group == g, ]
  p <- add_bars(
    p,
    data = x,
    x = ~label,
    y = ~rate,
    name = g,
    marker = list(color = group_colors[[g]], line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}, ", tolower(g), ": %{y:.2f} a year per 100,000<extra></extra>")
  )
}
p |>
  chart(
    "Disaster deaths a year per 100,000 people, by decade",
    paste0("EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain; population: HYDE, Gapminder, UN; via Our World in Data. 2020s: 2020–", last_year, "."),
    "Deaths a year per 100,000",
    barmode = "stack",
    legend = legend_top,
    margin = list(t = 110, b = 80, l = 60, r = 10),

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
text:
3. Which affect the most people?


Code
affected_since <- hit[hit$entity == "World" & hit$year %in% recent, ] |>
  group_by(kind) |>
  summarise(people = sum(value)) |>
  arrange(desc(people))
of_affected <- function(k) affected_since$people[affected_since$kind == k]
billion <- function(x) one(x / 1e9)


Floods and droughts. From 2000 to 2025, EM-DAT counted 1.9 billion people affected by floods, 1.8 billion by droughts and 0.9 billion by storms; earthquakes affected 159 million. These are not different people: someone hit by a flood in 2010 and again in 2020 is counted twice. EM-DAT counts as affected the people who needed immediate help, together with the injured and the homeless (EM-DAT, definitions).


Code
affected_since$label <- factor(label_of[affected_since$kind], levels = rev(label_of[affected_since$kind]))
plot_ly(
  affected_since,
  x = ~ people / 1e6,
  y = ~label,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(affected_since$kind %in% c("flood", "drought"), red, gray)),
  text = ~ number(people / 1e6),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:,.0f} million<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("People affected, millions, 2000–", last_year),
    "EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via Our World in Data.",
    x_axis = list(showticklabels = FALSE, showgrid = FALSE, zeroline = FALSE, range = c(0, 1.18 * max(affected_since$people) / 1e6)),
    margin = list(l = 140, t = 60, b = 50, r = 20),

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
section: 4. Where do disasters kill the most?
text:
4. Where do disasters kill the most?


Code
min_people <- 1e6 # countries with fewer people are left out of the rates: one event decides them
country_rates <- country_dead[country_dead$year %in% recent, ] |>
  group_by(code, entity, year) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value), worst_kind = kind[which.max(value)], .groups = "drop") |>
  inner_join(population[, c("code", "year", "people")], by = c("code", "year")) |>
  group_by(code, entity) |>
  summarise(
    worst_year = year[which.max(deaths)],
    worst_kind = worst_kind[which.max(deaths)],
    rate = 1e5 * sum(deaths) / sum(people),
    people_now = people[which.max(year)],
    deaths = sum(deaths),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
small <- country_rates[country_rates$people_now < min_people, ]
country_rates <- country_rates[country_rates$people_now >= min_people, ] |>
  arrange(desc(rate))
top_rates <- head(country_rates, 5)
world_rate <- 1e5 * sum(world_dead$value[world_dead$year %in% recent]) /
  sum(world_people$people[world_people$year %in% recent])

# each continent: the deaths since 2000 by kind
continent_dead <- dead[dead$entity %in% c("Africa", "Asia", "Europe", "North America", "South America", "Oceania", "World") &
  dead$year %in% recent, ] |>
  mutate(group = group_of[kind]) |>
  group_by(entity, group) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = 100 * deaths / sum(deaths)) |>
  ungroup()
share_in <- function(place, g) continent_dead$share[continent_dead$entity == place & continent_dead$group == g]
# the deadliest kind in each continent (of all eight kinds), as text
plural <- c(
  flood = "floods",
  extreme_temperature = "heat and cold",
  extreme_weather = "storms",
  drought = "droughts",
  earthquake = "earthquakes",
  volcanic_activity = "volcanic eruptions",
  landslide = "landslides",
  wildfire = "wildfires"
)
killers <- dead[dead$entity %in% c("Africa", "Asia", "Europe", "North America", "South America", "Oceania") &
  dead$year %in% recent, ] |>
  group_by(entity, kind) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = 100 * deaths / sum(deaths)) |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()
killer_text <- and_list(paste0("in ", killers$entity, ", ", plural[killers$kind], " (", percent(killers$share), ")"))
europe_heat <- dead[dead$entity == "Europe" & dead$kind == "extreme_temperature", ]
heat_in <- function(year) europe_heat$value[europe_heat$year == year]
greece <- country_dead[country_dead$entity == "Greece" & country_dead$year %in% recent, ]
greece_heat <- greece[greece$kind == "extreme_temperature", ]


Where one event struck a country hard. From 2000 to 2025, disasters killed 0.85 people a year for every 100,000 in the world. Among the countries of a million people or more, Haiti lost 88.4 a year, almost all in its earthquake of 2010; then Libya (47.5, storm of 2023), Myanmar (12.5, storm of 2008), Sri Lanka (6.9, earthquake of 2004) and Somalia (6.2, drought of 2010). The 58 places with fewer than a million people are left out of the rates and the map: on a small island, a single storm makes the rate enormous.


Code
classes <- c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, Inf)
class_names <- c("Under 0.1", "0.1–0.5", "0.5–1", "1–2", "2–5", "5–10", "10 or more")
country_rates$class <- as.integer(cut(country_rates$rate, classes, right = FALSE))
steps <- do.call(c, lapply(seq_along(reds), function(i) {
  list(list((i - 1) / 7, reds[i]), list(i / 7, reds[i]))
}))
plot_ly(
  country_rates,
  type = "choropleth",
  locations = ~code,
  z = ~class,
  zmin = 0.5,
  zmax = 7.5,
  colorscale = steps,
  marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.3)),
  text = ~ paste0(
    entity,
    ": ",
    two(rate),
    " deaths a year per 100,000<br>",
    number(deaths),
    " deaths in all; the worst year ",
    worst_year,
    " (",
    tolower(label_of[worst_kind]),
    ")"
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text",
  colorbar = list(
    title = list(text = "Deaths a year<br>per 100,000"),
    tickvals = 1:7,
    ticktext = class_names,
    len = 0.8,
    thickness = 14
  )
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Disaster deaths per 100,000 people a year, 2000–", last_year),
    "EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain; population: HYDE, Gapminder, UN; via Our World in Data. Grey: under a million people, or no data.",
    geo = list(
      showframe = FALSE,
      showcoastlines = FALSE,
      showland = TRUE,
      landcolor = "#e8e8e8",
      projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
      lataxis = list(range = c(-57, 85))
    ),
    margin = list(t = 50, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )






Each continent has its own killer. Of the people killed by disasters since 2000, the most died, in Africa, floods (34%), in Asia, earthquakes (63%), in Europe, heat and cold (99%), in North America, earthquakes (88%), in Oceania, landslides (28%) and in South America, floods (55%).
In Europe, heat, and its deaths are of another kind. For 2022 and 2023, EM-DAT’s heat deaths in Europe, 61,671 and 47,688, are almost exactly the heat-related deaths that epidemiologists estimated for those years, 61,672 and 47,690, with statistical models of temperature and the deaths recorded in 35 countries (Ballester et al. 2023; Gallo et al. 2024): estimates of the deaths that the heat added, not deaths counted one by one, as those of an earthquake are. In Greece, 14,831 of the 15,134 disaster deaths since 2000 are such heat deaths, 14,783 of them in the years from 2022 to 2025; for the summer of 2022, the first study found the second highest rate of heat deaths in Europe in Greece, after Italy.

section: 5. Where is the Earth itself restless?
text:
5. Where is the Earth itself restless?


Code
sf_use_s2(TRUE)
boundary <- st_union(st_geometry(plates))
quake_points <- st_as_sf(quakes, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
erupted <- volcanoes[!is.na(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year) & volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year >= 1900, ]
volcano_points <- st_as_sf(erupted, coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)
quake_km <- as.numeric(st_distance(quake_points, boundary)) / 1000
volcano_km <- as.numeric(st_distance(volcano_points, boundary)) / 1000
# how much of the Earth lies near a boundary: an even grid of points over the sphere (a Fibonacci
# lattice), each measured like the earthquakes
n_grid <- 60000
i <- 0:(n_grid - 1)
grid <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(
    lon = ((i * 180 * (3 - sqrt(5))) %% 360) - 180,
    lat = asin(-1 + 2 * (i + 0.5) / n_grid) * 180 / pi
  ),
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  crs = 4326
)
grid_km <- as.numeric(st_distance(grid, boundary)) / 1000
bands <- data.frame(km = c(100, 200, 300))
bands$earth <- sapply(bands$km, function(k) 100 * mean(grid_km <= k))
bands$quakes <- sapply(bands$km, function(k) 100 * mean(quake_km <= k))
bands$volcanoes <- sapply(bands$km, function(k) 100 * mean(volcano_km <= k))
in_band <- function(k, column) bands[[column]][bands$km == k]


Along the edges of the plates. The outer shell of the Earth is broken into plates that move against each other (Bird 2003). The map shows the 1,620 earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more since 1900 and the 439 volcanoes that have erupted since 1900: they line the boundaries of the plates, above all around the Pacific Ocean. Within 300 km of a boundary, a band that covers 24% of the Earth’s surface, lie 89% of those earthquakes and 87% of those volcanoes.

  from <- if (k == 1) 1 else breaks[k - 1] + 1
  c(segments[from:breaks[k], "X"], NA)
}))
lines_lat <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(breaks), function(k) {
  from <- if (k == 1) 1 else breaks[k - 1] + 1
  c(segments[from:breaks[k], "Y"], NA)
}))

title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
text:
So, what does it mean?

Floods and storms are the commonest disasters: 167 and 110 a year of the 393 that EM-DAT records.
Earthquakes have killed the most people since 2000, 796 thousand, then heat and cold, 377 thousand.
Disasters kill far fewer people than a century ago: 0.75 a year per 100,000 people in the 2020s, against 26.6 in the 1920s.
Floods and droughts affect the most people, billions since 2000; in Europe, by the estimates of recent years, heat kills more than any other disaster.
The ground shakes and erupts along the edges of the plates: a quarter of the Earth’s surface holds nearly nine in ten of the big earthquakes.

What this does not show. EM-DAT records the disasters that meet its criteria, and more of them get recorded as time goes on; its recent heat deaths in Europe are estimates from statistical models, while those of an earthquake or a flood are counted. The people affected are counted once for every disaster that hits them. The rates per person leave out small countries, and one event can decide the rate of a country for decades. And the numbers count the dead and the affected, not what the survivors lost.
For the details, see the pages on earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, floods, tornadoes and wildfires.

title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
text:
In August 2023 a fire near Alexandroupolis burnt more than 96,000 hectares, the largest single fire in Europe since the 1980s (JRC, 10 April 2024). A hectare is a square of 100 metres by 100; that fire burnt more than 960 square kilometres. Was it a sign that Greece burns more than it used to? This story asks five questions:

Is Greece burning more than it used to?
Which were the worst years, and why?
Is the fire season getting longer?
Where do the fires burn?
How does Greece compare with its neighbours?

The data come from three places, besides the boundaries of the regions from GISCO and the area of each country from Eurostat (reg_area3):

National statistics: the area burnt and the number of forest fires in each country, every year since 1980, which the countries report and the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission collects (country totals). Those of Greece count forest land, “wooded and non-wooded” (JRC 2025).
EFFIS, the European Forest Fire Information System, run by the JRC: satellites outline the land that burns. It has the area burnt in each country every year since 2006, in fires of about 30 hectares or more (statistics portal), and the outline of every fire mapped in Greece since 2016, at first of about 30 hectares or more and, since 2020, smaller ones too (rapid damage assessment).
NASA FIRMS: the hot spots that two satellites, Terra and Aqua, have seen in Greece since 2003 (FIRMS, with one file for each country and year).

They do not count the same things. The national statistics count forest land; the satellites outline all the land that burnt, farmland included, but miss the small fires. In 2007, for example, Greece counted 225,734 hectares of forest fires, and another 88,093 in fires outside forest land, 313,826 in all (JRC 2008); EFFIS mapped about 272,000 hectares, in fires of about 30 hectares or more. Where the two disagree, the page says which one it shows.

# the country totals: an Excel file with one sheet for the area burnt (hectares) and one for the

totals_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(

    "report_2024.xlsx"
  ),
  totals_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE

read_greece <- function(sheet) {
  x <- as.data.frame(readxl::read_excel(totals_file, sheet = sheet, col_types = "text"))
  # numbers are written with spaces between the thousands, such as "32 965"
  data.frame(year = as.integer(x$Year), value = as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.]", "", x$GRC)))
}
