# EFFIS's estimates for a country (its three-letter code): the area burnt each year, in hectares,
# and the number of fires of about 30 hectares or more, from satellite images
effis_annual <- function(code) {
  x <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(
    "https://api2.effis.emergency.copernicus.eu/statistics/v2/effis/",
    "estimatesbycountry?country=",
    code
  ))
  data.frame(code = code, year = x$year, area = x$ba, fires = x$nf)
}
countries <- data.frame(
  code = c("GRC", "PRT", "ESP", "ITA", "FRA", "CYP"),
  geo = c("EL", "PT", "ES", "IT", "FR", "CY"),
  name = c("Greece", "Portugal", "Spain", "Italy", "France", "Cyprus")
)
effis <- do.call(rbind, lapply(countries$code, effis_annual))
effis_greece <- effis[effis$code == "GRC", ]

# the area of each country, in square kilometres: for France, without its overseas departments

  "reg_area3",

)
area_now <- area_all[area_all$time == max(area_all$time), ]
land <- setNames(area_now$values, area_now$geo)

title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
section: 1. Is Greece burning more than it used to?
text:
1. Is Greece burning more than it used to?


Code
area_in <- function(year) national$area[national$year == year]
last_total <- max(national$year)
worst <- head(national$year[order(-national$area)], 5)
decade_of <- function(year) {
  ifelse(year >= 2020, paste0("2020–", last_total), paste0(10 * (year %/% 10), "s"))
}
by_decade <- national |>
  mutate(decade = decade_of(year)) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(
    years = n(),
    area_a_year = mean(area),
    fires_a_year = mean(fires),
    size_of_fire = sum(area) / sum(fires)
  )
of_decade <- function(decade, column) by_decade[[column]][by_decade$decade == decade]
last_decade <- tail(by_decade$decade, 1)
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance of a pattern as strong as this without one
trend_area <- cor.test(national$year, national$area, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
trend_fires <- cor.test(national$year, national$fires, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
# the area burnt by year, both sources side by side
both <- merge(national, effis_greece, by = "year", suffixes = c("_national", "_effis"))
ratio <- sum(both$area_effis) / sum(both$area_national)


Not steadily. The area burnt swings far more from one year to the next than it changes over the decades.
In the 45 years from 1980 to 2024, Greece’s forest fires burnt between 3,517 hectares (2003) and 225,734 (2007). Five years, 1988, 2000, 2007, 2021 and 2023, make up 36% of everything that burnt in those 45 years. The averages of the decades differ less:

The average fire grew from 25 hectares in the 1990s to 58 in 2020–2024, which is because the number of fires fell while a few of them were enormous. The number needs care, though: since 1998 the Fire Service has been responsible for forest fires, instead of the Forest Service, and the two did not count in the same way (European Commission 2001).

    p,
    x = c(min(years) - 0.45, max(years) + 0.45),
    y = rep(by_decade$area_a_year[k] / 1000, 2),
    name = "Average of the period",
    legendgroup = "average",
    showlegend = k == 1,
    line = list(color = "black", width = 2.5),
    hovertemplate = paste0(by_decade$decade[k], ": %{y:.1f} thousand ha a year<extra></extra>")
  )
}
p |>
  add_markers(
    data = effis_greece,
    x = ~year,
    y = ~ area / 1000,
    name = "Satellite maps (EFFIS)",
    marker = list(color = blue, size = 8, line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand ha<extra>EFFIS</extra>"
  ) |>
  chart(
    "Area burnt by fires in Greece each year, thousand hectares",
    paste0(
      "JRC, country totals (bars); EFFIS, fires of about 30 ha or more (dots). EFFIS's ",
      last_year,
      ": to ",
      date_text(last_fire),
      "."
    ),
    "Thousand hectares",
    legend = legend_top,
    margin = list(t = 110, b = 90)
  )






The 2010s were the quietest of the five periods, and the years from 2020 to 2024 the worst, 60,262 hectares a year, with two of the five worst years in them. But an average of five years says little when one of them burns 136,499 hectares and another 9,300.
The satellites agree, and go on to the present. EFFIS maps more land than the national statistics count, farmland included: 13% more in the years that both have, and their highs and lows are the same ones. After the country totals end, it has 47,819 hectares for 2025 and 35,454 for 2026, up to 21 November 2026. For 2025 the national figure, still provisional, is 41,540 hectares of forest land in 561 fires (JRC 2026).

title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
section: 2. Which were the worst years, and why?
text:
2. Which were the worst years, and why?


Code
largest <- st_drop_geometry(fires) |>
  arrange(desc(area)) |>
  head(10)
place_english <- c(
  Evvoia = "Evia",
  "Kalymnos, Karpathos, Kasos, Kos, Rodos" = "Rhodes and nearby islands",
  Ileia = "Ilia",
  "Dytiki Attiki" = "West Attica",
  "Lakonia, Messinia" = "Laconia and Messinia",
  "Anatoliki Attiki" = "East Attica",
  "Magnisia, Sporades" = "Magnesia and the Sporades"
)
latin <- places$NAME_LATN[match(largest$PROVINCE, places$NUTS_NAME)]
largest$place <- ifelse(latin %in% names(place_english), place_english[latin], latin)


Years of heat, drought or wind, when a few fires became huge. In the official record, the five worst years were:

2007, the worst year for forest fires ever recorded in Greece: 225,734 hectares of forest land. Three heatwaves in a row, with more than 46 °C in some places, a long drought and strong winds; at the end of August five fires in the Peloponnese burnt 170,000 hectares and two in Evia 25,000. 69 civilians, 9 seasonal firefighters and 2 pilots died (JRC 2008).
2000: 145,033 hectares, nearly three times the average of the two decades before (European Commission 2001).
2023: 136,499 hectares, after the warmest July in 64 years and a heatwave from 12 to 26 July. In July there were fires in Attica, Rhodes, Evia, Corfu and near Volos, and from the middle of August in Evros and Rodopi. 23 civilians and one firefighter died (JRC 2024).
1988: 110,501 hectares.
2021: 108,418 hectares, in a summer that approached 46 °C, with the most notable heatwave, in length, for 35 years. Most of the large fires came between 3 and 11 August, among them those of Attica, Evia, Eastern Mani and Ancient Olympia (JRC 2022).

The deadliest fire was not among the largest. In July 2018 a fire of just over 1,000 hectares at Mati, in Attica, killed 100 people, in a year that was “relatively light” for the area burnt (JRC 2019).
The ten largest fires that EFFIS has outlined in Greece since 2016:

Most fires are small: 80% of the outlined fires were under 100 hectares, and they made up 5% of the area. A year is bad because a few fires are huge, not because there are many.

title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
section: 3. Is the fire season getting longer?
text:
3. Is the fire season getting longer?


Code
# the heat that each day's fires gave off when the satellites passed, in megawatts: the sum of the
# fire radiative power of the day's hot spots
daily <- hot_spots |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(heat = sum(frp)) |>
  right_join(
    data.frame(
      date = seq(
        as.Date(paste0(min(hot_spot_years), "-01-01")),
        as.Date(paste0(max(hot_spot_years), "-12-31")),
        by = "day"
      )
    ),
    by = "date"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    heat = ifelse(is.na(heat), 0, heat),
    year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    day = as.Date(paste0("2001-", format(date, "%m-%d"))) # one calendar for every year
  )
big <- 2000 # a big-fire day: the fires gave off 2,000 megawatts or more when the satellites passed
big_days <- daily[daily$heat >= big, ]
big_days$j <- as.integer(format(big_days$date, "%j"))
big_days$summer <- as.integer(format(big_days$date, "%m")) %in% 6:9

# two periods of eleven years
periods <- list("2003–2013" = 2003:2013, "2015–2025" = 2015:2025)
period_numbers <- lapply(periods, function(years) {
  x <- big_days[big_days$year %in% years, ]
  first <- tapply(x$j, x$year, min)
  last <- tapply(x$j, x$year, max)
  list(
    per_year = nrow(x) / length(years),
    outside = 100 * mean(!x$summer),
    first = median(first),
    last = median(last)
  )
})
in_period <- function(k, what) period_numbers[[k]][[what]]
# the heat of a hot spot in each month (median of all years)
spot_heat <- tapply(hot_spots$frp, format(hot_spots$date, "%b"), median)


Not that the satellites can see. The chart shows every day since 2003, one row for each year and one square for each day. The colour is how much heat the fires of the day gave off when the satellites passed over, in megawatts: the sum of NASA’s fire radiative power of all the hot spots of the day, the presumed vegetation fires only (NASA’s description of the hot spots). The season of the big fires is the dark band of July and August. In the months around it there are many paler squares, especially in autumn, some of them probably farmers burning what is left in the fields: a hot spot gave off 10 megawatts in October and 46 in August (medians). The heat, not the number of hot spots, separates the big fires.


Code
daily$class <- cut(
  daily$heat,
  c(-Inf, 0, 200, 1000, big, Inf),
  labels = c(
    "No fire seen",
    "Under 200 MW",
    "200 to 999 MW",
    "1,000 to 1,999 MW",
    "2,000 MW or more"
  )
)
month_starts <- as.Date(paste0("2001-", 1:12, "-01"))
ggplot(daily[!is.na(daily$day), ], aes(x = day, y = year, fill = class)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#f7f7f7", "#fee6ce", "#fdae6b", "#e6550d", "#7f2704"),
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = month_starts + 14, labels = month.abb, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(2005, 2025, 5), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "When Greece burns",
    subtitle = "Heat of the fires that the satellites saw, each day, megawatts",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NASA FIRMS, MODIS on Terra and Aqua, presumed vegetation fires"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )









A big-fire day here is one on which the fires gave off 2,000 megawatts or more. In 2003–2013 there were 7.4 of them a year, in 2015–2025 8.2; 6% and 4% of them came outside the months from June to September. The first big-fire day of the year came on 29 June in 2003–2013 and 12 July in 2015–2025, and the last on 27 August and 5 September (medians of the years). Nothing in these numbers says that the season has become longer.
That is not the last word. The authors of Greece’s chapter in the JRC’s report for 2025 write that climate change has “systematically extended the fire season” (JRC 2026), and hot days do come earlier and last later, at least in Athens, as Athens Is Getting Hotter shows. But the hot spots show what did burn, not how much could have: in years without a spark in a dangerous week, or with firefighters who put a fire out in time, a longer dangerous season leaves no trace in them. There are other limits too:

A hot spot is not a fire. It is a square about a kilometre across in which the satellite saw heat (NASA’s frequently asked questions): a big fire makes many, and farm burning and other sources of heat make some too.
The satellites see a fire only when they pass over, without cloud. Their orbits have changed as well: since 2020 NASA has not been able to keep Terra’s passing time from drifting earlier (NASA), so the two periods were not seen at exactly the same hours.
23 years are few, and the fires of a year depend on the weather of a few weeks.

title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
text:
4. Where do the fires burn?


Code
fires_area <- st_transform(fires, 3035) # an equal-area projection
regions_area <- st_transform(st_make_valid(regions), 3035)
burnt <- st_union(st_geometry(fires_area)) # the land burnt at least once
inside <- st_intersection(regions_area[, "NUTS_ID"], st_sf(geometry = burnt))
region_share <- data.frame(
  NUTS_ID = regions_area$NUTS_ID,
  land = as.numeric(st_area(regions_area)) / 1e4,
  burnt = as.numeric(st_area(inside))[match(regions_area$NUTS_ID, inside$NUTS_ID)] / 1e4
)
region_share$share <- 100 * region_share$burnt / region_share$land
region_share$name <- region_names[region_share$NUTS_ID]
region_share <- region_share[order(region_share$share), ]
in_region <- function(id, column) region_share[[column]][region_share$NUTS_ID == id]
all_land <- sum(region_share$land)
burnt_share <- 100 * sum(region_share$burnt) / all_land

# what burnt: EFFIS gives, for each fire, the share of its area that was each kind of land
cover <- c(
  BROADLEA = "forest",
  CONIFER = "forest",
  MIXED = "forest",
  SCLEROPH = "other natural land",
  TRANSIT = "other natural land",
  OTHERNATLC = "other natural land",
  AGRIAREAS = "farmland",
  ARTIFSURF = "other",
  OTHERLC = "other"
)
cover_share <- sapply(names(cover), function(column) {
  as.numeric(fires[[column]]) / 100 * fires$area
})
cover_share <- cover_share[!is.na(rowSums(cover_share)), ]
cover_total <- tapply(colSums(cover_share), cover, sum)
cover_percent <- 100 * cover_total / sum(cover_total)


Attica the most for its size, then the north-east and the Aegean. By 21 November 2026, EFFIS had outlined 1,793 fires in Greece since 2016. They burnt 5,518 square kilometres, some land more than once; 4.0% of Greece burnt at least once in those 11 years.


Code
periods_map <- cut(
  fires$year,
  c(first_year - 1, 2020, 2023, last_year),
  labels = c(
    paste0(first_year, "–2020"),
    "2021–2023",
    paste0("2024–", last_year)
  )
)
fires_map <- st_transform(fires, 2100) # the Greek grid
fires_map$period <- periods_map
regions_map <- st_transform(regions, 2100)
# the names of the largest fires, at the middle of their outlines
labelled <- fires_map[order(-fires_map$area)[1:7], ]
labelled$label <- paste(
  c(largest$place[1:7]),
  labelled$year
)
xy <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(labelled)))
labels <- data.frame(x = xy[, 1], y = xy[, 2], label = labelled$label)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = regions_map, fill = "#ededed", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(
    data = fires_map[order(fires_map$period), ],
    aes(fill = period, colour = period),
    linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = labels,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    size = 3.6,
    min.segment.length = 0,
    segment.colour = "grey40",
    label.size = 0.2,
    fill = "white",
    seed = 1
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = period_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = period_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = NULL), colour = "none") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Every fire that EFFIS outlined in Greece",
    subtitle = paste0(first_year, "–", last_year, ", the seven largest fires named"),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Data: EFFIS (Copernicus); boundaries: GISCO © EuroGeographics.",
      "Fires of about 30 hectares or more until 2019, smaller ones too since 2020.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )









Attica has burnt the most for its size: 22.7% of its land burnt at least once from 2016 to 2026, more than one square kilometre in five. The chart shows the same share for every region; that of the whole country was 4.0%. East Macedonia and Thrace has the fire of Evros, and the North Aegean, Central Greece with Evia and the South Aegean are next.


Code
plot_ly(
  region_share,
  x = ~share,
  y = ~ factor(name, levels = name),
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(region_share$NUTS_ID == "EL30", red, gray)),
  text = percent(region_share$share, 1),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of its land<extra></extra>"
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Land burnt at least once, ", first_year, "–", last_year, ", % of the region"),
    "EFFIS outlines (Copernicus); regions: GISCO.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(region_share$share)), ticksuffix = "%"),
    margin = list(l = 190, t = 70, b = 70, r = 40),
    note_y = -0.1
  )








Code
# the mainland of Attica and its neighbours: the region also has islands far to the south
window <- st_bbox(c(xmin = 22.95, ymin = 37.5, xmax = 24.2, ymax = 38.45), crs = st_crs(4326))
box <- st_bbox(st_transform(st_as_sfc(window), 2100))
# the years of the larger fires in the window, at the middle of their outlines
in_window <- st_intersects(fires_map, st_as_sfc(box), sparse = FALSE)[, 1]
attica_fires <- fires_map[in_window & fires_map$area >= 3000, ]
attica_xy <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(attica_fires)))
attica_labels <- data.frame(x = attica_xy[, 1], y = attica_xy[, 2], label = attica_fires$year)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = regions_map, fill = "#ededed", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(
    data = fires_map[order(fires_map$period), ],
    aes(fill = period, colour = period),
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = period_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = period_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = NULL), colour = "none") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = attica_labels,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    size = 3.4,
    min.segment.length = 0,
    segment.colour = "grey40",
    label.size = 0.2,
    fill = "white",
    seed = 2
  ) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(box["xmin"], box["xmax"]),
    ylim = c(box["ymin"], box["ymax"]),
    datum = NA,
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Attica and its neighbourhood, close up",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Fires outlined ",
      first_year,
      "–",
      last_year,
      "\nLabels: the year of the fires of 3,000 hectares or more"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: EFFIS (Copernicus); boundaries: GISCO © EuroGeographics."
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )









What burns is mostly not forest: of the area inside the outlines, 23% was forest, 51% shrubland, grassland and other natural land, and 25% farmland; the rest, 2%, was built-up land or other cover. EFFIS gets these shares by laying the outlines on the EU’s CORINE map of land cover (EFFIS, fire damage assessment).

title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
section: 5. How does Greece compare with its neighbours?
text:
5. How does Greece compare with its neighbours?


Code
compare <- effis[effis$year %in% 2006:2025, ]
compare <- merge(compare, countries[, c("code", "name", "km2")])
# 1% of a square kilometre is one hectare, so hectares per square kilometre are a percentage
compare$share <- compare$area / compare$km2
means <- compare |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(share), worst = max(share), worst_year = year[which.max(share)]) |>
  arrange(mean)
in_country <- function(name, column) means[[column]][means$name == name]
top_of_year <- compare |>
  group_by(year) |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1)
first_place <- table(top_of_year$name)
times_first <- function(name) {
  if (name %in% names(first_place)) first_place[[name]] else 0
}


Portugal burns the most for its size, and Greece is second. In the years from 2006 to 2025, the satellites found that fires burnt on average 1.14% of Portugal every year and 0.38% of Greece: 3.0 times as much. Greece was ahead of Cyprus (0.26%), Spain (0.19%), Italy (0.19%) and France (0.03%). In 3 of the 20 years Greece had the highest share of all six, in 16 Portugal.
Here EFFIS’s satellites measure all six countries in the same way, in fires of about 30 hectares or more, so the comparison does not depend on how each country counts.


Code
set.seed(2026)
compare$position <- match(compare$name, means$name) + runif(nrow(compare), -0.17, 0.17)
plot_ly() |>
  add_markers(
    data = compare,
    x = ~share,
    y = ~position,
    marker = list(
      color = ifelse(compare$name == "Greece", red, gray),
      size = 9,
      line = list(color = "white", width = 1)
    ),
    text = ~ paste0(name, " ", year, ": ", two(share), "%"),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_markers(
    data = means,
    x = ~mean,
    y = ~ match(name, means$name),
    marker = list(
      color = ifelse(means$name == "Greece", red, dark_gray),
      symbol = "line-ns-open",
      size = 26,
      line = list(width = 4)
    ),
    text = ~ paste0(name, ", average 2006–2025: ", two(mean), "% a year"),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  chart(
    "Land burnt each year, % of the country, 2006–2025",
    paste0(
      "EFFIS, fires of about 30 ha or more; areas of the countries: Eurostat, reg_area3. ",
      "Dots: years. Bars: averages."
    ),
    x_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero", ticksuffix = "%"),
    y_axis = list(
      tickvals = seq_len(nrow(means)),
      ticktext = means$name,
      range = c(0.4, nrow(means) + 0.6),
      zeroline = FALSE
    ),
    annotations = lapply(seq_len(nrow(means)), function(i) {
      list(
        x = means$worst[i],
        y = i,
        text = paste0(means$worst_year[i]),
        showarrow = FALSE,
        xanchor = "left",
        xshift = 8,
        font = list(size = 12, color = dark_gray)
      )
    }),
    margin = list(l = 80, t = 70, b = 90, r = 40),
    note_y = -0.14
  )






The number beside each country’s row marks its worst year: 2017 in Portugal, 2007 in Greece, 2025 in Cyprus.

title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
text:
So, what does it mean?

Greece does not burn steadily more, but it burns in bursts. Five years, 1988, 2000, 2007, 2021 and 2023, have 36% of everything that burnt from 1980 to 2024, and there is no trend in the total.
A bad year is made of a few enormous fires. The ten largest fires made up 46% of the area of the 1,793 fires outlined since 2016.
The satellites see no longer season of big fires, though the heat that makes a fire dangerous does last longer, and the Greek authors of the JRC’s report say that the season has.
Attica burns the most for its size: more than a fifth of its land burnt at least once since 2016.
Greece is second to Portugal. Every year it burns about 0.38% of its land on average, against 0.19% in Spain and 0.19% in Italy.

What this does not show. It does not say what started the fires, how well they were fought, or what the climate will do to the next ones. The national statistics and the satellites do not count the same things, the satellites miss the small fires, and the outlines show where a fire burnt, not how severely. And the fires are counted in hectares here, which do not measure the people, the homes and the animals lost in them.
For the heat that dries out the land, see Athens Is Getting Hotter; for the temperature of the world, the NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
Greece is one of the most visited countries of Europe, and its tourism is squeezed into a few summer months and a few groups of islands. This story follows the tourists through the statistics of Eurostat:

How many come?
When do they come?
Where do they go?
Where do they come from?
How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
How much does Greece depend on them?
Where do they stay?

The data come from three places, all at Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU:

The statistics of tourist accommodation: the nights that guests spend in hotels, rented rooms and apartments, and campsites, each month since 1994, by region and by the country the guests live in. A night is one guest staying one night: a couple on a week’s holiday spend 14 nights. Since 2018 Eurostat also counts the nights booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor.
The survey of the trips of EU residents, which asks people in every EU country where they travelled and what they spent. It tells what a holiday in Greece costs its visitors, against a holiday in Spain, Italy or Croatia.
The balance of payments, which records what foreign visitors spend in each country, so it can be set against the size of its economy.

They are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
Greece is one of the most visited countries of Europe, and its tourism is squeezed into a few summer months and a few groups of islands. This story follows the tourists through the statistics of Eurostat:

How many come?
When do they come?
Where do they go?
Where do they come from?
How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
How much does Greece depend on them?
Where do they stay?

The data come from three places, all at Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU:

The statistics of tourist accommodation: the nights that guests spend in hotels, rented rooms and apartments, and campsites, each month since 1994, by region and by the country the guests live in. A night is one guest staying one night: a couple on a week’s holiday spend 14 nights. Since 2018 Eurostat also counts the nights booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor.
The survey of the trips of EU residents, which asks people in every EU country where they travelled and what they spent. It tells what a holiday in Greece costs its visitors, against a holiday in Spain, Italy or Croatia.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
The data


Code
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
# a monthly Eurostat dataset, the same way, with the year and the month of each value
eurostat_months <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "date", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x$year <- as.integer(format(x$time, "%Y"))
  x$month <- as.integer(format(x$time, "%m"))
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
eu <- eu_countries$code
eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27", TR = "Türkiye")

# Greece every year: the nights at all tourist accommodation (I551-I553), in hotels (I551), in rented
# rooms, apartments and holiday homes (I552, counted from 2009) and in campsites (I553), of all
# guests, of guests from abroad and of Greeks
kinds <- c(I551 = "Hotels", I552 = "Rented rooms and apartments", I553 = "Campsites")
annual <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_ninat", list(
  geo = "EL", unit = "NR", c_resid = c("TOTAL", "FOR", "DOM"), nace_r2 = c("I551-I553", names(kinds))
))
nights <- function(year, kind = "I551-I553", resid = "TOTAL") {
  annual$values[annual$time == year & annual$nace_r2 == kind & annual$c_resid == resid]
}
years <- annual$time[annual$nace_r2 == "I551-I553" & annual$c_resid == "TOTAL"]
year_now <- max(years)

# the nights of each month at all tourist accommodation, every EU country
monthly <- eurostat_months("tour_occ_nim", list(geo = c(eu, "EU27_2020"), unit = "NR", c_resid = "TOTAL", nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
greece <- monthly[monthly$geo == "EL", ]
month_now <- max(greece$time)   # the latest month
full_year <- max(as.integer(names(which(table(greece$year) == 12))))   # the latest year with all twelve months

# the regions of Greece (NUTS 2): the nights of each month since 2020, also per thousand inhabitants,
# of all guests and of guests from abroad
regions <- c(
  EL30 = "Attica", EL41 = "North Aegean", EL42 = "South Aegean", EL43 = "Crete",
  EL51 = "Eastern Macedonia and Thrace", EL52 = "Central Macedonia", EL53 = "Western Macedonia",
  EL54 = "Epirus", EL61 = "Thessaly", EL62 = "Ionian Islands", EL63 = "Western Greece",
  EL64 = "Central Greece", EL65 = "Peloponnese"
)
regional <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_nin2m", list(geo = names(regions), unit = c("NR", "P_THAB"), c_resid = c("TOTAL", "FOR"), nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
region_year <- max(regional$time)

# the nights in Greece by the country the guests live in; countries only, not groups such as EUR
origins <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_ninraw", list(geo = "EL", unit = "NR", nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
origins <- origins[nchar(origins$c_resid) == 2, ]
origin_nights <- function(country, year) origins$values[match(paste(country, year), paste(origins$c_resid, origins$time))]

# the survey of trips: what EU residents spend on holidays (trips for personal purposes of one night or
# more) in each country, by kind of spending, and the number of those trips and of their nights
destinations <- c("EL", "ES", "IT", "PT", "HR", "CY", "MT", "FR", "AT", "BG", "TR")
parts <- c(TRA = "Getting there and around", ACCOM = "Accommodation", OTHER = "Food, drinks and everything else")
survey <- list(geo = c("EU27_2020", setdiff(destinations, "TR")), c_dest = c(destinations, "DOM"), purpose = "PER", duration = "N_GE1")
# all spending (TOTXDUR, without durable goods), on transport and on accommodation; the rest is
# "everything else", as some countries count cafés and restaurants apart and others do not
per_trip <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_extotw", c(survey, list(statinfo = "AVG_TRP", expend = c("TOTXDUR", "TRA", "ACCOM"))))
trips <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_ttw", survey)
trip_nights <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_tnw", survey)
# Eurostat gives the totals of each kind of spending only for the trips at home; for the others they
# are the spending per trip times the trips
spent <- merge(per_trip[c("geo", "c_dest", "time", "expend", "values")], trips[c("geo", "c_dest", "time", "values")],
  by = c("geo", "c_dest", "time"), suffixes = c("_per_trip", "_trips"))
spent$values <- spent$values_per_trip * spent$values_trips

# consumer prices, 2015 = 100, in Greece and in the EU
prices <- eurostat_values("prc_hicp_aind", list(geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), coicop = "CP00", unit = "INX_A_AVG"))

# what foreign visitors spend in each country (travel, in the balance of payments) and GDP, million euros
receipts <- eurostat_values("bop_its6_det", list(geo = c(eu, "TR"), bop_item = "SD", stk_flow = "CRE", partner = "WRL_REST", currency = "MIO_EUR"))
gdp <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(geo = c(eu, "TR"), na_item = "B1GQ", unit = "CP_MEUR"))

# the nights booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor, Greece and its regions
platforms <- eurostat_values("tour_ce_omn12", list(geo = c("EL", names(regions)), indic_to = "NGT_SP", c_resid = "TOTAL", month = "TOTAL"))
platform_year <- max(platforms$time)
on_platforms <- function(geo, year = platform_year) platforms$values[platforms$geo == geo & platforms$time == year]




Code
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels
amber <- "#c97b1e"
# the three parts of a stacked bar, told apart also with colour blindness: light blue, amber, dark blue
stack_colors <- c("#5b8fd6", amber, "#1c5cab")
# a scale from few nights (white) to many (dark blue)
blues <- list(c(0, "#f4f8fd"), c(0.5, "#3987e5"), c(1, "#0d366b"))

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    # at the top, so that a legend of two or three rows fits under it in a larger top margin
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
months <- factor(month.abb, levels = month.abb)   # in this order on an axis
# a horizontal bar chart of countries or regions, from the highest at the top: by default one of
# them in red, the EU in blue and the others in gray
ranking_bars <- function(x, value, highlight, hover,
                         colors = function(x) ifelse(x$geo == highlight, greek_red, ifelse(x$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))) {
  x <- x[order(x[[value]]), ]
  plot_ly(
    y = factor(x$name, levels = x$name), x = x[[value]], type = "bar", orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = colors(x)), hovertext = hover(x), hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
  )
}

# short labels of numbers
million <- function(x, digits = 1) paste(format(round(x / 1e6, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "million")
euros <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))
billion_euros <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE), " billion")   # from million euros
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
# "A", "A and B", "A, B and C"
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) x else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
# the place of a country counted from the highest: 1 is the highest
highest <- function(k) {
  if (k > 8) return(paste0("the ", k, "th highest"))
  paste0("the ", c("", "second ", "third ", "fourth ", "fifth ", "sixth ", "seventh ", "eighth ")[k], "highest")
}

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
1. How many come?


Code
record <- years[which.max(sapply(years, nights))]
foreign_share <- function(year) 100 * nights(year, resid = "FOR") / nights(year)
hotels_growth <- 100 * (nights(year_now, "I551") / nights(min(years), "I551") - 1)
covid_fall <- 100 * (1 - nights(2020) / nights(2019))
recovered <- min(years[years > 2020 & sapply(years, nights) > nights(2019)])
# this year so far, against the same months of last year
latest_year <- as.integer(format(month_now, "%Y"))
latest_month <- as.integer(format(month_now, "%m"))
so_far <- function(year) sum(greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month <= latest_month])


156.3 million nights in 2025, more than ever.
In 2025, guests spent 156.3 million nights in the hotels, rented rooms and apartments, and campsites of Greece, 84% of them guests from abroad. Hotels alone had 119.0 million nights, 129% more than in 1994. In the first 8 months of 2026 there were 1.8% more nights than in the same months of 2025.
Until 2008 Greece counted only the nights in hotels and campsites; from 2009 it counts those in rented rooms, apartments and holiday homes too, so the bars jump in 2009. Since then the nights fell twice: in the debt crisis, to 80.6 million in 2012, and in 2020, when COVID closed the borders, by 73%. By 2023 there were more than in 2019.


Code
kind_colors <- c(I551 = stack_colors[3], I552 = stack_colors[2], I553 = stack_colors[1])
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(kinds)) {
  x <- annual[annual$nace_r2 == k & annual$c_resid == "TOTAL", ]
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = x$time, y = x$values / 1e6, type = "bar", name = kinds[[k]],
    marker = list(color = kind_colors[[k]], line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>", kinds[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart("Nights at tourist accommodation in Greece, million", "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninat", "Million",
  barmode = "stack", bargap = 0.15, legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "normal"), margin = list(t = 100, b = 90),
  annotations = list(list(x = 2009, y = nights(2009) / 1e6, text = "2009: rented rooms and<br>apartments counted too",
    showarrow = TRUE, ax = -70, ay = -45, font = list(color = dark_gray))))






More and more of the guests come from abroad: 69% of the nights in 2010, 84% in 2025. In 2020, with few foreigners able to travel, the share fell to 68%.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
2. When do they come?


Code
in_month <- function(year, month) greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month == month]
in_months <- function(year, months) sum(greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month %in% months])
summer <- 6:9
winter <- c(1:3, 11:12)
summer_share <- 100 * in_months(full_year, summer) / in_months(full_year, 1:12)
summer_growth <- in_months(full_year, summer) - in_months(2010, summer)
winter_growth <- in_months(full_year, winter) - in_months(2010, winter)


In August, 21 times as many nights as in January.
In 2025, guests spent 1.6 million nights in Greece in January and 34.0 million in August. 72% of the nights of the year fell in the four months from June to September. Each row of the chart is a year and each cell a month: the darker the cell, the more nights. Greece has added summer, not winter: from 2010 to 2025, the nights from June to September grew by 49.5 million, those from November to March by 4.2 million.


Code
heat <- greece[greece$year >= 2009, ]
z <- tapply(heat$values / 1e6, list(heat$year, factor(heat$month, levels = 1:12)), sum)   # years in rows, months in columns
plot_ly(
  x = months, y = rownames(z), z = z, type = "heatmap", colorscale = blues, xgap = 2, ygap = 2,
  colorbar = list(title = list(text = "Million<br>nights"), thickness = 12),
  hovertemplate = "%{x} %{y}: %{z:.1f} million nights<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Nights in Greece each month, million",
    paste0("Eurostat, tour_occ_nim, January 2009 to ", month.name[latest_month], " ", latest_year, "; blank: no data"), y_axis = list(type = "category", autorange = "reversed"), note_y = -0.08)








Code
season <- monthly[monthly$year == full_year, ]
complete <- names(which(table(season$geo) == 12))
by_season <- data.frame(geo = complete, name = eu_name[complete])
by_season$share <- sapply(complete, function(k) {
  x <- season[season$geo == k, ]
  100 * sum(x$values[x$month %in% summer]) / sum(x$values)
})
season_order <- by_season$geo[by_season$geo != "EU27_2020"][order(-by_season$share[by_season$geo != "EU27_2020"])]
more_seasonal <- season_order[seq_len(match("EL", season_order) - 1)]
eu_share <- by_season$share[by_season$geo == "EU27_2020"]


One of the most seasonal in the EU. In the EU as a whole, 52% of the nights at tourist accommodation fall from June to September; in Greece, 72%. Only Croatia packs more of its tourism into them. Hotels, restaurants and the people who work in them have to earn the year’s living in a few months.


Code
ranking_bars(by_season, "share", "EL", function(x) paste0(x$name, ": ", percent(x$share, 1), " of the year's nights")) %>%
  chart(paste0("Share of the nights of ", full_year, " spent from June to September, %"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nim",
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
3. Where do they go?


Code
year_total <- regional[regional$time == region_year & regional$month == "TOTAL", ]
region_value <- function(unit, resid) {
  year_total$values[match(paste(names(regions), unit, resid), paste(year_total$geo, year_total$unit, year_total$c_resid))]
}
by_region <- data.frame(geo = names(regions), name = regions)
by_region$nights <- region_value("NR", "TOTAL")
by_region$per_person <- region_value("P_THAB", "TOTAL") / 1000
by_region$foreign <- 100 * region_value("NR", "FOR") / by_region$nights
islands <- c("EL42", "EL43", "EL62")
islands_foreign <- min(by_region$foreign[by_region$geo %in% islands])
islands_share <- 100 * sum(by_region$nights[by_region$geo %in% islands]) / sum(by_region$nights)
in_region <- function(geo, column) by_region[[column]][by_region$geo == geo]
# the share of the nights of the year that a region has in each month
m <- regional[regional$time == region_year & regional$unit == "NR" & regional$c_resid == "TOTAL" & regional$month != "TOTAL", ]
m$month <- as.integer(sub("M", "", m$month))
by_month <- function(geo) {
  x <- m[m$geo == geo, ]
  x <- x[order(x$month), ]
  100 * x$values / sum(x$values)
}
summer_of <- function(geo) sum(by_month(geo)[summer])


62% of the nights on three groups of islands. In 2025, the South Aegean, the Cyclades and the Dodecanese with Santorini, Mykonos, Rhodes and Kos, had 41.8 million nights; Crete 35.2 million; the Ionian Islands, with Corfu, Zakynthos and Kefalonia, 20.4 million. Attica, with Athens, had 12.8 million. Against the people who live there, the islands are full: 128 nights a year for each inhabitant of the South Aegean and 103 in the Ionian Islands, against 3.4 in Attica. On the islands, 91% or more of the nights are those of guests from abroad.


Code
by_region$million_nights <- by_region$nights / 1e6
ranking_bars(by_region, "million_nights", "", function(x) {
  paste0(x$name, ": ", million(x$nights), " nights, ", round(x$per_person, 1), " per inhabitant, ", percent(x$foreign), " from abroad")
}, colors = function(x) ifelse(x$geo %in% islands, blue, gray)) %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights at tourist accommodation by region, ", region_year, ", million"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m",
    margin = list(l = 200, t = 70, b = 90))






Athens works all year, the islands in the summer. 80% of the nights of the Ionian Islands and 74% of those of the South Aegean fall from June to September, against 49% in Attica, where city breaks, business and conferences fill the hotels in spring and autumn too.


Code
shown <- c(EL62 = amber, EL42 = stack_colors[3], EL43 = stack_colors[1], EL30 = gray)
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(shown)) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = months, y = by_month(k), type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = regions[[k]],
    line = list(color = shown[[k]], width = if (k == "EL30") 2 else 3, dash = if (k == "EL30") "dash" else "solid"),
    marker = list(color = shown[[k]], size = 8),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of the year<extra>", regions[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart(paste0("Share of the nights of ", region_year, " in each month, %"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m", "% of the year",
  y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top, margin = list(t = 100, b = 90))

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
4. Where do they come from?


Code
origin_year <- max(origins$time)
latest <- origins[origins$time == origin_year, ]
latest <- latest[order(-latest$values), ]
latest$name <- as.character(label_eurostat(latest$c_resid, dic = "c_resid"))
latest$name[latest$c_resid == "EL"] <- "Greece (Greeks at home)"
abroad <- latest[latest$c_resid != "EL", ]
# a country's name in a sentence: "the United Kingdom"
in_text <- function(name) ifelse(name %in% c("United Kingdom", "United States", "Netherlands"), paste("the", name), name)
share_of_foreign <- function(country) 100 * origin_nights(country, origin_year) / nights(origin_year, resid = "FOR")
change <- function(country, from = 2019) origin_nights(country, origin_year) - origin_nights(country, from)


Most come from the United Kingdom and Germany. In 2025, guests from the United Kingdom spent 25.4 million nights in Greece and those from Germany 21.0 million: together 35% of the nights of guests from abroad. Greeks on holiday in their own country spent 25.3 million.
The list has changed since 2019. The Russians, who spent 6.6 million nights in Greece in 2019, have almost gone since the EU closed its skies to Russian planes in 2022: 0.36 million in 2025. The Americans came in their place: 6.1 million nights, against 3.9 million in 2019. Poland and Romania grew too, by 1.3 million and 1.9 million nights.


Code
top <- head(latest, 12)
top <- top[order(top$values), ]
plot_ly(
  y = factor(top$name, levels = top$name), x = top$values / 1e6, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(top$c_resid == "EL", gray, blue)),
  hovertext = paste0(top$name, ": ", million(top$values), " nights in ", origin_year, ", ",
    million(origin_nights(top$c_resid, 2019)), " in 2019"),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights in Greece by the country of the guests, ", origin_year, ", million"),
    "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninraw", margin = list(l = 190, t = 70, b = 90))

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
section: 5. How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
text:
5. How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
Eurostat’s survey of trips asks people in every EU country where they went on holiday and what it cost them. The trips to a country include those of its own people on holiday at home, which are cheaper, as there is no long journey: so they are taken out here, and what remains are the visitors from the other EU countries. Türkiye, outside the EU, is in the comparison as Greece’s nearest competitor; all its visitors in the survey come from abroad.


Code
# the value for the visitors to a country from the other EU countries: all EU residents, minus its
# own residents on holiday at home (Türkiye has none in the survey)
from_abroad <- function(x, country, year) {
  everyone <- x$values[x$geo == "EU27_2020" & x$c_dest == country & x$time == year]
  at_home <- if (country == "TR") 0 else x$values[x$geo == country & x$c_dest == "DOM" & x$time == year]
  if (length(everyone) != 1 || length(at_home) != 1) return(NA)
  everyone - at_home
}
spending <- function(year) {
  x <- data.frame(geo = destinations, name = eu_name[destinations])
  for (p in c("TOTXDUR", "TRA", "ACCOM")) x[[p]] <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(spent[spent$expend == p, ], d, year))
  x$OTHER <- x$TOTXDUR - x$TRA - x$ACCOM
  x$trips <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(trips, d, year))
  x$nights <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(trip_nights, d, year))
  x$per_trip <- x$TOTXDUR / x$trips
  x$per_night <- x$per_trip * x$trips / x$nights
  x$length <- x$nights / x$trips
  x[!is.na(x$per_trip), ]
}
survey_year <- max(trips$time[trips$geo == "EU27_2020" & trips$c_dest == "EL"])
costs <- spending(survey_year)
cost <- function(geo, column = "per_trip") costs[[column]][costs$geo == geo]
part_cost <- function(geo, part) cost(geo, part) / cost(geo, "trips")
by_trip <- costs$geo[order(-costs$per_trip)]
by_night <- costs$geo[order(-costs$per_night)]
by_length <- costs$geo[order(-costs$length)]
# the countries ahead of Greece in a ranking
before_greece <- function(ranking) ranking[seq_len(match("EL", ranking) - 1)]


A holiday in Greece costs its visitors €1,256, the third highest of the 11 holiday countries in the chart.
In 2025, visitors from the other EU countries spent €1,256 on a holiday trip to Greece, against €1,152 in Spain, €970 in Italy and €888 in Croatia; only Cyprus and Türkiye cost more. The money includes the journey: €379 of it went on getting there and around, mostly on the flights; €436 on accommodation; and €441 on food, drinks and everything else.


Code
costs <- costs[order(costs$per_trip), ]
labels <- ifelse(costs$geo == "EL", "<b>Greece</b>", costs$name)
y <- factor(labels, levels = labels)
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in seq_along(parts)) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    y = y, x = costs[[names(parts)[k]]] / costs$trips, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = parts[[k]],
    marker = list(color = stack_colors[k], line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: €%{x:,.0f}<extra>", parts[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart(paste0("What a holiday trip costs, ", survey_year, ", euros"),
  "Eurostat, tour_dem_extotw and tour_dem_ttw: visitors from the other EU countries; own calculation",
  x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(costs$per_trip))),
  barmode = "stack", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "normal"), margin = list(l = 110, t = 100, b = 90),
  annotations = lapply(seq_len(nrow(costs)), function(k) {
    list(x = costs$per_trip[k], y = labels[k], text = euros(costs$per_trip[k]), xanchor = "left", xshift = 4,
      showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))
  }))






Per night, too, Greece is among the dearest. Visitors stay long in Greece, 8.6 nights a trip (only in Türkiye and Spain do they stay longer), so the cost of the flight is spread over more nights. A night of holiday in Greece costs them €145, the third highest of the 11: Cyprus (€173) and Malta (€163) cost more.


Code
ranking_bars(costs, "per_night", "EL", function(x) {
  paste0(x$name, ": ", euros(x$per_night), " a night, ", one(x$length), " nights a trip")
}) %>%
  chart(paste0("What a night of holiday costs, ", survey_year, ", euros"),
    "Eurostat, tour_dem_extotw and tour_dem_tnw: visitors from the other EU countries; own calculation",
    margin = list(l = 110, t = 70, b = 90))








Code
trip_cost <- function(year) {
  x <- spending(year)
  x$per_trip[x$geo == "EL"]
}
price_year <- min(survey_year, max(prices$time))
price_change <- function(geo) 100 * (prices$values[prices$geo == geo & prices$time == price_year] / prices$values[prices$geo == geo & prices$time == 2019] - 1)
cost_change <- 100 * (trip_cost(survey_year) / trip_cost(2019) - 1)
real_change <- c(100 * ((1 + cost_change / 100) / (1 + price_change("EL") / 100) - 1),
                 100 * ((1 + cost_change / 100) / (1 + price_change("EU27_2020") / 100) - 1))
# within 5% of 2019 after inflation, by the prices of Greece and of the EU, is "about the same"
real_spending <- if (all(abs(real_change) < 5)) "about the same" else if (all(real_change > 0)) "more" else if (all(real_change < 0)) "less" else "about the same"


More visitors, not richer ones. In 2019, a holiday trip to Greece cost visitors from the other EU countries €1,025; in 2025, €1,256, 23% more. Consumer prices rose by 20% in Greece and by 26% in the EU over the same years, so after inflation each visitor spends about what they spent in 2019: what has grown is the number of visitors. The survey asks a sample of people, so the figure of a single year can jump: it is the change over several years that counts.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
section: 6. How much does Greece depend on them?
text:
6. How much does Greece depend on them?


Code
both <- merge(receipts[c("geo", "time", "values")], gdp[c("geo", "time", "values")], by = c("geo", "time"), suffixes = c("_receipts", "_gdp"))
both$share <- 100 * both$values_receipts / both$values_gdp
receipts_year <- max(both$time[both$geo == "EL"])
share_of <- function(geo, year = receipts_year) both$share[both$geo == geo & both$time == year]
earned <- function(geo, year = receipts_year) both$values_receipts[both$geo == geo & both$time == year]
dependence <- both[both$time == receipts_year, ]
dependence$name <- eu_name[dependence$geo]
by_share <- dependence$geo[order(-dependence$share)]
ahead_of_greece <- by_share[seq_len(match("EL", by_share) - 1)]


€23.6 billion in 2025, 9.5% of GDP. That is what visitors from abroad spent in Greece, on hotels, meals, transport and shopping, without the flights to get there. Of the countries in the chart, only Croatia (16.3%), Malta (12.1%) and Cyprus (10.9%) depend more on them; in Spain they spent 6.2% of GDP, in Italy 2.5%. The figure counts only what foreigners spend: the holidays of Greeks at home, and the farms, builders and shops that sell to hotels, add to what the economy owes to tourism.


Code
ranking_bars(dependence, "share", "EL", function(x) paste0(x$name, ": ", percent(x$share, 1), " of GDP, ", billion_euros(x$values_receipts))) %>%
  chart(paste0("What visitors from abroad spend, ", receipts_year, ", % of GDP"),
    "Eurostat, bop_its6_det (travel, credit) and nama_10_gdp", margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)






What a country depends on, it can lose. In 2020 visitors from abroad spent €4.3 billion in Greece, 2.6% of GDP, against €18.2 billion in 2019.


Code
greek <- both[both$geo == "EL", ]
plot_ly(greek,
  x = ~time, y = ~share, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 8),
  hovertext = paste0(greek$time, ": ", percent(greek$share, 1), " of GDP, ", billion_euros(greek$values_receipts)),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("What visitors from abroad spend in Greece, % of GDP", "Eurostat, bop_its6_det (travel, credit) and nama_10_gdp",
    "% of GDP", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"))

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
7. Where do they stay?


Code
compare_year <- min(platform_year, year_now)
platform_growth <- 100 * (on_platforms("EL", compare_year) / on_platforms("EL", 2019) - 1)
registered_growth <- 100 * (nights(compare_year) / nights(2019) - 1)
platforms_grew_more <- on_platforms("EL", compare_year) - on_platforms("EL", 2019) > nights(compare_year) - nights(2019)
stay_year <- min(platform_year, region_year)
stays <- regional[regional$time == stay_year & regional$month == "TOTAL" & regional$unit == "NR" & regional$c_resid == "TOTAL", ]
by_region$registered <- stays$values[match(by_region$geo, stays$geo)]
by_region$platforms <- sapply(by_region$geo, on_platforms, year = stay_year)
by_region$per_100 <- 100 * by_region$platforms / by_region$registered
platforms_per_100 <- function(geo) by_region$per_100[by_region$geo == geo]
more_than_attica <- by_region$name[by_region$per_100 > platforms_per_100("EL30")]


More and more of them in flats let through Airbnb and the like. In 2025, guests spent 52.1 million nights in places booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia or Tripadvisor, 115% more than in 2019. The nights in hotels, rented rooms and campsites grew by 9% in the same years. Some places are listed on the platforms and also counted as tourist accommodation, so the two cannot simply be added; but the platforms gained 27.8 million nights since 2019, the tourist accommodation 12.8 million: most of the growth has gone to the platforms.


Code
since <- min(platforms$time)
registered <- data.frame(time = since:year_now)
registered$values <- sapply(registered$time, nights)
greek_platforms <- platforms[platforms$geo == "EL", ]
plot_ly(registered,
  x = ~time, y = ~ values / 1e6, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Hotels, rented rooms and campsites",
  line = list(color = blue, width = 3), marker = list(color = blue, size = 8),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>Tourist accommodation</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = greek_platforms, x = ~time, y = ~ values / 1e6, name = "Booked through the platforms",
    line = list(color = amber, width = 3), marker = list(color = amber, size = 8),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>Platforms</extra>", inherit = FALSE,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers") %>%
  chart("Nights in Greece, million", "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninat and tour_ce_omn12 (Airbnb, Booking, Expedia, Tripadvisor)",
    "Million", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)






In Athens, 81 nights on the platforms for every 100 in tourist accommodation. That is what Attica had in 2025, more than any other region; the South Aegean had 22 and Crete 25. Many of the flats let to visitors in Athens were once let to people who live there, which is one reason given for the rise of rents in the city; the story of Greek housing follows rents and house prices against incomes.


Code
x <- by_region[order(by_region$registered), ]
y <- factor(x$name, levels = x$name)
plot_ly(
  y = y, x = x$registered / 1e6, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = "Hotels, rented rooms and campsites",
  marker = list(color = blue), hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} million nights<extra>Tourist accommodation</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(y = y, x = x$platforms / 1e6, name = "Booked through the platforms", marker = list(color = amber),
    hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} million nights<extra>Platforms</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights by region, ", stay_year, ", million"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m and tour_ce_omn12",
    barmode = "group", legend = legend_top, margin = list(l = 200, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.12)

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
So, what does it mean?
Tourism is one of the pillars of the Greek economy, and one of its risks. Visitors from abroad spend 9.5% of GDP in Greece, and they spend it:

In the summer: 72% of the nights fall from June to September. Greece has grown its summers, not its winters, so jobs and incomes in tourism remain seasonal.
On the islands: 62% of the nights are spent in the South Aegean, Crete and the Ionian Islands, where there are 128 nights for each inhabitant of the South Aegean every year, with what that means for water, roads and housing in August.
On long trips: a holiday in Greece costs its visitors from the rest of the EU €1,256, the third highest of the 11 holiday countries in the chart, and a night €145, the third highest. After inflation, each visitor spends about as much as before COVID: the growth comes from more visitors.
Through the platforms: since 2019, nights booked through Airbnb and the like grew by 115%, the registered tourist accommodation by 9%.

2020 showed the risk: when the visitors could not come, 73% of the nights were lost in one year. Longer seasons, more regions and more visitors from outside Europe would spread it.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
Sources

Eurostat, tourist accommodation: tour_occ_ninat (nights per year), tour_occ_nim (nights per month), tour_occ_nin2m (nights by month and region), tour_occ_ninraw (nights by the country of the guests), tour_ce_omn12 (short-stay accommodation booked through online platforms).
Eurostat, trips of EU residents: tour_dem_extotw (expenditure per trip by destination), tour_dem_ttw (trips by destination), tour_dem_tnw (nights by destination).
Eurostat, economy: bop_its6_det (international trade in services: travel), nama_10_gdp (GDP), prc_hicp_aind (consumer prices).

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
text:
Is Greece a good place to invest? The answer depends on the investor, whether they buy Greek bonds, build a factory or open a business, but some questions matter to all of them, and each can be measured in the same way for every EU country:

Do investors invest in Greece? What the economy invests, and what comes from abroad.
Is the country a financial risk? The interest rate on its bonds, and its debt.
What does it cost to produce there? Wages and electricity.
How well does the state work? Bureaucracy, regulation, the rule of law and corruption.
Do the courts protect investors? How long a case takes, and what companies think.
Can goods move? Ports, roads and customs.

The data come from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU, and from the World Bank, and are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures. Two sets of figures come from the European Commission’s 2026 EU Justice Scoreboard, a report, and are typed in below with the figure they come from. The charts of countries show the 27 EU countries, with Greece in red and the EU as a whole, where there is a figure for it, in blue.
Rankings of countries are a starting point, not a verdict: an investor in a Greek hotel and an investor in a Greek factory face different costs and different risks.

The data


Code
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
eu_codes <- eu_countries$code

# a World Bank indicator for the EU countries, with Eurostat's country codes (EL for Greece)
iso3 <- c(BE = "BEL", BG = "BGR", CZ = "CZE", DK = "DNK", DE = "DEU", EE = "EST", IE = "IRL", EL = "GRC",
          ES = "ESP", FR = "FRA", HR = "HRV", IT = "ITA", CY = "CYP", LV = "LVA", LT = "LTU", LU = "LUX",
          HU = "HUN", MT = "MLT", NL = "NLD", AT = "AUT", PL = "POL", PT = "PRT", RO = "ROU", SI = "SVN",
          SK = "SVK", FI = "FIN", SE = "SWE")
world_bank <- function(indicator, years = "2000:2025") {
  url <- paste0("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/", paste(iso3, collapse = ";"), "/indicator/", indicator,
                "?format=json&per_page=5000&date=", years)
  x <- jsonlite::fromJSON(url)[[2]]
  x <- data.frame(geo = names(iso3)[match(x$countryiso3code, iso3)], time = as.numeric(x$date), values = x$value)
  x[!is.na(x$values), ]
}

# investment: gross fixed capital formation (buildings, machines, equipment, software), % of GDP
investment_all <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(na_item = "P51G", unit = "PC_GDP"))

# labour cost per hour, euro, in the business economy
labour_all <- eurostat_values("lc_lci_lev", list(lcstruct = "D1_D4_MD5", nace_r2 = "B-S_X_O", unit = "EUR"))
# electricity for businesses using 2 to 20 GWh a year, euro per kWh without VAT, every six months
electricity_all <- eurostat_values("nrg_pc_205", list(nrg_cons = "MWH2000-19999", tax = "X_VAT", currency = "EUR", unit = "KWH"))
# renewable energy, % of the energy used
renewables_all <- eurostat_values("nrg_ind_ren", list(nrg_bal = "REN", unit = "PC"))
# World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators, from about -2.5 (worst) to +2.5 (best)

                      GOV_WGI_RL.EST = "Rule of law", GOV_WGI_CC.EST = "Control of corruption")

court_days <- c(EL = 740, CY = 680, IT = 590)




Code
# the EU countries and the EU in the latest year with data for Greece and for most EU countries
latest <- function(x, at_least = 20) {
  x <- x[x$geo %in% c(eu_codes, "EU27_2020"), ]
  for (y in sort(unique(x$time[x$geo == "EL"]), decreasing = TRUE)) {
    if (sum(x$geo %in% eu_codes & x$time == y) >= at_least) return(x[x$time == y, ])
  }
  stop("No year with data for Greece and for most EU countries")
}
greece <- function(x) x$values[x$geo == "EL"]
median_eu <- function(x) median(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])
# the EU: its own figure where there is one, otherwise the median of the countries
eu <- function(x) if (any(x$geo == "EU27_2020")) x$values[x$geo == "EU27_2020"] else median_eu(x)
countries <- function(x) sum(x$geo %in% eu_codes)
ordinal <- function(k) {
  paste0(k, if (k %% 100 %in% 11:13) "th" else c("th", "st", "nd", "rd", rep("th", 6))[k %% 10 + 1])
}
# the place of Greece among the EU countries, counted from the nearer end: "the highest",
# "the 3rd highest", "the 2nd lowest", ...
place <- function(x) {
  v <- x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes]
  from_top <- sum(v > greece(x)) + 1
  from_bottom <- sum(v < greece(x)) + 1
  k <- min(from_top, from_bottom)
  end <- if (from_top <= from_bottom) "highest" else "lowest"
  paste("the", if (k == 1) end else paste(ordinal(k), end))
}
# one series of a dataset, for Greece or the EU
series <- function(x, geo) x[x$geo == geo, c("time", "values")]

Code
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = modifyList(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = modifyList(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")

# the EU countries from the highest to the lowest, Greece in red and the EU in blue; where there is
# no figure for the EU, a dotted line marks the median country
ranking <- function(x, title, source, suffix = "%", digits = 1) {
  x <- x[x$geo %in% c(eu_codes, "EU27_2020"), ]
  x$name <- eu_name[x$geo]
  x <- x[order(x$values), ]
  x$name <- factor(x$name, levels = x$name)
  lines <- list()
  notes <- list()
  if (!any(x$geo == "EU27_2020")) {
    m <- median(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])
    lines <- list(list(type = "line", x0 = m, x1 = m, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper", line = list(color = blue, width = 2, dash = "dot")))
    notes <- list(list(x = m, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "Median EU country", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
                       xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = blue)))
  }
  # the source 45 px under the plot, below the numbers of the axis
  height <- knitr::opts_current$get("out.height.px")
  if (!is.numeric(height)) height <- 864
  plot_ly(x,
    x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = ifelse(x$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(x$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: %{x:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra></extra>")
  ) %>%
    chart(paste0(title, ", ", floor(x$time[1])), source, x_axis = list(ticksuffix = suffix), shapes = lines,
          annotations = notes, margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -45 / (height - 70 - 90))
}

# Greece and a second line (the EU, or another country) over time
two_lines <- function(a, b, name_b, title, source, y_title, suffix = "%", digits = 1, y_axis = list(), ...) {
  plot_ly(a, x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Greece",
    line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra>Greece</extra>")) %>%
    add_trace(data = b, x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = name_b,
      line = list(color = blue, width = 3), inherit = FALSE,
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra>", name_b, "</extra>")) %>%
    chart(title, source, y_title, y_axis = modifyList(list(ticksuffix = suffix), y_axis), legend = legend_top, ...)
}

# short labels of numbers
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
text:
1. Do investors invest in Greece?


Code
investment_line <- series(investment_all, "EL")
peak_year <- investment_line$time[which.max(investment_line$values)]
low_year <- investment_line$time[which.min(investment_line$values)]


Less than in almost all the EU, though more than at the bottom of the crisis. In 2025, Greece invested 18.0% of its GDP in buildings, machines, equipment and software, against 21.5% in the EU: the 3rd lowest share of the 27 countries. Before the crisis it invested more than the EU, 25.9% of GDP in 2000; by 2019 it had fallen to 11.0%. An economy that invests less than it did, and less than its neighbours, adds little to what it can produce.


Code
two_lines(investment_line, series(investment_all, "EU27_2020"), "EU-27",
          "Investment, % of GDP", "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp (gross fixed capital formation)", "% of GDP",
          y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"))








Code
fdi_median <- aggregate(values ~ time, fdi_all[fdi_all$geo %in% eu_codes, ], median)
fdi_years <- fdi_median$time[fdi_median$time >= max(fdi_median$time) - 4]
fdi_recent <- mean(at(fdi_all, "EL", fdi_years))
fdi_recent_eu <- mean(fdi_median$values[fdi_median$time %in% fdi_years])
fdi_before <- series(fdi_all, "EL")
fdi_before <- fdi_before[fdi_before$time < min(fdi_years), ]


Foreign investors have come back. Foreign direct investment, money from abroad that buys or builds a lasting share in Greek companies, averaged 3.0% of GDP a year in 2021-2025, against 3.0% in the median EU country; in 2000-2020 it had averaged 1.0%. The chart compares Greece with the median EU country, because the figures of a few countries, such as Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Ireland, swing by tens of percent of GDP with money that only passes through them.


Code
two_lines(series(fdi_all, "EL"), fdi_median, "Median EU country",
          "Foreign direct investment, net inflows, % of GDP", "World Bank, BX.KLT.DINV.WD.GD.ZS", "% of GDP")

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
section: 2. Is the country a financial risk?
text:
2. Is the country a financial risk?


Code
# since 2001, when Greece joined the euro: before, its bonds were in drachmas
greek_yields <- series(yields_all[yields_all$time >= 2001, ], "EL")
german_yields <- series(yields_all[yields_all$time >= 2001, ], "DE")
spread <- merge(greek_yields, german_yields, by = "time", suffixes = c("_el", "_de"))
spread$values <- spread$values_el - spread$values_de
worst <- spread[which.max(spread$values), ]
now <- spread[nrow(spread), ]
debt_line <- series(debt_all, "EL")
debt_peak <- debt_line[which.max(debt_line$values), ]


The markets no longer see Greece as a high risk, but its debt is the highest in the EU.
The interest rate that a country pays on its bonds is what the markets think of its risk. In 2012, in the debt crisis, Greece’s 10-year bonds paid 22.5% a year, 21.0 points more than Germany’s. In 2025 they paid 3.4%, only 0.8 points more than Germany’s and no more than the EU average of 3.4%. The credit rating agencies agree. They cut Greece to junk in the crisis, but S&P, Fitch, DBRS and Scope have rated it investment grade again since 2023, and Moody’s since 2025, so the large funds that may hold only such bonds can buy Greek debt again.


Code
two_lines(greek_yields, german_yields, "Germany",
          "Yield of 10-year government bonds, % a year", "Eurostat, irt_lt_mcby_a", "% a year",
          y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"))






The debt that worried the markets is still there: 145.4% of GDP in 2025, the highest in the EU, where it is 81.5%, though down from 209.4% in 2020. Much of it is owed to other euro countries on long terms and low interest rates, which is why the markets accept it. The economy grew by 2.1% in 2025, against 1.4% in the EU.


Code
two_lines(debt_line, series(debt_all, "EU27_2020"), "EU-27",
          "Government debt, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "% of GDP",
          y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"))

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
section: 3. What does it cost to produce there?
text:
3. What does it cost to produce there?
Cheap labour, electricity at about the EU’s price.
An hour of work cost employers in Greece €18.2 in 2025, wages and the employers’ contributions together, against €34.9 in the EU: the 6th lowest of 26 countries. Labour is cheap partly because it produces little: an hour of work in Greece produces about half of what it produces on average in the EU (see Greece at Work).


Code
ranking(labour, "Labour cost per hour, euro", "Eurostat, lc_lci_lev (business economy)", suffix = "", digits = 1)








Code
half <- function(t) paste0(if (t %% 1 == 0) "first" else "second", " half of ", floor(t))
greek_power <- series(electricity_all, "EL")
eu_power <- series(electricity_all, "EU27_2020")
power_peak <- greek_power[which.max(greek_power$values), ]


Electricity matters most for factories, data centres and cold storage. In the first half of 2026, a business that uses 2 to 20 GWh a year, a medium-sized factory, paid 16.0 cents per kWh in Greece before VAT, against 15.6 cents in the EU: the 11th highest of 27 countries. In the energy crisis the price rose to 22.9 cents, in the second half of 2022. Renewables, which keep the price of electricity from following the price of gas, gave 26.9% of the energy used in Greece in 2025, against 26.2% in the EU.


Code
power <- function(x) transform(x, values = 100 * values)
two_lines(power(greek_power[greek_power$time >= 2015, ]), power(eu_power[eu_power$time >= 2015, ]), "EU-27",
          "Electricity for medium-sized businesses, cents per kWh, without VAT",
          "Eurostat, nrg_pc_205 (2 to 20 GWh a year, every six months)", "Cents per kWh", suffix = "", digits = 1,
          y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"))

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
section: 4. How well does the state work?
text:
4. How well does the state work?


Code
gov_table <- data.frame(
  indicator = factor(governance_names, levels = rev(governance_names)),
  greece = sapply(governance, greece),
  median = sapply(governance, median_eu),
  low = sapply(governance, function(x) min(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])),
  high = sapply(governance, function(x) max(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])),
  place = sapply(governance, place),
  year = sapply(governance, function(x) x$time[1])
)
g <- function(name, column) gov_table[[column]][gov_table$indicator == name]


Bureaucracy and law and order: in the bottom third of the EU. The World Bank combines surveys of companies, households and experts into four measures of how well the state works: how good the public administration is (government effectiveness), how well regulation lets private business work (regulatory quality), how far contracts, property rights, the police and the courts can be relied on (rule of law), and how little public power is used for private gain (control of corruption). Each runs from about -2.5 to +2.5. In 2025, Greece had the 2nd lowest score of the EU for government effectiveness, the 6th lowest for regulatory quality, the 3rd lowest for the rule of law and the 7th lowest for control of corruption. All four are better than those of most countries in the world, but they are below the EU’s middle.


Code
plot_ly(gov_table) %>%
  add_segments(x = ~low, xend = ~high, y = ~indicator, yend = ~indicator, name = "EU countries, lowest to highest",
               line = list(color = "#d9d9d9", width = 10), hoverinfo = "skip") %>%
  add_markers(x = ~median, y = ~indicator, name = "Median EU country", marker = list(color = blue, size = 13, symbol = "line-ns-open", line = list(width = 3, color = blue)),
              hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.2f}<extra>Median EU country</extra>") %>%
  add_markers(x = ~greece, y = ~indicator, name = "Greece", marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 13),
              hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.2f}<extra>Greece</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Worldwide Governance Indicators, ", gov_table$year[1], " (-2.5 worst, +2.5 best)"),
        "World Bank, Worldwide Governance Indicators", legend = legend_top, margin = list(l = 170, t = 90, b = 90))

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
text:
5. Do the courts protect investors?
Greek courts are the slowest in the EU, and Greek companies trust them the least.
An investor needs to know that a contract will be enforced. In 2024, a civil or commercial dispute took about 740 days to be resolved at first instance in Greece, more than two years before any appeal: the longest of the EU countries with data. Cyprus and Italy, the next slowest, needed about 680 and 590 days, and most EU countries fewer than 300 (2026 EU Justice Scoreboard, Figure 5, from the CEPEJ study of the Council of Europe).


Code
unconfident <- function(code) {
  row <- protection[protection$geo == code, ]
  row$fairly_unconfident + row$very_unconfident
}


Companies see it. Asked in 2026 how well the law and the courts protect their investments, 25% of Greek companies said that they were confident, the lowest share in the EU, where it is 56% in the median country; 70% were not confident, and 36% very unconfident, more than in any other country.


Code
ranking(protection, "Companies confident that the law and courts protect their investments, %",
        "European Commission, 2026 EU Justice Scoreboard, Figure 52 (Eurobarometer)", digits = 0)

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
text:
6. Can goods move?
Ports, roads and customs: close to the EU’s middle. The World Bank’s Logistics Performance Index scores, from 1 to 5, how well a country’s customs, ports, roads and railways, shipping and tracking work, from a survey of the companies that move goods. In 2022, Greece scored 3.70, against 3.60 in the median EU country: the 10th highest of 27 countries. Its ports, Piraeus first among them, are among the busiest of the Mediterranean.


Code
ranking(logistics, "Logistics Performance Index (1 worst, 5 best)", "World Bank, LP.LPI.OVRL.XQ", suffix = "", digits = 2)

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts
section: So, is Greece a good place to invest?
text:
So, is Greece a good place to invest?
It depends on what an investor needs, and the data show which needs Greece meets:

Financial risk is low again: the bonds pay about what the EU’s pay, and the rating agencies call them investment grade, though the debt, 145% of GDP, is the EU’s highest.
Costs are low: labour costs €18.2 an hour against €34.9 in the EU, and electricity is at about the EU’s price.
Investors are coming back, but not enough: foreign investment has risen, yet the economy invests 18% of its GDP, the 3rd lowest share in the EU.
The state is the weak point: the public administration, regulation, the rule of law and the control of corruption are all in the bottom part of the EU.
And the courts most of all: about 740 days for a first judgment, the longest in the EU, and 25% of Greek companies confident that the law protects their investments, the lowest share.

For an investor who needs cheap labour and a growing market, and seldom goes to court, Greece has become a reasonable bet. For one whose investment depends on contracts and permits, the slow courts and the bureaucracy are the risk to price in.

title: Is Greece a Good Place to Invest? Risk, Costs, the State and the Courts

Sources

Eurostat: nama_10_gdp (investment), irt_lt_mcby_a (government bond yields), gov_10dd_edpt1 (government debt), tec00115 (GDP growth), lc_lci_lev (labour cost), nrg_pc_205 (electricity prices for non-household consumers), nrg_ind_ren (renewable energy).
World Bank: foreign direct investment, net inflows, Worldwide Governance Indicators, Logistics Performance Index.
