title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
From 2010 until August 2018, Greece lived on rescue loans, through three programmes (ESM). In those years many people left the country. This story asks five questions about them:

How many people left Greece, and when?
Who left? Their age and sex, and whether they were Greek citizens or foreigners.
Where did they go?
Did they come back?
Was it a brain drain? Did those who left have more education than those who stayed?

Fewer and Older shows how births, deaths and migration change the size and the age of Greece’s population. This story follows the people who left.
The data come from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU, and are downloaded when the page is rendered:

Greece’s figures on the people who leave the country and those who arrive, each year, from ELSTAT, the Hellenic Statistical Authority: by age and sex (migr_emi2), by citizenship (migr_emi1ctz, migr_imm1ctz), by country of birth (migr_imm3ctb) and by where they went (migr_emi5nxt); with the population (demo_pjan) and unemployment (une_rt_a).
The figures of the countries they moved to: the Greek citizens who arrive in each European country and those who leave it (migr_imm1ctz, migr_emi1ctz), and those who live there (migr_pop1ctz).
The Labour Force Survey, a survey of households in the countries of the EU and EFTA, which asks people where they were born and what education they have (lfst_lmbpcobed, edat_lfs_9912).

Most of these figures are estimates. In the statistics of the EU, an emigrant is someone who moves abroad for at least 12 months (Eurostat). Greece does not count them: nobody has to tell the authorities that they are leaving, so ELSTAT calls its data on emigration “essentially non-existent” and estimates it instead. For 2011 to 2021, emigration is the number of people who must have left for the population, as revised after the census of 2021, to add up with the births, the deaths and the people who arrived. Since 2022, it is worked out from the number of people that Germany counts arriving from Greece (ELSTAT). The countries the emigrants go to count the people who arrive, but not all in the same way: Norway, for example, counts as migrants the people who move for six months (Eurostat).

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
The data


Code
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
# the years that Eurostat flags as a break in one series (flag b); the eurostat package leaves the
# flags out when it filters, so they come from Eurostat's own API, in JSON-stat
breaks_in <- function(id, filters) {
  api <- "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/"
  query <- paste(paste0(names(filters), "=", unlist(filters)), collapse = "&")
  x <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(api, id, "?", query))
  years <- names(sort(unlist(x$dimension$time$category$index)))
  flags <- unlist(x$status)
  as.numeric(years[as.integer(names(flags)[flags == "b"]) + 1])
}
# all ages, both sexes, age in completed years, numbers of people
everyone <- list(age = "TOTAL", sex = "T", agedef = "COMPLET", unit = "NR")

# Greece: the people who left each year, by sex and single year of age, and the breaks in the series
emigration <- eurostat_values("migr_emi2", list(geo = "EL", agedef = "COMPLET", unit = "NR"))
breaks <- breaks_in("migr_emi2", c(list(geo = "EL"), everyone))
# Greece: everyone (TOTAL) and the Greek citizens (NAT) among the people who left and among those
# who arrived; the people who arrived who were born in Greece (NAT); and the people who left, by
# group of country of next residence: another EU country, or a country outside the EU
left <- eurostat_values("migr_emi1ctz", c(list(geo = "EL", citizen = c("NAT", "TOTAL")), everyone))
came <- eurostat_values("migr_imm1ctz", c(list(geo = "EL", citizen = c("NAT", "TOTAL")), everyone))
came_born <- eurostat_values("migr_imm3ctb", c(list(geo = "EL", c_birth = "NAT"), everyone))
next_residence <- eurostat_values("migr_emi5nxt", list(geo = "EL", unit = "NR"))

# every country that reports them, but not Greece itself or the EU as a whole: the Greek citizens
# (EL) who arrived there each year, those who left, and those who lived there on 1 January
abroad <- function(x) x[!x$geo %in% c("EL", "EU27_2020"), ]
greeks_came <- abroad(eurostat_values("migr_imm1ctz", c(list(citizen = "EL"), everyone)))
greeks_left <- abroad(eurostat_values("migr_emi1ctz", c(list(citizen = "EL"), everyone)))
greeks_living <- abroad(eurostat_values(
  "migr_pop1ctz",
  list(citizen = "EL", age = "TOTAL", sex = "T", unit = "NR")
))

# Greece: the population on 1 January, by sex and single year of age, and unemployment, % of the
# labour force aged 15 to 74
population <- eurostat_values("demo_pjan", list(geo = "EL", sex = c("T", "M", "F"), unit = "NR"))
unemployment <- eurostat_values(
  "une_rt_a",
  list(geo = "EL", age = "Y15-74", sex = "T", unit = "PC_ACT")
)

# Labour Force Survey: the people born in Greece who live in another EU or EFTA country, by age
# group and education, thousands; and those who live in Greece, aged 15 to 64, by education, %
born_abroad <- eurostat_values("lfst_lmbpcobed", list(c_birth = "EL", c_resid = "EU27_2020_EFTA"))
born_home <- eurostat_values(
  "edat_lfs_9912",
  list(geo = "EL", c_birth = "NAT", sex = "T", age = "Y15-64")
)

# the names of the countries of the EU and EFTA, and of the United Kingdom
country_name <- c(
  setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code),
  setNames(efta_countries$name, efta_countries$code),
  UK = "United Kingdom"
)




Code
# one series of a dataset, in the order of the years
by_year <- function(x, years) x$values[match(years, x$time)]

# Greece, year by year: the people who left, all of them and the Greek citizens; the people who
# arrived, all of them, the Greek citizens and those born in Greece; and the population
total_left <- emigration[emigration$age == "TOTAL" & emigration$sex == "T", ]
flows <- data.frame(year = total_left$time, left = total_left$values)
flows$left_greek <- by_year(left[left$citizen == "NAT", ], flows$year)
flows$came <- by_year(came[came$citizen == "TOTAL", ], flows$year)
flows$came_greek <- by_year(came[came$citizen == "NAT", ], flows$year)
flows$came_born <- by_year(came_born, flows$year)
flows$net_greek <- flows$came_greek - flows$left_greek
everyone_living <- population[population$age == "TOTAL" & population$sex == "T", ]
flows$population <- by_year(everyone_living, flows$year)
latest <- max(flows$year)
flow <- function(column, year) flows[[column]][match(year, flows$year)]

# the years of the rescue loans: the first programme started in 2010, and the third and last ended
# in August 2018 (ESM)
rescue <- c(2010, 2018)
rescue_years <- rescue[1]:rescue[2]




Code
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
orange <- "#ff7f0e"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
light_gray <- "#ebebeb"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the color of the notes

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the years of the rescue loans, shaded behind the data
rescue_band <- list(
  type = "rect",
  xref = "x",
  yref = "paper",
  x0 = rescue[1] - 0.5,
  x1 = rescue[2] + 0.5,
  y0 = 0,
  y1 = 1,
  fillcolor = light_gray,
  line = list(width = 0),
  layer = "below"
)
shaded <- paste0("Shaded: the rescue loans, ", rescue[1], "–", rescue[2], ".")

# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
thousands <- function(x) format(round(x, -3), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# years as ranges: 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2019 give "2014–2016, 2019"
years_text <- function(years) {
  years <- sort(unique(years))
  starts <- years[c(TRUE, diff(years) > 1)]
  ends <- years[c(diff(years) > 1, TRUE)]
  paste(ifelse(starts == ends, starts, paste0(starts, "–", ends)), collapse = ", ")
}

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
section: 1. How many people left Greece, and when?
text:
1. How many people left Greece, and when?


Code
in_2000s <- flows$left[flows$year %in% 2000:2009]
peak_year <- flows$year[which.max(flows$left)]
per_1000 <- function(year) 1000 * flow("left", year) / flow("population", year)
left_rescue <- sum(flows$left[flows$year %in% rescue_years])
left_greek_rescue <- sum(flows$left_greek[flows$year %in% rescue_years])
over_100k <- flows$year[flows$left > 1e5]
# the last year in which more people left than the year before: the fall since goes on to the
# latest year
rose <- flows$year[c(FALSE, diff(flows$left) >= 0)]
falling_since <- max(rose)
jobless <- function(year) unemployment$values[unemployment$time == year]
jobless_peak <- unemployment$time[which.max(unemployment$values)]
jobless_latest <- max(unemployment$time)


About 41,000 a year in the 2000s; more than 100,000 a year in 2011–2019.
From 2000 to 2009, between 37,433 and 46,993 people left Greece each year. Then came the crisis: 62,041 left in 2010, 106,398 in 2011 and 135,073 in 2012, the most since the figures start in 1991: 12.2 of every 1,000 people who lived in Greece. In the years of the rescue loans, from 2010 to 2018, 1,018,000 people left, 527,000 of them Greek citizens.
The number has fallen every year since 2018, to 78,014 in 2024, 1.9 times the average of the 2000s. It rose with unemployment, which went from 9.8% of the labour force in 2009 to 27.8% in 2013; both have fallen since, unemployment to 8.9% in 2025 (Eurostat, une_rt_a).


Code
bars <- flows[!is.na(flows$left), ]
rescue_label <- list(
  x = mean(rescue),
  y = 1,
  xref = "x",
  yref = "paper",
  yanchor = "bottom",
  text = paste0("Rescue loans, ", rescue[1], "–", rescue[2]),
  showarrow = FALSE,
  font = list(size = 12, color = dark_gray)
)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~year,
  y = ~ left / 1000,
  type = "bar",
  name = "People who left",
  marker = list(
    color = greek_red,
    pattern = list(
      shape = ifelse(bars$year %in% breaks, "/", ""),
      fillmode = "overlay",
      fgcolor = "white"
    )
  ),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(
    "People who left Greece each year, thousands",
    "Eurostat, migr_emi2 (estimates of ELSTAT). Striped: a break in the series.",
    "Thousands",
    annotations = list(rescue_label),
    shapes = list(rescue_band),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )






Eurostat marks a break in the series in 2002, 2008 and 2010 (the striped bars): the method changed, so the years before and after a break cannot be compared closely.

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
2. Who left?


Code
# the age of a Eurostat age code: Y_LT1 is under one, Y_OPEN and Y_GE100 are the oldest, and the
# codes of totals, such as TOTAL, give NA
age_of <- function(code) {
  age <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^Y", "", code)))
  age[code == "Y_LT1"] <- 0
  age[code %in% c("Y_OPEN", "Y_GE100")] <- 100
  age
}
group_names <- c(
  "0–14",
  "15–19",
  "20–24",
  "25–29",
  "30–34",
  "35–39",
  "40–44",
  "45–49",
  "50–54",
  "55–59",
  "60–64",
  "65+"
)
age_group <- function(code) {
  cut(age_of(code), c(-1, 14, 19, 24, 29, 34, 39, 44, 49, 54, 59, 64, Inf), labels = group_names)
}
# the people who left out of every 1,000 of the same sex and age group who lived in Greece on
# 1 January
rates <- function(year, sex) {
  out <- emigration[emigration$time == year & emigration$sex == sex, ]
  living <- population[population$time == year & population$sex == sex, ]
  1000 *
    tapply(out$values, age_group(out$age), sum) /
    tapply(living$values, age_group(living$age), sum)
}
rate <- function(year, sex, group) rates(year, sex)[[group]]
# the age that half of the people are younger than or as old as
median_age <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(age_of(x$age)), ]
  x <- x[order(age_of(x$age)), ]
  age_of(x$age)[which(cumsum(x$values) >= sum(x$values) / 2)[1]]
}
men_left <- emigration[emigration$age == "TOTAL" & emigration$sex == "M", ]
men_share <- data.frame(
  year = men_left$time,
  share = round(100 * men_left$values / flow("left", men_left$time), 1)
)
# the longest run of years in which the share of men is the same
runs <- rle(men_share$share)
run_end <- cumsum(runs$lengths)[which.max(runs$lengths)]
same_years <- men_share$year[(run_end - max(runs$lengths) + 1):run_end]
middle_aged <- c("35–39", "40–44", "45–49", "50–54")
men_to_women <- rates(peak_year, "M")[middle_aged] / rates(peak_year, "F")[middle_aged]


Mostly people in their twenties and thirties, and in the worst years, mostly men.
In 2012, 65% of the people who left Greece were men. Half of them were 32 or younger, while half of the people who lived in Greece were 41 or older.
The chart counts the people who left out of every 1,000 of the same sex and age who lived in Greece at the start of the year. In 2012, 44 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29 left, and 28 of every 1,000 women. From 35 to 54, men left at 2.3 to 3.5 times the rate of women. In 2024, fewer left: 31 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29, and 34 of every 1,000 women.


Code
profile <- data.frame(group = factor(group_names, levels = group_names))
lines <- data.frame(
  year = c(peak_year, peak_year, latest, latest),
  sex = c("M", "F", "M", "F"),
  name = paste(c("Men,", "Women,", "Men,", "Women,"), c(peak_year, peak_year, latest, latest)),
  color = c(blue, orange, blue, orange),
  dash = c("solid", "solid", "dot", "dot")
)
p <- plot_ly(profile, x = ~group)
for (k in seq_len(nrow(lines))) {
  p <- add_trace(
    p,
    y = as.numeric(rates(lines$year[k], lines$sex[k])),
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = lines$name[k],
    line = list(color = lines$color[k], width = 3, dash = lines$dash[k]),
    marker = list(color = lines$color[k]),
    hovertemplate = paste0("Aged %{x}: %{y:.1f} per 1,000<extra>", lines$name[k], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>%
  chart(
    "People who left Greece, per 1,000 of their sex and age",
    "Eurostat, migr_emi2 and demo_pjan (estimates of ELSTAT).",
    "Per 1,000",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"),
    legend = legend_top,
    margin = list(t = 100, b = 90)
  )






These shares are estimates too. ELSTAT does not measure the age and sex of the people who leave: it spreads its estimate of the total with fixed proportions (ELSTAT). In every year from 2016 to 2020, for example, 56.7% of those who left were men. So the chart shows the broad picture, not the changes from one year to the next.

Greek citizens and foreigners


Code
citizens <- flows[!is.na(flows$left_greek), ]
citizens$left_foreign <- citizens$left - citizens$left_greek
greek_share <- function(year) 100 * flow("left_greek", year) / flow("left", year)
mostly_greek <- citizens$year[citizens$left_greek > citizens$left_foreign]
most_greek <- citizens$year[which.max(citizens$left_greek / citizens$left)]
foreign <- function(year) citizens$left_foreign[citizens$year == year]


In 2008, 44% of the people who left Greece were Greek citizens; the rest were foreigners who had lived in Greece. In 2011–2017, most of those who left were Greek citizens: 58% in 2011, and 70,696 people in 2012. Foreigners left in larger numbers too, 64,377 in 2012 against 23,956 in 2008. In 2024, 32,141 Greek citizens left, 41% of all who left.


Code
plot_ly(
  citizens,
  x = ~year,
  y = ~ left_greek / 1000,
  type = "bar",
  name = "Greek citizens",
  marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Greek citizens</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(
    y = ~ left_foreign / 1000,
    name = "Foreign citizens",
    marker = list(color = gray),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Foreign citizens</extra>"
  ) %>%
  chart(
    "People who left Greece, by citizenship, thousands",
    paste("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz (estimates of ELSTAT).", shaded),
    "Thousands",
    shapes = list(rescue_band),
    barmode = "stack",
    legend = legend_top
  )

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
3. Where did they go?


Code
next_year <- max(next_residence$time)
went <- function(partner) {
  next_residence$values[next_residence$partner == partner & next_residence$time == next_year]
}
to_eu <- went("EU27_2020_FOR")
outside <- went("NEU27_2020_FOR")
# the years with figures for Germany, the main destination, after the gap of the crisis years
since <- min(greeks_came$time[greeks_came$geo == "DE" & greeks_came$time > 2008])
window <- since:latest
counted <- greeks_came[greeks_came$time %in% window, ]
destinations <- aggregate(values ~ geo, counted, sum)
destinations <- destinations[order(-destinations$values), ]
left_window <- sum(flows$left_greek[flows$year %in% window])
counted_total <- sum(destinations$values)
not_counted <- left_window - counted_total
shown <- head(destinations, 10)
other <- counted_total - sum(shown$values)
# a country's name, with the years it has figures for when they are not all the years
label <- function(geo) {
  name <- if (geo %in% names(country_name)) country_name[[geo]] else geo
  years <- counted$time[counted$geo == geo]
  if (length(years) == length(window)) name else paste0(name, " (", years_text(years), ")")
}
shown$label <- sapply(shown$geo, label)
share_of_counted <- function(geo) 100 * shown$values[shown$geo == geo] / counted_total
# the countries of the EU and EFTA without figures on Greek citizens arriving in these years
silent <- setdiff(names(country_name), c(unique(counted$geo), "EL", "UK"))
uk_years <- counted$time[counted$geo == "UK"]
uk_rank <- function(year) {
  in_year <- counted[counted$time == year, ]
  sum(in_year$values > in_year$values[in_year$geo == "UK"]) + 1
}


Above all to Germany. But the countries they went to counted only 54% of them arriving.
Greece’s figures say only whether the people who left went to another EU country or outside the EU, not to which country: in 2024, 28,047 went to another EU country and 49,967 outside the EU, foreigners leaving Greece included (migr_emi5nxt).
So the chart looks from the other end, at the countries that count the people who arrive, by citizenship. It follows the 545,000 Greek citizens who left Greece from 2014 to 2024, the years with figures for Germany, to the countries that counted them arriving.


Code
# where they went, from top to bottom: not counted, the countries from the most, the others
went_to <- data.frame(
  label = c(
    paste0("Not counted arriving in Europe: ", thousands(not_counted)),
    paste0(shown$label, ": ", thousands(shown$values)),
    paste0("Other European countries: ", thousands(other))
  ),
  value = c(not_counted, shown$values, other),
  color = c(gray, rep(blue, nrow(shown) + 1)),
  link = c("rgba(158, 158, 158, 0.35)", rep("rgba(31, 119, 180, 0.3)", nrow(shown) + 1))
)
# the place of each node, as a share of the width and of the height (its middle), fixed so that
# plotly keeps this order: the nodes share the height of the plot, less a gap of `pad` pixels
# between two
pad <- 10
margin <- list(t = 60, b = 80, l = 10, r = 10)
# opts_chunk has the dots per inch that set the height of a plotly chart; opts_current has them
# multiplied by fig.retina
dpi <- knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi")
plot_height <- knitr::opts_current$get("fig.height") * dpi - margin$t - margin$b
gap <- pad / plot_height
node_height <- went_to$value / sum(went_to$value) * (1 - gap * (nrow(went_to) - 1))
middle <- cumsum(node_height + gap) - gap - node_height / 2
plot_ly(
  type = "sankey",
  orientation = "h",
  arrangement = "fixed",
  valueformat = ",.0f",
  textfont = list(size = 12),
  node = list(
    label = c(paste0("Left Greece: ", thousands(left_window)), went_to$label),
    color = c(dark_gray, went_to$color),
    x = c(0.001, rep(0.999, nrow(went_to))),
    y = c(0.5, middle),
    pad = pad,
    thickness = 16,
    line = list(width = 0),
    hovertemplate = "%{label}<extra></extra>"
  ),
  link = list(
    source = rep(0, nrow(went_to)),
    target = seq_len(nrow(went_to)),
    value = went_to$value,
    color = went_to$link,
    hovertemplate = "%{target.label}<extra></extra>"
  )
) %>%
  chart(
    paste0("Where the Greek citizens who left went, ", since, "–", latest),
    paste0(
      "Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz (Greece's estimate) and migr_imm1ctz (the countries' counts). ",
      "In brackets: the years with figures."
    ),
    margin = margin,
    note_y = -0.04
  )






Germany counted 153,000 Greek citizens arriving, 52% of all those counted in Europe, and the Netherlands 37,000, 12%. The United Kingdom has figures only for 2015, when 12,148 Greek citizens arrived there, the most after Germany; Eurostat’s figures for the United Kingdom stop with its withdrawal from the EU (Eurostat).
The other 251,000, 46% of those who left, were not counted arriving in any European country. They may have gone to countries outside Europe; to European countries that have no figures on Greek citizens arriving, Cyprus, Ireland, Malta, Poland, Portugal and Spain; or to countries in years without figures, such as the United Kingdom after 2015. And part of the gap is the difference between Greece’s estimate and the counts of the other countries. The figures cannot tell how much of each.


Code
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    c(shown$label, "Other European countries"),
    number(c(shown$values, other))
  ),
  col.names = c(
    "Country (years with figures)",
    paste0("Greek citizens who arrived, ", since, "–", latest)
  ),
  align = "lr"
)

Where they live now


Code
living <- greeks_living[greeks_living$geo %in% names(country_name), ]
newest <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(living, living$geo), function(x) x[which.max(x$time), ]))
newest <- head(newest[order(-newest$values), ], 15)
living_year <- max(newest$time)
newest$label <- ifelse(
  newest$time == living_year,
  country_name[newest$geo],
  paste0(country_name[newest$geo], " (", newest$time, ")")
)
newest <- newest[order(newest$values), ]
newest$label <- factor(newest$label, levels = newest$label)
lived <- function(geo, year) living$values[living$geo == geo & living$time == year]
uk_last <- max(living$time[living$geo == "UK"])
uk_place <- sum(living$values[living$time == uk_last] > lived("UK", uk_last)) + 1


The countries also count the people who live there, by citizenship. Germany had by far the most Greek citizens: 298,398 on 1 January 2025. Its Greek community was as large before the crisis, 297,668 in 2010: the number of people living in a country does not grow by all who arrive, as people also leave, die, or take the citizenship of the country. In the Netherlands, the number of Greek citizens grew from 7,781 in 2010 to 32,924 in 2025. The United Kingdom had 74,970 in 2019, its last year in the figures, the most after Germany.


Code
plot_ly(
  newest,
  x = ~values,
  y = ~label,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = blue),
  text = number(newest$values),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:,.0f}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(
    paste0("Greek citizens living elsewhere in Europe, 1 January ", living_year),
    "Eurostat, migr_pop1ctz. In brackets: the last year with figures.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.2 * max(newest$values)), tickformat = ","),
    margin = list(l = 150, t = 70, b = 70, r = 30),
    note_y = -0.08
  )

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
4. Did they come back?


Code
turn <- min(flows$year[flows$year > rescue[1] & !is.na(flows$net_greek) & flows$net_greek > 0])
after_turn <- flows$year[flows$year >= turn]
before_turn <- max(flows$year[
  flows$year < rescue[1] & !is.na(flows$net_greek) & flows$net_greek > 0
])
lost <- -sum(flows$net_greek[flows$year %in% rescue[1]:(turn - 1)])
gained <- sum(flows$net_greek[flows$year %in% after_turn])
born_elsewhere <- flow("came_greek", latest) - flow("came_born", latest)

germany <- data.frame(year = min(greeks_came$time[greeks_came$geo == "DE"]):latest)
germany$came <- by_year(greeks_came[greeks_came$geo == "DE", ], germany$year)
germany$left <- by_year(greeks_left[greeks_left$geo == "DE", ], germany$year)
both <- germany[!is.na(germany$came) & !is.na(germany$left), ]
before <- both[both$year < rescue[1], ]
restart <- min(both$year[both$year > rescue[1]])
since_restart <- both[both$year >= restart, ]
peak_in <- since_restart$year[which.max(since_restart$came - since_restart$left)]
more_left <- since_restart$year[since_restart$left > since_restart$came]
# the years without figures between the last year before the crisis and the restart
gap_years <- (max(before$year) + 1):(restart - 1)
in_germany <- function(column, year) germany[[column]][germany$year == year]
left_germany_first <- length(more_left) == 1 && more_left == latest


Some have. Since 2023, more Greek citizens move to Greece each year than leave it, by ELSTAT’s estimates, but they have made up only a small part of what the crisis took.
From 2010 to 2022, 328,000 more Greek citizens left Greece than moved to it. In 2023 and 2024, for the first time since 2009, more moved to Greece than left: 9,160 and 19,852 more. Together, that is 9% of what was lost from 2010 to 2022.
Not all the Greek citizens who move to Greece were born there: in 2024, 51,993 Greek citizens moved to Greece, but only 44,336 people born in Greece, of any citizenship, so at least 7,657 of the Greek citizens were born abroad. The people born in Greece who move to Greece are coming back to the country of their birth: 44,336 in 2024, against 27,604 in 2022 and 17,350 in 2008.


Code
greek_flows <- flows[!is.na(flows$left_greek), ]
plot_ly(
  greek_flows,
  x = ~year,
  y = ~ left_greek / 1000,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines+markers",
  name = "Greek citizens who left Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
  marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Greek citizens who left</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(
    y = ~ came_greek / 1000,
    name = "Greek citizens who moved to Greece",
    line = list(color = blue, width = 3),
    marker = list(color = blue),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Greek citizens who came</extra>"
  ) %>%
  add_trace(
    y = ~ came_born / 1000,
    name = "People born in Greece who moved to Greece",
    line = list(color = blue, width = 2, dash = "dot"),
    marker = list(color = blue, symbol = "circle-open"),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Born in Greece, came</extra>"
  ) %>%
  chart(
    "Leaving Greece and moving to Greece, thousands a year",
    paste("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz, migr_imm1ctz and migr_imm3ctb (estimates of ELSTAT).", shaded),
    "Thousands",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"),
    shapes = list(rescue_band),
    legend = legend_top,
    margin = list(t = 110, b = 90)
  )






These figures are ELSTAT’s estimates as well. Since 2022, it estimates the people who arrive, apart from those granted protection, such as refugees, with a model: from the number of the year before and the growth of the economy. It splits them by citizenship and country of birth as in the census of 2021 (ELSTAT).

A check from Germany
Germany counts the Greek citizens who move there and those who leave, and its figures point the same way. Before the crisis, more Greek citizens left Germany than moved there, in every year with figures from 1998 to 2008: in 2008, 16,079 left and 8,266 arrived. There are no figures for 2009–2013. In 2015, 18,970 Greek citizens moved to Germany and 5,796 left it. In 2024, 8,833 moved there and 9,025 left: for the first time since the figures restart in 2014, more left than came.


Code
plot_ly(
  germany,
  x = ~year,
  y = ~ came / 1000,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines+markers",
  name = "Greek citizens who moved to Germany",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
  marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Moved to Germany</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(
    y = ~ left / 1000,
    name = "Greek citizens who left Germany",
    line = list(color = blue, width = 3),
    marker = list(color = blue),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Left Germany</extra>"
  ) %>%
  chart(
    "Greek citizens arriving in and leaving Germany, thousands",
    paste0(
      "Eurostat, migr_imm1ctz and migr_emi1ctz (figures of Germany; none for ",
      years_text(gap_years),
      "). ",
      shaded
    ),
    "Thousands",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"),
    shapes = list(rescue_band),
    legend = legend_top
  )

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
5. Was it a brain drain?


Code
education_names <- c(
  "ED5-8" = "Higher education",
  "ED3_4" = "Upper secondary",
  "ED0-2" = "At most lower secondary"
)
education_colors <- c("ED5-8" = greek_red, "ED3_4" = gray, "ED0-2" = dark_gray)
adults_abroad <- born_abroad[born_abroad$age == "Y20-64" & born_abroad$time >= 2005, ]
level <- function(isced, year) {
  adults_abroad$values[adults_abroad$isced11 == isced & adults_abroad$time == year]
}
edu_latest <- max(adults_abroad$time)
# the share with higher education: abroad, of those whose education is known; in Greece, as Eurostat
# publishes it
working_age <- born_abroad[born_abroad$age == "Y15-64" & born_abroad$time >= 2005, ]
known <- working_age[working_age$isced11 %in% names(education_names), ]
share <- aggregate(values ~ time, known, sum)
names(share) <- c("year", "known")
share$abroad <- 100 * by_year(known[known$isced11 == "ED5-8", ], share$year) / share$known
share$home <- by_year(born_home[born_home$isced11 == "ED5-8", ], share$year)
share <- share[!is.na(share$home), ]
behind <- share$year[share$abroad <= share$home]
ahead_since <- max(behind) + 1
first_share <- min(share$year)
last_share <- max(share$year)
higher <- function(where, year) share[[where]][share$year == year]


Partly. The people born in Greece who live elsewhere in Europe used to have less education than those at home; now they have more, and many more of them have a degree.
No statistic follows the people who left, so none can say exactly how much education they had. The nearest is Eurostat’s Labour Force Survey, which counts the people born in Greece, aged 20 to 64, who live in another EU or EFTA country, by the highest level of education they finished.
From 2010 to 2024, the number of them with higher education, a university degree or similar, rose from about 40,000 to 113,000: 2.8 times as many. The number with at most lower secondary schooling hardly changed: about 102,000 in 2010 and 98,000 in 2024.


Code
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(education_names)) {
  p <- add_trace(
    p,
    data = adults_abroad[adults_abroad$isced11 == k, ],
    x = ~time,
    y = ~values,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = education_names[[k]],
    line = list(color = education_colors[[k]], width = if (k == "ED5-8") 3 else 2),
    marker = list(color = education_colors[[k]]),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>", education_names[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>%
  chart(
    "Greek-born aged 20 to 64 in other EU and EFTA countries",
    paste("Eurostat, lfst_lmbpcobed (Labour Force Survey), by education.", shaded),
    "Thousands",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"),
    shapes = list(rescue_band),
    legend = legend_top
  )






So the Greeks abroad have changed. In 2005, 12% of the people born in Greece aged 15 to 64 who lived in another EU or EFTA country had higher education, against 18% of those who lived in Greece. In 2024, it was 36% against 32%, and those abroad have had more education than those at home in every year since 2017. To change the Greeks abroad so much, those who left in the crisis must have had much more education than those who had left before them. That they also had more than those who stayed is likely, but the survey cannot prove it: it counts the people who live abroad, not those who left. The share with higher education rose in Greece too, from 18% to 32%.


Code
plot_ly(
  share,
  x = ~year,
  y = ~abroad,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines+markers",
  name = "Living in another EU or EFTA country",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
  marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}%<extra>Living abroad</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(
    y = ~home,
    name = "Living in Greece",
    line = list(color = blue, width = 3),
    marker = list(color = blue),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}%<extra>Living in Greece</extra>"
  ) %>%
  chart(
    "Born in Greece, aged 15 to 64: share with higher education",
    paste("Eurostat, lfst_lmbpcobed and edat_lfs_9912 (Labour Force Survey).", shaded),
    "% of the age group",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero", ticksuffix = "%"),
    shapes = list(rescue_band),
    legend = legend_top
  )






What the data cannot tell:

Who left when. The survey counts the people who live abroad, whenever they left, not those who left in a given year.
Where they studied. It does not say whether the degree was earned in Greece or abroad.
All the countries. It covers the EU and EFTA countries: not the United Kingdom, which is left out of this series, nor the countries outside Europe.
Exact numbers. The survey asks a sample of households, so its figures move from year to year more than the people do.
What it cost. No statistic here says whether those who left would have found work in Greece, or what their education cost the country.

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
So, what does it mean?

The crisis drove a wave of emigration. By ELSTAT’s estimates, 1,018,000 people left Greece in the years of the rescue loans, 527,000 of them Greek citizens. In 2012, 12.2 of every 1,000 people who lived in Greece left.
They were young, and many were men. In 2012, 44 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29 left.
Germany took the most: 52% of the Greek citizens counted arriving in Europe from 2014 to 2024. For 46% of those who left, the figures do not say where they went.
The flow has turned, a little. Since 2023, more Greek citizens come to Greece than leave it, and in 2024 more Greek citizens left Germany than moved there. But 29,012 more Greek citizens in 2023 and 2024 make up only 9% of the 328,000 lost from 2010 to 2022.
It was partly a brain drain. The people born in Greece with higher education who live elsewhere in the EU and EFTA are 2.8 times as many as in 2010, and those abroad now have more education than those at home.

Most of these numbers are estimates: Greece does not count the people who leave, and the countries they go to count them in their own ways. The direction is clear; the exact numbers are not.

title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
text:
Sources

Eurostat, migration: migr_emi2 (emigration by age and sex), migr_emi1ctz (emigration by citizenship), migr_emi5nxt (emigration by group of country of next residence), migr_imm1ctz (immigration by citizenship), migr_imm3ctb (immigration by country of birth), migr_pop1ctz (population by citizenship), and the metadata of the migration statistics (definitions, breaks in the series, countries’ methods).
Eurostat, population and work: demo_pjan (population by age and sex), une_rt_a (unemployment).
Eurostat, Labour Force Survey: lfst_lmbpcobed (people born in an EU or EFTA country who live in another one, by education), edat_lfs_9912 (education by country of birth).
ELSTAT, Migration flows: Methodological note for the estimation of migration flows for the years 2022, 2023 and 2024 and population on 1st January of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and Short Methodological Note on Population Revision for the Intercensal years 2012 – 2021 and Estimation of Post-census Migration Models, both of 18 December 2025.
ESM: Greece successfully concludes ESM programme.

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
text:
Greece went through one of the deepest debt crises of any modern European economy. More than fifteen years after the first bailout, this story answers four questions with official data:

Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?
Whom does it owe?
How much is that compared with the size of the economy, and with the rest of the EU?
Will Greece be able to repay?

The data come from three places:

Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU: the debt, the deficit, the interest, who holds the debt and when it falls due. They are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest figures.
The World Bank: interest payments as a share of the government’s revenue, back to 1972.
The Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) of Greece: who the creditors are, from its Annual Debt Bulletin 2025. The bulletin is a PDF, so its figures are typed in below, with the page they come from.

It follows two other stories of this site: Greece Since 2000 goes through the boom, the crisis and the recovery of the economy, and Same Crisis, Different Endings compares Greece with the other countries of the euro crisis; this one follows the debt.
Two measures of the same debt. Eurostat and the EU count the debt of the whole general government (the State, public bodies, local government and the pension funds) and leave out what one public body owes another: that is the figure of the EU rules, and of the headlines. The PDMA also reports the debt of the State alone, which includes the short-term loans that other public bodies make to the State with their spare cash. At the end of 2025 the first was €362.9 billion, the second €406.2 billion. This story uses the first, except where it names the creditors of the State.

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
text:
The data


Code
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
}

# debt, deficit and interest of the general government of Greece
edp <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(
  geo = "EL", sector = "S13",
  na_item = c("GD", "GD_F3", "GD_F4", "B9", "D41PAY"),
  unit = c("MIO_EUR", "PC_GDP")
))
# gross domestic product at current prices, million euros
gdp <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(geo = "EL", na_item = "B1GQ", unit = "CP_MEUR"))

# one series of the deficit and debt data, by year
series <- function(item, unit, years) {
  s <- edp[edp$na_item == item & edp$unit == unit, ]
  s$values[match(years, s$time)]
}
years <- sort(unique(edp$time[edp$na_item == "GD"]))
greece <- data.frame(
  year = years,
  debt_bn = series("GD", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,          # debt, billion euros
  debt_gdp = series("GD", "PC_GDP", years),                 # debt, % of GDP
  bonds_bn = series("GD_F3", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,      # of which bonds and bills
  loans_bn = series("GD_F4", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,      # of which loans
  balance_gdp = series("B9", "PC_GDP", years),              # surplus (+) or deficit (-), % of GDP
  interest_gdp = series("D41PAY", "PC_GDP", years),         # interest, % of GDP
  interest_bn = series("D41PAY", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,
  gdp_bn = gdp$values[match(years, gdp$time)] / 1000
)
# the balance before interest: what the State collects minus what it spends on everything else
greece$primary_gdp <- greece$balance_gdp + greece$interest_gdp
last <- max(greece$year)
at <- function(column, year) greece[[column]][greece$year == year]

# who holds the debt (from 2020), and when it falls due
holders <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_ggd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "MIO_EUR"))
due <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD"))

# debt of every EU country, % of GDP, and the countries with the most
eu <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", unit = "PC_GDP"))
eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27")
most <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ]
most <- most[order(-most$values), ]

# the average years to repayment of the debt of every EU country, the longest first
maturities <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "YR"))
maturities <- maturities[maturities$time == max(maturities$time) & maturities$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ]
maturities <- maturities[order(-maturities$values), ]

# World Bank: interest payments, % of revenue
world_bank <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/GRC/indicator/GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS?format=json&per_page=100")[[2]]
interest_revenue <- data.frame(year = as.integer(world_bank$date), value = world_bank$value)
interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[!is.na(interest_revenue$value), ]
interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[order(interest_revenue$year), ]




Code
greek_red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
blue <- "#1f77b4"

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left"),
    yaxis = list(title = y_title),
    xaxis = list(title = ""),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
# a short label of an amount
billion <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x), big.mark = ","), " bn")

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
section: 1. Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?
text:
1. Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?
In euros, yes. As a share of the economy, slightly less — and far less than at the peak.
At the end of 2010 the Greek state owed €331 bn; at the end of 2025 it owed €363 bn, that is €32 bn more. The debt fell only once, in 2012, when private holders of Greek bonds took a loss in the restructuring known as the PSI: between 2011 and 2012 the debt went down by €51 bn, although new bailout loans came in at the same time.


Code
highlight <- ifelse(greece$year %in% c(2010, last), greek_red, gray)
plot_ly(greece,
  x = ~year, y = ~debt_bn, type = "bar", marker = list(color = highlight),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(
    "Greek government debt, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros",
    annotations = list(list(
      x = 2012, y = at("debt_bn", 2012), text = "2012: bondholders' haircut (PSI)",
      showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = -60
    ))
  )






What matters for paying a debt is the size of the economy that carries it. As a share of the gross domestic product (GDP), the debt was 147.8% in 2010 and 145.4% in 2025: about the same. In between it rose to 209.4% in 2020, when the pandemic made the economy shrink, and it has fallen by 64 points since.


Code
plot_ly(greece,
  x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_lines(x = range(greece$year), y = c(60, 60), line = list(color = gray, dash = "dash"), hoverinfo = "skip", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart(
    "Greek government debt, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "% of GDP",
    showlegend = FALSE,
    annotations = list(
      list(x = greece$year[1], y = 60, text = "60%: the limit of the EU rules", showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(color = gray)),
      list(x = greece$year[which.max(greece$debt_gdp)], y = max(greece$debt_gdp), text = "Pandemic", showarrow = TRUE, ax = -50, ay = -30)
    )
  )

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
text:
2. Whom does Greece owe?
Mostly the rest of the euro area, through the rescue funds of the bailouts. In 2010, 79% of the debt was bonds sold to investors; in 2025, 71% is loans. The bailouts replaced most of the bonds with long, cheap loans from the euro area and, until 2022, the IMF.


Code
plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~bonds_bn, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Bonds and bills",
  line = list(color = gray, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in bonds<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~loans_bn, name = "Loans", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in loans<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("From bonds to loans: the debt by instrument, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros",
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))






The PDMA names the creditors of the State. At the end of 2025:


Code
# PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025 (June 2026), debt of the State at 31.12.2025, million euros (pages 13-14).
# The bulletin gives 211,421 for the loans of the EFSF, the ESM and the GLF together, and says
# that the EFSF and the ESM hold 45.58% of the debt; the GLF is the difference.
total <- 406181
creditors <- data.frame(
  creditor = c(
    "EFSF and ESM: the euro area rescue funds",
    "Bonds held by investors and the Bank of Greece",
    "Repos: short-term loans, mostly from public bodies",
    "GLF: bilateral loans of euro area countries",
    "Other EU and international loans (RRF, SURE, EIB)",
    "Treasury bills"
  ),
  million = c(round(0.4558 * total), 100759, 62852, 211421 - round(0.4558 * total), 23057, 7969)
)
creditors$share <- 100 * creditors$million / total
creditors <- creditors[order(creditors$million), ]
creditors$creditor <- factor(creditors$creditor, levels = creditors$creditor)

plot_ly(creditors,
  x = ~ million / 1000, y = ~creditor, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = c(rep(gray, nrow(creditors) - 1), greek_red)),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share, 1), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: €%{x:.1f} billion<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Who lends to the Greek State, end of 2025, billion euros",
    "PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025; the GLF as calculated in the code above",
    margin = list(l = 330, r = 60, t = 70, b = 90))







The EFSF and the ESM, the rescue funds of the euro area, hold almost half of the debt of the State. Their loans are repaid over decades: those of the EFSF from 2023 to 2070, those of the ESM from 2034 to 2060 (ESM).
The GLF loans of the first bailout come from the other euro area countries. Their interest rate floats, so Greece is paying them back early: €5.3 billion in 2025.
The IMF was repaid in full in 2022.
The repos are mostly the cash of other public bodies, lent to the State for a few days or weeks; the EU measure of the debt leaves them out.

Eurostat’s view of the same debt, by who holds it rather than by instrument:


Code
groups <- c(
  S2 = "Abroad (the rescue funds, foreign investors)",
  S121 = "Bank of Greece",
  S122_S123 = "Greek banks",
  `S124-S129` = "Other Greek financial companies",
  S11 = "Greek companies",
  S14_S15 = "Greek households"
)
latest_holders <- holders[holders$time == max(holders$time), ]
held <- data.frame(holder = groups, million = latest_holders$values[match(names(groups), latest_holders$sector2)])
held$million[is.na(held$million)] <- 0
held$share <- 100 * held$million / latest_holders$values[latest_holders$sector2 == "S1_S2"]
held <- held[order(held$share), ]
held$holder <- factor(held$holder, levels = held$holder)

plot_ly(held,
  x = ~share, y = ~holder, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(held$holder == groups[["S2"]], greek_red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of the debt<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Who holds the Greek government debt, ", max(holders$time), ", % of the debt"),
    "Eurostat, gov_10dd_ggd", margin = list(l = 300, t = 70, b = 90))

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
section: 3. How much is it, compared with the economy and with the EU?
text:
3. How much is it, compared with the economy and with the EU?
At 145.4% of GDP, Greece still has the highest debt in the EU, 8.7 points above Italy.


Code
eu_latest <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% c(eu_countries$code, "EU27_2020"), ]
eu_latest$name <- eu_name[eu_latest$geo]
eu_latest <- eu_latest[order(eu_latest$values), ]
eu_latest$name <- factor(eu_latest$name, levels = eu_latest$name)

plot_ly(eu_latest,
  x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))),
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Government debt in the EU, ", last, ", % of GDP"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1",
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90))

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
section: 4. Will Greece be able to repay?
text:
4. Will Greece be able to repay?
Countries rarely pay their debt off; they repay old loans with new ones. The question is whether the debt stays affordable — whether the interest leaves enough for everything else — and whether it keeps shrinking against the economy. On both, the numbers now look good, for four reasons.

Interest takes far less of the budget
In 2011 interest cost Greece 7.7% of GDP; in 2025, 3.1%. The World Bank’s series shows the same from the side of the budget: interest took 17.8% of the government’s revenue in 2011, and 7.5% in 2024.


Code
subplot(
  plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~interest_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    name = "% of GDP (Eurostat)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"),
  plot_ly(interest_revenue, x = ~year, y = ~value, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = blue, width = 3),
    name = "% of revenue (World Bank)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of revenue<extra></extra>"),
  nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE
) %>%
  chart("Interest paid by the Greek government", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; World Bank, GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS",
    "% of GDP", yaxis2 = list(title = "% of revenue"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))








The debt is long, fixed and in euros


Code
years_left <- due[due$unit == "YR" & due$maturity == "TOTAL", ]
buckets <- c(Y_LE1 = "Up to 1 year", `Y1-5` = "1 to 5 years", `Y5-10` = "5 to 10 years", `Y10-30` = "10 to 30 years", Y_GT30 = "Over 30 years")
falling_due <- due[due$unit == "MIO_EUR" & due$time == max(due$time) & due$maturity %in% names(buckets), ]
falling_due$label <- factor(buckets[falling_due$maturity], levels = buckets)
falling_due$share <- 100 * falling_due$values / sum(falling_due$values)

plot_ly(falling_due,
  x = ~label, y = ~share, type = "bar", marker = list(color = greek_red),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of the debt<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("When the debt falls due, ", max(due$time), ", % of the debt"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_rmd", "% of the debt")







On average the debt falls due in 18.4 years (Eurostat), the longest in the EU: next comes Austria, with 11.3 years.
After interest rate swaps, none of it has a floating rate and none is in a foreign currency (PDMA): higher interest rates reach only the debt that is renewed, a little each year.
In 2025 the State needed €17.6 billion to repay maturing debt and cover its budget, about 7% of GDP, and borrowed it at 2.89% for 14.6 years on average (PDMA). When the euro area eased the terms of its loans in 2018, it set out to keep these needs below 15% of GDP in the medium term and below 20% after that (Eurogroup, June 2018).
The State keeps a cash reserve: the general government held €39.6 billion in cash at the end of 2025, so its debt minus its cash was €323 billion (PDMA).



Why the ratio fell so fast
The change of the debt ratio each year adds up from four parts:

Interest adds to the debt.
The primary balance (the budget before interest) adds a deficit or takes away a surplus.
Growth of the economy in euros — real growth plus inflation — shrinks the ratio, as the same debt is divided by a bigger GDP.
Other changes: debt that changes without a deficit, such as the PSI haircut of 2012 or the cash the State borrows ahead and keeps.



Code
d <- greece[greece$year >= 2010 & !is.na(greece$gdp_bn), ]
n <- nrow(d)
ratio <- 100 * d$debt_bn / d$gdp_bn
growth <- d$gdp_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-n] - 1
parts <- data.frame(
  year = d$year[-1],
  change = diff(ratio),
  interest = 100 * d$interest_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-1],
  primary = -d$primary_gdp[-1],
  growth = -ratio[-n] * growth / (1 + growth)
)
parts$other <- parts$change - parts$interest - parts$primary - parts$growth

plot_ly(parts, x = ~year, y = ~interest, type = "bar", name = "Interest", marker = list(color = greek_red)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~primary, name = "Primary deficit (+) or surplus (-)", marker = list(color = "#ff9896")) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~growth, name = "Growth of GDP in euros", marker = list(color = blue)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~other, name = "Other", marker = list(color = gray)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~change, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = "Change of the debt ratio",
    marker = list(color = "black", size = 10, symbol = "diamond")) %>%
  chart("What changed the debt ratio each year, points of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1 and nama_10_gdp; own calculation",
    "Points of GDP", barmode = "relative", note_y = -0.34, margin = list(t = 70, b = 160),
    # under the chart, as its five entries take two lines
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.1, yanchor = "top"))






From 2021 the economy grew fast in euros — partly real growth, partly inflation — while the interest rate on the debt stayed low: growth alone took 71 points off the ratio between 2021 and 2025. The budget before interest was in deficit in the pandemic and then turned to surplus: from 2023, the surpluses took 12 points more.


Where it could go: three scenarios
The debt ratio of next year is this year’s, grown by the interest rate and shrunk by the growth of GDP in euros, minus the primary surplus:
\[d_{t} = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + i_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t\]
The scenarios below start from the 2025 debt and its average interest rate of 2.1%, which climbs over ten years as cheap loans are replaced by new borrowing at market rates. They are illustrations of what drives the debt, not forecasts.


Code
start_rate <- at("interest_bn", last) / at("debt_bn", last - 1)
assumptions <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Strong", "Steady", "Weak"),
  growth = c(0.050, 0.040, 0.025),    # growth of GDP in euros, a year
  rate_to = c(0.025, 0.030, 0.040),   # average interest rate on the debt after ten years
  primary = c(3.5, 2.5, 1.0)          # primary surplus, % of GDP
)
project <- function(growth, rate_to, primary, years = (last + 1):2040) {
  debt <- at("debt_gdp", last)
  path <- numeric(length(years))
  for (k in seq_along(years)) {
    rate <- start_rate + (rate_to - start_rate) * min(1, k / 10)
    debt <- debt * (1 + rate) / (1 + growth) - primary
    path[k] <- debt
  }
  data.frame(year = c(last, years), debt_gdp = c(at("debt_gdp", last), path))
}
paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(assumptions)), function(k) {
  cbind(scenario = assumptions$scenario[k], project(assumptions$growth[k], assumptions$rate_to[k], assumptions$primary[k]))
}))
in_2040 <- setNames(paths$debt_gdp[paths$year == 2040], paths$scenario[paths$year == 2040])

knitr::kable(transform(assumptions,
  growth = paste0(100 * growth, "%"), rate_to = paste0(100 * rate_to, "%"), primary = paste0(primary, "% of GDP"),
  debt_2040 = paste0(round(in_2040[scenario]), "% of GDP")
), col.names = c("Scenario", "GDP growth in euros, a year", "Interest rate after ten years", "Primary surplus", "Debt in 2040"))

Code
plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual",
  line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Strong", ], name = "Strong", line = list(color = blue, dash = "dot")) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Steady", ], name = "Steady", line = list(color = greek_red, dash = "dot")) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Weak", ], name = "Weak", line = list(color = gray, dash = "dot")) %>%
  chart("Greek government debt to 2040: three scenarios, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; own scenarios", "% of GDP",
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))






In the steady scenario the debt falls to about 86% of GDP by 2040. In the weak one it ends near 150%, a little above today’s level: with long, fixed and cheap loans, a bad decade would stop the fall rather than send the debt back to the heights of 2020.


So, will Greece repay?
On today’s numbers, yes: the debt is large, but it is cheap, it falls due slowly, and it is shrinking against the economy. The markets agree: Greece is back in the investment grade (Moody’s raised it to Baa3 in March 2025), and at the end of 2025 its ten-year bonds paid only 0.59 percentage points more than Germany’s (PDMA).
What could still go wrong:

A recession, or years of slow growth: growth did most of the work since 2021.
Higher interest rates on the debt that is renewed each year, and more of it once the cheap rescue loans start falling due in the 2030s.
Smaller surpluses: the scenarios need primary surpluses for many years, which is a political choice, not only an economic one.
An ageing population, which raises the cost of pensions and health care.

title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
text:
Sources

Eurostat: gov_10dd_edpt1 (deficit, debt and interest), gov_10dd_ggd (holders of the debt), gov_10dd_rmd (remaining maturity), nama_10_gdp (GDP).
World Bank: Interest payments (% of revenue), GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS.
PDMA, Ministry of Finance: Annual Debt Bulletin 2025 (in Greek, June 2026).
ESM: When will Greece repay ESM and EFSF loans?

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
In 2006, Hans Rosling gave a TED talk that changed how people think about global development. His animated bubble chart showed 200 years of data in 4 minutes, revealing that the world is far less divided between “rich” and “poor” than most people assume.
This tutorial shows you how to recreate that chart in R using freely available packages — no API keys, no paid data, just a few lines of code.

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("gapminder", "ggplot2", "gganimate", "gifski", "scales"))

library(gapminder)   # the data
library(ggplot2)     # plotting
library(gganimate)   # animation
library(gifski)      # GIF renderer
library(scales)      # axis formatting

data(gapminder)

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
The data
The gapminder package ships with a clean, ready-to-use dataset. No downloading required.


Code
head(gapminder, 12)


# A tibble: 12 × 6
   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
 4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
 5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
 6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.
 7 Afghanistan Asia       1982    39.9 12881816      978.
 8 Afghanistan Asia       1987    40.8 13867957      852.
 9 Afghanistan Asia       1992    41.7 16317921      649.
10 Afghanistan Asia       1997    41.8 22227415      635.
11 Afghanistan Asia       2002    42.1 25268405      727.
12 Afghanistan Asia       2007    43.8 31889923      975.


It covers 142 countries across 5 continents, with observations every 5 years from 1952 to 2007.
Each row is one country in one year, with:



Column
Description




country
Country name


continent
Continent


year
Year (every 5 years)


lifeExp
Life expectancy at birth


pop
Population


gdpPercap
GDP per capita (inflation-adjusted USD)

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
section: Building the chart step by step
text:
Building the chart step by step

Step 1 — the basic scatter
Start with a single year to get the layout right before adding animation.


Code
gapminder_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()









Three things are already encoded: wealth (x), health (y), and population (bubble size). Continent gets color.


Step 2 — improve the axes
GDP per capita spans from ~$200 to ~$100,000. A log scale is essential — on a linear scale, poor countries are crushed into the left margin and you lose all the variation that matters.


Code
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()









range = c(2, 24) in scale_size maps the smallest population to a 2px bubble and the largest (China, India) to 24px. The guide = "none" removes the size legend — it’s not readable anyway.


Step 3 — label the big ones


Code
big_countries <- c("China", "India", "United States", "Brazil", "Nigeria")

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()











Step 4 — dark theme + colors


Code
continent_colors <- c(
  Africa   = "#E74C3C",
  Americas = "#F39C12",
  Asia     = "#3498DB",
  Europe   = "#2ECC71",
  Oceania  = "#9B59B6"
)

dark_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text             = element_text(color = "white"),
    axis.text        = element_text(color = "#90A4AE"),
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    legend.text      = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.caption     = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 8, hjust = 1)
  )

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, stroke = 0.2) +
  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = continent_colors,
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))
  ) +
  labs(
    title   = "2007",
    x       = "GDP per capita (log scale)",
    y       = "Life expectancy at birth",
    color   = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Gapminder  |  Bubble size = population"
  ) +
  dark_theme











Step 5 — animate it
gganimate extends ggplot2 with transition_* functions. transition_time(year) moves through the year variable. shadow_mark() leaves a faint ghost trail so you can see where countries have been.


Code
p <- ggplot(gapminder,
            aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +

  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, stroke = 0.2) +

  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +

  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = continent_colors,
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))
  ) +

  labs(
    title   = "{as.integer(frame_time)}",   # <-- the magic: year as title
    x       = "GDP per capita (log scale)",
    y       = "Life expectancy at birth",
    color   = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Gapminder  |  Bubble size = population"
  ) +

  dark_theme +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 54, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)) +

  transition_time(year) +      # animate over year
  ease_aes("linear") +         # constant speed between frames
  shadow_mark(alpha = 0.06, size = 0.4)   # ghost trail

animate(p,
        nframes  = 120,
        fps      = 12,
        width    = 900,
        height   = 650,
        units    = "px",
        res      = 96,
        renderer = gifski_renderer("gapminder.gif"))










Note: rendering takes ~1–2 minutes. The GIF will appear in your working directory (getwd()).

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
What the chart shows

Africa (red) clusters bottom-left in 1952 — low income, low life expectancy — and moves right and up over 55 years, but more slowly than other continents.
Asia (blue) shows the most dramatic movement. South Korea, Singapore, and China all make huge leaps.
Europe (green) starts already in the upper-right and pushes further right.
The gap between rich and poor narrows dramatically — the world Rosling called “two humps” in 1952 becomes one.

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
Customising it

Change which countries get labels


Code
big_countries <- c("China", "India", "United States", "Germany", "Japan")




Change the speed


Code
animate(p, nframes = 60, fps = 6, ...)   # slower
animate(p, nframes = 240, fps = 24, ...) # smoother




Filter to one continent


Code
gapminder_asia <- gapminder[gapminder$continent == "Asia", ]
# then replace gapminder with gapminder_asia in the ggplot() call




Save as MP4 instead of GIF


Code
# install.packages("av")
animate(p, renderer = av_renderer("gapminder.mp4"), fps = 24, width = 1280, height = 720)

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Between 2010 and 2013 six euro countries ran into deep trouble: Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Cyprus and Italy. Five of them needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, and all six went through years of cuts and lost jobs. They started from the same crisis, but they did not end up in the same place: in 2024 the average person in Ireland produced almost twice as much as in 2008, while in Greece it was still less than in 2008.
This data story compares the six countries, in plain words, on:

borrowing — how much more each country bought from abroad than it sold, before the crisis,
income — how much the country produces per person,
jobs — how many people who want work cannot find it,
investment — what the country spends on its future,
exports — how much it sells to the rest of the world,
people — whether its population grew or shrank.

Greece is in red throughout and the other five in gray. It follows on from Greece Since 2000, which tells the Greek story on its own. All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators; the page carries its own copy of the data for these six countries and of the one function it uses, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub.
