title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "plotly"))
# The data and indicator_change() come from golemworldbank, copied next to this page:
# R/code_golemworldbank.R (sourced above) and R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds. For every country,
# install golemworldbank itself; its data is in Git LFS, so install it from a clone
# (install_github() can download LFS pointer files instead of the data):
#   git lfs install
#   git clone https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank.git
# then in R:
#   devtools::install_local("golemworldbank")

library(dplyr)
library(plotly)          # interactive charts

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
The data
golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds holds its rows for the six countries from 2000 onwards, every indicator. We keep the indicators this story needs, each with a short name:


Code
# golemworldbank's mfi, six countries from 2000 (with the package installed, its mfi has every country)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds"))

countries <- c("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Cyprus", "Italy")
last_year <- 2024   # the latest year with complete numbers: 2025 is still incomplete
indicators <- c(
  income             = "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  income_gni         = "GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  unemployment       = "Unemployment, total (% of total labor force) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  youth_unemployment = "Unemployment, youth total (% of total labor force ages 15-24) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  investment         = "Gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)",
  current_account    = "Current account balance (% of GDP)",
  exports            = "Exports of goods and services (% of GDP)",
  population         = "Population, total"
)

df_peers <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Country Name` %in% countries, `Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(country = `Country Name`,
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  select(country, measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(country, measure, year)

head(df_peers, 12)


   country         measure year      value
1   Cyprus current_account 2000  -4.887475
2   Cyprus current_account 2001  -3.099168
3   Cyprus current_account 2002  -3.320125
4   Cyprus current_account 2003  -2.007671
5   Cyprus current_account 2004  -4.773275
6   Cyprus current_account 2005  -5.266826
7   Cyprus current_account 2006  -6.367948
8   Cyprus current_account 2007  -7.636691
9   Cyprus current_account 2008 -14.385541
10  Cyprus current_account 2009  -6.670743
11  Cyprus current_account 2010 -10.762276
12  Cyprus current_account 2011  -2.093436


Each row is one country, one indicator, one year:







Column
Description




country
Country name


measure
Short name of the indicator (the names of indicators above)


year
Year of observation


value
The World Bank’s value for that country and year



A few of these need a word of explanation:

Income (GDP per person) is the value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by the number of people who live there, in US dollars with price rises removed, so that years can be compared fairly. It is a rough measure of how well off the average person is.
Borrowing from abroad (the current account) is what a country earns from the rest of the world minus what it pays to it, as a share of everything it produces. A minus means it bought more than it sold and borrowed to pay the difference.
Investment is the money spent on things that help a country earn more later: new buildings, factories, machines, roads and equipment, as a share of everything the economy produces.

Every chart shades the euro crisis (2008 to 2013) and COVID (2020), and writes each country’s latest value at the end of its line; labels that would overlap are moved apart and joined to their line:


Code
# a measure's value for one country and year, and the change between two values
at <- function(m, cty, y) df_peers$value[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$country == cty & df_peers$year == y]
change_pct <- function(from, to) round((to - from) / from * 100)
big <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")

# Greece in red, the others in gray (as in the Greek Wages and Housing races)
highlight <- "Greece"
colour_of <- function(cty) ifelse(cty == highlight, "#E74C3C", "#B3B3B3")

shocks <- list(list(from = 2008,   to = 2013,   label = "Euro crisis"),
               list(from = 2019.5, to = 2020.5, label = "COVID"))

# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}

# data source as a footnote inside each chart, at the bottom of the bottom
# margin `b` (in pixels), so it lands in the same place whatever the height
source_note <- function(b) {
  list(text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
       xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
       font = list(size = 11, color = "#7F7F7F"))
}

# end labels: each sits right of its line's last point; labels closer than
# `gap` pixels are pushed upwards and joined to their point by a leader line.
# `per_px` is how many y units one pixel of the plot is worth
end_labels <- function(ends, per_px, unit, gap = 17) {
  o <- order(ends$value)
  y <- ends$value[o]
  for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + gap * per_px)
  ends$label_y[o] <- y
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(ends)), function(i) {
    name <- if (ends$country[i] == highlight) paste0("<b>", ends$country[i], "</b>") else ends$country[i]
    list(x = ends$year[i], y = ends$value[i], xref = "x", yref = "y",
         ax = 24, ay = -(ends$label_y[i] - ends$value[i]) / per_px,
         showarrow = TRUE, arrowhead = 0, arrowwidth = 1, arrowcolor = "#B3B3B3",
         xanchor = "left", text = paste0(name, " ", ends$text[i]),
         font = list(size = 12, color = "#404040"))
  })
}

# one line per country, Greece drawn last so it sits on top. `index_year`
# turns each line into "that year = 100"; `ref` draws a dotted reference line
peer_chart <- function(m, title, ytitle, unit = "", index_year = NULL, ref = NULL,
                       tozero = TRUE, h = 520) {
  d <- df_peers[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$year >= 2000 & df_peers$year <= last_year, ]
  if (!is.null(index_year)) {
    d <- d %>% group_by(country) %>%
      mutate(value = value / value[year == index_year] * 100) %>% ungroup()
  }
  fmt <- function(v) if (unit == "$") paste0("$", big(v)) else paste0(round(v, 1), unit)
  p <- plot_ly()
  for (cty in c(setdiff(countries, highlight), highlight)) {
    dc <- d[d$country == cty, ]
    p <- add_lines(p, data = dc, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = cty,
                   line = list(color = colour_of(cty), width = if (cty == highlight) 3 else 2),
                   text = paste0(cty, " · ", dc$year, "<br>", fmt(dc$value)), hoverinfo = "text")
  }
  ends <- d %>% filter(!is.na(value)) %>% group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year) %>% ungroup() %>%
    mutate(text = fmt(value))
  b <- 110
  lo <- if (tozero) min(0, d$value, na.rm = TRUE) else min(d$value, na.rm = TRUE)
  per_px <- (max(d$value, na.rm = TRUE) - lo) * 1.1 / (h - 90 - b)
  shapes <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(type = "rect", xref = "x", yref = "paper", x0 = s$from, x1 = s$to, y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
         fillcolor = "#EBEBEB", line = list(width = 0), layer = "below")
  })
  if (!is.null(ref)) {
    shapes <- c(shapes, list(list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = ref, y1 = ref,
                                  line = list(dash = "dot", color = "gray"))))
  }
  tags <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(x = (s$from + s$to) / 2, y = 1, xref = "x", yref = "paper", yanchor = "bottom",
         text = s$label, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "#666666"))
  })
  plotly::layout(p,
    title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 90, r = 150, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, range = c(1999.5, max(d$year) + 0.5)),
    yaxis  = list(title = ytitle, ticksuffix = if (unit == "%") "%" else "",
                  rangemode = if (tozero) "tozero" else "normal"),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    shapes = shapes,
    annotations = c(tags, end_labels(ends, per_px, unit), list(source_note(b))),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "#404040")) %>%
    sized(h)
}

# one bar per country, largest at the top, Greece in red; a negative bar
# carries its value inside, where it cannot run into the country names
ranked_bars <- function(values, title, h = 380) {
  d <- data.frame(country = names(values), value = unname(values))
  d <- d[order(d$value), ]
  b <- 80
  plot_ly(d, x = ~value, y = ~factor(country, levels = country), type = "bar", orientation = "h",
          marker = list(color = colour_of(d$country)),
          # rounding first (+ 0 turns -0 into 0) so -0.3 reads "+0%", never "-0%"
          text = sprintf("%+.0f%%", round(d$value) + 0),
          textposition = ifelse(d$value < 0, "inside", "outside"),
          textfont = list(color = ifelse(d$value < 0, "white", "#404040")), cliponaxis = FALSE,
          hovertext = paste0(d$country, ": ", sprintf("%+.1f%%", d$value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
    plotly::layout(
      title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.95, yanchor = "top"),
      margin = list(t = 70, r = 60, b = b, l = 90),
      xaxis  = list(title = "", ticksuffix = "%", zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "gray"),
      yaxis  = list(title = ""),
      annotations = list(source_note(b)),
      font   = list(size = 13, color = "#404040")) %>%
    sized(h)
}

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Before the crisis: living on borrowed money
text:
Before the crisis: living on borrowed money


Code
peer_chart("current_account",
           title  = "Buying more from abroad than selling (-) or less (+), % of the economy",
           ytitle = "% of the economy", unit = "%", ref = 0, tozero = FALSE)






In the 2000s borrowing was cheap across the euro area, and for years Greece, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus bought far more from the rest of the world than they sold, borrowing the difference. In 2008 the gap was -14.6% of everything Greece produced, -14.4% in Cyprus and -11.9% in Portugal. When the 2008 financial crisis made lenders nervous, the money stopped coming, and each country had to close the gap fast. By 2013 every one of them was close to zero. Italy borrowed little from abroad and Ireland less than the others: their problems came from a government that already owed a lot (Italy) and from banks that had lent too much on houses (Ireland).
Five of the six then needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, the International Monetary Fund or both, and in return had to cut spending and raise taxes:

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Income: from almost double to still below
text:
Income: from almost double to still below
To compare countries of different sizes, each line starts at 100 in 2008: 110 means 10% more than in 2008, 90 means 10% less.


Code
peer_chart("income", index_year = 2008, ref = 100, tozero = FALSE,
           title  = "Income per person, 2008 = 100 (price rises removed)",
           ytitle = "2008 = 100")








Code
income_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("income", cty, 2008), at("income", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(income_change, "Income per person: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")






All six fell into the crisis, but they came out of it at very different speeds. By 2024 income per person was +91% in Ireland against 2008, +19% in Cyprus, +13% in Portugal, +8% in Spain and +3% in Italy. Greece is the only one still below 2008, at -10%: its fall was the deepest and its rescue the longest.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Ireland’s numbers need a second look
text:
Ireland’s numbers need a second look
Ireland’s line shoots up from 2015 because of how GDP is counted. GDP includes everything produced in the country, and many large international companies have made Ireland the base of their business for tax reasons, so their profits count as Irish production. Much of that money goes back to the companies’ owners abroad. GNI subtracts it and counts only the income that stays with people in Ireland:


Code
d <- df_peers %>%
  filter(country == "Ireland", measure %in% c("income", "income_gni"), year <= last_year, !is.na(value)) %>%
  mutate(what = ifelse(measure == "income", "GDP per person (everything produced)", "GNI per person (income that stays)"))

p <- plot_ly(d, x = ~year, y = ~value, color = ~what, colors = c("#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
             type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", marker = list(size = 7),
             text = ~paste0("Ireland · ", year, "<br>", what, ": $", big(value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  plotly::layout(title  = list(text = "Ireland: what is produced and what stays (US$ per person, price rises removed)",
                               x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
                 margin = list(t = 80, b = 150),
                 xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90),
                 yaxis  = list(title = "US$ per person", rangemode = "tozero"),
                 legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
                 annotations = list(source_note(150)),
                 font   = list(size = 13, color = "#404040"))
sized(p, 520)






In 2024 Ireland’s GDP per person was $94,475, but its GNI per person $67,024. Even GNI is lifted by these companies, which is why Ireland’s own statistics office publishes a third measure that removes them; the World Bank does not carry it. The same companies explain the strange jumps in Ireland’s investment and borrowing lines below, such as investment of 53% of the economy in 2019, the year some of them moved patents and other intangible assets to Ireland. Ireland did recover strongly — its unemployment is among the lowest of the six — but by less than its GDP suggests.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Jobs: the deepest wound
The unemployment rate counts people who want a job and are looking for one, but cannot find one.


Code
peer_chart("unemployment", unit = "%",
           title  = "People looking for work who cannot find it (%)",
           ytitle = "% of people looking for work")






In 2013, 28% of people looking for work in Greece and 26% in Spain could not find a job — more than 1 in 4. Among young people (15 to 24) it was 58% in Greece and 55% in Spain, more than half. Unemployment has fallen everywhere since, but not to the same level: by 2024 it was 4.3% in Ireland and 4.9% in Cyprus, against 10% in Greece and 11.4% in Spain.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Investment: Greece stopped building


Code
peer_chart("investment", unit = "%",
           title  = "Investment in buildings, machines and roads (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")






Investment fell in every country during the crisis. Most of them went back to around a fifth of what they produce, but Greece fell furthest — from 23% in 2008 to 12% in 2013 — and stayed there until 2019. In 2024 it was still 16%, the lowest of the six. A country that invests little for a decade has fewer new factories, machines and roads to earn from, which is one reason Greek incomes have been slowest to recover. (Ireland’s line jumps around for the reasons in the section above.)

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Exports: everyone sells more abroad


Code
peer_chart("exports", unit = "%",
           title  = "Exports of goods and services (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")








Code
exports_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) round(at("exports", cty, 2024) - at("exports", cty, 2008)))
ranked_bars(exports_change, "Exports: change from 2008 to 2024 (percentage points of the economy)")






The one thing all six did after the crisis was to sell more to the rest of the world. Greek exports went from 23% of the economy in 2008 to 42% in 2024, Portugal’s from 31% to 46%. The bar chart shows the change in percentage points: Greece’s exports grew by 19 points of its economy. Ireland’s exports are bigger than its whole economy, and Cyprus’s almost as big, because exports count the full value of what is sold, including parts that were imported first.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: People: who stayed and who left
text:
People: who stayed and who left


Code
population_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("population", cty, 2008), at("population", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(population_change, "Population: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")






During the crisis many people, often young and well educated, left to find work elsewhere. In the countries that recovered quickly, people came back and newcomers arrived: from 2008 to 2024 the population grew by 24% in Cyprus and 20% in Ireland. Greece’s shrank by 6%, also because Greek families have few children; Italy’s stayed about the same.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Comparing 2008 with 2024 with indicator_change()
golemworldbank’s indicator_change() compares every indicator a country has in two years — the same comparison as the app’s Change (%) tab. Running it for each country from 2008 to 2024 and keeping the indicators of this story gives one table of percentage changes:


Code
change_2008_2024 <- bind_rows(lapply(countries, function(cty) {
  res <- indicator_change(mfi, country = cty, year1 = 2008, year2 = 2024)
  both <- rbind(res$increased, res$decreased)
  both <- both[both$Indicator %in% indicators[names(indicators) != "current_account"], ]
  data.frame(measure = names(indicators)[match(both$Indicator, indicators)],
             country = cty, change = round(both$`Change %`))
}))

change_2008_2024 %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = change) %>%
  arrange(match(measure, names(indicators))) %>%
  as.data.frame()


             measure Greece Ireland Portugal Spain Cyprus Italy
1             income    -10      91       13     8     19     3
2         income_gni     -7      70       22    10     10     4
3       unemployment     31     -37      -14     1     30    -3
4 youth_unemployment      4     -23       31     9     51    -5
5         investment    -31     -30      -11   -27    -24     0
6            exports     85      71       47    45     94    21
7         population     -6      20        1     6     24     0


Each number is the percentage change from 2008 to 2024: income -10 for Greece means 10% less than in 2008. Unemployment, investment and exports are themselves percentages, so their change is relative to the 2008 level (unemployment in Ireland going from 6.8% to 4.3% is a change of -37%). Borrowing from abroad is left out: it is a number that can be below zero, and a percentage change of a negative number, or of one that turns from a minus into a plus, has no clear meaning.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
What the charts show


Code
snapshot <- df_peers %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2008, 2013, 2024), measure %in% c("income", "unemployment", "investment", "exports")) %>%
  mutate(value = round(value, 1)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = value) %>%
  arrange(match(measure, names(indicators)), year) %>%
  as.data.frame()
snapshot


        measure year  Cyprus  Greece Ireland   Italy Portugal   Spain
1        income 2008 27449.2 23923.9 49461.2 33550.6  20014.5 27112.5
2        income 2013 22711.7 17644.9 47928.0 30330.0  18597.7 24498.6
3        income 2024 32757.5 21494.7 94475.0 34508.1  22664.0 29245.2
4  unemployment 2008     3.8     7.7     6.8     6.7      7.6    11.3
5  unemployment 2013    16.1    27.7    13.7    12.1     16.2    26.1
6  unemployment 2024     4.9    10.0     4.3     6.5      6.5    11.4
7    investment 2008    27.2    23.3    24.8    21.6     22.9    27.9
8    investment 2013    14.1    11.5    18.3    17.3     14.8    17.6
9    investment 2024    20.5    16.0    17.3    21.5     20.4    20.3
10      exports 2008    50.1    22.8    84.3    26.7     31.3    25.5
11      exports 2013    61.3    30.3   109.7    28.2     39.6    32.8
12      exports 2024    97.0    42.1   144.0    32.3     45.8    37.1



The same start: before 2008, Greece, Cyprus, Portugal and Spain bought far more from abroad than they sold and borrowed the difference. When the borrowing stopped, all of them had to cut back at once.
Different endings: from 2008 to 2024 income per person rose by 91% in Ireland (less in reality, see GNI), 19% in Cyprus, 13% in Portugal, 8% in Spain and 3% in Italy, and fell by 10% in Greece.
Jobs came back everywhere, but Greece and Spain still have the highest unemployment of the six: 10% and 11.4% in 2024, against 4.3% to 6.5% in the other four.
Investment is where Greece differs most: it has invested the least of the six every year since 2010.
Exports grew in all six — the one recipe every country followed.
People voted with their feet: the countries that recovered fastest gained population, Greece lost it.

title: NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly
text: Attribution: This document is a modification of original work by hrbrmstr (Bob Rudis). The visualizations have been updated to use the most recent NASA GISS surface temperature data and adapted with additional chart types.

title: NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly
text:
Load Data


Code
library(highcharter)

df_nasa <- read.csv(
  "https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv",
  header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = "***", skip = 1
)

dfm <- df_nasa <- df_nasa[, c("Year", "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                               "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")]

dfma <- data.frame(
  Year   = df_nasa$Year,
  lower  = apply(dfm[, 2:length(dfm)], 1, min, na.rm = TRUE),
  upper  = apply(dfm[, 2:length(dfm)], 1, max, na.rm = TRUE),
  decade = paste0(substr(df_nasa$Year, 1, 3), 0)
)

dfr     <- reshape::melt(df_nasa, id.vars = "Year", variable_name = "month")
df_nasa <- merge(dfr, dfma, sort = FALSE)
df_nasa$month <- as.character(df_nasa$month)
df_nasa$year_mon <- paste0(
  df_nasa$Year, "-",
  stringr::str_pad(
    sapply(df_nasa$month, function(x) grep(paste("(?i)", x, sep = ""), month.abb)),
    2, pad = "0"
  ),
  "-01"
)
names(df_nasa) <- tolower(names(df_nasa))
df_nasa <- df_nasa[, c("year_mon", "value", "lower", "upper", "year", "decade", "month")]
df_nasa$decade <- as.numeric(df_nasa$decade)
df <- df_nasa[order(df_nasa$year_mon), ]

caption_text <- "Temperature deviation (°C) from the 1951–1980 baseline, combining land surface and ocean measurements (1880–2026). Negative values indicate cooler periods; positive values indicate warming. Recent years (2023–2024) exceed +1.2°C, approaching the Paris Agreement 1.5°C threshold. Source: NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4)."

title: NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly
text:
Prepare Series


Code
df <- dplyr::mutate(df,
  date    = lubridate::ymd(year_mon),
  tmpstmp = datetime_to_timestamp(date),
  year    = lubridate::year(date),
  month   = lubridate::month(date, label = TRUE),
  unite   = colorize(value, viridis::viridis(10, option = "B")),
  unite   = hex_to_rgba(unite, 0.65)
)

dfcolyrs <- df %>%
  dplyr::group_by(year) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(value = median(value)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    color_y = colorize(value, viridis::viridis(10, option = "B")),
    color_y = hex_to_rgba(color_y, 0.65)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-value)

df <- dplyr::left_join(df, dfcolyrs, by = "year")

lsseries <- df %>%
  dplyr::group_by(year) %>%
  dplyr::do(data = .$value, color = dplyr::first(.$color_y)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(name = year) %>%
  list_parse()

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
text:
Since ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022, more and more companies have said that they are cutting jobs because of artificial intelligence, and some of them have later had to hire people back. This page puts together the data there are on what happens then:

How many jobs are cut “because of AI”?
Does the labour market show a wave of AI layoffs?
How many of the people laid off are hired back, and how fast?
Does it save money?
What happened at Klarna, Commonwealth Bank of Australia and Ford?
What do employers and analysts say?
Why does it happen, and what can a company do instead?

The data are of four kinds, and they are not equally solid:

Counts of what happened: the layoffs and hires of the whole US economy, from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, downloaded from FRED when the document is knitted; and the records of 2.4 million employees, in which Visier counted how many of the people laid off were hired back by the same employer.
Counts of what companies said: the job cuts announced by US employers, with the reason they gave, counted by the outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
Surveys of HR professionals and business leaders: Careerminds, Orgvue and Gartner.
Forecasts of analysts: Forrester and Gartner.

Challenger, Visier and the surveys publish their figures in press releases and reports, not as datasets, so the figures are typed in below, and the page each one comes from is listed under Sources.
What these numbers can and cannot say. No source counts the people who were replaced by AI and then hired back. Challenger counts the reason a company gives for a cut, and “AI” may sound better to investors than “weak sales”. Visier counts people hired back after any layoff, not only after cuts blamed on AI. The surveys ask the people who made the decisions, and the firms that run them sell outplacement, people analytics or workforce planning. Together they show the size of what is happening and its direction, not exact numbers, and almost all of them are about the United States.

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages("plotly")
library(plotly)

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
text:
The data


Code
# a FRED series as dates and values; FRED leaves the months without a value empty
fred <- function(id) {
  url <- paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=", id)
  x <- tryCatch(read.csv(url),
                error = function(e) stop("Could not download ", id, " from FRED: ", conditionMessage(e), call. = FALSE))
  names(x) <- c("date", "value")
  x$date <- as.Date(x$date)
  x$value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x$value))
  x[!is.na(x$value), ]
}
# JOLTS, all US non-farm employers, seasonally adjusted, monthly: layoffs and discharges and hires as
# % of employment, and layoffs and discharges in thousands
layoffs_rate <- fred("JTSLDR")
hires_rate <- fred("JTSHIR")
layoffs <- fred("JTSLDL")

# job cuts announced by US employers, for all reasons and those for which the employer cited
# artificial intelligence; Challenger started counting AI as a reason in 2023. The AI cuts of 2024
# are not published on their own: they are the 71,825 AI cuts from 2023 to 2025 minus those of 2023
# and of 2025
challenger <- data.frame(
  period = c("2023", "2024", "2025", "2026, Jan-Oct"),
  from = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2024-01-01", "2025-01-01", "2026-01-01")),
  to = as.Date(c("2023-12-01", "2024-12-01", "2025-12-01", "2026-10-01")),
  ai = c(4247, 71825 - 4247 - 54836, 54836, 121401),
  all = c(721677, 761358, 1206374, 617189)
)
challenger$months <- 12 * (as.numeric(format(challenger$to, "%Y")) - as.numeric(format(challenger$from, "%Y"))) +
  as.numeric(format(challenger$to, "%m")) - as.numeric(format(challenger$from, "%m")) + 1
# the AI cuts of 2026 from the start of the year to the end of each month; the cuts of a month are the
# difference between two months
ai_2026 <- data.frame(
  month = seq(as.Date("2026-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 10),
  to_date = c(7624, 12304, 27645, 49135, 87714, 101743, 112713, 116175, 120136, 121401)
)
ai_2026$cuts <- diff(c(0, ai_2026$to_date))

# Visier: rehiring by the same employer after a layoff, in the records of 2.4 million employees of 142
# organisations (actual records, not a survey)
visier <- list(rehired = 5.3, months = "just under six", pay_back = 5, pay_stayed = 2,
               high_performers = 120, managers = 68)

# Careerminds: 600 HR professionals whose organisations made layoffs in the 12 months before
# February 2026. The share of the roles that were cut and then filled again, the time until they
# were filled again, and the money the layoffs saved after the rehiring, % of the HR professionals
roles_back <- data.frame(
  answer = c("The rest: under a quarter, or none", "A quarter to a half", "More than half"),
  share = c(100 - 32.7 - 35.6, 32.7, 35.6)
)
time_back <- data.frame(
  answer = c("Under 3 months", "3 to 6 months", "6 to 12 months", "Over 12 months"),
  share = c(17.8, 52.1, 27.8, 2.1)
)
money <- data.frame(
  answer = c("Rehiring cost more than the layoffs saved", "Broke even", "Came out ahead"),
  share = c(30.9, 42.37, 26.69)
)
careerminds <- list(lost_skills = 32.9, oversight = 54.6, fully_replaced = 21.4, some_replaced = 66.1,
                    worse = 12.3, repeat_unchanged = 8.4, never_discussed = 55.1,
                    redeploy_quarter = 51.3, redeploy_half = 28.3, ai_understanding = 53.8, skills_data = 40.6)




Code
red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(),
                  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = modifyList(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = modifyList(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")

# the answers to one survey question as horizontal bars, the first answer at the top, with the share
# at the end of each bar; color is one color, or one per answer
answers <- function(x, title, source, color = blue) {
  x$answer <- factor(x$answer, levels = rev(x$answer))
  plot_ly(x,
    x = ~share, y = ~answer, type = "bar", orientation = "h", marker = list(color = color),
    text = ~paste0(format(round(share, 1), nsmall = 1), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
    textfont = list(color = dark_gray), hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}%<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
    chart(title, source, x_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", range = c(0, max(x$share) * 1.2)),
          margin = list(l = 10, t = 70, b = 80), note_y = -0.25, bargap = 0.35) %>%
    layout(yaxis = list(automargin = TRUE))
}

# short labels of numbers
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
thousands <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
month_year <- function(d) format(d, "%B %Y")

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
section: 1. How many jobs are cut “because of AI”?
text:
1. How many jobs are cut “because of AI”?


Code
challenger$share <- 100 * challenger$ai / challenger$all
peak <- ai_2026[which.max(ai_2026$cuts), ]
last <- ai_2026[nrow(ai_2026), ]


More every year, from almost nothing. In 2023, the first year that Challenger counted it, US employers cited AI for 4,247 job cuts, 0.6% of all the cuts they announced. In 2025 they cited it for 54,836, 4.5% of all cuts, and in the first ten months of 2026 for 121,401, 20%: more than in the three years before put together. In the spring of 2026 AI was the reason that employers cited most often.


Code
plot_ly(challenger,
  x = ~factor(period, levels = period), y = ~ai, type = "bar", marker = list(color = blue),
  text = ~paste0(thousands(ai), "<br>", percent(share, 1), " of all cuts"), textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE, textfont = list(color = dark_gray),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:,} job cuts<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Job cuts for which US employers cited AI", "Challenger, Gray & Christmas, job cuts reports",
        y_axis = list(range = c(0, max(challenger$ai) * 1.25), tickformat = ","), bargap = 0.45)






But not a steady rise. The AI cuts of 2026 came in a few large announcements: 38,579 in May 2026, the most of any month since Challenger started counting, then fewer every month, down to 1,265 in October 2026.


Code
plot_ly(ai_2026,
  x = ~month, y = ~cuts, type = "bar", marker = list(color = blue),
  hovertemplate = "%{x|%B %Y}: %{y:,} job cuts<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("AI-cited job cuts by month, 2026", "Challenger, Gray & Christmas, job cuts reports",
        y_axis = list(tickformat = ","), x_axis = list(tickformat = "%b", dtick = "M1"), bargap = 0.3)






These are announcements and reasons given, not people who lost their job because a machine now does it. An announced cut can take months or years, or never happen, and a company that cuts jobs to save money can choose to say that AI made it possible. A Gartner analyst, Kathy Ross, said that most recent reductions “were influenced by broader economic conditions rather than automation alone”.

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
section: 2. Does the labour market show a wave of AI layoffs?
text:
2. Does the labour market show a wave of AI layoffs?


Code
latest_layoffs <- layoffs_rate[nrow(layoffs_rate), ]
latest_hires <- hires_rate[nrow(hires_rate), ]
before <- function(x) mean(x$value[x$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01") & x$date <= as.Date("2019-12-01")])
peak_layoffs <- layoffs_rate[which.max(layoffs_rate$value), ]


No. If companies were replacing many workers with AI, more people would lose their jobs. JOLTS counts every layoff and discharge in the US every month, and since ChatGPT came out the share of workers laid off or discharged in a month has stayed at about 1%: 1.0% in September 2026, against 1.2% on average in 2015 to 2019, before COVID-19. A real wave of layoffs looks like March 2020, when 8.6% of all workers were laid off in one month.
What has changed is hiring: 3.4% of workers were hired in September 2026, against 3.8% in 2015 to 2019. Companies are not firing more people; they are taking on fewer. A hiring freeze is also the quietest way to replace people with AI: no one is laid off, the people who leave are not replaced, and the work that they did goes to the software or to the people who stay.


Code
chatgpt <- as.Date("2022-11-30")
plot_ly() %>%
  add_lines(data = hires_rate, x = ~date, y = ~value, name = "Hires", line = list(color = blue, width = 2),
            hovertemplate = "%{x|%B %Y}: %{y:.1f}% of employment<extra>Hires</extra>") %>%
  add_lines(data = layoffs_rate, x = ~date, y = ~value, name = "Layoffs and discharges", line = list(color = red, width = 2),
            hovertemplate = "%{x|%B %Y}: %{y:.1f}% of employment<extra>Layoffs and discharges</extra>") %>%
  chart("US hires and layoffs in a month, % of employment", "US Bureau of Labor Statistics, JOLTS, via FRED (JTSHIR, JTSLDR)",
        y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top,
        shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = chatgpt, x1 = chatgpt, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper",
                           line = list(color = dark_gray, width = 1, dash = "dot"))),
        annotations = list(list(x = chatgpt, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "ChatGPT", xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top",
                                xshift = -4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))))






AI-cited cuts are a small part of all layoffs. Even in 2026, the job cuts for which employers cited AI were less than 1% of the people laid off or discharged in the US. The comparison is rough, as Challenger counts announcements and JOLTS counts people who left, and JOLTS also counts people fired for their work, but the difference is of a hundred times or more.


Code
# the AI cuts per month against the layoffs and discharges per month, over the months of each period
# that JOLTS has published
challenger$layoffs <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(challenger)), function(i) {
  1000 * mean(layoffs$value[layoffs$date >= challenger$from[i] & layoffs$date <= challenger$to[i]])
})
challenger$of_layoffs <- 100 * (challenger$ai / challenger$months) / challenger$layoffs
plot_ly(challenger,
  x = ~factor(period, levels = period), y = ~of_layoffs, type = "bar", marker = list(color = blue),
  text = ~percent(of_layoffs, 2), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE, textfont = list(color = dark_gray),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.2f}%<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Job cuts citing AI, % of all layoffs and discharges in the US", "Challenger, Gray & Christmas; BLS, JOLTS, via FRED (JTSLDL)",
        y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", range = c(0, max(challenger$of_layoffs) * 1.25)), bargap = 0.45)

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
section: 3. How many are hired back, and how fast?
text:
3. How many are hired back, and how fast?
“Hired back” means two different things, and the data on them are very different:

The same person comes back. In the records of 2.4 million employees, Visier found that about 5.3% of the people laid off were later hired again by the employer that laid them off, after just under six months on average. This is after any layoff, not only those blamed on AI. The people who come back are not a random group: high performers were rehired 120% more often than others, and managers 68% more often than employees who manage no one. The company calls back the people it most needs.
The job is filled again, by the same person or by someone else, perhaps with another title, at a lower wage, through an agency or in another country. This is what the surveys ask about, and it is much more common. Of 600 HR professionals whose organisations had made layoffs in the previous year, 35.6% said that their organisation had filled again more than half of the roles it cut, and 32.7% between a quarter and a half.



Code
answers(roles_back, "Roles cut and then filled again, % of HR professionals", "Careerminds, survey of 600 HR professionals, February 2026")






And fast. Of the organisations that filled the roles again, 69.9% did so within six months of the cuts, 17.8% within three.


Code
answers(time_back, "Time until the roles were filled again, % of HR professionals", "Careerminds, survey of 600 HR professionals, February 2026")

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
text:
4. Does it save money?
For most, it did not. Asked what the layoffs saved once the roles had been filled again, 30.9% of the HR professionals said that the rehiring cost more than the layoffs saved, and 42.4% that they broke even. Only 26.7% came out ahead.


Code
answers(money, "Savings after the rehiring, % of HR professionals",
        "Careerminds, survey of 600 HR professionals, February 2026", color = c(red, gray, blue))






The reason is simple arithmetic. Cutting a job saves its pay for every month that it stays empty, but the cut and the rehiring cost money once: the severance pay, the recruiting and the onboarding, the months before the new person does the job well, and, for people who come back, a higher wage. Visier found that the people hired back got a pay rise of 5%, against 2% for those who had stayed. If the job is filled again soon, the months of pay saved do not cover these costs.
The model below makes that concrete. Its numbers are assumptions, not data: every cost is in months of the pay of the job that is cut, so that it fits any job and any country. Change them to fit a real case.


Code
severance <- 2           # months of pay paid when the job is cut; depends on the country and the years of service
hiring <- 1              # recruiting, interviews and onboarding when the job is filled again
ramp_up <- 3 * 0.5       # the new person does half the work in the first 3 months
premium <- 12 * 0.05     # a 5% higher wage for a year, the rise that Visier found for people hired back
ai_cost <- 0.10          # what the AI costs per month, as a share of the pay that the cut saves
one_off <- severance + hiring + ramp_up + premium
saving <- data.frame(months = 0:24)
saving$net <- saving$months * (1 - ai_cost) - one_off
break_even <- one_off / (1 - ai_cost)


With these assumptions the cut costs 5.1 months of pay once, and saves 0.9 of a month’s pay for every month that the job stays empty. A job filled again in less than 5.7 months costs more than it saves, and the shaded area shows that, in the Careerminds survey, 70% of the roles were filled again in the first six months.


Code
plot_ly(saving,
  x = ~months, y = ~net, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = blue, width = 2),
  hovertemplate = "Filled again after %{x} months: %{y:.1f} months of pay<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("What a job cut saves, by the months until the job is filled again", "the assumptions of the model above",
        y_title = "Months of pay saved (net)", x_axis = list(title = "Months until the job is filled again", dtick = 3),
        y_axis = list(zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = dark_gray),
        shapes = list(list(type = "rect", x0 = 0, x1 = 6, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper",
                           fillcolor = gray, opacity = 0.15, line = list(width = 0))),
        annotations = list(
          list(x = 3, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = paste0("Filled again within 6 months:<br>",
                                                           percent(time_back$share[1] + time_back$share[2]), " of the roles"),
               yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)),
          list(x = break_even, y = 0, text = paste("Break-even:", one(break_even), "months"), ax = 70, ay = 35, xanchor = "left",
               arrowcolor = dark_gray, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray))),
        margin = list(t = 70, b = 110), note_y = -0.3)






The model leaves out the costs that are hardest to count, and the next section shows that they can be the larger part: service that gets worse, overtime for the people who stayed, and knowledge that left with the people who were let go. In the Careerminds survey, 32.9% said that their organisation lost critical skills and expertise with the layoffs. It also leaves out the cheaper ways of filling a job again, with lower pay or in another country, which make the cut save more.

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
text:
5. Three cases


Code
cases <- data.frame(
  Company = c("Klarna (payments, Sweden)", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia", "Ford (cars, US)"),
  `What it did` = c(
    "Stopped hiring anyone but engineers in December 2023. In February 2024 it said that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 full-time customer service agents, most of whom worked for outside providers. Its staff fell from 5,441 in 2022 to 4,201 in 2023.",
    "In July 2025 it told the union that 45 customer service jobs were no longer needed, because a new AI voice bot had reduced the calls.",
    "Relied \"more and more on automated quality systems\" to find faults in its cars."
  ),
  `What happened` = c(
    "In May 2025 its CEO said that cost had been \"a too predominant evaluation factor\" and the result was \"lower quality\". Klarna started hiring people for customer service again, and now says that human service will be \"a VIP thing\", while AI answers the simple questions.",
    "The union said that the calls had in fact increased, and that the staff were doing overtime and team leaders were answering phones. It took the case to the Fair Work Commission. In August 2025 the bank said that it had been wrong, apologised, and kept the jobs.",
    "In June 2026 it said that it had hired 350 veteran engineers, some of them former Ford employees and others from its suppliers, to find faults before parts reach the plant, to train younger engineers and to reprogram its AI tools. Ford keeps using AI."
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(cases, caption = "Companies that replaced people with AI and then needed people again")



Companies that replaced people with AI and then needed people again







Company
What it did
What happened




Klarna (payments, Sweden)
Stopped hiring anyone but engineers in December 2023. In February 2024 it said that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 full-time customer service agents, most of whom worked for outside providers. Its staff fell from 5,441 in 2022 to 4,201 in 2023.
In May 2025 its CEO said that cost had been “a too predominant evaluation factor” and the result was “lower quality”. Klarna started hiring people for customer service again, and now says that human service will be “a VIP thing”, while AI answers the simple questions.


Commonwealth Bank of Australia
In July 2025 it told the union that 45 customer service jobs were no longer needed, because a new AI voice bot had reduced the calls.
The union said that the calls had in fact increased, and that the staff were doing overtime and team leaders were answering phones. It took the case to the Fair Work Commission. In August 2025 the bank said that it had been wrong, apologised, and kept the jobs.


Ford (cars, US)
Relied “more and more on automated quality systems” to find faults in its cars.
In June 2026 it said that it had hired 350 veteran engineers, some of them former Ford employees and others from its suppliers, to find faults before parts reach the plant, to train younger engineers and to reprogram its AI tools. Ford keeps using AI.





The three cases are different from each other, and each is different from the headline “fired for AI, hired back”:

Klarna did not fire 700 people: most of its customer service agents worked for outside providers, and the company shrank mainly by not hiring. What failed was the quality of the service, and the CEO said so.
Commonwealth Bank measured the wrong thing. The bot answered some calls, but the work did not go away: it went to the people who stayed.
Ford did not say that it had laid these engineers off because of AI. Its case is about knowledge: the experience of veteran engineers was not in the data from which its automated systems learned, and Ford needed people who had it.

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
section: 6. What do employers and analysts say?
text:
6. What do employers and analysts say?


Code
surveys <- data.frame(
  Source = c("Orgvue", "Careerminds", "Gartner", "Gartner", "Forrester"),
  Date = c("April 2025", "February 2026", "October 2025", "March 2026", "November 2025"),

    "Only about 20% had reduced their number of customer service agents because of AI; most kept them stable.",

The surveys agree on the direction: many of the companies that cut jobs for AI regret it, and many fill the jobs again. The two forecasts agree on what happens next: the jobs come back in another form, with other titles, at lower pay or in another country. Neither form shows up as a company “hiring back the people it replaced”, which is one reason why the counts of rehiring are low and the counts of roles filled again are high.

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
section: 7. Why does it happen, and what can a company do instead?
text:
7. Why does it happen, and what can a company do instead?
Why it happens:

AI does tasks, but companies cut jobs. Almost every job has a part that AI does well and a part that it does not. In the Careerminds survey, only 21.4% said that AI fully replaced the roles with no problems; 66.1% said that it replaced some of them, and 54.6% that the layoffs were not worth it because of the human oversight the AI needed.
Decisions are made on promises, not on results. 53.8% said that they would have decided better with a clearer understanding of what AI could do.
Cost is measured, quality is not. Klarna’s CEO said so in as many words, and Commonwealth Bank counted the calls that the bot answered, not the work that was left.
Knowledge that is not written down leaves with the people. AI learns from the data it is given, and the experience of people who know the exceptions, the customers and the history is rarely in those data. This is what Ford found.
“AI” is sometimes only the label. A cut made to save money can be announced as a cut made possible by AI, and the work comes back when it turns out that someone still has to do it.

What a company can do instead:

Split each job into tasks before cutting jobs, and cut only where AI can do the whole job, or join the parts that remain into new jobs.
Run the AI next to the people first, for long enough, and measure quality, mistakes, the work that is left and customer satisfaction, not only cost and speed.
Move people instead of letting them go. 55.1% of the HR professionals said that moving people to other roles was never formally discussed, and 51.3% that up to a quarter of the roles cut could have been redeployed (28.3% said a quarter to a half). Knowing the skills of the people who are already there makes this possible: 40.6% said that they would have needed more data on skills.
Keep the knowledge: write down how the work is done, and keep a core of experienced people who can train others and correct the AI.
If people must go, let them go well. The people a company most often hires back are its high performers and managers, and they come back only if they left on good terms.

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
text:
So, what happens?

More and more job cuts are blamed on AI: 121,401 in the first ten months of 2026, 20% of all job cuts announced in the US, against 4,247 in all of 2023.
But there is no wave of layoffs: the share of US workers laid off in a month is still about 1%, as before ChatGPT, and AI-cited cuts are less than 1% of all layoffs. What has fallen is hiring.
The same people rarely come back, about 5.3% of those laid off, but the jobs often do: two in three organisations that made layoffs filled at least a quarter of the roles again, most of them within six months.
It usually does not save money: once the roles were filled again, 73% of the organisations had saved nothing or lost money. A job filled again within a few months costs more than it saves, before counting the service, the overtime and the knowledge that were lost.
The jobs come back changed: with other titles, at lower pay, through agencies or in other countries, which is what both Gartner and Forrester expect.

The data are thin: one count of announcements, one count of people hired back, and surveys run by firms with an interest in the answer. But they point the same way: replacing people with AI before the AI can do the whole job tends to cost a company twice, once to let people go and once to get the work done again.

title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
text:
Sources

US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS), via FRED: JTSHIR (hires rate), JTSLDR (layoffs and discharges rate), JTSLDL (layoffs and discharges, level).
Challenger, Gray & Christmas, job cuts reports: December 2023, December 2024, 2025 year-end, May 2026, June 2026, August 2026, October 2026; the AI cuts from the start of 2026 to the end of January, February, March, April, July and September as reported by HRD America, which match Challenger’s own figures for the other months.
Visier, The true cost of layoff boomerangs (February 2026) and The Layoff Boomerang Report (November 2025).
Careerminds, AI-led layoffs: what HR leaders wish they knew before making job cuts (February 2026). The headings of the page give some rounded or combined figures (75% cost more than they saved, 52.1% within six months) that do not match its own charts; this page uses the figures of the charts.
Orgvue, as reported by HR Dive and TechRadar (April 2025).
Gartner, as reported by TechRepublic (March 2026) and CX Today (June 2025).
Forrester, Predictions 2026: The Workforce Muddles Through Ambient Disruption (November 2025).
Klarna: CX Today, February 2024, CX Today, May 2025, TechCrunch, June 2025.
Commonwealth Bank of Australia: The Register, Bloomberg (August 2025).
Ford: TechCrunch (June 2026).

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
1. Find the station
NOAA ISD identifies stations by USAF and WBAN codes. The easiest way to find them is by ICAO airport code.


Code
stations <- isd_stations(refresh = FALSE)

# explore Greek stations
stations[stations$ctry %in% "GR", c("station_name","icao","usaf","wban","lat","lon")]

lgav    <- stations[stations$icao %in% "LGAV", ]
station <- lgav$station_name
usaf    <- lgav$usaf[1]
wban    <- lgav$wban[1]

message("Station : ", station)

Change "LGAV" to any ICAO code — "EGLL" for Heathrow, "KJFK" for New York, etc.

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
2. Download hourly ISD data
rnoaa::isd() replaces the old wget + FTP workflow. It downloads, decompresses, and parses the ISD binary format automatically. Each call fetches one year; a loop collects all years into a list.


Code
years     <- 2001:2026
data_list <- list()

for (yr in years) {
  tryCatch({
    d <- rnoaa::isd(usaf = usaf, wban = wban, year = yr, progress = FALSE)
    data_list[[as.character(yr)]] <- d
    message("  downloaded ", yr, " (", nrow(d), " rows)")
  }, error = function(e) message("  skip ", yr, ": ", conditionMessage(e)))
}

df_raw <- bind_rows(data_list)
message("Total rows: ", nrow(df_raw))



Years where data are unavailable are silently skipped by tryCatch. 2026 data may be partial depending on when you run this.

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
section: 3. Clean: sentinel values and date parsing
text:
3. Clean: sentinel values and date parsing

Why sentinel values matter
NOAA ISD encodes missing measurements as 9999 in the raw file. After dividing by 10 (ISD stores all values as tenths of the unit), missing temperature becomes 999.9°C — a physically impossible value that will corrupt any aggregate (mean, max, min) if not removed.


Code
df_data <- df_raw |>
  mutate(
    date     = as.Date(date, format = "%Y%m%d"),   # isd() returns "YYYYMMDD" strings
    temp     = as.numeric(temperature) / 10,
    dew      = as.numeric(temperature_dewpoint) / 10,
    wind_spd = as.numeric(wind_speed) / 10,
    slp      = as.numeric(air_pressure) / 10
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(temp, dew, wind_spd, slp),
                ~ ifelse(. > 900 | . < -200, NA, .))) |>
  filter(!is.na(date))

df_data[df_data == 999.9] <- NA          # catch any remaining sentinels
df_data$month <- sub("-\\d{2}$", "", df_data$date)   # "YYYY-MM" column


Two-pass sentinel removal:

ifelse(. > 900 | . < -200, NA, .) — catches the scaled sentinels immediately after division
df_data[df_data == 999.9] <- NA — safety net for any that slipped through

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
4. Daily and monthly aggregates
plyr::ddply with numcolwise applies a function (here max or min) to every numeric column, grouped by date or month. Columns are then renamed with _max / _min suffixes before merging.


Code
daily_max <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "date",  plyr::numcolwise(max, na.rm = TRUE))
daily_min <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "date",  plyr::numcolwise(min, na.rm = TRUE))
month_max <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "month", plyr::numcolwise(max, na.rm = TRUE))
month_min <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "month", plyr::numcolwise(min, na.rm = TRUE))

names(daily_max)[2:length(daily_max)] <- paste0(names(daily_max)[2:length(daily_max)], "_max")
names(daily_min)[2:length(daily_min)] <- paste0(names(daily_min)[2:length(daily_min)], "_min")
names(month_max)[2:length(month_max)] <- paste0(names(month_max)[2:length(month_max)], "_max")
names(month_min)[2:length(month_min)] <- paste0(names(month_min)[2:length(month_min)], "_min")

daily <- merge(daily_max, daily_min)
month <- merge(month_max, month_min)

daily$date       <- as.Date(daily$date)
month$month_date <- as.Date(paste0(month$month, "-01"))
month            <- month[order(month$month_date), ]

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
5. Plots

Daily temperature ribbon
geom_ribbon fills the area between the daily min and max. The fill colour is mapped to temp_max through a diverging gradient — cold days are blue, hot days are red.


Code
plot_daily <- ggplot(daily, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = temp_min, ymax = temp_max, fill = temp_max), alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#2166ac","#74add1","#fee090","#f46d43","#a50026"),
    name    = "Max °C"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "white", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = str_aes(station),
    subtitle = "Daily temperature range",
    x        = NULL, y = "Temperature (°C)",
    caption  = "Source: NOAA ISD via rnoaa"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
  )

plot_daily











Monthly ribbon
Aggregating to monthly level removes the noise and makes the seasonal pattern clearer. The max temperature gets a coloured gradient line; the min stays white.


Code
plot_monthly <- ggplot(month, aes(x = month_date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = temp_min, ymax = temp_max), fill = "#74add1", alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(aes(y = temp_max, color = temp_max), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = temp_min), color = "white", linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_gradientn(
    colours = c("#2166ac","#74add1","#fee090","#f46d43","#a50026"),
    name    = "Max °C"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "white", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = str_aes(station),
    subtitle = "Monthly temperature range",
    x        = NULL, y = "Temperature (°C)",
    caption  = "Source: NOAA ISD via rnoaa"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
  )

plot_monthly











Heatmaps
A calendar heatmap puts year on the x-axis and month on the y-axis, with temperature encoded as fill colour. This format is ideal for spotting anomalies — an unusually hot August or a cold February stands out immediately.


Code
month$year <- substr(month$month, 1, 4)
month$mon  <- substr(month$month, 6, 7)

plot_heat_max <- ggplot(month, aes(x = year, y = mon, fill = temp_max)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(temp_max, 1), "°C")),
            color = "grey20", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low      = "#256abf", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#e34948",
    midpoint = median(month$temp_max, na.rm = TRUE),
    name     = "°C"

plot_heat_min <- ggplot(month, aes(x = year, y = mon, fill = temp_min)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(temp_min, 1), "°C")),
            color = "grey20", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low      = "#256abf", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#e34948",

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
6. Seasonal decomposition
decompose() splits a time series into three additive components:

Trend — the long-term direction (is the station getting warmer?)
Seasonal — the repeating annual cycle (summer peaks, winter troughs)
Random — what’s left after removing trend and seasonal (unusual events, measurement noise)

The frequency = 365 tells R the series repeats annually. yday() sets the correct starting position within the first year.


Code
ts_temp <- ts(
  daily$temp_max,
  frequency = 365,
  start     = c(year(min(daily$date)), yday(min(daily$date)))
)

fit <- decompose(ts_temp)

autoplot(fit) +
  labs(title = paste("Seasonal decomposition —", str_aes(station), "daily max")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)










Reading the decomposition: If the trend panel slopes upward over 20+ years, that is a local warming signal. The random panel should look like white noise — large spikes indicate extreme weather events.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
text:
Summers in Athens feel hotter than they used to. This data story checks that feeling against the measurements of one weather station, which has measured the highest and the lowest temperature of the day since 1955, with some gaps, and asks five questions:

Is Athens hotter than it used to be?
How many hot days does a summer have?
Do the nights still cool down?
Is the hot season longer?
Which were the worst heatwaves?

The station is at Hellinikon, on the coast south of the city centre, where Athens had its airport until 2001. Its record comes from NOAA, the US agency for weather and climate data, which publishes it in the Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCN-Daily), an archive of daily measurements from weather stations around the world (Menne et al. 2012). It is downloaded when the page is knitted, so the charts show the latest days in NOAA’s archive.
The words of this page:

a hot day reaches 35 °C or more, and a very hot day 40 °C or more;
on a tropical night the temperature stays above 20 °C, as in the climate change indices of the ETCCDI, an international team of experts; on a very warm night it stays above 25 °C;
a heatwave is three days or more in a row above 37 °C (section 5 says why 37);
summer is June, July and August.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "RColorBrewer"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
text:
The data

One station since 1955
GHCN-Daily lists its stations with where they are, and in the Athens area it has only one: Hellinikon, station GR000016716. It is also what this story needs, a long record from one place. The new airport, Eleftherios Venizelos, replaced Hellinikon in 2001 (Wikipedia), so its own record is much shorter, and joining the two would join two different places. The station at Hellinikon kept measuring after the airport moved.
NOAA keeps one file per station, with a row for each day:


Code
station <- "GR000016716" # Athens Hellinikon
ghcnd_url <- paste0(
  "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/global-historical-climatology-network-daily/access/",
  station,
  ".csv"
)
raw <- read.csv(ghcnd_url)
head(raw[, c("DATE", "TMAX", "TMAX_ATTRIBUTES", "TMIN", "TMIN_ATTRIBUTES")])


        DATE TMAX TMAX_ATTRIBUTES TMIN TMIN_ATTRIBUTES
1 1955-01-01  185             ,,I  102             ,,E
2 1955-01-02  144             ,,I   70             ,,E
3 1955-01-03  158             ,,I   96             ,,E
4 1955-01-04  188             ,,I   73             ,,E
5 1955-01-05  179             ,,I   84             ,,E
6 1955-01-06  195             ,,I   90             ,,E


TMAX and TMIN are the highest and the lowest temperature of the day, in tenths of a degree. Each comes with three flags, separated by commas (NOAA’s description of the flags): how it was measured, whether it failed one of NOAA’s quality checks, and where NOAA got it. The values that failed a check are left out, and the days missing from the file are added as empty rows:


Code
# the three flags of a value are "measurement,quality,source": a quality flag means that the value
# failed one of NOAA's checks, and the source flag says where NOAA got it
quality_flag <- function(attributes) sub("^[^,]*,([^,]*),.*$", "\\1", attributes)
source_flag <- function(attributes) sub("^.*,", "", attributes)

days <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(raw$DATE),
  tmax = raw$TMAX / 10,
  tmin = raw$TMIN / 10,
  tmax_source = source_flag(raw$TMAX_ATTRIBUTES),
  tmin_source = source_flag(raw$TMIN_ATTRIBUTES)
)
failed_max <- !is.na(days$tmax) & quality_flag(raw$TMAX_ATTRIBUTES) != ""
failed_min <- !is.na(days$tmin) & quality_flag(raw$TMIN_ATTRIBUTES) != ""
days$tmax[failed_max] <- NA
days$tmin[failed_min] <- NA
cbind(left_out = c(maximum = sum(failed_max), minimum = sum(failed_min)))


        left_out
maximum       12
minimum       13


Code
# every day from the first to the last day with a temperature, the missing ones as empty rows
measured <- days$date[!is.na(days$tmax) | !is.na(days$tmin)]
first_day <- min(measured)
last_day <- max(measured)
days <- merge(data.frame(date = seq(first_day, last_day, by = "day")), days, all.x = TRUE)
days$year <- as.integer(format(days$date, "%Y"))
days$month <- as.integer(format(days$date, "%m"))

# for the text: "1 January 1955" in English, whatever the language of the computer, numbers with
# one or two decimals, and lists such as "2021, 2024 and 2025"
date_text <- function(d) {
  paste(as.integer(format(d, "%d")), month.name[as.integer(format(d, "%m"))], format(d, "%Y"))
}
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}


So the record runs from 1 January 1955 to 24 August 2025, the latest day that NOAA has for this station. NOAA checks the values but does not correct them for new instruments or new ways of measuring (NOAA): the record is what the station measured.


Three sources, one record
NOAA put the record together from three sources:


Code
source_names <- c(
  I = "NOAA's International collection",
  E = "European Climate Assessment & Dataset",
  S = "Global Summary of the Day"
)
# from when to when each source gives a measure, and for how many days
from_source <- function(value, source, measure) {
  data.frame(date = days$date, value = value, source = source) |>
    filter(!is.na(value)) |>
    group_by(source) |>
    summarise(from = min(date), to = max(date), days = n()) |>
    arrange(from) |>
    mutate(measure = measure, source = source_names[source])
}
sources <- rbind(
  from_source(days$tmax, days$tmax_source, "Maximum"),
  from_source(days$tmin, days$tmin_source, "Minimum")
)
knitr::kable(
  sources[, c("measure", "source", "from", "to", "days")],
  col.names = c("Measure", "Source", "From", "To", "Days")
)

Code
# the first day of each measure from the Global Summary of the Day, and the year before it
gsod_from <- c(
  maximum = min(days$date[days$tmax_source %in% "S" & !is.na(days$tmax)]),
  minimum = min(days$date[days$tmin_source %in% "S" & !is.na(days$tmin)])
)
year_before <- as.integer(format(gsod_from, "%Y")) - 1
names(year_before) <- names(gsod_from)


Until 2000 the maximum comes from NOAA’s International collection, data that weather services sent to NOAA, and until 2022 the minimum from the European Climate Assessment & Dataset (Klein Tank et al. 2002). After that, both come from the reports that the station sends every hour or every few hours to the weather services of the world, as NOAA’s Global Summary of the Day (GSOD) collects them.
A change of source can put a step into a record, the same as moving a station. But GSOD also has the station’s reports for the years before, so in the last year before each change the two can be compared, day by day:


Code
# GSOD of the same station (167160 99999) for a year: degrees Fahrenheit, 9999.9 when missing. A
# "*" flag marks a value worked out from the readings of the day instead of reported: left out
gsod <- function(year) {
  x <- read.csv(paste0(
    "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/global-summary-of-the-day/access/",
    year,
    "/16716099999.csv"
  ))
  reported <- function(value, flag) ifelse(value > 9000 | trimws(flag) == "*", NA, value)
  data.frame(
    date = as.Date(x$DATE),
    gsod_max = (reported(x$MAX, x$MAX_ATTRIBUTES) - 32) * 5 / 9,
    gsod_min = (reported(x$MIN, x$MIN_ATTRIBUTES) - 32) * 5 / 9
  )
}
gsod_years <- lapply(setNames(unique(year_before), unique(year_before)), gsod)

# the two sources on the days that both have: the average gap between them, and the days on
# which they are more than 1 °C apart
compare <- function(measure) {
  year <- year_before[[measure]]
  both <- merge(days, gsod_years[[as.character(year)]], by = "date")
  gap <- if (measure == "maximum") both$gsod_max - both$tmax else both$gsod_min - both$tmin
  data.frame(
    measure = measure,
    year = year,
    days = sum(!is.na(gap)),
    average_gap = mean(abs(gap), na.rm = TRUE),
    apart = sum(abs(gap) > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
overlap <- rbind(compare("maximum"), compare("minimum"))
knitr::kable(
  overlap,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Year", "Days in both", "Average gap (°C)", "Days over 1 °C apart")
)

They are the same measurements: on the days that both have, they differ by 0.07 °C or less on average, and by more than 1 °C on 7 days out of 546. The change of source is not a step in the record.


A check without gaps: ERA5-Land
One station can mislead: the place around it changes, and it misses days. So this story also downloads ERA5-Land, a reconstruction of the weather of every day since 1950 by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (Muñoz-Sabater et al. 2021; data: Muñoz Sabater 2019). It is a model of the land surface, driven by the weather of ERA5, the Centre’s reconstruction of the weather of the whole world, and it does not use the measurements of any station directly. It describes squares of land 9 km across, so it cannot see what happens around one station: it is a check on the station, not a replacement for it. It comes through the historical weather API of Open-Meteo (Zippenfenig 2023), for the nearest point of its grid that Open-Meteo counts as land:


Code
# ERA5-Land through Open-Meteo, from the station's first day to yesterday, as one CSV file: two
# lines about the point of the grid, an empty line, then the days
era5_url <- paste0(
  "https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive",
  "?latitude=",
  raw$LATITUDE[1],
  "&longitude=",
  raw$LONGITUDE[1],
  "&start_date=",
  first_day,
  "&end_date=",
  Sys.Date() - 1,
  "&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min",
  "&timezone=Europe%2FAthens&models=era5_land&format=csv"
)
era5_lines <- readLines(era5_url)
era5_point <- read.csv(text = era5_lines[1:2])
era5 <- read.csv(text = era5_lines[-(1:3)], col.names = c("date", "tmax", "tmin"))
era5 <- era5[!is.na(era5$tmax) & !is.na(era5$tmin), ] # the last few days are not ready yet
era5$date <- as.Date(era5$date)
era5$year <- as.integer(format(era5$date, "%Y"))
era5$month <- as.integer(format(era5$date, "%m"))
era5_point[, c("latitude", "longitude", "elevation")]


  latitude longitude elevation
1     37.9      23.8        62


Code
# the average temperature of each whole summer, day and night together
era5_summers <- era5 |>
  filter(month %in% 6:8) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(summer = mean((tmax + tmin) / 2), days = n()) |>
  filter(days == 92)




Missing days


Code
enough <- 0.8 # the share of a season's days that must have a measurement

# for each year: the share of its summer days with a maximum, with both a maximum and a minimum,
# and of its days from May to October with a minimum; the average temperature of its summer, and
# its hot days, very hot days, tropical nights and very warm nights
years <- days |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    summer_max = sum(!is.na(tmax[month %in% 6:8])) / 92,
    summer_both = sum(!is.na(tmax[month %in% 6:8] + tmin[month %in% 6:8])) / 92,
    warm_season_min = sum(!is.na(tmin[month %in% 5:10])) / 184,
    summer = mean((tmax[month %in% 6:8] + tmin[month %in% 6:8]) / 2, na.rm = TRUE),
    hot = sum(tmax >= 35, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_hot = sum(tmax >= 40, na.rm = TRUE),
    tropical = sum(tmin > 20, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_warm = sum(tmin > 25, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    summer = ifelse(summer_both >= enough, summer, NA),
    hot = ifelse(summer_max >= enough, hot, NA),
    very_hot = ifelse(summer_max >= enough, very_hot, NA),
    tropical = ifelse(warm_season_min >= enough, tropical, NA),
    very_warm = ifelse(warm_season_min >= enough, very_warm, NA)
  )

# the year with the fewest days with a maximum
max_days <- days |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(days = sum(!is.na(tmax)))
fewest <- max_days[which.min(max_days$days), ]

left_out <- function(x) and_list(years$year[is.na(x)])
dropped <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Summer average", "Hot days", "Tropical nights"),
  needs = c(
    "June to August, maximum and minimum",
    "June to August, maximum",
    "May to October, minimum"
  ),
  kept = c(sum(!is.na(years$summer)), sum(!is.na(years$hot)), sum(!is.na(years$tropical))),
  left_out = c(left_out(years$summer), left_out(years$hot), left_out(years$tropical))
)


The weak point of the record is its gaps. The station’s reports often leave out the maximum of the day: in 2013, only 4 days have one. A year with many missing days would seem to have fewer hot days than it had, so a year counts only if at least 80% of its days in the season that matters have a measurement: June to August for the summer average and the hot days, May to October for the warm nights, when almost all of them come. Of the 71 years from 1955 to 2025, this leaves out 9 for the summer average, 9 for the hot days and 4 for the tropical nights:


Code
knitr::kable(
  dropped,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Days that must have a measurement", "Years kept", "Years left out")
)
