Code
# ERA5-Land has every day: for each summer kept, its average over the days that the station has,
# against its average over all the days of the summer
measured_summer <- days$date[days$month %in% 6:8 & !is.na(days$tmax + days$tmin)]
shift <- era5 |>
  filter(month %in% 6:8, year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$summer)]) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    all_days = mean((tmax + tmin) / 2),
    station_days = mean(((tmax + tmin) / 2)[date %in% measured_summer])
  )
largest_shift <- max(abs(shift$station_days - shift$all_days))


How much can the missing days change the average of a summer? ERA5-Land has every day, so it can tell: for each summer kept, its average over the days that the station has is at most 0.2 °C away from its average over all the days of that summer. Counts are another matter: a missing day may hide a hot day or a tropical night, so the counts of the years with missing days are, if anything, too low.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
section: 1. Is Athens hotter than it used to be?
text:
1. Is Athens hotter than it used to be?


Code
# three periods: 1961-1990, the usual reference for the climate of a place, and the two after it
last_year <- max(years$year)
recent <- paste0("2011–", last_year)
period_of <- function(year) {
  cut(year, c(1960, 1990, 2010, last_year), labels = c("1961–1990", "1991–2010", recent))
}
years$period <- period_of(years$year)
by_period <- years |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    summers = sum(!is.na(summer)),
    summer_average = mean(summer, na.rm = TRUE),
    hot_years = sum(!is.na(hot)),
    hot_days = mean(hot, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_hot_days = sum(very_hot, na.rm = TRUE),
    night_years = sum(!is.na(tropical)),
    tropical_nights = mean(tropical, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_warm_nights = mean(very_warm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
base <- by_period$summer_average[1]
now <- by_period$summer_average[3]


Yes. The summers of 2011–2025 were 2.4 °C warmer than those of 1961–1990.
Each stripe below is one summer, from 1955 on the left to 2025 on the right, coloured by its average temperature, day and night together: blue for the cooler summers, red for the warmer ones. They follow Ed Hawkins’ warming stripes (#ShowYourStripes), which show in the same way how the world, a country or a city has warmed. As there, the colours change from blue to red at the average of 1961–2010, and reach their darkest three standard deviations away from it, a measure of how much summers differ from one another (theirs is that of 1901–2000, here it is that of 1961–2010): here 2.8 °C below and above 26.6 °C. Grey stripes are the summers with too many missing days.


Code
reference <- years$summer[years$year %in% 1961:2010]
centre <- mean(reference, na.rm = TRUE)
spread <- sd(reference, na.rm = TRUE)
# 8 blues and 8 reds of ColorBrewer, from the coolest to the warmest
stripe_colours <- c(
  rev(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(9, "Blues")[-1]),
  RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(9, "Reds")[-1]
)
# from 3 standard deviations below the centre to 3 above, in 16 steps
z <- pmin(pmax((years$summer - centre) / spread, -3), 3)
step <- as.integer(cut(z, seq(-3, 3, length.out = 17), include.lowest = TRUE))
years$stripe <- ifelse(is.na(step), "grey75", stripe_colours[step])

ggplot(years, aes(x = year, y = 1, fill = stripe)) +
  geom_tile(width = 1) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 20), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Summers at Athens Hellinikon, ", min(years$year), "–", last_year),
    subtitle = "One stripe for each summer: blue cooler, red warmer\nGrey: too many days missing",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Data: NOAA GHCN-Daily, station GR000016716",
      "Graphic: after Ed Hawkins' #ShowYourStripes",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(12, 12, 12, 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 4)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey25", margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour = "grey30", margin = margin(t = 4))
  )











Code
kept <- years |>
  filter(!is.na(summer)) |>
  arrange(desc(summer))
warmest <- kept[1, ]
top_five <- sort(kept$year[1:5])
# the last summer of the record is counted only up to its last day, if that is before September
partial <- last_day < as.Date(paste0(last_year, "-08-31"))


In 1961–1990, a summer at Hellinikon averaged 26.2 °C, day and night together. The 8 summers of 2011–2025 that can be counted averaged 28.5 °C. The five warmest summers since 1955 were those of 2008, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and the warmest of all, 2024, averaged 31.0 °C, 4.8 °C more than the summers of 1961–1990. (The summer of 2025 is counted up to 24 August 2025, the last day of the record.)

A check: the station and ERA5-Land


Code
station_base <- mean(years$summer[years$year %in% 1961:1990], na.rm = TRUE)
era5_base <- mean(era5_summers$summer[era5_summers$year %in% 1961:1990])
anomalies <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    year = years$year,
    series = "Hellinikon station",
    anomaly = years$summer - station_base
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = era5_summers$year,
    series = "ERA5-Land",
    anomaly = era5_summers$summer - era5_base
  )
)
anomalies$series <- factor(anomalies$series, levels = c("Hellinikon station", "ERA5-Land"))
ends <- anomalies |>
  filter(!is.na(anomaly)) |>
  group_by(series) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1)

ggplot(anomalies, aes(x = year, y = anomaly, colour = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = year), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Hellinikon station" = "#eb6834", "ERA5-Land" = "#2a78d6")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 10), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    title = "Summers against those of 1961–1990",
    subtitle = "Average temperature of June to August, difference in °C",
    x = NULL,
    y = "°C",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA GHCN-Daily, station GR000016716; ERA5-Land via Open-Meteo"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )











Code
# the station and ERA5-Land in the summers of the last period that the station can count
recent_kept <- years$year[years$period %in% recent & !is.na(years$summer)]
station_warming <- mean(years$summer[years$year %in% recent_kept]) - station_base
era5_warming <- mean(era5_summers$summer[era5_summers$year %in% recent_kept]) - era5_base
# and ERA5-Land in all the summers of the last period
era5_recent <- mean(era5_summers$summer[era5_summers$year %in% 2011:last_year]) - era5_base
# the place of a summer among all the summers of ERA5-Land, the warmest first
era5_place_of <- function(year) {
  sum(era5_summers$summer >= era5_summers$summer[era5_summers$year == year])
}
both_kept <- merge(
  data.frame(year = years$year, station = years$summer - station_base),
  data.frame(year = era5_summers$year, era5 = era5_summers$summer - era5_base)
)
together <- cor(both_kept$station, both_kept$era5, use = "complete.obs")
# ERA5-Land's latest summer, which the station's record may not reach
era5_latest <- era5_summers[era5_summers$year == max(era5_summers$year), ]
era5_place <- era5_place_of(era5_latest$year)
place_text <- function(k) {
  if (k == 1) {
    return("the warmest")
  }
  words <- c("second", "third", "fourth", "fifth", "sixth", "seventh", "eighth", "ninth", "tenth")
  if (k <= 10) paste("the", words[k - 1], "warmest") else paste0("the ", k, "th warmest")
}


The station and ERA5-Land agree. The warm and the cool summers are the same in both (their correlation is 0.94, where 1 would be a perfect match), and both have warmed: compared with 1961–1990, the summers of 2011–2025 that the station can count were 2.4 °C warmer at the station and 1.6 °C warmer in ERA5-Land. The summers that the station cannot count do not change the picture: over all the summers of 2011–2025, ERA5-Land was 1.6 °C warmer.
The station warmed by 0.8 °C more. Part of the difference may come from the place around it. Cities cool more slowly than the countryside at night (Founda and Santamouris 2017), and the station’s own surroundings have changed: the airport around it closed in 2001, and since 2020 the old airfield has been a building site (Wikipedia). NOAA’s file gives the station the same place for the whole record, so it does not say whether the station itself moved within the old airport. ERA5-Land cannot see any of this, and it warmed too: the warming is not only the station’s.
ERA5-Land also has the summer of 2026, which NOAA’s record of the station does not reach yet: it was 1.5 °C warmer than its summers of 1961–1990, the 13th warmest of its 72 summers since 1955.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
section: 2. How many hot days does a summer have?
text:
2. How many hot days does a summer have?


Code
hot_days <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = years$year, days = years$hot - years$very_hot, kind = "35 to 39.9 °C"),
  data.frame(year = years$year, days = years$very_hot, kind = "40 °C or more")
)
hot_days$kind <- factor(hot_days$kind, levels = c("35 to 39.9 °C", "40 °C or more"))
gaps <- data.frame(year = years$year[is.na(years$hot)], days = 0, what = "Too many days missing")
most <- years[which.max(years$hot), ]

ggplot(hot_days, aes(x = year, y = days)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = kind), width = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = gaps, aes(shape = what), colour = "grey45", size = 2.4, stroke = 0.9) +

    data = most,

    vjust = -0.6,
    hjust = 0.8,

  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("35 to 39.9 °C" = "#fd8d3c", "40 °C or more" = "#a63603")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Too many days missing" = 4)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(order = 1), shape = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Hot days at Athens Hellinikon",
    subtitle = "Days with a maximum of 35 °C or more, each year",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Days",
    fill = NULL,
    shape = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA GHCN-Daily, station GR000016716"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +

    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )











Code
hottest <- days[which.max(days$tmax), ]
summer_2024 <- days[days$year == 2024 & days$month %in% 6:8, ]
above_37_2024 <- sum(summer_2024$tmax > 37, na.rm = TRUE)
missing_2024 <- sum(is.na(summer_2024$tmax))


Many more. In 1961–1990 Hellinikon had 5 hot days a year on average, in 1991–2010 15, and in the 8 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted 30. The most were in 2024: 70 days of 35 °C or more.
Very hot days, of 40 °C or more, were rare and still are, but less so: 2 in the 30 years of 1961–1990, 6 in the 8 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted. The hottest day of the record was 3 August 2021, at 43.0 °C.
Can the station be trusted for a summer like that of 2024? The National Observatory of Athens has its own stations, and counted the days of that summer above 37 °C: 45 at Harokopio University in Kallithea and 30 in Piraeus (meteo.gr, 3 September 2024). Hellinikon had 32, with 8 days of the summer missing: in the same range.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
section: 3. Do the nights still cool down?
text:
3. Do the nights still cool down?


Code
nights <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = years$year, nights = years$tropical - years$very_warm, kind = "20 to 25 °C"),
  data.frame(year = years$year, nights = years$very_warm, kind = "Above 25 °C")
)
nights$kind <- factor(nights$kind, levels = c("20 to 25 °C", "Above 25 °C"))
night_gaps <- data.frame(
  year = years$year[is.na(years$tropical)],
  nights = 0,
  what = "Too many days missing"

ggplot(nights, aes(x = year, y = nights)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = kind), width = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +

    subtitle = "Nights when the temperature stayed above 20 °C, each year",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Nights",
    fill = NULL,
    shape = NULL,

  ) +

    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),

    plot.caption.position = "plot",

    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )











Code
most_nights <- years[which.max(years$tropical), ]
most_very_warm <- years[which.max(years$very_warm), ]
warmest_night <- days[which.max(days$tmin), ]


Less and less. At Hellinikon, by the sea, a summer night often stays above 20 °C anyway: in 1961–1990 there were 86 tropical nights a year on average. In the 11 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted there were 102, and the most were in 2012: 118. The change is larger for the very warm nights, above 25 °C: from 9 a year in 1961–1990 to 28 in 2011–2025, with 49 in 2024. The warmest night of the record was that of 26 July 2025, when the temperature did not fall below 31.7 °C.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
text:
4. Is the hot season longer?
Each row of the chart below is one year, from 1955 at the bottom to 2025 at the top, and each small square one day from May to October, coloured by the maximum of that day. A season that starts earlier or ends later shows as colour spreading to the left or to the right; grey squares are the days with no measurement.


Code
season_days <- days |>
  filter(month %in% 5:10) |>
  mutate(day = as.Date(paste0("2001-", format(date, "%m-%d")))) # one calendar for every year
band <- cut(
  season_days$tmax,
  c(-Inf, 30, 35, 40, Inf),
  right = FALSE,
  labels = c("Below 30 °C", "30 to 34.9 °C", "35 to 39.9 °C", "40 °C or more")
)
levels(band) <- c(levels(band), "No measurement")
band[is.na(band)] <- "No measurement"
season_days$band <- band
month_starts <- as.Date(paste0("2001-", 5:10, "-01"))

ggplot(season_days, aes(x = day, y = year, fill = band)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Below 30 °C" = "#fff3e2",
      "30 to 34.9 °C" = "#fdd0a2",
      "35 to 39.9 °C" = "#fd8d3c",
      "40 °C or more" = "#a63603",
      "No measurement" = "grey70"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = month_starts + 14,
    labels = month.abb[5:10],
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 10), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Every day from May to October",
    subtitle = "Daily maximum at Athens Hellinikon",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA GHCN-Daily, station GR000016716"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )









The orange spreads both ways. To put numbers on it, the next chart pools the years of each period that can be counted, and shows for every date how often it was a hot day: a share of 50% means that the date reached 35 °C in half of those years.


Code
chance <- days |>
  filter(month %in% 5:10, year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$hot)], !is.na(tmax)) |>
  mutate(period = period_of(year), day = as.Date(paste0("2001-", format(date, "%m-%d")))) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(period, day) |>
  summarise(share = 100 * mean(tmax >= 35), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(smooth = as.numeric(stats::filter(share, rep(1 / 15, 15), sides = 2))) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(chance, aes(x = day, y = smooth, colour = period)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#fd8d3c", "#e6550d", "#a63603")) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = month_starts + 14, labels = month.abb[5:10]) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title = "How often each date was a hot day",
    subtitle = "Share of the years with 35 °C or more on that date, average of 15 days",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA GHCN-Daily, station GR000016716"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )











Code
# the share of hot days in two parts of the season, in each period
share_between <- function(from, to) {
  days |>
    filter(year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$hot)], !is.na(tmax)) |>
    mutate(period = period_of(year), md = format(date, "%m-%d")) |>
    filter(!is.na(period), md >= from, md <= to) |>
    group_by(period) |>
    summarise(share = 100 * mean(tmax >= 35)) |>
    pull(share)
}
late_june <- share_between("06-16", "06-30")
late_august <- share_between("08-16", "08-31")

# the first and the last tropical night of each year that can be counted, as days of the year,
# and their average in each period, as a date
warm_nights <- days |>
  filter(year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$tropical)], tmin > 20) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    first = as.integer(format(min(date), "%j")),
    last = as.integer(format(max(date), "%j"))
  ) |>
  mutate(period = period_of(year)) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(first = mean(first), last = mean(last))
day_text <- function(d) {
  x <- as.Date(round(d) - 1, origin = "2001-01-01")
  paste(as.integer(format(x, "%d")), month.name[as.integer(format(x, "%m"))])
}
season_length <- warm_nights$last - warm_nights$first
longer <- season_length[3] - season_length[1]


Yes: it starts earlier and ends later. In 1961–1990 a day in the second half of June reached 35 °C in 1% of the years; in 2011–2025, in 26%. In the second half of August the share went from 5% to 30%.
The nights tell the same story. In 1961–1990 the first tropical night of the year came, on average, on 31 May, and the last on 6 October. In 2011–2025 the first came on 19 May and the last on 13 October: the season of warm nights is 19 days longer.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
text:
5. Which were the worst heatwaves?


Code
# runs of days above 37 °C. A single missing day between two such days does not end a run, and a
# run counts as a heatwave if at least three of its days were measured above 37 °C
above <- days$tmax > 37
bridge <- is.na(above) &
  c(FALSE, head(above, -1) %in% TRUE) &
  c(tail(above, -1) %in% TRUE, FALSE)
in_run <- above %in% TRUE | bridge
run <- cumsum(in_run & !c(FALSE, head(in_run, -1)))
heatwaves <- days |>
  mutate(run = run) |>
  filter(in_run) |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(
    start = min(date),
    end = max(date),
    days = n(),
    measured = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
    hottest = max(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    warmest_night = if (all(is.na(tmin))) NA else max(tmin, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(measured >= 3) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(format(start, "%Y")), period = period_of(year))

# how rare a day above 37 °C was in the summers of 1961-1990
summers_1961_1990 <- days$tmax[days$year %in% 1961:1990 & days$month %in% 6:8]
share_above_37 <- 100 * mean(summers_1961_1990 > 37, na.rm = TRUE)


Why 37 °C? At Hellinikon, in the summers of 1961–1990, only 1.1% of the days were warmer than 37 °C, about one in 89; the National Observatory of Athens, too, counts the days above 37 °C in its reviews of the summer (meteo.gr, 3 September 2024). Three such days in a row are a heatwave here. Each dot below is one heatwave, as high as it was long:


Code
longest <- heatwaves |>
  arrange(desc(days), desc(hottest)) |>
  head(3)
longest$label <- paste(month.abb[as.integer(format(longest$start, "%m"))], longest$year)
# the label is to the left of the dot, or to its right for the latest of the three
longest$side <- ifelse(longest$start == max(longest$start), -0.2, 1.2)
# the years with too many days missing, as grey bands
no_data <- data.frame(year = years$year[is.na(years$hot)])
no_data$from <- as.Date(paste0(no_data$year, "-01-01"))
no_data$to <- as.Date(paste0(no_data$year + 1, "-01-01"))

ggplot(heatwaves, aes(x = start, y = days)) +
  geom_rect(
    data = no_data,
    aes(xmin = from, xmax = to, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "grey87"
  ) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = start, y = 0, yend = days), colour = "#a63603", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = "#a63603", size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = longest, aes(label = label, hjust = side), size = 3.8, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_x_date(
    limits = c(first_day, last_day),
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1960, 2020, 10), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max(heatwaves$days) * 1.15),
    breaks = seq(0, 30, 3),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Every heatwave at Athens Hellinikon",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Three days or more in a row above 37 °C; the height is the length in days",
      "Grey: years with too many days missing",
      sep = "\n"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Days",
    caption = "Data: NOAA GHCN-Daily, station GR000016716"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )









The ten longest:


Code
# "8–24 July 2024", or "27 July – 5 August 2021" when a heatwave runs into the next month
when <- function(start, end) {
  day <- function(d) as.integer(format(d, "%d"))
  month <- function(d) month.name[as.integer(format(d, "%m"))]
  ifelse(
    month(start) == month(end),
    paste0(day(start), "–", day(end), " ", month(end), " ", format(end, "%Y")),
    paste0(day(start), " ", month(start), " – ", day(end), " ", month(end), " ", format(end, "%Y"))
  )
}
ten <- heatwaves |>
  arrange(desc(days), desc(hottest)) |>
  head(10)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    when = when(ten$start, ten$end),
    days = ten$days,
    missing = ten$days - ten$measured,
    hottest = ten$hottest,
    night = ten$warmest_night
  ),
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c(
    "When",
    "Days",
    "Days missing",
    "Hottest day (°C)",
    "Warmest night (°C)"
  )
)

Code
per_period <- heatwaves |>
  filter(!is.na(period), year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$hot)]) |>
  count(period, .drop = FALSE)
first_long <- heatwaves$year[heatwaves$days >= 7][1]
july_2023 <- sum(!is.na(days$tmax[days$year == 2023 & days$month == 7]))
summer_2012 <- sum(!is.na(days$tmax[days$year == 2012 & days$month %in% 6:8]))
heatwave_1987 <- heatwaves[heatwaves$year == 1987, ]


More of them, and longer. In the 30 years of 1961–1990 Hellinikon had 4 heatwaves; in the 8 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted, 8. Before 2021 no heatwave that the station measured lasted a week. The longest, of 17 days, was that of 8–24 July 2024, with 3 days missing in it; the hottest day of a heatwave was 43.0 °C, in that of 27 July – 5 August 2021.
What these numbers mean for people is clearest in July 1987: in that month, when a major heatwave hit Greece, almost twice as many people died in Athens (97% more) as in July of the six years before (Katsouyanni et al. 1993). At Hellinikon, by the sea, the heatwave lasted 3 days, 22–24 July 1987, and reached 41.6 °C.
Some heatwaves are missing. The station has a maximum for only 3 days of July 2023, when the National Observatory of Athens counted, in Greece as a whole, a heatwave of 15 days, the longest until then; that of July 2024 beat it, with 16 (meteo.gr, 25 July 2024). And it has a maximum for only 11 of the 92 days of the summer of 2012, the second warmest of the 72 in ERA5-Land.

title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
text:
So, what does it mean?
Athens is getting hotter, by day and by night. At Hellinikon, comparing 1961–1990 with the years of 2011–2025 that can be counted:


Code
measures <- rbind(
  "Summer average (°C)" = by_period$summer_average,
  "Hot days a year" = by_period$hot_days,
  "Very hot days a year" = by_period$very_hot_days / by_period$hot_years,
  "Tropical nights a year" = by_period$tropical_nights,
  "Very warm nights a year" = by_period$very_warm_nights,
  "Heatwaves a year" = per_period$n / by_period$hot_years
)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(rownames(measures), measures),
  row.names = FALSE,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Measure", as.character(by_period$period))
)

Summers are warmer: 2.4 °C warmer than in 1961–1990, and ERA5-Land, which cannot see the city, warmed too.
Hot days are much more common: 30 a year instead of 5.
The nights cool down less: 28 very warm nights a year instead of 9.
The hot season is longer: its warm nights start earlier and end later, 19 days longer in all.
Heatwaves come more often and last longer: the longest at Hellinikon lasted 17 days, in 2024.

What this does not show. It is one station, at the edge of the city and by the sea; the centre of Athens and the plains inland are hotter by day, and some of the station’s warming may come from the city around it, which this record cannot separate from the climate. NOAA’s record of the station has gaps, worst in the 2010s, and ends on 24 August 2025; ERA5-Land, which goes on to the present, is a model, not a measurement.
For the world as a whole, see the NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly; for more of what a weather station measures, hour by hour, the Airport Weather Analysis of the new Athens airport; and for the fires that burn in Greek summers, Greece Burning.

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
text:
R ships with a built-in palette of named colors, returned by colors(). As of this writing (and for a long time now) it holds 657 names — things like "steelblue", "tomato3", or "gray42". This document walks through a classic script by efg (Stowers Institute) that turns that list into a printable reference chart, and along the way explains the underlying R color machinery: how names map to RGB, how RGB maps to HSV, and how to pick readable text/background combinations automatically.
The original script writes everything to a file called COLOR_CHART.pdf. Here we reproduce each piece as an inline, explained chunk so it renders directly in this document; the full original (PDF-producing) script is included as an appendix at the end for reference.


Code
# The chart layout below hard-codes 25 columns x 27 rows = 675 slots for 657 colors.
# This assumes the palette size hasn't changed between R versions.
length(colors())

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
text:
R ships with a built-in palette of named colors, returned by colors(). As of this writing (and for a long time now) it holds 657 names — things like "steelblue", "tomato3", or "gray42". This document walks through a classic script by efg (Stowers Institute) that turns that list into a printable reference chart, and along the way explains the underlying R color machinery: how names map to RGB, how RGB maps to HSV, and how to pick readable text/background combinations automatically.
The original script writes everything to a file called COLOR_CHART.pdf. Here we reproduce each piece as an inline, explained chunk so it renders directly in this document; the full original (PDF-producing) script is included as an appendix at the end for reference.


Code
# The chart layout below hard-codes 25 columns x 27 rows = 675 slots for 657 colors.
# This assumes the palette size hasn't changed between R versions.
length(colors())


[1] 657

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
text:
How R represents colors
R gives you three interchangeable ways to specify a color:

By name — a string from colors(), e.g. "firebrick".
By hex code — "#FF0000", the familiar web-style RRGGBB (optionally with alpha, RRGGBBAA).
By numeric index — a legacy palette (palette()), rarely used now.

col2rgb() converts any of the first two into the underlying 0–255 RGB triplet:


Code
col2rgb("yellow")


      [,1]
red    255
green  255
blue     0


Code
col2rgb("steelblue")


      [,1]
red     70
green  130
blue   180


RGB is how the color is stored, but it is not how humans reason about color. For that, R (via rgb2hsv()) can convert to HSV — Hue, Saturation, Value — which separates what color (hue, as an angle 0–1 representing 0–360°) from how vivid (saturation) and how bright (value):


Code
rgb2hsv(col2rgb("steelblue"))


       [,1]
h 0.5757576
s 0.6111111
v 0.7058824


Sorting colors by hue-then-saturation-then-value is what makes the second chart below (“sorted by hue”) group visually similar colors together, instead of the arbitrary alphabetical-ish order colors() returns them in.

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
section: Choosing readable text color: a contrast heuristic
text:
Choosing readable text color: a contrast heuristic
Rectangles need a label (the color’s name and index) drawn on top of them. White text on "yellow" is unreadable; black text on "navy" is unreadable. The script uses a cheap luminance heuristic: average the R, G, and B channels, and if that average is above the midpoint (127.5), the background is “light” so use black text; otherwise use white text.


Code
SetTextContrastColor <- function(color) {
  ifelse(mean(col2rgb(color)) > 127, "black", "white")
}

SetTextContrastColor("white")


[1] "black"


Code
SetTextContrastColor("black")


[1] "white"


Code
SetTextContrastColor("red")


[1] "white"


Code
SetTextContrastColor("yellow")


[1] "black"


This is a simplification — perceptual luminance weights green much more heavily than blue (roughly 0.299*R + 0.587*G + 0.114*B), so a plain channel average can misjudge some saturated blues or reds. It’s good enough for a quick reference chart, though, which is the point here.
We precompute the contrast color for every entry in colors() once, so the plotting loops below can just look it up instead of recomputing it per rectangle:


Code
TextContrastColor <- unlist(lapply(colors(), SetTextContrastColor))
table(TextContrastColor)


TextContrastColor
black white 
  416   241

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
text:
Chart 1a: colors in index order
The simplest chart just walks colors() in the order R returns it, laying out 25 colors per row. Each rectangle is drawn with rect(), positioned by its row/column, filled with the color itself, and labeled with its numeric index (SetTextContrastColor decides whether that label is black or white).


Code
colCount <- 25  # number of rectangles per row
rowCount <- ceiling(length(colors()) / colCount)

oldpar <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))

plot(c(1, colCount), c(0, rowCount), type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "",
     axes = FALSE, ylim = c(rowCount, 0))
title("R colors (index order)")

for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  base <- j * colCount
  remaining <- length(colors()) - base
  RowSize <- ifelse(remaining < colCount, remaining, colCount)
  rect((1:RowSize) - 0.5, j - 0.5, (1:RowSize) + 0.5, j + 0.5,
       border = "black", col = colors()[base + (1:RowSize)])
  text((1:RowSize), j, paste(base + (1:RowSize)), cex = 0.7,
       col = TextContrastColor[base + (1:RowSize)])
}









Code
par(oldpar)


Notice how little visual structure there is: R’s colors() order is alphabetical by name (with numbered variants like "blue1".."blue4" interleaved), not by appearance, so neighboring cells jump around the color wheel.

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
section: Chart 1b: colors sorted by hue, saturation, value
text:
Chart 1b: colors sorted by hue, saturation, value
To get a chart that actually reads as a gradient, we convert every color to HSV and sort by hue first, then saturation, then value. order() gives us the permutation of indices that achieves that sort, and we index into colors() with it.


Code
RGBColors <- col2rgb(colors())
HSVColors <- rgb2hsv(RGBColors[1, ], RGBColors[2, ], RGBColors[3, ], maxColorValue = 255)
HueOrder <- order(HSVColors[1, ], HSVColors[2, ], HSVColors[3, ])

oldpar <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))

plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE,
     ylim = c(rowCount, 0), xlim = c(1, colCount))
title("R colors -- sorted by hue, saturation, value")

for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  for (i in 1:colCount) {
    k <- j * colCount + i
    if (k <= length(colors())) {
      rect(i - 0.5, j - 0.5, i + 0.5, j + 0.5,
           border = "black", col = colors()[HueOrder[k]])
      text(i, j, paste(HueOrder[k]), cex = 0.7,
           col = TextContrastColor[HueOrder[k]])
    }
  }
}









Code
par(oldpar)


The label in each cell is still the original index into colors() — so you can look up a color visually here, then use that number (or better, colors()[index]) to reference it by name in code.

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
section: Getting a color’s hex and decimal RGB
text:
Getting a color’s hex and decimal RGB
For a reference sheet you usually want the exact hex code (for CSS/HTML/design tools) alongside the decimal RGB triplet (for R/plotting code). sprintf() builds both from col2rgb()’s output in one line:


Code
GetColorHexAndDecimal <- function(color) {
  c <- col2rgb(color)
  sprintf("#%02X%02X%02X %3d %3d %3d", c[1], c[2], c[3], c[1], c[2], c[3])
}

GetColorHexAndDecimal("yellow")


[1] "#FFFF00 255 255   0"


Code
GetColorHexAndDecimal("steelblue")


[1] "#4682B4  70 130 180"

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
section: Chart 2: paginated detail sheet (name + hex + decimal)
text:
Chart 2: paginated detail sheet (name + hex + decimal)
The final part of the original script produces a multi-page listing: two columns of 50 colors each per page, each row showing a filled swatch, the color’s index, its name, and its hex/decimal RGB (in a monospace font so the numbers align). Below is a single representative page reproduced inline; the appendix has the full paging loop that generates every page (this is what the original script writes across the multi-page PDF).


Code
index <- paste(1:length(colors()))
HexAndDec <- unlist(lapply(colors(), GetColorHexAndDecimal))
PerColumn <- 50
PerPage <- 2 * PerColumn

page <- 1
oldpar <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1))

plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE,
     ylim = c(PerColumn, 0), xlim = c(0, 1))
title("R colors")
mtext(paste("page", page), side = 1, adj = 1, line = -1)

base <- PerPage * (page - 1)

# Column 1
remaining <- length(colors()) - base
ColumnSize <- ifelse(remaining < PerColumn, remaining, PerColumn)
rect(0.00, 0:(ColumnSize - 1), 0.49, 1:ColumnSize,
     border = "black", col = colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
text(0.045, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 1, index[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)],
     cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
text(0.06, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)],
     cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
save <- par(family = "mono")
text(0.25, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, HexAndDec[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)],
     cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
par(save)

# Column 2
if (remaining > PerColumn) {
  remaining2 <- remaining - PerColumn
  ColumnSize2 <- ifelse(remaining2 < PerColumn, remaining2, PerColumn)
  rect(0.51, 0:(ColumnSize2 - 1), 1.00, 1:ColumnSize2,
       border = "black", col = colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  text(0.545, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize2 - 1)), adj = 1,
       index[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)],
       cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  text(0.56, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize2 - 1)), adj = 0,
       colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)],
       cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  save <- par(family = "mono")
  text(0.75, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize2 - 1)), adj = 0,
       HexAndDec[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)],
       cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  par(save)
}









Code
par(oldpar)


To generate every page (not just page 1) and get the full multi-page reference sheet, wrap that same block in a loop over page in 1:ceiling(length(colors()) / PerPage) and, when knitting, either emit one PDF page per iteration or (for HTML) let each iteration produce its own plot — see the appendix for the loop as written in the original script.

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
text:
Takeaways

colors() is R’s built-in named palette (657 entries); col2rgb() and rgb2hsv() convert between name/hex, RGB, and HSV representations.
Sorting by HSV hue (not the default alphabetical order) is what makes a color chart visually navigable.
A simple average-of-channels test is a cheap-but-imperfect way to auto-pick readable black/white text on an arbitrary background color.
sprintf("#%02X%02X%02X ...") is the idiomatic way to format an RGB triplet as both hex and decimal in one string.

title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
text:
Appendix: original script (writes COLOR_CHART.pdf)


Code
# efg, Stowers Institute for Medical Research
# efg's Research Notes: http://research.stowers-institute.org/efg/R/Color/Chart 6 July 2004. Modified 23 May 2005.
pdf("COLOR_CHART.pdf", width = 10, height = 10)
# save to reset at end
oldparameters <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1), mfrow = c(2, 1))
# Be cautious in case definition of "colors" changes. Use some hard-coded constants since this is not expected to change.
stopifnot(length(colors()) == 657)
# 0. Setup
SetTextContrastColor <- function(color) {ifelse(mean(col2rgb(color)) > 127, "black", "white")}
TextContrastColor <- unlist(lapply(colors(), SetTextContrastColor))
# 1a. Plot matrix of R colors, in index order, 25 per row.
colCount <- 25
rowCount <- 27
plot(c(1, colCount), c(0, rowCount), type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE, ylim = c(rowCount, 0))
title("R colors")
mtext("http://research.stowers-institute.org/efg/R/Color/Chart", cex = 0.6)
for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  base <- j * colCount
  remaining <- length(colors()) - base
  RowSize <- ifelse(remaining < colCount, remaining, colCount)
  rect((1:RowSize) - 0.5, j - 0.5, (1:RowSize) + 0.5, j + 0.5, border = "black", col = colors()[base + (1:RowSize)])
  text((1:RowSize), j, paste(base + (1:RowSize)), cex = 0.7, col = TextContrastColor[base + (1:RowSize)])
}
# 1b. Plot matrix of R colors, in "hue" order, 25 per row.
RGBColors <- col2rgb(colors()[1:length(colors())])
HSVColors <- rgb2hsv(RGBColors[1, ], RGBColors[2, ], RGBColors[3, ], maxColorValue = 255)
HueOrder <- order(HSVColors[1, ], HSVColors[2, ], HSVColors[3, ])
plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE, ylim = c(rowCount, 0), xlim = c(1, colCount))
title("R colors -- Sorted by Hue, Saturation, Value")
for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  for (i in 1:colCount) {
    k <- j * colCount + i
    if (k <= length(colors())) {
      rect(i - 0.5, j - 0.5, i + 0.5, j + 0.5, border = "black", col = colors()[HueOrder[k]])
      text(i, j, paste(HueOrder[k]), cex = 0.7, col = TextContrastColor[HueOrder[k]])
    }
  }
}
# 2. Create 7-page color chart showing rectangle block of color, along with index, color name, and RGB constants in hex and decimal.
GetColorHexAndDecimal <- function(color) {
  c <- col2rgb(color)
  sprintf("#%02X%02X%02X %3d %3d %3d", c[1], c[2], c[3], c[1], c[2], c[3])
}
par(oldparameters)
oldparameters <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1))
index <- paste(1:length(colors()))
HexAndDec <- unlist(lapply(colors(), GetColorHexAndDecimal))
PerColumn <- 50
PerPage <- 2 * PerColumn
for (page in 1:(trunc(length(colors()) + (PerPage - 1)) / PerPage)) {
  plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE, ylim = c(PerColumn, 0), xlim = c(0, 1))
  title("R colors")
  mtext(paste("page ", page), SOUTH <- 1, adj = 1, line = -1)
  base <- PerPage * (page - 1)
  # Column 1
  remaining <- length(colors()) - base
  ColumnSize <- ifelse(remaining < PerColumn, remaining, PerColumn)
  rect(0.00, 0:(ColumnSize - 1), 0.49, 1:ColumnSize, border = "black", col = colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  text(0.045, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 1, index[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  text(0.06, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  save <- par(family = "mono")
  text(0.25, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, HexAndDec[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  par(save)
  # Column 2
  if (remaining > PerColumn) {
    remaining <- remaining - PerColumn
    ColumnSize <- ifelse(remaining < PerColumn, remaining, PerColumn)
    rect(0.51, 0:(ColumnSize - 1), 1.00, 1:ColumnSize, border = "black", col = colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    text(0.545, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 1, index[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    text(0.56, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    save <- par(family = "mono")
    text(0.75, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, HexAndDec[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    par(save)
  }
}
par(oldparameters)
dev.off()

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
text:
For a population to stay the same size, without people moving in or out, women need to have about 2.1 children each: two to replace the parents, and a little more because some children die young and slightly more boys than girls are born. In 1960 almost every country in the world was far above that. Today more than half of all countries are below it, and some are far below: in South Korea women have fewer than one child each.
This data story shows, in plain words:

how many countries have dropped below 2.1, year by year since 1960,
where — a world map that changes year by year,
how fast — the path of ten countries, from Niger to South Korea, with Greece in red,
what it does to a country — population pyramids that turn upside down as fewer children are born and people live longer.

All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators; the page carries its own copy of the data it needs, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub.

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "plotly"))
# The data comes from golemworldbank, copied next to this page in R/mfi_fertility.rds.
# For every country and indicator, install golemworldbank itself; its data is in
# Git LFS, so install it from a clone (install_github() can download LFS pointer
# files instead of the data):
#   git lfs install
#   git clone https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank.git
# then in R:
#   devtools::install_local("golemworldbank")

library(dplyr)
library(plotly)          # interactive charts

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
text:
The data
golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_fertility.rds holds four of its indicators for every country, and the age of the population for six countries:


Code
# part of golemworldbank's mfi (with the package installed, its mfi has every indicator)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_fertility.rds"))

indicators <- c(
  fertility  = "Fertility rate, total (births per woman)",
  aged_65    = "Population ages 65 and above (% of total population)",
  children   = "Population ages 0-14 (% of total population)",
  population = "Population, total"
)

df_world <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(country = recode(`Country Name`, "Korea, Rep." = "South Korea"),
         code    = `Country Code`,
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  select(country, code, measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(country, measure, year)

# the population pyramids: the share of men, and of women, in each five-year age group
ages <- c(sprintf("%02d-%02d", seq(0, 75, 5), seq(4, 79, 5)), "80 and above")
df_ages <- mfi %>%
  filter(grepl("^Population ages .*, (male|female) \\(% of (male|female) population\\)$", `Indicator Name`)) %>%
  mutate(country = recode(`Country Name`, "Korea, Rep." = "South Korea"),
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         sex     = ifelse(grepl(", female", `Indicator Name`), "Women", "Men"),
         age     = sub("^Population ages (.*), (male|female).*$", "\\1", `Indicator Name`)) %>%
  filter(age %in% ages) %>%
  mutate(age = factor(sub("80 and above", "80+", age), levels = sub("80 and above", "80+", ages))) %>%
  select(country, year, sex, age, value)

head(df_world, 12)

Column
Description




country
Country name (World Bank names, except “South Korea” for “Korea, Rep.”)


code
Three-letter country code, for the map


measure
fertility children per woman, aged_65 and children the share of people aged 65 and over and under 15, population the number of people


year
Year of observation


value
The World Bank’s value for that country and year



The fertility rate is the number of children a woman would have over her life if, at each age, she had children at the rate women of that age had them that year. It describes one year, not one family: a rate of 1.5 means that at that year’s pace, ten women would have fifteen children between them.


Code
replacement <- 2.1   # children per woman that keep a population steady
last_year <- max(df_world$year[df_world$measure == "fertility"])
at <- function(m, cty, y) df_world$value[df_world$measure == m & df_world$country == cty & df_world$year == y]

# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}

# data source as a footnote inside each chart, at the bottom of the bottom
# margin `b` (in pixels), so it lands in the same place whatever the height
source_note <- function(b) {
  list(text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
       xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
       font = list(size = 11, color = "gray50"))
}

# end labels: each sits right of its line's last point. Labels closer than
# `gap` pixels are pushed apart, each group of crowded labels centred on its
# lines, and joined to their point by a leader line. `per_px` is how many y
# units one pixel of the plot is worth
end_labels <- function(ends, per_px, highlight = "", gap = 17) {
  o <- order(ends$value)
  y <- ends$value[o]
  step <- gap * per_px
  for (pass in 1:3) {
    for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + step)
    group <- cumsum(c(TRUE, diff(y) > step + 1e-9))
    y <- y - ave(y - ends$value[o], group)            # centre each group on its lines
  }
  for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + step)
  ends$label_y[o] <- y
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(ends)), function(i) {
    name <- if (ends$country[i] == highlight) paste0("<b>", ends$country[i], "</b>") else ends$country[i]
    list(x = ends$year[i], y = ends$value[i], xref = "x", yref = "y",
         ax = 24, ay = -(ends$label_y[i] - ends$value[i]) / per_px,
         showarrow = TRUE, arrowhead = 0, arrowwidth = 1, arrowcolor = "#B3B3B3",
         xanchor = "left", text = paste0(name, " ", ends$text[i]),
         font = list(size = 12, color = "gray25"))
  })
}

# the dotted 2.1 line
replacement_line <- list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = replacement, y1 = replacement,
                         line = list(dash = "dot", color = "gray"))

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
section: More than half the world is below 2.1
text:
More than half the world is below 2.1


Code
counts <- df_world %>%
  filter(measure %in% c("fertility", "aged_65", "children")) %>%
  select(-code) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(countries     = sum(!is.na(fertility)),
            low_fertility = sum(fertility < replacement, na.rm = TRUE),
            more_old      = sum(aged_65 > children, na.rm = TRUE),
            median        = median(fertility, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(year <= last_year)
first <- counts[counts$year == min(counts$year), ]
latest <- counts[counts$year == last_year, ]

h <- 520; b <- 150
p <- plot_ly(counts, x = ~year) %>%
  add_lines(y = ~low_fertility, name = "Women have fewer than 2.1 children",
            line = list(color = "#0082c8", width = 3),
            text = ~paste0(year, ": ", low_fertility, " of ", countries, " countries"), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  add_lines(y = ~more_old, name = "More people over 65 than under 15",
            line = list(color = "#E74C3C", width = 3),
            text = ~paste0(year, ": ", more_old, " countries"), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title  = list(text = "Number of countries where...", x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 80, r = 60, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, dtick = 5),
    yaxis  = list(title = "countries", rangemode = "tozero"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
    annotations = list(
      list(x = last_year, y = latest$low_fertility, xanchor = "left", xshift = 6, showarrow = FALSE,
           text = latest$low_fertility, font = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")),
      list(x = last_year, y = latest$more_old, xanchor = "left", xshift = 6, showarrow = FALSE,
           text = latest$more_old, font = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")),
      source_note(b)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
sized(p, h)






In 1960, women had fewer than 2.1 children in just 5 of 216 countries. By 2024 it was 119 of 217 — more than half. In the middle country of the world, the number of children per woman fell from 6.1 to 1.9.
Fewer children, and people living longer, change the shape of a country. In 1960 there was 1 country with more people over 65 than children under 15; in 2024 there were 53. The red line follows the blue one about 35 years later — 20 countries in 1972 and 2006, 50 in 1987 and 2024: the children who are not born today are the working-age people who will be missing a generation later.

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
text:
Where: the map turns blue
Press Play to watch the years go by, or drag the slider. Red countries are above 2.1 children per woman, blue ones below, and the closer to gray, the closer to 2.1.


Code
d <- df_world %>% filter(measure == "fertility", !is.na(code), year <= last_year)
lo <- 0.5; hi <- 8   # fixed colour range, so a colour means the same thing in every year

p <- plot_ly(d, type = "choropleth", locations = ~code, z = ~value, frame = ~year,
             zmin = lo, zmax = hi,
             colorscale = list(list(0, "#0082c8"), list((replacement - lo) / (hi - lo), "#f0efec"), list(1, "#E74C3C")),
             marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.3)),
             text = ~paste0(country, " · ", year, "<br>", round(value, 2), " children per woman"),
             hoverinfo = "text",
             colorbar = list(title = list(text = "children<br>per woman"), tickvals = c(1, 2.1, 4, 6, 8), len = 0.6)) %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title  = list(text = "Children per woman, by country", x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    geo    = list(showframe = FALSE, showcoastlines = FALSE, projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
                  bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    margin = list(t = 60, r = 10, l = 10, b = 170),   # room for the slider, then the source
    annotations = list(source_note(170)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 300, transition = 0, redraw = TRUE) %>%
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "Year ", font = list(size = 18, color = "gray40")))
sized(p, 600)






In 1960 almost the whole map is red: only 5 countries were below 2.1. Over the decades blue spreads, first through Europe, North America and East Asia, later through much of Latin America, North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. By 2024 the deepest red is in Africa south of the Sahara, where women in many countries still have four to six children; Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, Iraq and parts of Central Asia are also still well above 2.1. Even there, the numbers are falling.

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
text:
How fast: ten countries
The dotted line is 2.1 children per woman, the level that keeps a population steady.


Code
paths <- c("Niger", "Nigeria", "Israel", "India", "France", "United States", "Italy", "China", "South Korea", "Greece")
highlight <- "Greece"

d <- df_world %>% filter(measure == "fertility", country %in% paths, year <= last_year)
h <- 600; b <- 110; t <- 90
p <- plot_ly()
for (cty in c(setdiff(paths, highlight), highlight)) {
  dc <- d[d$country == cty, ]
  p <- add_lines(p, data = dc, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = cty,
                 line = list(color = if (cty == highlight) "#E74C3C" else "#B3B3B3", width = if (cty == highlight) 3 else 2),
                 text = paste0(cty, " · ", dc$year, "<br>", round(dc$value, 2), " children per woman"), hoverinfo = "text")
}
ends <- d %>% group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year) %>% ungroup() %>% mutate(text = round(value, 2))
per_px <- max(d$value) * 1.1 / (h - t - b)
plotly::layout(p,
  title  = list(text = "Children per woman, 1960 to today", x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
  margin = list(t = t, r = 160, b = b),
  xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, dtick = 5, range = c(1959.5, last_year + 0.5)),
  yaxis  = list(title = "children per woman", rangemode = "tozero"),
  showlegend = FALSE,
  shapes = list(replacement_line),
  annotations = c(end_labels(ends, per_px, highlight), list(source_note(b))),
  font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
  sized(h)






The fall did not happen everywhere at the same time or the same speed:

South Korea went from 6 children per woman in 1960 to 0.75 in 2024, the lowest of any country with more than 10 million people. China fell from 4.5 to 1; its jagged start is the famine of 1959 to 1961, when births collapsed, and the rebound in births that followed it.
Italy and Greece have been below 2.1 for decades — Greece since 1981 — and are now at about 1.2. Of 217 countries, Greece has the 22nd lowest rate.
France and the United States stayed close to 2.1 for a long time and have only recently slipped further, to about 1.6.
India crossed below 2.1 around 2020. Israel is the exception among rich countries, at 2.9.
Nigeria and Niger are still far above, at 4.4 and 5.9, but falling.

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
section: What it does: the pyramid turns upside down
text:
What it does: the pyramid turns upside down
A population pyramid shows how many people there are of each age: men on the left, women on the right, the youngest at the bottom. A country with many children is wide at the bottom, like a pyramid.


Code
pyramid_data <- function(cty, years = NULL) {
  d <- df_ages[df_ages$country == cty, ]
  if (!is.null(years)) d <- d[d$year %in% years, ]
  d$x <- ifelse(d$sex == "Men", -d$value, d$value)   # men to the left of the middle
  d$label <- paste0(d$sex, " ", d$age, " · ", d$year, "<br>", round(d$value, 1), "% of all ", tolower(d$sex))
  d
}
# x axis in % either side of the middle, labelled without the minus sign
pyramid_axis <- function(m) {
  ticks <- seq(-floor(m / 5) * 5, floor(m / 5) * 5, by = 5)
  list(title = "% of men (left) and of women (right)", range = c(-m, m),
       tickvals = ticks, ticktext = paste0(abs(ticks), "%"), zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "gray")
}

left <- "Nigeria"; right <- "Greece"
pair <- pyramid_data(left, last_year) %>% bind_rows(pyramid_data(right, last_year))
m <- max(pair$value) * 1.1
one <- function(cty, legend) {
  dc <- pair[pair$country == cty, ]
  plot_ly(dc, x = ~x, y = ~age, color = ~sex, colors = c(Men = "#0082c8", Women = "#E74C3C"),
          type = "bar", orientation = "h", text = ~label, hoverinfo = "text", textposition = "none",
          legendgroup = ~sex, showlegend = legend) %>%
    plotly::layout(xaxis = pyramid_axis(m))
}
b <- 150
p <- subplot(one(left, TRUE), one(right, FALSE), shareY = TRUE, titleX = TRUE, margin = 0.03) %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title  = list(text = paste0(left, " and ", right, " in ", last_year, ": share of the population in each age group"),
                  x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    barmode = "overlay", bargap = 0.1,
    margin = list(t = 110, b = b),
    yaxis  = list(title = "age"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.5, xanchor = "center", y = 1.08),
    annotations = list(
      list(text = paste0("<b>", left, "</b>"), x = 0.24, y = 1.0, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "center", yanchor = "bottom", showarrow = FALSE),
      list(text = paste0("<b>", right, "</b>"), x = 0.76, y = 1.0, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "center", yanchor = "bottom", showarrow = FALSE),
      source_note(b)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
sized(p, 560)






Nigeria, at 4.4 children per woman, is still a pyramid: the youngest group is the biggest. Greece, below 2.1 for more than forty years, has more people in their fifties than in any other group and fewer children under five than people in their seventies. People aged 65 and over are 24% of Greece’s population, children under 15 only 13%.

title: The World Is Having Fewer Babies: Fertility and Ageing Since 1960
text:
What the charts show


Code
peaks <- df_world %>%
  filter(measure == "population", country %in% c("China", "South Korea", "Italy", "Greece"), year <= last_year) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(peak_year = year[which.max(value)],
            peak      = round(max(value) / 1e6, 1),
            now       = round(value[year == last_year] / 1e6, 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
peaks


      country peak_year   peak    now
1       China      2021 1412.4 1409.0
2      Greece      2010   11.1   10.4
3       Italy      2014   60.3   59.0
4 South Korea      2020   51.8   51.8



More than half the world is below 2.1: 119 of 217 countries in 2024, against 5 in 1960.
Countries are getting older: 53 countries now have more people over 65 than children under 15; in 1960 there was 1.
Some populations have started to shrink: the table above shows when the population peaked in four of them. Greece’s population peaked in 2010, Italy’s in 2014, South Korea’s in 2020 and China’s in 2021.
A low rate does not shrink a country at once. The large generations born earlier are still having children, people live longer, and people move in from other countries. Many countries below 2.1 are still growing; but without immigration, a rate below 2.1 for long enough means fewer people.
Caveats: the fertility rate is an estimate built from birth registrations, censuses and surveys, and the latest years are often projections that are revised later, especially where births are not all registered. The 2.1 level is for countries where few children die; where more die young, a population needs a little more.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
If you compare Greece in 2000 with Greece in 2020, you get a confusing picture. Both years are unusual: in 2000 Greece did not yet use the euro, and 2020 was the year COVID shut the world down. In between, Greece went through a boom, a very deep crisis and a slow recovery, and two snapshots cannot show that.
This data story follows Greece year by year, in plain words, through the World Bank’s numbers on:

income — how much the country produces per person,
jobs — how many people who want work cannot find it,
investment — what the country spends on its future,
people — who moves in and out, and how old the population is,
energy — where the electricity comes from.

All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators. The page carries its own copy of the Greek data and of the one function it uses, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub; install golemworldbank to do the same for any other country, or to explore the data in the app.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "plotly"))
# The data and indicator_change() come from golemworldbank, copied next to this page:
# R/code_golemworldbank.R (sourced above) and R/mfi_greece.rds. For every country,
# install golemworldbank itself; its data is in Git LFS, so install it from a clone
# (install_github() can download LFS pointer files instead of the data):
#   git lfs install
#   git clone https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank.git
# then in R:
#   devtools::install_local("golemworldbank")

library(dplyr)
library(plotly)          # interactive charts

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
The data
golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_greece.rds holds its rows for Greece, every indicator and year. We keep the years from 2000 onwards and the indicators this story needs, each with a short name:


Code
# golemworldbank's mfi, Greece only (with the package installed, its mfi has every country)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_greece.rds"))

indicators <- c(
  income             = "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  unemployment       = "Unemployment, total (% of total labor force) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  youth_unemployment = "Unemployment, youth total (% of total labor force ages 15-24) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  investment         = "Gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)",
  net_migration      = "Net migration",
  population         = "Population, total",
  aged_65            = "Population ages 65 and above (% of total population)",
  fertility          = "Fertility rate, total (births per woman)",
  coal               = "Electricity production from coal sources (% of total)",
  renewables         = "Renewable electricity output (% of total electricity output)",
  gas                = "Electricity production from natural gas sources (% of total)",
  tourism            = "International tourism, receipts (current US$)",
  life_expectancy    = "Life expectancy at birth, total (years)",
  internet           = "Individuals using the Internet (% of population)",
  exports            = "Exports of goods and services (% of GDP)",
  poverty            = "Poverty headcount ratio at societal poverty line (% of population)"
)

df_greece <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Country Name` == "Greece", `Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  filter(year >= 2000) %>%
  select(measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(measure, year)

head(df_greece, 12)


   measure year    value
1  aged_65 2000 17.02536
2  aged_65 2001 17.26438
3  aged_65 2002 17.53454
4  aged_65 2003 17.83265
5  aged_65 2004 18.10322
6  aged_65 2005 18.32481
7  aged_65 2006 18.48934
8  aged_65 2007 18.60483
9  aged_65 2008 18.71140
10 aged_65 2009 18.88299
11 aged_65 2010 19.15789
12 aged_65 2011 19.50739


Each row is one indicator in one year:







Column
Description




measure
Short name of the indicator (the names of indicators above)


year
Year of observation


value
The World Bank’s value for Greece in that year



Two of these need a word of explanation:

Income is the value of everything Greece produces in a year, divided by the number of people who live there, in US dollars with price rises removed, so that years can be compared fairly. It is a rough measure of how well off the average person is.
Investment is the money spent on things that help a country earn more later: new buildings, factories, machines, roads and equipment, as a share of everything the economy produces.

Every chart below shades the two shocks of the period — the debt crisis (2008 to 2013) and COVID (2020) — and writes the latest value at the end of each line:


Code
# the latest value of a measure, and its value in a given year
at <- function(m, y) df_greece$value[df_greece$measure == m & df_greece$year == y]
last_year <- function(m) max(df_greece$year[df_greece$measure == m])
latest <- function(m) at(m, last_year(m))
change_pct <- function(from, to) round((to - from) / from * 100)
big <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")

# "$21,922" for dollars, "8.5%" for percentages
fmt <- function(v, unit) {
  if (unit == "$") paste0("$", big(v)) else paste0(round(v, 1), unit)
}

shocks <- list(list(from = 2008,   to = 2013,   label = "Debt crisis"),
               list(from = 2019.5, to = 2020.5, label = "COVID"))

# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}

# title, shaded shocks, end labels and the data source in one layout() call
# (a second layout(annotations = ...) would replace the first one's). The
# source sits at the bottom of the bottom margin `b`, in pixels, so it lands
# in the same place whatever the chart's height; the x axis range is fixed,
# because plotly would otherwise widen it to make room for the end labels
finish <- function(p, title, ytitle, labels, unit = "", legend = TRUE, b = if (legend) 150 else 110) {
  shapes <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(type = "rect", xref = "x", yref = "paper", x0 = s$from, x1 = s$to, y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
         fillcolor = "#EBEBEB", line = list(width = 0), layer = "below")
  })
  tags <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(x = (s$from + s$to) / 2, y = 1, xref = "x", yref = "paper", yanchor = "bottom",
         text = s$label, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "#666666"))
  })
  source_note <- list(
    text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
    xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = "#7F7F7F"))
  plotly::layout(p,
    title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 90, r = 130, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, range = c(1999.5, max(df_greece$year) + 0.5)),
    yaxis  = list(title = ytitle, ticksuffix = if (unit == "%") "%" else "", rangemode = "tozero"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
    showlegend = legend,
    shapes = shapes,
    annotations = c(tags, labels, list(source_note)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "#404040"))
}

# one line per measure, each with its value written at the end; `nudge` lifts
# a label (in pixels) off a line it would otherwise be written over
story_chart <- function(measures, names, short, colors, title, ytitle, unit = "", h = 520,
                        nudge = rep(0, length(measures))) {
  p <- plot_ly()
  ends <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(measures)) {
    d <- df_greece[df_greece$measure == measures[i], ]
    p <- add_trace(p, data = d, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = names[i],
                   type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
                   line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                   marker = list(color = colors[i], size = 7),
                   text = paste0(names[i], " · ", d$year, "<br>", fmt(d$value, unit)),
                   hoverinfo = "text")
    ends[[i]] <- list(x = last_year(measures[i]), y = latest(measures[i]), xref = "x", yref = "y",
                      xanchor = "left", xshift = 8, yshift = nudge[i], showarrow = FALSE,
                      text = trimws(paste(short[i], fmt(latest(measures[i]), unit))),
                      font = list(size = 13, color = "#404040"))
  }
  finish(p, title, ytitle, ends, unit, legend = length(measures) > 1) %>% sized(h)
}

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Greece at a glance


Code
peak   <- df_greece %>% filter(measure == "income", year <= 2010) %>% slice_max(value)
bottom <- df_greece %>% filter(measure == "income", year > 2008, year <= 2016) %>% slice_min(value)

p <- plot_ly(df_greece[df_greece$measure == "income", ], x = ~year, y = ~value,
             type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
             line = list(color = "#0082c8", width = 2), marker = list(color = "#0082c8", size = 7),
             text = ~paste0("Greece · ", year, "<br>", fmt(value, "$"), " per person"), hoverinfo = "text")
finish(p, "Greece: how much the country produces per person (US$, price rises removed)", "US$ per person",
       labels = list(
         list(x = peak$year, y = peak$value, yshift = 10, yanchor = "bottom", showarrow = FALSE,
              text = paste0("Peak ", peak$year, ": ", fmt(peak$value, "$")), font = list(color = "#404040")),
         list(x = bottom$year, y = bottom$value, yshift = -10, yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
              text = paste0("Bottom ", bottom$year, ": ", fmt(bottom$value, "$")), font = list(color = "#404040")),
         list(x = last_year("income"), y = latest("income"), xanchor = "left", xshift = 8, showarrow = FALSE,
              text = fmt(latest("income"), "$"), font = list(color = "#404040"))),
       legend = FALSE) %>%
  sized(520)






The line has five chapters:

2000 to 2008: boom. Joining the euro made borrowing cheap for the government and for families, and money flowed in. Income per person grew by 33%. Part of that growth was paid for with borrowed money.
2008 to 2013: crisis. In late 2009 it came out that the government’s finances were far worse than it had reported. From 2010 Greece needed rescue loans from other euro countries and the International Monetary Fund, and in return it had to cut wages, pensions and public spending and raise taxes. Income per person fell by 26% in five years.
2013 to 2019: slow recovery. The economy grew again, slowly. The last rescue programme ended in 2018.
2020: COVID. Tourists stopped coming and the economy fell again.
2021 onwards: rebound. Growth returned, but in 2025 income per person was still 8% below 2008.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
section: Jobs: the deepest wound, now healing
text:
Jobs: the deepest wound, now healing
The unemployment rate counts people who want a job and are looking for one, but cannot find one.


Code
story_chart(c("unemployment", "youth_unemployment"),
            names  = c("Everyone", "Young people (15 to 24)"),
            short  = c("Everyone", "Young"),
            colors = c("#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
            title  = "Greece: people looking for work who cannot find it (%)",
            ytitle = "% of people looking for work", unit = "%")






In 2013, 28% of people looking for work could not find a job — more than 1 in 4. Among young people it was 58%, almost 6 in 10. Since then unemployment has fallen every year, and by 2025 it was back near its level before the crisis (8.5%, against 7.7% in 2008).

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
section: Investment: what has not come back
text:
Investment: what has not come back


Code
story_chart("investment", names = "Investment", short = "",
            colors = "#0082c8",
            title  = "Greece: investment in buildings, machines and roads (% of the economy)",
            ytitle = "% of the economy", unit = "%")






Before the crisis Greece invested about a quarter of what it produced. During the crisis this fell to about a tenth (11.5% in 2013) and stayed there until 2019. It is rising again (16.9% in 2025), but it is still well below where it was. A decade of low investment is one reason incomes have not fully recovered.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
People: fewer and older
Net migration is the number of people who moved into the country minus the number who moved out. Blue bars mean more people arrived than left; red bars mean more people left than arrived.


Code
d <- df_greece %>%
  filter(measure == "net_migration") %>%
  mutate(color = ifelse(value >= 0, "#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
         what  = ifelse(value >= 0, "more arrived than left", "more left than arrived"))

p <- plot_ly(d, x = ~year, y = ~value, type = "bar",
             marker = list(color = ~color),
             text = ~paste0("Greece · ", year, "<br>", big(value), " people: ", what),
             hoverinfo = "text", textposition = "none")
finish(p, "Greece: people who moved in, minus people who moved out, per year", "people per year",
       labels = list(), legend = FALSE) %>%
  sized(520)






During the crisis many people, often young and well educated, moved abroad to find work: between 2011 and 2015 about 250,000 more people left Greece than arrived. Treat the latest years with care — the World Bank’s estimates for them jump sharply from one year to the next.
At the same time, Greek families have few children: about 1.2 per woman, while about 2 are needed to keep a population steady. Together these explain why there are fewer Greeks now (10.4 million in 2025, down from 11.1 million around 2010) and why they are older: people aged 65 and over were 17% of the population in 2000 and 24% in 2025.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Energy: much less coal
Most of Greece’s electricity used to come from lignite, a cheap and dirty kind of coal. Those power stations are being closed, and solar parks, wind farms and power stations that burn natural gas have taken their place.


Code
story_chart(c("coal", "renewables", "gas"),
            names  = c("Coal", "Renewable (sun, wind, water)", "Natural gas"),
            short  = c("Coal", "Renewable", "Gas"),
            colors = c("#E74C3C", "#0082c8", "#999999"),
            title  = "Greece: where the electricity comes from (% of all electricity)",
            ytitle = "% of all electricity", unit = "%",
            nudge  = c(0, 14, 0))   # renewables stop in 2021, above the gas line






In 2000 coal made 64% of Greece’s electricity; by 2025 it made 5%. Renewable sources went from 8% to 41% (2021 is the last year the World Bank reports), and natural gas from 11% to 39%.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Comparing two years with indicator_change()
golemworldbank’s indicator_change() compares every indicator a country has in two years and splits them into those that went up and those that went down, each sorted by percentage change — the same comparison as the app’s Change (%) tab. The result depends entirely on which two years you pick. Comparing 2000 with 2020 mixes twenty years of change with one very bad year: in 2019 tourists spent $23 billion in Greece, in 2020 $6 billion, a fall of 73% in one year.
These pairs each answer one clear question:



Question
From
To




What did the boom look like?
2000
2008


How bad was the crisis?
2008
2013


How strong was the recovery?
2013
2019


Is Greece back to where it was?
2008
2024



Avoid 2020 and 2021 as end points, because COVID makes almost everything look worse than the real trend, and use 2024 as the latest year, because the 2025 numbers are still incomplete. The crisis, for example:


Code
crisis <- indicator_change(mfi, country = "Greece", year1 = 2008, year2 = 2013)
c(increased = nrow(crisis$increased), decreased = nrow(crisis$decreased))


increased decreased 
      319       474 


Code
# the indicators of this story, by their short names
headline <- function(tab) {
  tab <- tab[tab$Indicator %in% indicators, ]
  tab$Indicator <- names(indicators)[match(tab$Indicator, indicators)]
  # 3 significant digits, with thousands separators and no scientific notation
  tab[, 2:4] <- lapply(tab[, 2:4], function(x) {
    vapply(x, function(v) format(signif(v, 3), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE), "")
  })
  tab
}
