Code
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = modifyList(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = modifyList(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")

# the EU countries from the highest to the lowest, Greece in red and the EU in blue; where Eurostat
# publishes no figure for the EU, a dotted line marks the median country
ranking <- function(x, title, source, suffix = "%", digits = 1) {
  x$name <- eu_name[x$geo]
  x <- x[order(x$values), ]
  x$name <- factor(x$name, levels = x$name)
  lines <- list()
  notes <- list()
  if (!any(x$geo == "EU27_2020")) {
    m <- median(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])
    lines <- list(list(type = "line", x0 = m, x1 = m, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper", line = list(color = blue, width = 2, dash = "dot")))
    notes <- list(list(x = m, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "Median EU country", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
                       xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = blue)))
  }
  # the source 45 px under the plot, below the numbers of the axis: in a chart this tall a fixed
  # fraction of the plot would put it below the bottom of the chart
  height <- knitr::opts_current$get("out.height.px")
  if (!is.numeric(height)) height <- 864
  plot_ly(x,
    x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = ifelse(x$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(x$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: %{x:.", digits, "f}", suffix, "<extra></extra>")
  ) %>%
    chart(paste0(title, ", ", x$time[1]), source, x_axis = list(ticksuffix = suffix), shapes = lines,
          annotations = notes, margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -45 / (height - 70 - 90))
}

# short labels of numbers
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)
thousands <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
section: 1. How much schooling do Greeks have?
text:
1. How much schooling do Greeks have?
About as many university graduates as the rest of the EU, and almost no one leaves school early.
In 2025, 42.8% of Greeks aged 25 to 34 had a university degree or another tertiary qualification, against 44.8% in the EU: the 11th lowest share of the 27 countries.


Code
ranking(tertiary, "People aged 25 to 34 with tertiary education, %", "Eurostat, edat_lfse_03")






Almost every young Greek finishes secondary school. Only 3.0% of Greeks aged 18 to 24 left education with at most lower secondary school and are not in any education or training, the 2nd lowest share in the EU, where it is 9.1%. The older generations had less schooling: 18.0% of Greeks aged 25 to 64 have no more than lower secondary education, against 18.8% in the EU.


Code
ranking(early, "Early leavers from education and training, % of people aged 18 to 24", "Eurostat, edat_lfse_14")

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
text:
2. What do they know?

Maths, reading and science at 15


Code
pisa_year <- pisa$EF461$time[1]
maths <- pisa_all[pisa_all$field == "EF461" & pisa_all$geo %in% c("EL", "EU27_2020"), ]
first_year <- min(intersect(maths$time[maths$geo == "EL"], maths$time[maths$geo == "EU27_2020"]))
maths_then <- function(geo) maths$values[maths$geo == geo & maths$time == first_year]


50% of Greek 15-year-olds are below the basic level in maths, against 34% in the EU.
PISA, the OECD’s test of 15-year-olds, measures whether students can use what they have learned. Below level 2, its basic level, a student can at most answer questions about a familiar, clearly stated situation with all the information given: in maths, for example, apply a simple formula when told which one. In 2025, 50% of Greek 15-year-olds were below that level in maths, against 34% in the EU, the 4th highest share of the 27 countries. In reading the shares are 44% and 31%, and in science 41% and 26%. The EU’s target for 2030 is fewer than 15% in each.


Code
pisa_table <- data.frame(
  subject = factor(subjects, levels = subjects),
  greece = sapply(pisa, greece),
  eu = sapply(pisa, eu)
)
plot_ly(pisa_table,
  x = ~subject, y = ~greece, type = "bar", name = "Greece", marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}%<extra>Greece</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~eu, name = "EU-27", marker = list(color = blue), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}%<extra>EU-27</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("15-year-olds below the basic level of PISA, ", pisa_year, ", %"), "Eurostat, sdg_04_40 (OECD PISA)", "%",
        y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%"), legend = legend_top, barmode = "group")






It was not always as far behind: in 2006, 32% of Greek 15-year-olds were below the basic level in maths, against 25% in the EU. These are results of schooling, not of ability: PISA tests what students have been taught, and how well, by the age of 15.


Code
ranking(pisa$EF461, "15-year-olds below the basic level of PISA in mathematics, %", "Eurostat, sdg_04_40 (OECD PISA)")








Computer skills
51% of Greek adults have at least basic computer skills, against 60% in the EU.
Eurostat counts people as having at least basic digital skills when they can do at least one basic task in each of five areas: finding and judging information, communicating online, making digital content, using a device safely, and solving problems with it. In 2025, 51% of Greeks aged 16 to 74 could, against 60% in the EU, the 6th lowest share of the 27 countries; 27% had above basic skills, against 31%. Few Greeks work with computers for a living: ICT specialists are 2.5% of the people in work, the lowest share in the EU, where they are 5.0%.


Code
ranking(digital, "People aged 16 to 74 with at least basic digital skills, %", "Eurostat, isoc_sk_dskl_i21")








Learning as adults
Greeks rarely go back to learning once they work. In 2025, 5.2% of Greeks aged 25 to 64 had taken part in a course or other training in the four weeks before the survey, against 13.7% in the EU: the lowest share.


Code
ranking(learning, "People aged 25 to 64 in education or training in the last four weeks, %", "Eurostat, trng_lfse_01")

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
text:
3. Do they find work?


Code
greek_rates <- unemployment_all[unemployment_all$geo == "EL" & unemployment_all$age == "Y15-74", ]
peak_year <- greek_rates$time[which.max(greek_rates$values)]


More of them are out of work than in most of the EU, and for longer. Unemployment in Greece rose to 27.8% of the labour force in 2013, in the debt crisis, and has fallen to 8.9% in 2025. That is still the 3rd highest rate in the EU, where it is 6.0%. Among the young, aged 15 to 24, it is 19.1%, against 15.2%.


Code
line <- function(geo, age) unemployment_all[unemployment_all$geo == geo & unemployment_all$age == age, ]
series <- data.frame(
  geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020", "EL", "EU27_2020"),
  age = c("Y15-74", "Y15-74", "Y15-24", "Y15-24"),
  name = c("Greece, 15 to 74", "EU-27, 15 to 74", "Greece, 15 to 24", "EU-27, 15 to 24"),
  color = c(greek_red, blue, greek_red, blue),
  dash = c("solid", "solid", "dot", "dot")
)
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in seq_len(nrow(series))) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    data = line(series$geo[k], series$age[k]), x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    name = series$name[k], line = list(color = series$color[k], width = 3, dash = series$dash[k]),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f}%<extra>", series$name[k], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart("Unemployment, % of the labour force", "Eurostat, une_rt_a", "%",
            y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)






Unemployment in Greece lasts: 56% of the unemployed have been looking for work for a year or longer, against 32% in the EU, which makes the long-term unemployed 5.0% of the labour force, the highest share in the EU. 13.6% of Greeks aged 15 to 29 are neither in work nor in education or training, against 11.0% in the EU.
Of the Greeks aged 20 to 64, 71.0% have a job, against 76.1% in the EU. The gap is mostly among women: 62.3% of Greek women have a job, against 71.3% of women in the EU, while for men the rates are 79.7% and 80.9%.

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
section: 4. How hard do they work, and how much do they produce?
text:
4. How hard do they work, and how much do they produce?
Hours of work: the highest in the EU. Output per hour: the lowest.
Greeks in work usually work 41.0 hours a week, the highest in the EU, where the average is 37.0. Yet an hour of work in Greece produces 54% of what an hour produces on average in the EU, the lowest in the EU, and a person in work, with the longer hours, 67%. These figures count output in purchasing power standards, which allow for the lower prices of Greece.


Code
both <- merge(hours[hours$geo %in% eu_codes, c("geo", "values")],
              per_hour[per_hour$geo %in% eu_codes, c("geo", "values")],
              by = "geo", suffixes = c("_hours", "_output"))
both$label <- ifelse(both$geo == "EL", "Greece", both$geo)
both$name <- eu_name[both$geo]
plot_ly(both,
  x = ~values_hours, y = ~values_output, type = "scatter", mode = "markers+text",
  text = ~label, textposition = "top center", customdata = ~name,
  marker = list(size = ifelse(both$geo == "EL", 14, 9), color = ifelse(both$geo == "EL", greek_red, gray)),
  textfont = list(color = ifelse(both$geo == "EL", greek_red, dark_gray)),
  hovertemplate = "%{customdata}: %{x:.1f} hours a week, %{y:.0f}% of the EU's output per hour<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Hours of work and output per hour, ", hours$time[1]), "Eurostat, lfsa_ewhun2 and tesem160",
        "Output per hour worked, EU = 100", x_axis = list(title = "Usual hours of work a week"),
        margin = list(t = 70, b = 110), note_y = -0.2)






Output per hour depends less on how hard people work than on what they work with, and where. A large share of Greeks work for themselves or in very small firms: 24.3% of Greeks in work are self-employed, the highest share in the EU, where it is 12.9%. They run farms, shops, taxis, cafés and workshops, often with no employees. Small businesses like these have less machinery and technology behind each hour of work than large firms, and long opening hours add hours more than they add output.


Code
ranking(self_employed, "The self-employed, % of the people in work aged 15 to 64", "Eurostat, lfsa_egaps")

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
section: 5. Do their jobs use their education?
text:
5. Do their jobs use their education?
Often not. 31.4% of the Greeks with tertiary education who work have jobs that do not need it, such as clerical, sales or manual jobs, the 2nd highest share in the EU, where it is 21.4%. The schools and universities produce graduates; the economy has too few jobs that need them.


Code
ranking(overqualified, "People in work with tertiary education in jobs that do not need it, %", "Eurostat, lfsa_eoqgan")

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
text:
6. Is there much crime?
Recorded crime is around the middle of the EU, but the share of Greeks who see crime around them is the highest in the EU.
Crime is hard to compare between countries. The police can only count the offences that people report, and people report more where they trust the police or need a report for their insurance; and each country defines and counts offences in its own way. Eurostat therefore warns against comparing the levels of most offences between countries. The exception is intentional homicide, which is almost always recorded, and recorded in the same way.


Code
homicide <- offences$ICCS0101
median_eu <- function(x) median(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes])


In 2024, the police in Greece recorded 0.78 intentional homicides for every 100,000 inhabitants, against 0.85 in the median EU country: the 11th lowest rate of 27 countries.


Code
ranking(homicide, "Intentional homicides recorded by the police, per 100,000 inhabitants", "Eurostat, crim_off_cat",
        suffix = "", digits = 2)






For the other offences, with the warning above, Greece is near the middle or below it:


Code
# homicides with two decimals, as there are few of them
decimals <- function(i, v) if (i == "ICCS0101") two(v) else one(v)
offence_table <- data.frame(
  Offence = offence_names,
  Year = sapply(offences, function(x) x$time[1]),
  Greece = sapply(names(offences), function(i) decimals(i, greece(offences[[i]]))),
  `Median EU country` = sapply(names(offences), function(i) decimals(i, median_eu(offences[[i]]))),
  `Place of Greece` = sapply(offences, function(x) paste(sum(x$values[x$geo %in% eu_codes] > greece(x)) + 1, "of", countries(x))),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(offence_table, align = "lrrrr",
             caption = "Offences recorded by the police per 100,000 inhabitants; place 1 is the country with the most")

How many are in prison?


Code
prison_year <- max(prisoners_ctz$time)
held <- function(citizen) prisoners_ctz$values[prisoners_ctz$citizen == citizen & prisoners_ctz$time == prison_year]
# the Greek citizens living in Greece on 1 January of the next year, or of the same year
greek_citizens <- citizens$values[match(prison_year + 1, citizens$time)]
if (is.na(greek_citizens)) greek_citizens <- citizens$values[match(prison_year, citizens$time)]
greek_rate <- 1e5 * held("NAT") / greek_citizens


Greece holds 111 people in prison for every 100,000 inhabitants, against 111 in the median EU country (the 14th highest rate of 27). Of the 11,484 people held in Greek prisons in 2024, 5,511 were Greek citizens: 57 for every 100,000 Greek citizens living in Greece, or one in 1,748. The other 52% were foreign citizens, a group that also includes people who did not live in Greece, so it cannot be turned into a rate in the same way.
A prison count is not a count of criminals: it includes people waiting for their trial, and most people who commit an offence are never caught, or are fined or given a suspended sentence instead of prison.


Code
ranking(prisoners, "People held in prison, per 100,000 inhabitants", "Eurostat, crim_pris_cap", suffix = "", digits = 0)








How safe do Greeks feel?
Less safe than anyone else in the EU. In 2023, 20.9% of Greeks said that there is crime, violence or vandalism in the area where they live, against 10.0% of people in the EU: the highest share. The gap between the crime that is recorded and the crime that people see around them can have many causes, among them petty crime and vandalism that are never reported, and trust in the police.


Code
ranking(area, "People who say that their area has crime, violence or vandalism, %", "Eurostat, ilc_mddw03 (EU-SILC)")

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
text:
So, are they good workers?
The data cannot say whether Greeks are good workers, but they can say what Greek workers bring and what the economy does with it:

They work long hours: 41.0 hours a week, the highest in the EU.
They stay in education: the 2nd lowest share of early school leavers in the EU, and about as many graduates as the EU, 43% of people aged 25 to 34.
But what they learn at school is weak: 50% of 15-year-olds are below the basic level in maths, against 34% in the EU; fewer adults have basic computer skills (51%, against 60%), and almost none go back to learning (5.2%, the lowest share in the EU).
And the economy does not use what they have: an hour of work produces 54% of the EU average, the lowest; 24% of the people in work are self-employed, mostly in very small businesses; 31% of the graduates in work have jobs that do not need a degree; and 9% of the labour force cannot find work.
Crime is not the problem it is felt to be: the homicide rate and the prison population are around the middle of the EU, and 57 in every 100,000 Greek citizens are in prison, yet 21% of Greeks say that there is crime where they live, the highest share in the EU.

The picture is of people who work hard and stay in school, in an economy of small businesses that turns their hours into little output and leaves much of their education unused, and with schools that teach less than those of most of the EU.

title: Greece at Work: Education, Skills, Jobs and Crime Compared with the EU
text:
Sources

Eurostat, education and skills: edat_lfse_03 (educational attainment), edat_lfse_14 (early leavers from education and training), sdg_04_40 (low achieving 15-year-olds, from the OECD’s PISA), isoc_sk_dskl_i21 (digital skills), trng_lfse_01 (adult learning), isoc_sks_itspt (ICT specialists).
Eurostat, work: une_rt_a (unemployment), une_ltu_a (long-term unemployment), edat_lfse_20 (young people neither in employment nor in education or training), lfsi_emp_a (employment), lfsa_ewhun2 (hours of work), tesem160 (labour productivity), lfsa_egaps (employment by professional status), lfsa_eoqgan (over-qualification).
Eurostat, crime: crim_off_cat (recorded offences), crim_pris_cap (prison population), crim_pris_ctz (prisoners by citizenship), migr_pop1ctz (population by citizenship), ilc_mddw03 (crime, violence or vandalism in the area).

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Every September the Arctic sea ice reaches its annual minimum after the summer melt season. The National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) has been tracking this since 1979 using satellite passive-microwave sensors. Their Sea Ice Index v4.0 is the authoritative public record.
This document shows you exactly how to download the real data and reproduce the charts below — no manual downloads, no hardcoded numbers.

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Every September the Arctic sea ice reaches its annual minimum after the summer melt season. The National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) has been tracking this since 1979 using satellite passive-microwave sensors. Their Sea Ice Index v4.0 is the authoritative public record.
This document shows you exactly how to download the real data and reproduce the charts below — no manual downloads, no hardcoded numbers.

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Packages


Code
# Install any missing packages before running
# install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "sf", "rnaturalearth", "rnaturalearthdata"))

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Part 1 — Time series

Download the data
NSIDC publishes one CSV per month. September (month 09) is the annual minimum.


Code
csv_url <- "https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/north/monthly/data/N_09_extent_v4.0.csv"

arctic <- read.csv(csv_url, strip.white = TRUE) |>
  select(year, extent) |>
  filter(year >= 1979)

head(arctic)


  year extent
1 1979   7.05
2 1980   7.67
3 1981   7.14
4 1982   7.30
5 1983   7.39
6 1984   6.81




Plot


Code
avg_baseline <- arctic |> filter(year <= 1990) |> pull(extent) |> mean()
loss_pct     <- round((1 - min(arctic$extent) / avg_baseline) * 100)

col_fill   <- "#B3E5FC"
col_line   <- "#0277BD"
col_trend  <- "#C62828"
col_record <- "#E65100"
col_ref    <- "#78909C"
col_title  <- "#0D1B40"

records <- filter(arctic, year %in% c(2007, 2012, 2020))

ggplot(arctic, aes(x = year, y = extent)) +
  geom_area(fill = col_fill, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = avg_baseline, linetype = "dotted",
             color = col_ref, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 1981, y = avg_baseline + 0.18,
           label = "1979-1990 mean", size = 2.9, color = col_ref, hjust = 0) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              color = col_trend, fill = "#FFCDD2", alpha = 0.25,
              linewidth = 1.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = col_line, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = records, color = col_record, fill = col_record,
             size = 4, shape = 21, stroke = 1.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2012, xend = 2012,
           y = min(arctic$extent), yend = min(arctic$extent) - 0.6,
           color = col_record, linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 2012, y = min(arctic$extent) - 0.75,
           label = paste0("Record low\n", round(min(arctic$extent), 2),
                          " M km²  (", arctic$year[which.min(arctic$extent)], ")"),
           color = col_record, size = 2.9, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = max(arctic$year), y = max(arctic$extent) * 0.93,
           label = paste0("-", loss_pct, "% vs.\n1979-1990 avg"),
           color = col_trend, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting",
    subtitle = "September minimum sea ice extent, 1979 to present",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Extent  (million km²)",
    caption  = "Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0 | noaadata.apps.nsidc.org"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1980, 2030, 5), expand = c(0.01, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, " M")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#F0F8FF", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray88", linewidth = 0.35),

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Part 2 — Maps (overview)

How the shapefiles work
NSIDC also publishes the sea ice boundary as a polygon shapefile for every month. We download and cache them locally, then read with sf.


Code
month_dirs <- c("01_Jan","02_Feb","03_Mar","04_Apr","05_May","06_Jun",
                "07_Jul","08_Aug","09_Sep","10_Oct","11_Nov","12_Dec")

fetch_ice_extent <- function(year, month = "09", pole = "N",
                             tmpdir = file.path(tempdir(), "nsidc_ice")) {
  dir.create(tmpdir, showWarnings = FALSE)
  mm       <- sprintf("%02d", as.integer(month))
  yymm     <- paste0(year, mm)
  pole_dir <- ifelse(pole == "N", "north", "south")
  mon_dir  <- month_dirs[as.integer(mm)]
  url <- paste0(
    "https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/",
    pole_dir, "/monthly/shapefiles/shp_extent/", mon_dir, "/",
    "extent_", pole, "_", yymm, "_polygon_v4.0.zip"
  )
  zip_path <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm, ".zip"))
  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000) {
    message("Downloading ", year, "-", mm, " ...")
    tryCatch(
      download.file(url, zip_path, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb"),
      error = function(e) { message("  failed: ", e$message); return(NULL) }
    )
  }
  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000) return(NULL)
  exdir <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm))
  suppressWarnings(unzip(zip_path, exdir = exdir, overwrite = FALSE))
  shp <- list.files(exdir, "\\.shp$", full.names = TRUE)[1]
  if (is.na(shp)) return(NULL)
  shape <- tryCatch(sf::st_read(shp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(shape)) return(NULL)
  shape$year <- year
  shape
}




Download shapefiles (every 5 years)


Code
years_overview <- c(1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2024)

ice_list <- lapply(years_overview, fetch_ice_extent, month = "09", pole = "N")
ice_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), ice_list)
ice_all  <- do.call(rbind, ice_list)




Build the map


Code
world     <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
crs_polar <- "+proj=stere +lat_0=90 +lat_ts=70 +lon_0=0 +datum=WGS84 +units=m"

ice_proj   <- st_transform(ice_all,  crs_polar)
world_proj <- st_transform(world,    crs_polar)

clip_large <- st_buffer(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 90)), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(crs_polar),
  dist = 1e7
)
world_clip <- st_intersection(world_proj, clip_large)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = clip_large, fill = "#AED6F1", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = ice_proj,   fill = "white",  color = "white",   linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = world_clip, fill = "#8D6E63", color = "#6D4C41", linewidth = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title   = "Arctic Sea Ice Extent - September",
    caption = "Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#1A237E", color = NA),
    strip.text      = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 9),
    plot.title      = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 14,
                                   margin = margin(12, 0, 8, 12)),
    plot.caption    = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 7, hjust = 1,
                                   margin = margin(8, 12, 8, 0)),
    panel.spacing   = unit(0.4, "lines")
  )

text:
Part 3 — Maps (zoomed comparison)
Four key years in a closer view, with the actual extent area computed from the polygon geometry.


Code
years_zoom <- c(1985, 2000, 2012, 2024)

ice_zoom_list <- lapply(years_zoom, fetch_ice_extent, month = "09", pole = "N")
ice_zoom_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), ice_zoom_list)
ice_zoom_all  <- do.call(rbind, ice_zoom_list)




Code
ice_zoom_proj <- st_transform(ice_zoom_all, crs_polar)

clip_tight <- st_buffer(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 90)), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(crs_polar),
  dist = 5.5e6
)
world_clip_tight <- st_intersection(world_proj, clip_tight)
ice_zoom_clip    <- st_intersection(ice_zoom_proj, clip_tight)

# Compute area per year (million km²) from the actual geometry
ice_areas <- sapply(years_zoom, function(y) {
  sub <- ice_zoom_proj[ice_zoom_proj$year == y, ]
  if (nrow(sub) == 0) return(NA)
  as.numeric(sum(st_area(sub))) / 1e12
})
base_area <- ice_areas[1]

labels_df <- data.frame(
  year  = years_zoom,
  label = ifelse(seq_along(years_zoom) == 1,
                 sprintf("%.2f M km²\n(baseline)", ice_areas),
                 sprintf("%.2f M km²\n(-%.0f%% vs %d)",
                         ice_areas, (1 - ice_areas / base_area) * 100, years_zoom[1]))
)
ice_zoom_clip <- merge(ice_zoom_clip, labels_df, by = "year")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = clip_tight,        fill = "#AED6F1", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = ice_zoom_clip,     fill = "white",   color = "#c8e0f0", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = world_clip_tight,  fill = "#6D4C41", color = "#4E342E", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf_text(
    data = ice_zoom_clip |> group_by(year) |> slice(1),
    aes(label = label, geometry = geometry),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    color = "white", size = 3, fontface = "bold",
    nudge_x = -3.2e6, nudge_y = -4.0e6, hjust = 0
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Arctic Sea Ice Shrinkage - September Minimum",
    subtitle = "Polar stereographic projection, zoomed to 55N+",
    caption  = "Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#0D1B2A", color = NA),
    strip.text      = element_text(color = "white",  face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title      = element_text(color = "white",  face = "bold", size = 16,
                                   margin = margin(14, 0, 4, 14)),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "#90CAF9", size = 9,
                                   margin = margin(0, 0, 10, 14)),
    plot.caption    = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 7.5, hjust = 1,
                                   margin = margin(8, 14, 10, 0)),
    panel.spacing   = unit(0.8, "lines")
  )

title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
text:
An earthquake comes without warning, and the strongest can wreck a city in a minute. This story asks where they strike, and four more questions:

Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?
How often, and how strong?
How deep are they?
Which were the deadliest?
Are there more of them than there used to be?

For the other hazards of the series, see Tsunamis, Volcanoes and the overview of natural disasters.
The data come from three places, downloaded when the page is rendered:

The earthquakes: the catalogue of the United States Geological Survey (USGS), called ComCat, which collects the earthquakes that seismic networks around the world report: the date, the place, the magnitude and the depth (ComCat, queried through its web service). The page uses every earthquake of magnitude 6 and above since 1900, and every one of magnitude 5 and above since 1973.
The deaths: the Significant Earthquake Database of the US National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI, part of NOAA), which lists destructive earthquakes with the number of people they killed (NCEI). The USGS catalogue has no deaths.
The map: the boundaries of the tectonic plates, from Peter Bird’s digital model (Bird 2003) in the version of Hugo Ahlenius and Nordpil (tectonicplates), and the outlines of the countries, from Natural Earth.

The magnitude is the size of the earthquake. Each whole number up is a tenfold increase in the ground motion that a seismograph records and 32 times more energy released (USGS). So a magnitude 7 earthquake releases 32 times the energy of a magnitude 6, and about a thousand times (32 × 32) that of a magnitude 5. This page writes magnitude 6 as M6, and “M6+” for magnitude 6 and above.
The depth is how far below the surface the rock starts to break, in kilometres. The USGS calls an earthquake shallow when it is between 0 and 70 km deep, intermediate between 70 and 300 km and deep between 300 and 700 km (USGS).
The tectonic plates are the large slabs that make up the outer shell of the Earth. They move against each other, and the earthquakes are not spread evenly: look at where the plates meet.

title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "sf", "jsonlite"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(sf)
library(jsonlite)

title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
text:
The data


Code
# only complete years: from 1 January of this year, the catalogue is incomplete
last_year <- as.integer(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")) - 1
# the USGS catalogue as a table: the earthquakes between two dates, of at least a magnitude
# (a query returns 20,000 earthquakes at most, so the magnitude 5 and above come in pieces)
usgs <- function(from, to, magnitude) {
  read.csv(paste0(
    "https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=csv",
    "&starttime=", from, "-01-01&endtime=", to, "-01-01",
    "&minmagnitude=", magnitude, "&orderby=time-asc&limit=20000"
  ))
}
# magnitude 6 and above, since 1900
big <- usgs(1900, last_year + 1, 6)
# magnitude 5 and above, since 1973, eight years at a time
starts <- seq(1973, last_year, by = 8)
ends <- c(starts[-1], last_year + 1)
middle <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(a, b) usgs(a, b, 5), starts, ends))
# the destructive earthquakes of NCEI, with deaths, since 1900, 200 to a page
noaa_url <- "https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/earthquakes?minYear=1900&minDeaths=1"
first_page <- fromJSON(noaa_url)
deadly <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(first_page$totalPages), function(i) {
  fromJSON(paste0(noaa_url, "&page=", i))$items[, c(
    "year", "locationName", "country", "eqMagnitude", "deaths", "deathsTotal", "latitude", "longitude"
  )]
}))
# the plate boundaries (Bird 2003), and the countries (Natural Earth, 1:50 million)
plates <- st_read(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json",
  quiet = TRUE
)
land <- st_read(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/geojson/ne_50m_admin_0_countries.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
)[, c("NAME_LONG", "ADM0_A3", "CONTINENT")]




Code
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# the three depths, in order, whose neighbours were checked for colour blindness
depth_colors <- c(Shallow = "#d97706", Intermediate = "#be123c", Deep = "#5b3fb5")
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the map of the countries
blues <- c("#eff3ff", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c", "#08306b")

# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}

# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}
# the distance in kilometres between two points (longitude and latitude in degrees)
distance_km <- function(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2) {
  r <- pi / 180
  h <- sin((lat2 - lat1) * r / 2)^2 + cos(lat1 * r) * cos(lat2 * r) * sin((lon2 - lon1) * r / 2)^2
  12742 * asin(sqrt(h))
}




Code
# only earthquakes: the catalogue also holds explosions, and more
all_types <- table(c(big$type, middle$type))
n_blasts <- sum(all_types[names(all_types) == "nuclear explosion"])
n_other <- sum(all_types[!names(all_types) %in% c("earthquake", "nuclear explosion")])
quakes <- function(x) {
  x <- x[x$type == "earthquake", ]
  x$year <- as.integer(substr(x$time, 1, 4))
  x
}
n_before <- nrow(big) + nrow(middle)
big <- quakes(big)
middle <- quakes(middle)
magnitude_types <- sort(table(middle$magType), decreasing = TRUE)

# the depth classes of the USGS
depth_class <- function(depth) {
  cut(depth, c(-Inf, 70, 300, Inf), labels = names(depth_colors), right = FALSE)
}
middle$depth_class <- depth_class(middle$depth)
big$depth_class <- depth_class(big$depth)
# depths that a location program sets when the data do not fix the depth (USGS: 10 and 33 km)
fixed_depth <- mean(middle$depth %in% c(10, 33))
other_depth <- max(table(middle$depth[!middle$depth %in% c(10, 33)])) / nrow(middle)
above_sea <- sum(middle$depth < 0)

# each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above: the country it is in; or the nearest country, if the
# sea is less than 200 km wide between the two; or nowhere. Planar geometry on longitude and latitude
# is accurate enough to find the nearest country; the distance itself is then worked out on the globe.
sf_use_s2(FALSE)
points <- st_as_sf(middle[, c("id", "longitude", "latitude")], coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
inside <- st_intersects(points, land)
on_land <- lengths(inside) > 0
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(points[!on_land, ], land)
lines <- st_nearest_points(points[!on_land, ], land[nearest, ], pairwise = TRUE)
ends_xy <- st_coordinates(st_cast(lines, "POINT"))
from_xy <- ends_xy[seq(1, nrow(ends_xy), by = 2), ]
to_xy <- ends_xy[seq(2, nrow(ends_xy), by = 2), ]
offshore_km <- distance_km(from_xy[, 1], from_xy[, 2], to_xy[, 1], to_xy[, 2])
middle$place_index <- NA_integer_
middle$place_index[on_land] <- vapply(inside[on_land], `[`, 1L, 1L)
reach <- 200
middle$place_index[!on_land][offshore_km <= reach] <- nearest[offshore_km <= reach]
land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG == "Russian Federation"] <- "Russia"
land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG == "South Georgia and the Islands"] <- "South Georgia"
middle$country <- land$NAME_LONG[middle$place_index]
middle$code <- land$ADM0_A3[middle$place_index]
middle$continent <- land$CONTINENT[middle$place_index]

# each earthquake of magnitude 6 and above since 1973: its distance from the nearest plate boundary
big_now <- big[big$year >= 1973, ]
points_now <- st_as_sf(big_now[, c("id", "longitude", "latitude")], coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
near_boundary <- st_nearest_feature(points_now, plates)
lines_now <- st_nearest_points(points_now, plates[near_boundary, ], pairwise = TRUE)
xy_now <- st_coordinates(st_cast(lines_now, "POINT"))
big_now$boundary_km <- distance_km(
  xy_now[seq(1, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 1], xy_now[seq(1, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 2],
  xy_now[seq(2, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 1], xy_now[seq(2, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 2]
)
# the same distance for points spread evenly over the globe: how much of the world is near a boundary
set.seed(2026)
n_random <- 4000
random_points <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(lon = runif(n_random, -180, 180), lat = asin(runif(n_random, -1, 1)) * 180 / pi),
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  crs = 4326
)
near_random <- st_nearest_feature(random_points, plates)
lines_random <- st_cast(st_nearest_points(random_points, plates[near_random, ], pairwise = TRUE), "POINT")
xy_random <- st_coordinates(lines_random)
random_km <- distance_km(
  xy_random[seq(1, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 1], xy_random[seq(1, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 2],
  xy_random[seq(2, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 1], xy_random[seq(2, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 2]
)
sf_use_s2(TRUE)

# the deaths: the NCEI total where it has one
deadly$deaths_all <- ifelse(is.na(deadly$deathsTotal), deadly$deaths, deadly$deathsTotal)
deadly <- deadly[!is.na(deadly$deaths_all) & deadly$year <= last_year, ]
deadly$name <- ifelse(deadly$country == "USA", "United States", tools::toTitleCase(tolower(deadly$country)))
# the place as NCEI writes it, in words: the parts between colons, without compass points
place_text <- function(x) {
  parts <- strsplit(tolower(x), "\\s*:\\s*")
  vapply(parts, function(p) {
    p <- trimws(p)
    paste(tools::toTitleCase(p[!p %in% c("n", "s", "e", "w", "ne", "nw", "se", "sw", "")]), collapse = ", ")
  }, "")
}
deadly$place <- place_text(deadly$locationName)


Only earthquakes. The catalogue also holds explosions, mine collapses and landslides. Of the 102,788 events that the two downloads found, 494 were nuclear explosions and 69 were other things (an explosion, a rock burst, a volcanic eruption and so on). The page uses the other 102,225, labelled earthquakes. 14,358 of them are magnitude 6 and above since 1900 and 87,867 magnitude 5 and above since 1973, and the second group includes most of the first from 1973 on.
Only whole years. The page stops at the end of 2025, so that every year counts in full.
Many magnitudes. The catalogue gives each earthquake the magnitude that its source chose, of several kinds: from 1973 on, 47% of the magnitude 5 and above are of the kind called mb, and the others are of kinds such as Mw (the moment magnitude, the one that scientists prefer for large earthquakes). Section 5 shows what that means for counting earthquakes over the years.
Which country? The catalogue’s place is a piece of text, not a country code, so each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above is placed on the map of the countries. Only 20% fall inside a country: the rest happen under the sea. An earthquake at sea is given to the nearest country when it is within 200 km of its coast (56% of all of them); the other 24%, in the open sea, belong to no country. Countries are those of Natural Earth, which counts overseas territories (Puerto Rico, Guam) as places of their own, and a country’s earthquakes are the ones under it and near it.
The depth is the least certain number. It is the least constrained of all the parameters of an earthquake, says the USGS, and where the data do not fix it, the location program sets a default, often 10 or 33 km (ComCat). 40% of the magnitude 5 and above have exactly 10 or 33 km (the next most common depth has 3%), so the depths on this page are good for classes (shallow, intermediate, deep) and not for the exact kilometre. 27 of them are negative, which means above the reference level that the source used.

title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
section: 1. Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?
text:
1. Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?


Code
n_big <- nrow(big_now)
within <- function(km) percent(100 * mean(big_now$boundary_km <= km))
world_within <- function(km) percent(100 * mean(random_km <= km))
places <- middle |>
  filter(!is.na(country)) |>
  group_by(country, code, continent) |>
  summarise(n = n(), strong = sum(mag >= 6), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(n), country)
n_years <- last_year - 1973 + 1
n_places <- nrow(places)
top <- head(places, 15)
sea_share <- 100 * mean(is.na(middle$country))
place_of <- function(name, column) places[[column]][places$country == name]
rank_of <- function(name) match(name, places$country)
# Europe: the continent of Natural Earth, without Russia (most of its earthquakes are in Kamchatka and
# the Kuril Islands, in the east) and with Turkey, which Natural Earth puts in Asia, counted on its own
europe <- places |>
  filter(continent == "Europe", country != "Russia") |>
  head(4)


Along narrow belts, and mostly under the sea. The 7,327 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above from 1973 to 2025 do not fall at random: 65% of them are within 100 km of a plate boundary and 92% within 300 km. Of the surface of the globe, only 10% is within 100 km of a boundary and 24% within 300 km (worked out for 4,000 points spread evenly over the globe). Where plates meet, one slides under the other, or they grind side by side, and the rock breaks.


Code
# the plate boundaries as one line with gaps
coords <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(plates))
gaps <- coords |>
  group_by(L1) |>
  group_modify(~ bind_rows(.x[, c("X", "Y")], data.frame(X = NA, Y = NA)))
shown <- big_now
shown$text <- paste0("M", format(shown$mag, nsmall = 1), ", ", shown$year, ", ", round(shown$depth), " km deep")
p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "lines",
    lon = round(gaps$X, 2),
    lat = round(gaps$Y, 2),
    line = list(color = dark_gray, width = 0.8),
    name = "Plate boundaries",
    hoverinfo = "skip"
  )
for (k in names(depth_colors)) {
  x <- shown[shown$depth_class == k, ]
  p <- add_trace(
    p,
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "markers",
    lon = x$longitude,
    lat = x$latitude,
    text = x$text,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    name = paste0(k, " (", ifelse(k == "Shallow", "under 70 km", ifelse(k == "Deep", "300 km or more", "70–300 km")), ")"),
    marker = list(color = depth_colors[[k]], size = 4.5, opacity = 0.75, line = list(width = 0))
  )
}
p |>
  chart(
    paste0("Earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above, 1973–", last_year),
    "USGS ComCat; plate boundaries: Bird (2003), via Ahlenius/Nordpil; countries: Natural Earth.",
    geo = list(
      showframe = FALSE,
      showcoastlines = TRUE,
      coastlinecolor = "#cccccc",
      showland = TRUE,
      landcolor = "#f0f0f0",
      projection = list(type = "natural earth"),

    margin = list(t = 80, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )






Indonesia leads, then Papua New Guinea and Japan. Counting every earthquake of magnitude 5 and above from 1973 to 2025 under a country or within 200 km of its coast, Indonesia had 11,920, Papua New Guinea 5,488 and Japan 5,093: 224.9, 103.5 and 96.1 a year. 24% of all the earthquakes of this size were farther than 200 km from any country.

In Europe, Greece comes first. In 172 countries and territories with at least one earthquake of magnitude 5 and above, Greece is number 22: 552 earthquakes since 1973, 58 of magnitude 6 and above, 10.4 a year. title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
text:
2. How often, and how strong?


Code
modern <- 1990
# the magnitude classes: the lower end and the name
classes_m <- list(
  "5–5.9" = c(5, 6),
  "6–6.9" = c(6, 7),
  "7–7.9" = c(7, 8),
  "8 and above" = c(8, 11)
)
per_year <- sapply(classes_m, function(r) {
  sum(middle$mag >= r[1] & middle$mag < r[2] & middle$year >= modern) / (last_year - modern + 1)
})
big_per_year <- sapply(classes_m[3:4], function(r) {
  sum(big$mag >= r[1] & big$mag < r[2]) / (last_year - 1900 + 1)
})
largest <- big[order(-big$mag, big$time), ][1:10, ]
largest$place_short <- sub("^[0-9.]+ km [A-Z]+ of ", "", largest$place)
n8 <- sum(big$mag >= 8)
n8_years <- big |>
  filter(mag >= 8) |>
  count(year)


About 1,500 a year of magnitude 5 and 0.9 of magnitude 8. From 1990 to 2025, the catalogue records on average 1,547 earthquakes of magnitude 5 to 5.9 a year, 135 of magnitude 6 to 6.9, 14 of magnitude 7 to 7.9 and 0.9 of magnitude 8 and above. title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
text:
3. How deep are they?


Code
share_of <- function(x, k) 100 * mean(x$depth_class == k)
by_size <- list(
  "5–5.9" = middle[middle$mag < 6, ],
  "6–6.9" = middle[middle$mag >= 6 & middle$mag < 7, ],
  "7 and above" = middle[middle$mag >= 7, ]
)
shares <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(by_size), function(s) {
  data.frame(size = s, k = names(depth_colors), share = sapply(names(depth_colors), function(k) share_of(by_size[[s]], k)))
}))
deep <- middle[middle$depth_class == "Deep", ]
deep_places <- sort(table(deep$country), decreasing = TRUE)
deepest <- middle[which.max(middle$depth), ]
deep_share_n <- sum(deep$mag >= 7)


Nearly all of them are shallow. 79% of the earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above since 1973 began less than 70 km down, 16% between 70 and 300 km and 4.8% below 300 km. Among those of magnitude 7 and above, 77% were shallow.


Code

shares$k <- factor(shares$k, levels = names(depth_colors))
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(depth_colors)) {
  x <- shares[shares$k == k, ]
  p <- add_bars(
    p,
    x = x$share,
    y = x$size,
    name = k,
    orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = depth_colors[[k]], line = list(color = "white", width = 1.5)),
    text = ifelse(x$share >= 10, percent(x$share), ""),
    textposition = "inside",
    insidetextanchor = "middle",
    textfont = list(color = "white"),
    hovertemplate = paste0("Magnitude %{y}: %{x:.1f}% ", tolower(k), "<extra></extra>")
  )
}

The deep ones are in a few places. 4,201 earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above were deep, 61 of them of magnitude 7 and above. The countries (or the coasts) with the most were Fiji (1,694), Indonesia (430) and Russia (122); 32% were in the open sea. The deepest of all, of magnitude 5.5, was 700 km down: 281 km SE of Levuka, Fiji, in 1985.

4. Which were the deadliest?


Code
worst <- deadly[order(-deadly$deaths_all), ] |> head(10)

  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths_all), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>

# the ten largest earthquakes of section 2: the deaths of the earthquake of the same year within 500 km

  near <- deadly$year == as.integer(substr(largest$time[i], 1, 4)) &
    distance_km(largest$longitude[i], largest$latitude[i], deadly$longitude, deadly$latitude) <= 500
  near[is.na(near)] <- FALSE
  if (any(near)) max(deadly$deaths_all[near]) else 0
})
# the events where the NCEI total differs from its deaths, and the largest example
all_rows <- deadly[!is.na(deadly$deaths) & !is.na(deadly$deathsTotal) & deadly$deathsTotal > deadly$deaths, ]
example <- all_rows[which.max(all_rows$deathsTotal - all_rows$deaths), ]

title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
section: 5. Are there more of them than there used to be?
text:
5. Are there more of them than there used to be?


Code
years_big <- 1900:last_year
count_by_year <- function(x, lo, years) {
  tab <- table(factor(x$year[x$mag >= lo], levels = years))
  data.frame(year = years, n = as.integer(tab))
}
m7 <- count_by_year(big, 7, 1900:last_year)
m6 <- count_by_year(big, 6, 1900:last_year)
m6_modern <- m6[m6$year >= 1973, ]
m5 <- count_by_year(middle, 5, 1973:last_year)
# the year after which the yearly counts of magnitude 6 and above are on another level (the split
# of the years that leaves the least spread within the two parts)
split_cost <- sapply(1976:(last_year - 3), function(y) {
  a <- m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year < y]
  b <- m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year >= y]
  sum((a - mean(a))^2) + sum((b - mean(b))^2)
})
step_year <- (1976:(last_year - 3))[which.min(split_cost)]
before_step <- mean(m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year < step_year])
after_step <- mean(m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year >= step_year])
m6_first <- mean(m6$n[m6$year <= 1904])
m6_next <- mean(m6$n[m6$year %in% 1905:1914])
m7_first <- mean(m7$n[m7$year <= 1904])
m7_all <- mean(m7$n)
m7_periods <- c(
  early = mean(m7$n[m7$year <= 1949]),
  middle = mean(m7$n[m7$year %in% 1950:1989]),
  late = mean(m7$n[m7$year >= 1990])
)
tests <- data.frame(
  what = c("M7+", "M7+", "M6+", "M5+"),
  from = c(1900, modern, step_year, step_year),
  chance = c(
    chance(m7$n, m7$year),
    chance(m7$n[m7$year >= modern], m7$year[m7$year >= modern]),
    chance(m6$n[m6$year >= step_year], m6$year[m6$year >= step_year]),
    chance(m5$n[m5$year >= step_year], m5$year[m5$year >= step_year])
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
means_of <- function(x, from, to) mean(x$n[x$year >= from & x$year <= to])
# one big earthquake brings its aftershocks: the Tohoku earthquake of 2011 and the following year
in_2011 <- big[big$year == 2011, ]
tohoku <- in_2011[which.max(in_2011$mag), ]
tohoku_time <- as.POSIXct(tohoku$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")
middle_time <- as.POSIXct(middle$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")
after <- middle_time > tohoku_time & middle_time <= tohoku_time + 365 * 86400 &
  distance_km(tohoku$longitude, tohoku$latitude, middle$longitude, middle$latitude) <= 500
after_n <- sum(after)
year_2011 <- m5$n[m5$year == 2011]
peak_year <- m5$year[which.max(m5$n)]


No clear trend in the big ones; the smaller ones are counted in steps. Earthquakes of magnitude 7 and above are the only ones that the catalogue seems to record in full since 1900 (see below). They averaged 12.4 a year from 1900 to 1949, 11.1 from 1950 to 1989 and 15.0 from 1990 to 2025: not a steady rise. From 1990 on, a rank test finds no trend in them (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 64 in 100). Over all the years from 1900 the test leans slightly upwards (3 in 100), because of the dip in the middle of the century; the page does not take that for a lasting rise, since magnitudes were worked out differently in each period.
For the smaller earthquakes the catalogue is the problem, not the Earth. From 1900 to 1904 it holds 15.4 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above a year, and from 1905 to 1914 55.8; for magnitude 7 and above the same years give 12.0 and 15.7, so only the strongest were recorded in those years. Even from 1973 the counts of magnitude 6 and above are not on one level: they average 93.1 a year before 1983 and 148.7 from 1983 on, a step of 60%. The page does not know why the catalogue steps there. So the tests for magnitude 6 and above and for 5 and above start in 1983, where the rank test finds no clear trend either (the last column):


Code
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    what = c("Magnitude 7 and above", "Magnitude 7 and above", "Magnitude 6 and above", "Magnitude 5 and above"),
    from = paste0(tests$from, "–", last_year),
    average = c(
      one(means_of(m7, 1900, last_year)),
      one(means_of(m7, modern, last_year)),
      one(means_of(m6, step_year, last_year)),
      number(means_of(m5, step_year, last_year))
    ),
    chance = tests$chance
  ),
  col.names = c("", "Years", "A year, on average", "By chance, in 100"),
  align = "llrr",
  row.names = FALSE
)

Aftershocks can make a year. A large earthquake is followed by many smaller ones, and a simple count does not tell them from new earthquakes. After the Tohoku earthquake in Japan (magnitude 9.1, 2011-03-11), 779 earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above happened within 500 km in the following year, 29% of the 2,701 of the whole of 2011, and 779 is 46% of the average year since 1983. The year with the most of magnitude 5 and above was 2011, with 2,701.


Code
series <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = "Magnitude 7 and above, since 1900", year = m7$year, n = m7$n),
  data.frame(panel = "Magnitude 6 and above, since 1973", year = m6_modern$year, n = m6_modern$n),
  data.frame(panel = "Magnitude 5 and above, since 1973", year = m5$year, n = m5$n)
)
series$panel <- factor(series$panel, levels = unique(series$panel))
step_lines <- data.frame(
  panel = factor("Magnitude 6 and above, since 1973", levels = levels(series$panel)),
  x = c(1973 - 0.4, step_year - 0.5),
  xend = c(step_year - 0.5, last_year + 0.4),
  y = c(before_step, after_step)
)
ggplot(series, aes(x = year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(colour = dark_gray, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = dark_gray, size = 1) +
  geom_segment(data = step_lines, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = y), colour = red, linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2020, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title = "Earthquakes counted each year",
    subtitle = paste0("Red: the average before and from ", step_year, ", for magnitude 6 and above"),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: USGS ComCat"
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
  )

title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
text:
So, what does it mean?

Earthquakes come in belts. 65% of the 7,327 of magnitude 6 and above since 1973 struck within 100 km of a plate boundary, which is near only 10% of the surface of the globe. 24% of those of magnitude 5 and above were farther than 200 km from any country.
Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Japan have the most. Greece is number 22 among 172 countries and territories, and the first in Europe without Russia.
There are about 0.9 earthquakes of magnitude 8 a year and about 14 of magnitude 7, and each step down in magnitude is several times as common.
Nearly all are shallow, 79% of those of magnitude 5 and above. The deaths come in a few events: the ten deadliest earthquakes killed 61% of the 2,531,015 recorded since 1900.
There is no clear sign of more earthquakes in this catalogue. From 1990 on there is no trend in those of magnitude 7 and above; the smaller ones are counted in steps, and the page does not claim a trend for them.

What this does not show. The catalogue is of the earthquakes that instruments record, and the earlier years of it are patchy for all but the strongest. The magnitude is of several kinds, and the depth is uncertain. The countries come from the places of the earthquakes, not from where the shaking was felt. The deaths are those NCEI recorded for its significant earthquakes: some counts are estimates, and the tsunamis that follow some earthquakes are not told apart here. And earthquakes of the same size do not do the same harm.
For the waves that some of these earthquakes send across the sea, see Tsunamis; for the mountains that melt rock instead, Volcanoes; and for the hazards side by side, Natural Disasters.

title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
text:
A tornado is a narrow, violently rotating column of air that reaches from a storm cloud to the ground. People think of the American Plains, and the United States does report more tornadoes than any other country we can count. But there is no single open database of the world’s tornadoes, so this story does what the data allow: it counts the United States closely, sets Canada beside it, and says plainly what cannot be compared. It asks five questions:

Where do tornadoes happen?
When do they strike?
How strong and how deadly are they?
Which were the worst?
Are there more of them than there used to be?

This is one of a series on natural disasters: see the overview and Floods.
The data come from two places, downloaded when the page is rendered:

The United States: the tornado database of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Storm Prediction Center (SPC), one row for each tornado since 1950, with its date and time, the state, the start and end points, the length and width of its path, the rating, and the people injured and killed (SPC severe weather database). It is made of the reports that the National Weather Service’s offices send in (format description). The file used here is the one with single tracks: a tornado that crosses a state line is one row, in the state where it touched down.
Canada: the event summaries of the Northern Tornadoes Project, founded at Western University in 2017, which investigates tornadoes by ground, drone, aerial and satellite surveys (Northern Tornadoes Project).

The rating of a tornado is not a measurement of its wind. Since February 2007 the National Weather Service rates a tornado on the Enhanced Fujita scale, from EF0 to EF5, from the damage that it leaves: an EF0 is estimated at 65 to 85 miles per hour (the gust of three seconds), an EF1 at 86 to 110, an EF2 at 111 to 135, an EF3 at 136 to 165, an EF4 at 166 to 200 and an EF5 at more than 200 (National Weather Service). Before 2007 the original Fujita scale (F0 to F5) was used, in the same way. This page writes EF0 to EF5 for both. A tornado is rated by what it destroys, so one that crosses empty land can get a low rating whatever its wind.
Europe is missing, on purpose. The European Severe Weather Database, kept by the European Severe Storms Laboratory, lets a guest browse only recent events; the full data need a request for restricted access (ESWD). A study of its reports from 1950 to 2015 finds that tornadoes do occur in Europe, with injuries, deaths and damage, “although their reported frequencies and intensities are lower compared with the United States” (Antonescu et al. 2017). That is all this page can say about Europe from what it has read.

title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
text:
The data


Code
# the SPC file of single tornado tracks since 1950, named after the last year it holds: try the
# latest years first
this_year <- as.integer(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y"))
tor <- NULL
for (y in this_year:2020) {
  tor <- tryCatch(
    read.csv(paste0("https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/1950-", y, "_actual_tornadoes.csv")),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(tor)) break
}
# the Northern Tornadoes Project's event summaries (Canada), a thousand rows at a time
ntp_url <- paste0(
  "https://services.arcgis.com/rGKxabTU9mcXMw7k/arcgis/rest/services/",
  "NTP_Event_Summaries_stakeholder/FeatureServer/0/query"
)
ntp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq(0, 9000, by = 1000), function(offset) {
  r <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(
    ntp_url,
    "?where=1%3D1&outFields=Year,event_type,province&returnGeometry=false&resultOffset=",
    offset,
    "&resultRecordCount=1000&f=json"
  ))
  if (length(r$features) == 0) NULL else r$features$attributes
}))




Code
first_year <- min(tor$yr)
last_year <- max(tor$yr)
first_ten <- first_year:(first_year + 9)
last_ten <- (last_year - 9):last_year
# the rating: -9 means that the tornado has no rating
ratings <- c("EF0", "EF1", "EF2", "EF3", "EF4", "EF5")
tor$rating <- factor(ifelse(tor$mag < 0, "Unrated", ratings[pmax(tor$mag, 0) + 1]), levels = c("Unrated", ratings))
n_unrated <- sum(tor$mag < 0)
unrated_modern <- tor[tor$mag < 0 & tor$yr >= 2007, ]
estimated <- sum(tor$fc == 1, na.rm = TRUE)

state_name <- function(s) ifelse(s %in% state.abb, state.name[match(s, state.abb)], s)
# the states: 50 states, with their area (the R datasets) and the census division they are in
areas <- data.frame(
  st = state.abb,
  state = state.name,
  km2 = state.area * 2.589988,
  division = as.character(state.division)
)
tor_states <- tor[tor$st %in% areas$st, ]

# the time of day: the SPC puts all times, but a few, on central standard time (3 in the column tz);
# the sun's time at the place is the clock in Greenwich (central standard time plus six hours) plus one
# hour for every 15 degrees of longitude
hms <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(tor$time, ":"))
tor$clock <- as.numeric(hms[, 1]) + as.numeric(hms[, 2]) / 60
tor$sun_hour <- floor((tor$clock + 6 + tor$slon / 15) %% 24)
timed <- tor[tor$tz == 3 & tor$slon != 0, ]
n_other_clock <- sum(tor$tz != 3)




Code
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
blue <- "#2171b5"
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the maps and the calendar
blues <- c("#eff3ff", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#4292c6", "#2171b5", "#084594")
# one hue for the ratings, from EF0 to EF5; the unrated are grey
rating_colors <- c(Unrated = "#d9d9d9", EF0 = "#c6dbef", EF1 = "#9ecae1", EF2 = "#6baed6", EF3 = "#4292c6", EF4 = "#2171b5", EF5 = "#084594")

# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}

# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
# a change in per cent, with its sign (the bold font of the charts has no minus sign: a dash there)
change_text <- function(x, minus = "−") paste0(ifelse(x >= 0, "+", minus), round(abs(x)), "%")
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}
# a date as "27 April 2011"
long_date <- function(x) format(as.Date(x), "%e %B %Y") |> trimws()




Code
# the unrated tornadoes in the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale, and the tornadoes that the SPC rated
# afterwards from the damage (fc = 1, from 1953 to 1982)
n_all <- nrow(tor)
unrated_years <- tor |>
  filter(yr >= 2007) |>
  group_by(yr) |>
  summarise(share = 100 * mean(mag < 0))
first_unrated <- min(tor$yr[tor$mag < 0 & tor$yr >= 2007])
rated_early <- tor[tor$fc == 1, ]


Some tornadoes have no rating. 1,546 of the 73,458 tornadoes (2.1%) are coded -9, “unknown”. For 1953 to 1982 the SPC has filled in an estimated rating, from the property loss and the length of the path, for 1,863 tornadoes that had none; the file marks them. The 1,546 that remain unrated come from 2007 on, and from 2019 on they are 10% to 20% of the tornadoes of a year. The documentation does not say why. This page counts them in the totals, shows them apart in the tables, and, where a trend depends on the ratings, tests what happens if all of them were strong (section 5).
Times are those of the sun. The SPC converts the time of a tornado to central standard time, whatever the state (37 tornadoes are on another clock). A tornado in Georgia at 17:00 central standard time struck at six in the evening by the clock there. To compare places, section 2 turns each time into the sun’s time at the place where the tornado began, from its longitude: an hour for every 15 degrees.

title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
text:
1. Where do tornadoes happen?


Code
last_eight <- (last_year - 7):last_year
us_a_year <- tor |>
  filter(yr %in% last_eight) |>
  nrow() / length(last_eight)
ntp$Year <- as.integer(ntp$Year)
canada_tornadoes <- ntp[ntp$event_type %in% c("tornado_over_land", "tornado_over_water") & ntp$Year %in% last_eight, ]
canada_a_year <- nrow(canada_tornadoes) / length(last_eight)
canada_provinces <- sort(table(canada_tornadoes$province), decreasing = TRUE) / length(last_eight)
canada_water <- 100 * mean(canada_tornadoes$event_type == "tornado_over_water")

# the states since 2006, the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale
since <- 2006
years_since <- last_year - since + 1
by_state <- tor_states |>
  filter(yr >= since) |>
  group_by(st) |>
  summarise(all = n(), ef2 = sum(mag >= 2), ef3 = sum(mag >= 3)) |>
  left_join(areas, by = "st") |>
  mutate(
    per_10k = all / years_since / km2 * 1e4,
    ef2_per_10k = ef2 / years_since / km2 * 1e4,
    a_year = all / years_since
  )
by_count <- by_state |> arrange(desc(all))
by_density <- by_state |> arrange(desc(per_10k))
by_strong <- by_state |> arrange(desc(ef2_per_10k))
top_density <- by_density$state[1:3]
# the state with the most tornadoes, and its density
texas <- by_state[by_state$st == "TX", ]
rank_texas_density <- which(by_density$st == "TX")
n_states <- nrow(by_state)


The United States reports about 1,346 tornadoes a year; Canada’s project finds about 112, and for Europe there is no open count. From 2018 to 2025 the United States had 1,346 a year on average and Canada 112 (15% of them over water, which the Canadian figures count). The two numbers are not a fair comparison. They come from different ways of finding tornadoes, and a tornado that nobody reports or surveys is not counted anywhere.


Code
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    place = c("United States", "Canada", "Europe"),
    a_year = c(number(us_a_year), number(canada_a_year), "no open count"),
    source = c(
      "SPC database: reports sent in by National Weather Service offices",
      "Northern Tornadoes Project: surveys on the ground, by drone, from the air and from satellites",
      "European Severe Weather Database: browsing is limited to recent events; the study of Antonescu et al. finds fewer reports than in the United States"
    )
  ),
  col.names = c("", paste0("Tornadoes a year, ", min(last_eight), "–", max(last_eight)), "Where it comes from"),
  align = "lrl"
)











Tornadoes a year, 2018–2025
Where it comes from




United States
1,346
SPC database: reports sent in by National Weather Service offices


Canada
112
Northern Tornadoes Project: surveys on the ground, by drone, from the air and from satellites


Europe
no open count
European Severe Weather Database: browsing is limited to recent events; the study of Antonescu et al. finds fewer reports than in the United States





In the United States, Texas has the most tornadoes, but the most for their size are in Mississippi. Texas had the most tornadoes from 2006 to 2025, 119 a year, but it is large. Per area, Mississippi, Alabama and Illinois come first, with 5.40, 4.92 and 4.51 tornadoes a year for every 10,000 square kilometres; Texas is only 24th of the 50 states, with 1.72. For the strong tornadoes (EF2 and above) the order is Mississippi, Alabama and Kentucky: 0.90, 0.81 and 0.54. Hover over a state to see its numbers.


Code
classes <- c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, Inf)
class_names <- c("Under 0.1", "0.1–0.5", "0.5–1", "1–2", "2–3", "3–4", "4 or more")
by_state$class <- as.integer(cut(by_state$per_10k, classes, right = FALSE))
steps <- do.call(c, lapply(seq_along(blues), function(i) {
  list(list((i - 1) / 7, blues[i]), list(i / 7, blues[i]))
}))
plot_ly(
  by_state,
  type = "choropleth",
  locationmode = "USA-states",
  locations = ~st,
  z = ~class,
  zmin = 0.5,
  zmax = 7.5,
  colorscale = steps,
  marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.6)),
  text = ~ paste0(
    state,
    ": ",
    two(per_10k),
    " a year per 10,000 km²<br>",
    one(a_year),
    " tornadoes a year, ",
    one(ef2 / years_since),
    " of them EF2 or above"
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text",
  colorbar = list(
    title = list(text = "Tornadoes<br>a year per<br>10,000 km²"),
    tickvals = 1:7,
    ticktext = class_names,
    len = 0.8,
    thickness = 14
  )
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Tornadoes a year per 10,000 km², ", since, "–", last_year),
    "NOAA Storm Prediction Center; areas: R datasets (state.area). 50 states.",
    geo = list(scope = "usa", projection = list(type = "albers usa"), showlakes = FALSE),
    margin = list(t = 50, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )






The strongest tornadoes show where the damage is. The map shows where the most violent ones began, every EF3, EF4 and EF5 tornado from 1950 to 2025:


Code
strong <- tor[tor$mag >= 3 & tor$slon != 0 & tor$slat != 0, ]
strong_dots <- function(p, x, color, name) {
  add_trace(
    p,
    data = x,
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "markers",
    lon = ~ round(slon, 2),
    lat = ~ round(slat, 2),
    name = name,
    marker = list(color = color, size = 4, opacity = 0.55),
    hoverinfo = "skip"
  )
}
plot_ly() |>
  strong_dots(strong[strong$mag == 3, ], blue, "EF3") |>
  strong_dots(strong[strong$mag >= 4, ], red, "EF4 and EF5") |>
  chart(
    paste0("Where EF3 or stronger tornadoes began, ", first_year, "–", last_year),
    "NOAA Storm Prediction Center. A dot is the start of a tornado.",
    geo = list(scope = "usa", projection = list(type = "albers usa"), showlakes = FALSE),
    legend = c(legend_top, list(y = 1.0)),
    margin = list(t = 70, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )








Code
strong_states <- tor_states |>
  filter(mag >= 3) |>
  count(st) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
violent <- tor_states[tor_states$mag >= 4, ]
division_of <- function(s) areas$division[match(s, areas$st)]
violent_by_division <- sort(table(division_of(violent$st)), decreasing = TRUE)
violent_share <- 100 * violent_by_division / sum(violent_by_division)
divisions_names <- function(d) and_list(areas$state[areas$division == d])


Most of the violent ones, the EF4 and EF5, began in two census divisions: the West North Central division (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota) had 32% of them and the West South Central division (Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas) 24%.

title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
text:
2. When do they strike?


Code
month_share <- function(x) 100 * tabulate(x$mo, 12) / nrow(x)
all_months <- month_share(tor)
strong_months <- month_share(tor[tor$mag >= 3, ])
peak_month <- which.max(all_months)
three_months <- function(s) sapply(1:12, function(m) sum(s[(m - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1]))
best_three <- which.max(three_months(all_months))
best_three_share <- max(three_months(all_months))
winter_share <- sum(all_months[c(12, 1, 2)])
strong_winter <- sum(strong_months[c(12, 1, 2)])
hour_share <- 100 * tabulate(timed$sun_hour + 1, 24) / nrow(timed)
peak_hour <- which.max(hour_share) - 1
afternoon <- sum(hour_share[(15:19) + 1]) # 15:00 to 19:59
night <- timed$sun_hour <= 5
night_tornadoes <- 100 * mean(night)
night_deaths <- 100 * sum(timed$fat[night]) / sum(timed$fat)
night_strong <- 100 * mean(night[timed$mag >= 3]) # the share of the EF3 and above that began at night
hour_label <- function(h) paste0(sprintf("%02d", h), ":00")


May is the peak month, and each part of the country peaks at its own time. 22% of all tornadoes since 1950 began in May, and 54% in the three months of April to June. The strong ones (EF3 and above) are more spread out over the year than the weak ones: 11% of them came in December, January and February, against 8% of all tornadoes.
The calendar shows, for each census division, the share of its tornadoes that came in each month. The divisions are ordered from the one with the most tornadoes.


Code
by_division <- tor_states |>
  mutate(division = division_of(st)) |>
  group_by(division, mo) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
division_order <- tor_states |>
  mutate(division = division_of(st)) |>
  count(division, sort = TRUE) |>
  pull(division)
by_division$class <- cut(
  by_division$share,
  c(-Inf, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, Inf),
  labels = c("Under 2%", "2–5%", "5–10%", "10–15%", "15–20%", "20% or more")
)
ggplot(by_division, aes(x = mo, y = factor(division, levels = rev(division_order)), fill = class)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = blues[2:7], drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "When each part of the country has its tornadoes",
    subtitle = paste0("Share of a division's tornadoes in each month, ", first_year, "–", last_year),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA Storm Prediction Center. Census divisions of the 50 states."
  ) +
  theme_page(12) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.75)))











Code
division_peak <- by_division |>
  group_by(division) |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
peak_of <- function(d) month.name[division_peak$mo[division_peak$division == d]]
peak_share_of <- function(d) percent(division_peak$share[division_peak$division == d])
south_east <- "East South Central"
plains <- "West North Central"


In the East South Central division (Alabama, Kentucky, Mississippi and Tennessee) the busiest month is April (22% of its tornadoes); in the West North Central division (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota) it is June (27%). The chart shows the seasons of each division; it does not say why they differ.
Late afternoon and evening. By the sun’s time at the place where they began, the busiest hour of the day is 16:00 to 17:00, and 52% of all tornadoes began between 15:00 and 20:00.

Few begin at night, and they are somewhat deadlier. Between midnight and 06:00 began 7% of the tornadoes, and 9% of the deaths were from them. Among the EF3 and stronger tornadoes, 8% began at night.

3. How strong and how deadly are they?


Code
by_rating <- tor |>
  group_by(rating) |>
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(fat), injured = sum(inj)) |>
  mutate(
    share = 100 * n / sum(n),
    death_share = 100 * deaths / sum(deaths),
    per_thousand = 1000 * deaths / n
  )

weak_share <- 100 * sum(by_rating$n[by_rating$rating %in% c("EF0", "EF1")]) / rated_n

violent_tor_share <- 100 * violent_n / sum(by_rating$n)
violent_death_share <- sum(by_rating$death_share[by_rating$rating %in% c("EF4", "EF5")])

total_injured <- sum(tor$inj)
deaths_ef0 <- of_rating("EF0", "deaths")


Most tornadoes are weak; most of the deaths come from the strongest. Of the tornadoes that have a rating, 81% were EF0 or EF1. The 656 EF4 and EF5 tornadoes were 0.9% of all of them, and 61% of the 6,341 people killed from 1950 to 2025 died in them. An EF5 killed on average 22 people, an EF0 one in 1,389 (the chart and the table count the unrated too).
