title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
section: 5. Are there more of them than there used to be?
text:
5. Are there more of them than there used to be?


Code
count_after <- function(x, years) mean(x[by_year$yr %in% years])
trend_row <- function(name, x) {
  data.frame(
    name = name,
    start = count_after(x, first_ten),
    end = count_after(x, last_ten),
    chance = chance(x, by_year$yr),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}
# the days of the year with at least one tornado of rating EF1 or above, and the days with ten or more
ef1_days <- tor[tor$mag >= 1, ] |>
  count(yr, date) |>
  group_by(yr) |>
  summarise(days = n(), big_days = sum(n >= 10))
ef1_days <- left_join(data.frame(yr = by_year$yr), ef1_days, by = "yr")
ef1_days[is.na(ef1_days)] <- 0
changes <- rbind(
  trend_row("All tornadoes", by_year$n),
  trend_row("EF1 or above", by_year$ef1),
  trend_row("EF2 or above", by_year$ef2),
  trend_row("EF3 or above", by_year$ef3),
  trend_row("People killed", by_year$deaths),
  trend_row("Days with an EF1 or above", ef1_days$days),
  trend_row("Days with ten or more EF1 or above", ef1_days$big_days)
)
changes$change <- 100 * (changes$end / changes$start - 1)
of_change <- function(name, column) changes[[column]][changes$name == name]
# what if every unrated tornado were EF1 or above?
chance_if_strong <- chance(by_year$ef1 + by_year$unrated, by_year$yr)
before_2007 <- by_year$yr < 2007
chance_before <- chance(by_year$ef1[before_2007], by_year$yr[before_2007])
chance_after <- chance(by_year$ef1[!before_2007], by_year$yr[!before_2007])
ef2_peak <- by_year$yr[which.max(by_year$ef2)]
ef0 <- by_year$n - by_year$ef1 - by_year$unrated
ef0_start <- count_after(ef0, first_ten)
ef0_end <- count_after(ef0, last_ten)


More are reported, but the rise is mostly in the weak tornadoes. In 1950–1959 the SPC database had 479 tornadoes a year, in 2016–2025 1,318: 175% more, and a rank test of all the years finds the rise (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is less than 1 in 100). Much of the rise is in the weakest tornadoes: EF0 tornadoes went from 105 a year to 534. A study of the database found that the doubling of the count from the 1950s to the 2000s “is likely not related to meteorological causes alone”, and that the count of F1 and stronger tornadoes was steadier than that of F2 and stronger (Verbout et al. 2006); another says that changes in how tornadoes are reported “have made it difficult” to read the trend, and leaves out the weakest (Brooks et al. 2014). Counting from EF1 up, the rise is smaller: 374 a year at the start and 632 at the end (+69%), and the test does not clearly find a trend (6 in 100).
The table compares the first and the last ten years. The last column is the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as that of all the years without a trend.

)

  data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels), x0 = min(first_ten) - 0.4, x1 = max(first_ten) + 0.4, y = ten_year$start, who = "first"),

)

    data = bands,
    aes(x = x0, xend = x1, y = y, yend = y, colour = who),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(first = blue, last = red), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1950, 2020, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "More tornadoes, or only more found?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Tornadoes in each year. Blue: the average of ",
      min(first_ten),
      "–",
      max(first_ten),
      "; red: of ",
      min(last_ten),
      "–",
      max(last_ten)
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA Storm Prediction Center. Unrated tornadoes are in the first panel only."
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
  )









The strongest tornadoes are fewer, but be careful with that. The EF2 and stronger tornadoes fell from 189 a year to 142 (by chance less than 1 in 100), the EF3 and stronger from 50 to 28 (less than 1 in 100). Their peak year was 1973. But ratings are judgements of damage, they changed from one scale to the other in 2007, and from 2007 the unrated tornadoes grew in number, so this page does not conclude that the strong tornadoes have become rarer. The unrated tornadoes matter for the count of EF1 and above: if every one of them is counted in it, the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend becomes 1 in 100, against 6. For the years before 2007 alone it is 95 in 100, and for 2007 on 3 in 100. People killed fell from 142 a year to 51 (4 in 100); these data do not say why.
What changed more is how the tornadoes come. The days with at least one tornado of EF1 or above fell from 120.4 a year to 110.0, while the days with ten or more of them rose from 6.7 to 17.9 (the chances of the two patterns, less than 1 and less than 1 in 100). That is what a study of the database found, after setting aside the weakest tornadoes: the mean annual number “has remained relatively constant”, but the variability has increased since the 1970s, with fewer days with tornadoes and more days with many (Brooks et al. 2014).

title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
text:
So, what does it mean?

A few states have the most tornadoes for their size, and they are not the largest. Mississippi, Alabama and Illinois had the most per area from 2006 to 2025, and Texas, the state with the most tornadoes, only 24th. Canada’s project finds about 112 a year, against 1,346 in the United States, but the two are not counted the same way.
They come in the afternoon and evening, mostly in spring. 22% of them began in May, and each part of the country has its own busiest month.
Most are weak and most deaths come from the strongest. EF4 and EF5 tornadoes were 0.9% of the tornadoes and 61% of the deaths.
The worst years and days are far from the average. 27 April 2011 had 210 tornadoes in one day, and 2011 killed 553 people.
More are counted, but that is not the same as more. The tornadoes of EF2 and above did not rise; what has changed is that the tornadoes of EF1 and above come on fewer days and in bigger groups.

What this does not show. There is no worldwide count: the data cover the United States and, in outline, Canada, and say nothing of the many countries where tornadoes are not systematically recorded, so this page cannot say that the United States has the most tornadoes in the world, only the most that are counted. Reports depend on who is there to see a tornado, and the ratings on what it destroyed. Averages by state hide the differences inside a state, and a rank test says whether a pattern is likely to be chance, not what causes it. And the counts say nothing of the people who live where tornadoes land.
For floods, see Floods; for all the hazards together, the overview.

title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
text:
Most people know a few volcanoes: Vesuvius, Etna, Krakatau, perhaps Santorini. They are a small part of the whole. More than a thousand volcanoes have erupted in the last 10,000 years, and some of them erupt again every year. This story asks five questions:

Where in the world are the volcanoes?
Which volcanoes erupt, and how often?
How big do eruptions get?
Which were the deadliest eruptions?
How many people live close to a volcano, and where does Greece stand?

Where the Earth Shakes looks at earthquakes, Waves from the Sea at tsunamis, and Natural Disasters puts the hazards side by side.
The data come from two sources, downloaded when the page is rendered:

The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program (GVP), which keeps the Volcanoes of the World database, no key needed (GVP): the list of volcanoes that have erupted in the Holocene (the last 10,000 years or so), where they are and what kind they are; their eruptions, with the year they began and how explosive they were; and the number of people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 kilometres of each volcano.
NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), whose Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database lists the eruptions that did the most harm, with the number of deaths where it is known (NCEI volcanoes).

The map also draws the boundaries between the plates of the Earth’s crust, from Peter Bird’s model (Bird 2003), in the version of the GitHub repository fraxen/tectonicplates.
The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measures how big an explosive eruption was, on a scale that starts at 0 for a gentle eruption and is open-ended, with 8 for the largest eruptions in history. It is mainly based on the volume of ash thrown out, and also on the height of the eruption cloud. Each step up is about ten times more ash, apart from the first (USGS; Newhall and Self 1982).
A volcano here is a volcano of the GVP’s list. A large volcanic field, with hundreds of small vents, counts as one volcano.

  )

# the volcanoes of the Holocene: place, type, tectonic setting and last eruption
volcanoes <- gvp("Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Volcanoes")
# the eruptions of the Holocene: one row for each eruption, with the year it began and its VEI
eruptions <- gvp("Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Eruptions")
# the people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 km of each volcano
people <- gvp("E3WebApp_HoloceneVolcanoes")

# NOAA's significant eruptions: 200 to a page
noaa_page <- function(page) {
  fromJSON(paste0("https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/volcanoes?page=", page))
}
first_page <- noaa_page(1)
significant <- bind_rows(c(
  list(first_page$items),
  lapply(seq_len(first_page$totalPages)[-1], function(page) noaa_page(page)$items)
))

# the boundaries of the plates (Bird 2003), as lines
plates <- fromJSON(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json",
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)




Code
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts
oranges <- c("#feedde", "#fdd0a2", "#fdae6b", "#fd8d3c", "#f16913", "#d94801", "#8c2d04")
# the colour of a volcano that has erupted in the time of the complete records (the dark orange of
# the scale) and of the plate boundaries
erupted_color <- "#d94801"
plate_color <- "#6b6b6b"

# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}

# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
# millions of people: one decimal below 10 million
million <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) >= 1e7, number(x / 1e6), one(x / 1e6))
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# country names that take "the" in a sentence
with_the <- function(x) ifelse(x %in% c("United States", "United Kingdom"), paste("the", x), x)
# the first letter of a sentence in capitals
cap <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substring(x, 2))
# a volcano name as people say it: "Ruiz, Nevado del" is Nevado del Ruiz
flip <- function(x) sub("^(.*), (.*)$", "\\2 \\1", x)
# a year, as in the text: years before the year 1 are BCE
year_text <- function(y) ifelse(y < 0, paste(-y, "BCE"), as.character(y))
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}




Code
# the eruptions that are certain: the GVP also lists eruptions that are only possible
confirmed <- eruptions[eruptions$Activity_Type == "Confirmed Eruption" & !is.na(eruptions$StartDateYear), ]
n_uncertain <- sum(eruptions$Activity_Type != "Confirmed Eruption")
# the country of each eruption: the country of its volcano
confirmed$country <- volcanoes$Country[match(confirmed$Volcano_Number, volcanoes$Volcano_Number)]
# the year of the data is not complete: its eruptions so far are left out of the rates
current_year <- max(confirmed$StartDateYear)
last_full_year <- current_year - 1
so_far <- sum(confirmed$StartDateYear == current_year)
# the records are complete from 1960 (explained below)
complete_from <- 1960
modern <- confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= complete_from & confirmed$StartDateYear <= last_full_year, ]
n_years <- last_full_year - complete_from + 1
# NOAA's rows are events with a date of their own: one volcano can have several in a year
same_year <- sum(duplicated(significant[, c("name", "year")]))


The list of eruptions has 11,109 rows, but not all of them are certain. 1,169 are marked by the GVP as uncertain, and they are left out: this page counts the 9,940 confirmed eruptions with a year, over the whole Holocene. An eruption counts in the year it began, and one that goes on for years counts once.
The records of eruptions are far more complete in recent times, so the page counts eruptions only from 1960. Newhall and Self, who invented the VEI, wrote that only the largest eruptions have a complete record back to the early 19th century, and that other important explosive events went unrecorded before about 1960 (Newhall and Self 1982). Section 2 shows the numbers. From 1960 to 2025 the list has 2,231 confirmed eruptions, 33.8 a year. For 2026 only 28 eruptions are listed so far, the year is not over, and it is left out of every rate and every trend.
The deaths are not always known. NOAA lists 903 significant eruptions, from 4360 BCE to 2026, but only 480 have a number of deaths. An empty cell means that the number is not known, not that nobody died, so the deaths below are a minimum. NOAA’s total deaths count the eruption and its secondary effects, whenever possible; where it has no total, this page takes the direct deaths. Each row of the database is an event with its own date, so the same volcano can appear more than once in a year (66 times here), and the deadliest eruptions below are rows of the database, which may be one phase of a longer eruption.


Code
# the deaths of an eruption: the total if there is one, and never less than the direct deaths
significant$dead <- ifelse(
  is.na(significant$deathsTotal) & is.na(significant$deaths),
  NA,
  pmax(significant$deathsTotal, significant$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
)
with_deaths <- significant[!is.na(significant$dead), ]

title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
section: 1. Where in the world are the volcanoes?
text:
1. Where in the world are the volcanoes?


Code
n_volcanoes <- nrow(volcanoes)
# volcanoes by country (a volcano on a border has both countries in its name: they stay together)
by_country <- volcanoes |>
  count(Country, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / n_volcanoes)
top_countries <- head(by_country, 10)
top_ten_share <- sum(top_countries$n) / n_volcanoes * 100
# the tectonic setting that the GVP gives each volcano: the first part, before the crust
volcanoes$setting <- sub(" /.*", "", volcanoes$Tectonic_Setting)
settings <- table(volcanoes$setting)
setting_share <- function(x) percent(100 * settings[[x]] / sum(settings))
# volcanoes whose last eruption is known (the year is empty when it is not)
n_since <- function(year) sum(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year >= year, na.rm = TRUE)
in_country <- function(name) by_country$n[by_country$Country == name]
type_top <- volcanoes |> count(Primary_Volcano_Type, sort = TRUE)
n_undersea <- sum(volcanoes$Elevation < 0, na.rm = TRUE)


Along the plate boundaries, and in a few countries. The GVP lists 1,209 volcanoes that have erupted in the Holocene. The 10 countries with the most have 59% of them: the United States (165), Japan (105) and Indonesia (101) lead, followed by Russia, Chile and Ethiopia. 69% of the volcanoes sit in what the GVP calls a subduction zone, a place where one plate of the crust slides under another, 18% in a rift zone, where plates pull apart, and 12% inside a plate, away from its edges. On the map the volcanoes follow the plate boundaries.


Code
volcanoes$recent <- !is.na(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year) & volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year >= complete_from
volcanoes$label <- paste0(
  volcanoes$Volcano_Name,
  " (",
  volcanoes$Country,
  ")<br>",
  ifelse(
    is.na(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year),
    "last eruption not known",
    paste("last eruption:", year_text(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year))
  )
)
# the plate boundaries as one line with gaps, rounded to a tenth of a degree
boundary_lines <- do.call(rbind, lapply(plates$features, function(f) {
  xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(f$geometry$coordinates, unlist))
  rbind(round(xy[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], 1), c(NA, NA))
}))
older <- volcanoes[!volcanoes$recent, ]
recent <- volcanoes[volcanoes$recent, ]
plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "lines",
    lon = boundary_lines[, 1],
    lat = boundary_lines[, 2],
    line = list(color = plate_color, width = 1),
    name = "Plate boundaries",
    hoverinfo = "skip"
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "markers",
    lon = older$Longitude,
    lat = older$Latitude,
    text = older$label,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    marker = list(color = gray, size = 5, line = list(color = "#8a8a8a", width = 0.4)),
    name = paste("No eruption since", complete_from)
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "markers",
    lon = recent$Longitude,
    lat = recent$Latitude,
    text = recent$label,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    marker = list(color = erupted_color, size = 6, line = list(color = "white", width = 0.4)),
    name = paste("Erupted since", complete_from)
  ) |>
  chart(
    paste0("The ", number(n_volcanoes), " volcanoes of the Holocene"),
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World; plates: Bird (2003), via fraxen/tectonicplates.",
    geo = list(
      showframe = FALSE,
      showcoastlines = TRUE,
      coastlinecolor = "#d0d0d0",
      coastlinewidth = 0.5,
      showland = TRUE,
      landcolor = "#f3f3f3",
      projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
      lataxis = list(range = c(-70, 85))
    ),
    legend = c(legend_top, list(itemsizing = "constant")),
    margin = list(t = 70, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )






334 of the volcanoes have erupted since 1960, 439 since 1900. For 360 the year of the last eruption is not known: the evidence of an eruption in the Holocene is there, but not its date.


Code
bars <- top_countries[order(top_countries$n), ] # the largest at the top
bars$Country <- factor(bars$Country, levels = bars$Country)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~n,
  y = ~Country,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$n == max(bars$n), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(n, " (", percent(share), ")"),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} volcanoes<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    "Countries with the most volcanoes",
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Share of the world in brackets.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.5 * max(bars$n)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 60, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )






The United States is first, with 165 volcanoes, 14% of the world’s; Japan has 105 and Indonesia 101. In Europe, Iceland has 35, Italy 13 and Greece 5. The 113 volcanoes of the list whose summit is below the sea are counted too, but the seafloor is far less surveyed than the land, and the list is surely less complete there.

title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
section: 2. Which volcanoes erupt, and how often?
text:
2. Which volcanoes erupt, and how often?


Code
by_year <- as.data.frame(table(factor(modern$StartDateYear, levels = complete_from:last_full_year)))
by_year$year <- complete_from:last_full_year
by_year$n <- by_year$Freq
trend_chance <- chance(by_year$n, by_year$year)
first_ten <- mean(by_year$n[by_year$year < complete_from + 10])
last_ten <- mean(by_year$n[by_year$year > last_full_year - 10])
n_erupted <- n_distinct(modern$Volcano_Number)
# the eruptions of each volcano since 1960
by_volcano <- modern |>
  group_by(Volcano_Number, Volcano_Name, country) |>
  summarise(eruptions = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(eruptions))
# volcanoes that erupted since 1960, by country
erupting <- modern |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(volcanoes = n_distinct(Volcano_Number), eruptions = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(volcanoes), desc(eruptions))
erupting$in_list <- by_country$n[match(erupting$country, by_country$Country)]
# the GVP's "country" of volcanoes under the sea that belong to no country
erupting$country[erupting$country == "Undersea Features"] <- "Undersea (no country)"
top_erupting <- head(erupting, 10)
# the eruptions in 50 years and in decades since 1600, per year: the part before the complete records
# is shown in grey
decades <- confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= 1600 & confirmed$StartDateYear <= last_full_year, ]
decades$decade <- 10 * (decades$StartDateYear %/% 10)
per_decade <- decades |>
  count(decade) |>
  mutate(years = pmin(decade + 9, last_full_year) - decade + 1, per_year = n / years)
per_year_in <- function(from, to) {
  nrow(confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= from & confirmed$StartDateYear <= to, ]) / (to - from + 1)
}


About 34 eruptions begin each year, and the number has not changed since 1960. From 1960 to 2025, between 23 and 49 eruptions began in a year, 34.1 a year on average in the first ten years and 32.0 in the last ten. A rank test of all the years finds no clear trend: the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 25 in 100. And 329 different volcanoes erupted at least once, 27% of the list: most volcanoes are quiet, and a few erupt again and again.


Code
ggplot(per_decade, aes(x = decade, y = per_year, fill = decade >= complete_from)) +
  geom_col(width = 8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = erupted_color, "FALSE" = gray), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1600, 2000, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "The records get more complete",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Eruptions that began each year, average of each decade (dark: from ",
      complete_from,
      ")"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Confirmed eruptions."
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())









Before 1960 the list is not a count of eruptions, but of what people recorded. In 1600–1699 the list has 3.4 eruptions a year, in 1800–1899 15.0, in 1900–1959 27.8, and since 1960 33.8. Volcanoes did not wake up in the 20th century: the records improved.


Code
bars <- top_erupting[order(top_erupting$volcanoes), ]
bars$country <- factor(bars$country, levels = bars$country)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~volcanoes,
  y = ~country,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$volcanoes == max(bars$volcanoes), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(volcanoes, " of ", in_list),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} volcanoes erupted<br>%{customdata} eruptions<extra></extra>",
  customdata = ~eruptions,
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Volcanoes that erupted, ", complete_from, "–", last_full_year),
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Confirmed eruptions; \"of\": volcanoes of the country in the list.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.6 * max(bars$volcanoes)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 60, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )






A few countries have most of the eruptions. Since 1960, Indonesia had 54 different volcanoes erupt, the United States (39), Japan (37) and Russia (24) come next, and the ten countries of the chart have 67% of all the volcanoes that erupted. The volcanoes with the most eruptions are Piton de la Fournaise in France (54), Bezymianny in Russia (50) and Klyuchevskoy in Russia (44). Whether the GVP splits a long period of activity into many eruptions or counts one affects such numbers, so they are best read as rough.

title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
text:
3. How big do eruptions get?


Code
vei_total <- table(factor(modern$ExplosivityIndexMax, levels = 0:8))
vei_known <- sum(vei_total)
vei_missing <- nrow(modern) - vei_known
vei_share <- function(levels) percent(100 * sum(vei_total[as.character(levels)]) / vei_known)
vei_n <- function(levels) sum(vei_total[as.character(levels)])
big <- confirmed[!is.na(confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax) & confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax >= 6 &
  confirmed$StartDateYear >= 1800, ]
big <- big[order(big$StartDateYear), ]
big$country <- with_the(big$country)
# the largest eruptions of the Holocene (VEI 7 and 8) in the list
huge <- confirmed[!is.na(confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax) & confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax >= 7, ]
since_1800 <- confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= 1800 & confirmed$StartDateYear <= last_full_year &
  !is.na(confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax), ]


Most eruptions are small; a few are enormous. Of the 2,225 eruptions since 1960 with a VEI, 83% are VEI 0 to 2, 14% are VEI 3, 2% VEI 4, and only 7 VEI 5 or more (6 at VEI 5, 1 at VEI 6, none higher). 6 have no VEI in the list.


Code
sizes <- data.frame(vei = 0:7, n = as.integer(vei_total[as.character(0:7)]))
plot_ly(
  sizes,
  x = ~vei,
  y = ~n,
  type = "bar",
  marker = list(color = colorRampPalette(oranges)(8)),
  text = ~n,
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "VEI %{x}: %{y} eruptions<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Eruptions by size, ", complete_from, "–", last_full_year),
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Confirmed eruptions with a VEI.",
    x_axis = list(title = "Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI)", dtick = 1),
    y_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(sizes$n)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 20, t = 60, b = 80, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.25
  )






The largest eruptions are rare: 5 of VEI 6 or more since 1800, and none above VEI 7. The table lists them.


Code
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    year = big$StartDateYear,
    volcano = flip(big$Volcano_Name),
    country = big$country,
    vei = big$ExplosivityIndexMax
  ),
  col.names = c("Year", "Volcano", "Country", "VEI"),
  align = "rllr"
)

The biggest are much older. The list has 7 eruptions of VEI 7 or more in the whole Holocene, Santorini (1610 BCE), Kurile Lake (6440 BCE), Kikai (4350 BCE), Cerro Blanco (2300 BCE), Rinjani (1257), Tambora (1812) and Crater Lake (5680 BCE). The GVP dates Tambora’s eruption from 1812 to 1815, and NOAA gives the year of its great explosion, 1815; the table gives the year each eruption began. The date of an old eruption is an estimate: the GVP gives each one a margin of error, and some dates are marked as uncertain.
Big eruptions are rare, and small ones are the easiest to miss. From 1960 the list has 33.6 of them a year, but only 0.1 of VEI 5 or more, about one in 9 years. The VEI is also missing more often for older eruptions: for 5% of the eruptions from 1800 to 1959, against 0.3% since.

title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
text:
4. Which were the deadliest eruptions?


Code
worst <- with_deaths[order(-with_deaths$dead), ]
top_dead <- head(worst, 10)
top_dead$label <- paste0(flip(top_dead$name), " ", year_text(top_dead$year))
total_dead <- sum(with_deaths$dead)
top_five_share <- 100 * sum(head(worst$dead, 5)) / total_dead
since_1900 <- with_deaths[with_deaths$year >= 1900, ]
n_1900 <- sum(significant$year >= 1900)
dead_1900 <- sum(since_1900$dead)
by_dead_country <- with_deaths |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(dead = sum(dead), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(dead))
n_100k <- sum(with_deaths$dead >= 10000)
# eruptions with a given number of deaths, since 1900, whose VEI is below 4
low_vei <- since_1900[!is.na(since_1900$vei) & since_1900$vei <= 3, ]
low_vei <- low_vei[order(-low_vei$dead), ]
tam <- worst[1, ]


4 eruptions have killed more than 25,000 people each. NOAA’s list has 480 eruptions with a known number of deaths, 335,768 deaths together. The five deadliest, Tambora 1815, Krakatau 1883, Ilopango 450, Pelee 1902 and Nevado del Ruiz 1985, account for 53% of them. The deadliest, Tambora in 1815, has 60,000 deaths on record, of which NOAA puts 11,000 directly on the eruption and the rest on its secondary effects.


Code
bars <- top_dead[order(top_dead$dead), ]
bars$label <- factor(bars$label, levels = bars$label)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~dead,
  y = ~label,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$dead == max(bars$dead), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(number(dead), ifelse(is.na(vei), "", paste0(" (VEI ", vei, ")"))),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:,} deaths<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    "The ten deadliest eruptions on record",
    "NOAA NCEI, Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database; VEI: the database. Total deaths where known.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.8 * max(bars$dead)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 150, t = 60, b = 60, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )






The deadliest are not always the biggest. Of the ten, Nevado del Ruiz and Unzendake had a VEI of 3 or less, and the Nevado del Ruiz 1985 eruption, with 23,080 deaths, was VEI 3. How big an eruption is and how many people it kills are two different things.


Code
timeline <- with_deaths[with_deaths$year >= 1500, ]
timeline$labelled <- timeline$dead >= 20000


The deaths on record are concentrated in a few countries. Indonesia has 43% of the deaths on the list, El Salvador (9%), Martinique (9%) and Colombia (8%) follow. And the list is not constant over time: since 1900 NOAA lists 530 significant eruptions, 344 of them with a number of deaths, 94,831 deaths in all, 28% of the total.


Code
ggplot(timeline, aes(x = year, y = dead)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = labelled), size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    data = timeline[timeline$labelled, ],
    aes(label = paste0(flip(name), " ", year)),
    colour = "grey20",
    size = 3.2,
    vjust = -0.9,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = red, "FALSE" = dark_gray), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(
    breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000),
    labels = c("1", "10", "100", "1,000", "10,000"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Few eruptions kill many",
    subtitle = "Deaths in each eruption with a known number, since 1500, on a log scale",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA NCEI, Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database.\nEruptions without a known number of deaths are not shown."
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
section: 5. How many people live close to a volcano, and where does Greece stand?
text:
5. How many people live close to a volcano, and where does Greece stand?


Code
people$country <- people$Country
known <- people[!is.na(people$Within_100km), ]
n_known <- nrow(known)
near <- function(km) known[[paste0("Within_", km, "km")]]
share_over <- function(km, n) percent(100 * mean(near(km) >= n))
close <- known[order(-known$Within_30km), ]
top_close <- head(close, 10)
hundred <- known[order(-known$Within_100km), ]
greece <- known[known$Country == "Greece", ]
greece <- greece[order(-greece$Within_30km), ]
# the volcanoes of Greece in the list, the last eruption first
greece_list <- volcanoes[volcanoes$Country == "Greece", ]
greece_list <- greece_list[order(-greece_list$Last_Eruption_Year), ]
santorini <- known[known$VolcanoName == "Santorini", ]
italy_top <- known[known$Country == "Italy", ]
italy_top <- italy_top[order(-italy_top$Within_30km), ]


Many volcanoes have millions of people near them, but the figures cannot simply be added up. The GVP counts, for each volcano, the people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 km. A person who lives near two volcanoes is counted for both, so the numbers of different volcanoes must not be added; this page compares volcanoes, and does not total the people. The GVP gives the numbers for 1,172 of the 1,209 volcanoes.


Code
bars <- top_close[order(top_close$Within_30km), ]
bars$name <- paste0(flip(bars$VolcanoName), ", ", bars$Country)
bars$name <- factor(bars$name, levels = bars$name)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~ Within_30km / 1e6,
  y = ~name,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$Within_30km == max(bars$Within_30km), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(one(Within_30km / 1e6), " million"),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = paste0(
    "%{y}<br>%{x:.1f} million people within 30 km<br>",
    "%{customdata:,.0f} people within 100 km<extra></extra>"
  ),
  customdata = ~Within_100km,
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    "Most people within 30 km of a volcano",
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. People within 30 km.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.6 * max(bars$Within_30km) / 1e6), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 240, t = 60, b = 60, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )






In 76 volcanoes, more than a million people live within 30 km. The top of the list is Tatun Volcanic Group in Taiwan (6.7 million), Michoacan-Guanajuato in Mexico (5.8 million) and Tangkuban Parahu in Indonesia (5.7 million). Some of the volcanoes at the top are volcanic fields, which cover a large area and count as one volcano. Within 100 km, 30% of the volcanoes have a million people or more, and 4% have ten million or more; the most is 41 million, near Gede-Pangrango in Indonesia. And the other end: 39% of the volcanoes have fewer than 1,000 people within 30 km. The GVP’s counts come from a gridded population map whose year the data do not give, so they may not match today’s population.
Greece has 5 volcanoes in the list: Santorini (last eruption 1950), Nisyros (last eruption 1888), Kolumbo (last eruption 1650), Milos (last eruption 140) and Methana (last eruption 258 BCE). That is far fewer than Italy’s 13 or Iceland’s 35.


Code
greece_eruptions <- confirmed[confirmed$country %in% "Greece", ]
santorini_eruptions <- greece_eruptions[greece_eruptions$Volcano_Name == "Santorini", ]
minoan <- santorini_eruptions[which.max(santorini_eruptions$ExplosivityIndexMax), ]
last_santorini <- max(santorini_eruptions$StartDateYear)
kolumbo <- significant[significant$name == "Kolumbo", ]
kolumbo_year <- greece_eruptions$StartDateYear[greece_eruptions$Volcano_Name == "Kolumbo"][1]
kolumbo_vei <- greece_eruptions$ExplosivityIndexMax[greece_eruptions$Volcano_Name == "Kolumbo"][1]
kolumbo_dead <- sum(kolumbo$dead, na.rm = TRUE)
santorini_dead <- with_deaths[with_deaths$name == "Santorini", ]


Santorini’s recent eruptions were small, but its largest was far older. The GVP lists 11 confirmed eruptions of Santorini in the Holocene, the last in 1950, with a VEI of 2; the largest, dated to 1610 BCE, was VEI 7, one of the 7 of VEI 7 or more in the Holocene in the list. Kolumbo, whose summit is 18 metres below the sea, erupted in 1650 (VEI 4), and NOAA’s database gives its 4 entries of that year 140 deaths together. Within 30 km of Santorini live 12,336 people, and within 100 km 67,468. Of the 4 volcanoes with a population count, the most people live near Methana (48,917 within 30 km). By the same measure Campi Flegrei, in Italy, has 3.0 million.

title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
text:
So, what does it mean?

Volcanoes are where the plates meet, and in a few countries. The 10 countries with the most volcanoes have 59% of the 1,209 in the list, and 69% sit in subduction zones. The United States, Japan and Indonesia lead.
About 34 eruptions begin a year, and the number has not changed since 1960. The apparent rise before that is a rise in what was recorded.
Most eruptions are small. 83% of the eruptions since 1960 are VEI 0 to 2; 5 since 1800 were VEI 6 or more.
The deadliest eruptions are not always the biggest. The five deadliest on record have 53% of the deaths of the eruptions with a known number, Tambora 1815, Krakatau 1883, Ilopango 450, Pelee 1902 and Nevado del Ruiz 1985.
Many volcanoes have people near them. In 76 volcanoes of the list, more than a million people live within 30 km; Greece has 5 volcanoes in the list, and Santorini is the one that erupted last.

What this does not show. A list of eruptions is a list of what people recorded: it is incomplete before about 1960, and eruptions on the seafloor are the hardest to see. The VEI measures the explosion, not the harm, and it is missing for some eruptions. NOAA lists only significant eruptions, and for many of them the deaths are not known, so the totals are minimums, and a death toll is partly a matter of who counted and how. The numbers of people near volcanoes come from a population map whose year the data do not give, and each person near several volcanoes is counted several times. Nothing here says when or where the next eruption will be: a count of past eruptions is not a forecast.
For earthquakes, see Where the Earth Shakes; for tsunamis, Waves from the Sea; for all the hazards together, Natural Disasters.

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text: Eurostat publishes yearly average full-time adjusted salaries (nama_10_fte) for every EU/EFTA country. This vignette pulls that series directly from the Eurostat API and turns it into three progressively more polished visualisations: an interactive time series, an animated bar chart, and a “bar chart race” — with Greece highlighted in red against the rest of Europe in gray.

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text: Eurostat publishes yearly average full-time adjusted salaries (nama_10_fte) for every EU/EFTA country. This vignette pulls that series directly from the Eurostat API and turns it into three progressively more polished visualisations: an interactive time series, an animated bar chart, and a “bar chart race” — with Greece highlighted in red against the rest of Europe in gray.

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "countrycode", "plotly",
#                     "eurostat", "gganimate", "gifski", "scales", "ragg"))

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(countrycode)  # geo codes -> country names / ISO codes
library(plotly)       # interactive charts
library(eurostat)     # Eurostat data API
library(gganimate)    # animation
library(gifski)       # GIF renderer
library(scales)       # axis formatting

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
The data
get_eurostat() downloads the raw dataset table by its Eurostat code. We keep only country-level rows (dropping the EU27_2020 and EA20 aggregates), derive a plain-language country name and ISO code with countrycode, and rank countries by salary within each year.


Code
df_eusalary <- get_eurostat("nama_10_fte", filters = list(unit = "EUR"))
df_eusalary <- df_eusalary[!df_eusalary$geo %in% c("EU27_2020", "EA20"), ]

df_eusalary$year    <- lubridate::year(df_eusalary$time)
df_eusalary$country <- countrycode(df_eusalary$geo, origin = "eurostat", destination = "country.name")
df_eusalary$iso     <- countrycode(df_eusalary$geo, origin = "eurostat", destination = "iso2c")

df_eusalary$rank  <- NA
df_eusalary$color <- NA
for (i in unique(df_eusalary$year)) {
  df_eusalary[df_eusalary$year %in% i, "rank"] <-
    rank(-df_eusalary[df_eusalary$year %in% i, "values"], ties.method = "min")
}

df_eusalary[df_eusalary$country %in% "Greece", "color"]  <- "#E74C3C"
df_eusalary[!df_eusalary$country %in% "Greece", "color"] <- "#B3B3B3"

title <- "Average full time adjusted salary [nama_10_fte]"

head(df_eusalary[, c("country", "year", "values", "rank")], 12)


# A tibble: 12 × 4
   country  year values  rank
   <chr>   <dbl>  <int> <int>
 1 Belgium  1995  27855     3
 2 Belgium  1996  27875     3
 3 Belgium  1997  27774     3
 4 Belgium  1998  28200     3
 5 Belgium  1999  29691     3
 6 Belgium  2000  30506     4
 7 Belgium  2001  31777     3
 8 Belgium  2002  32985     3
 9 Belgium  2003  33678     3
10 Belgium  2004  34447     4
11 Belgium  2005  35009     4
12 Belgium  2006  36327     4


Each row is one country in one year, with:



Column
Description




country
Country name (derived from Eurostat’s geo code)


year
Year of observation


values
Average full-time adjusted salary, in EUR


rank
Country’s salary rank within that year (1 = highest)


color
Highlight color — red for Greece, gray for everyone else

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
Building the visualisations

Step 1 — interactive time series
A line per country lets you trace how each economy moved over time, and hovering reveals the exact value.


Code
colors <- c("#e6194b", "#3cb44b", "#ffe119", "#0082c8", "#f58231", "#911eb4", "#46f0f0",
            "#f032e6", "#d2f53c", "#fabebe", "#008080", "#e6beff", "#aa6e28", "#fffac8",
            "#800000", "#aaffc3", "#808000", "#ffd8b1", "#000080", "#808080", "#ffffff",
            "#000000")

plot_ly(df_eusalary[df_eusalary$values > 0, ],
        x = ~year,
        y = ~values,
        color = ~country,
        mode = "lines+markers",
        type = "scatter",
        text = ~paste("Year:", year,
                      "<br>Value:", values,
                      "<br>Country Name:", country),
        hoverinfo = "text",
        colors = colors,
        showlegend = TRUE,
        marker = list(size = 8)) %>%
  plotly::layout(title = "",
                 autosize = TRUE,
                 margin = list(l = 50, r = 50, b = 50, t = 50, pad = 0),
                 legend = list(orientation = "vertical", xanchor = "right", x = 30, y = 1),
                 xaxis = list(title = "Year", tickangle = -90),
                 yaxis = list(title = ""),
                 font = list(size = 20, color = "#404040", weight = "bold"))








Step 2 — animated bar chart
Sliding a frame argument to plot_ly turns a static bar chart into a play/pause animation stepping through each year.


Code
plot_ly(df_eusalary,
        x = ~country,
        y = ~values,
        frame = ~year,
        ids = ~country,
        type = "bar",
        text = ~paste("Year:", year,
                      "<br>Value:", values,
                      "<br>Country:", country),
        hoverinfo = "text",
        colors = colors,
        showlegend = FALSE) %>%
  layout(
    title  = title,
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Euro"),
    font   = list(size = 20, color = "#404040", weight = "bold"),
    margin = list(l = 50, r = 50, b = 200, t = 100)
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(
    frame = 500,
    transition = 500,
    easing = "linear",
    redraw = FALSE,
    mode = "immediate"
  )








Step 3 — bar chart race, ranked
Instead of plotting by country name, we plot by rank, so the bars physically reorder every year as economies overtake each other. Greece is layered on top in red so it’s always visible against the gray field.


Code
plot_ly() %>%
  add_bars(
    data         = df_eusalary[df_eusalary$color == "#B3B3B3", ],
    x            = ~rank,
    y            = ~values,
    frame        = ~year,
    ids          = ~rank,
    marker       = list(color = "#B3B3B3"),
    text         = ~country,
    hoverinfo    = "text",
    textposition = "outside",
    textangle    = 90,
    showlegend   = FALSE
  ) %>%
  add_bars(
    data         = df_eusalary[df_eusalary$color %in% "#E74C3C", ],
    x            = ~rank,
    y            = ~values,
    frame        = ~year,
    ids          = ~rank,
    marker       = list(color = "#E74C3C"),
    text         = ~country,
    hoverinfo    = "text",
    textposition = "outside",
    textangle    = 90,
    showlegend   = FALSE
  ) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis  = list(title = "Rank", tickmode = "array"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Euro"),
    title  = title,
    margin = list(l = 50, r = 50, b = 200, t = 100),
    font   = list(size = 20, color = "#404040", weight = "bold")
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 1000, transition = 0, easing = "linear", redraw = TRUE)








Step 4 — dark themed GIF with gganimate
The interactive versions above are great for exploring in a browser, but a rendered GIF is easier to share. ggplot2 + gganimate recreates the same ranked race as a horizontal bar chart with a dark background, country labels, and a large year watermark.


Code
p <- ggplot(df_eusalary, aes(x = rank, y = values, fill = color, group = country)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0, label = country, color = color),
            hjust = 1, nudge_y = -400,
            size = 3.8, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(values, accuracy = 1)),
            hjust = 0, nudge_y = 400,
            color = "gray80", size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    breaks = seq(0, 100000, by = 20000),
    limits = c(-8000, NA),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = df_eusalary %>% dplyr::distinct(year),
    aes(x = 23, y = 85000, label = year),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1, vjust = 1,
    size = 20, color = "white", alpha = 0.15,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  labs(title   = title,
       x       = NULL,
       y       = "Euros",
       caption = "Source: Eurostat  |  Greece highlighted in red") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D", linewidth = 0.4),
    axis.text.x   = element_text(color = "#90A4AE", size = 10),
    axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
    plot.title    = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 10,
                                  margin = margin(12, 0, 2, 0)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray80", face = "bold", size = 10,
                                  hjust = 0.98,
                                  margin = margin(0, 0, 6, 0)),
    plot.caption  = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 8, hjust = 1,
                                  margin = margin(8, 0, 8, 0)),
    plot.margin   = margin(10, 30, 10, 120)) +
  transition_states(year, transition_length = 0, state_length = 5) +
  ease_aes("cubic-in-out")

animate(p,
        nframes  = 100,
        fps      = 10,
        duration = 20,
        width    = 900,
        height   = 800,
        units    = "px",
        res      = 100,   # set explicitly: when knitting, gganimate otherwise uses the chunk dpi (300 x retina 2)
        renderer = gifski_renderer(paste0(directory,"eu_salary_race.gif")))










Note: rendering the GIF takes a couple of minutes and requires an internet connection to reach the Eurostat API. The GIF is written to the working directory (getwd()).

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
What the chart shows

Northern and Western European economies (e.g. Denmark, Luxembourg, Ireland) consistently occupy the top ranks across the whole period.
Greece sits in the lower half of the ranking throughout, and its relative position (highlighted in red) makes the post-2010 economic crisis visible as a plateau while other countries continue climbing.
Ranks shuffle more among mid-table countries than at the extremes — the top and bottom of the distribution are comparatively stable year to year.

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
Customising it

Highlight a different country


Code
df_eusalary[df_eusalary$country %in% "Portugal", "color"]  <- "#E74C3C"
df_eusalary[!df_eusalary$country %in% "Portugal", "color"] <- "#B3B3B3"




Change the animation speed


Code
animate(p, nframes = 50, fps = 5, duration = 10, ...)   # faster / shorter
animate(p, nframes = 200, fps = 20, duration = 30, ...) # smoother / longer




Save as MP4 instead of GIF


Code
# install.packages("av")
animate(p, renderer = av_renderer("eu_salary_race.mp4"), fps = 24, width = 1280, height = 720)
